Well ..................................... yeah. That is how I'm feeling after reading The Hunt series. I will say that out of the 3 books, The Trap was the least weird and random. The Hunt talked about shoving elbows into armpits and The Prey talked about foot binding. The Trap, fortunately, left out a lot of those super out-there concepts. There were some weird moments but overall, it was fast paced, exhilarating and wild. This one gets a lower rating because many things were unbelievable and the ending left me with more questions than answers. Gene and Sissy always seemed to get into these situations where neither would have survived. But somehow, they both survive. Every time! Gene even gave the whole 'its over, let's stop running and graciously die' speech not once, but twice!! You can't give the same speech twice in a book and have the reader believe it. Towards the end, I just rolled my eyes at each death scenario. One such narrow death escape was a serious plot hole and made no sense at all! So Sissy and Gene are the cure to vampirism. But in order to escape the vampires who are about to kill them, they need to turn into vampires themselves? So they do, with the plan that they will cure themselves with their own blood later and return to being human. How the hell does that work????? First of all, both Gene and Sissy had survived vampire scratches and bites previously, so why does an injection of vampire saliva work? Was it because there were multiple vampires who had contributed their saliva? The previous book showed that they were immune and are actually the cure, but now they're vampires. Totally logical. Also, does vampirism not alter your blood or DNA, even though it alters everything else i.e. your senses, abilities, agility, and the fact that you can't be in the sun! ??? So how can they just cure themselves by using their human blood after becoming vampires? The author kind of hits on that, but still, it made no freaking sense. I'm actually not mad about the big plot twist. It was kind of cool that vampires are the norm and humans the mutation! When that was revealed, I was actually happy! A cool twist on a vampire story that it was the vampires that changed into humans and not the other way around. So Gene and Sissy aren't the cure, but the contagion. Cool twist! But everything else about the ending was horrible. They never ever answer some of the biggest questions and don't even mention the fates of certain important characters Gene's dad, the Scientist! He's presumably alive and somewhere out East. But the author kept switching between him being presumed dead and presumed alive for the entire book, so how can we trust that. To not know if they ever find him was a major cop-out for the author. Also, Clair and Ben, not even mentioned in this book at all. Last we heard of them they had escaped on a hang glider to find Gene's dad. How hard would it have been to add an additional 20 pages to explain the fates of those 3 characters, since they were so important throughout the entire series?? This series was definitely gripping and a real page turner, but had so many issues I can't really recommend it.

This book really surprised me. Despite how long I've been wanting to read it, I didn't really know much about it, which I was okay with. I was expecting it to be a lot more action, fighting, death, battles, danger, etc. Instead, what I found was more of a Pretty Little Liars-esque drama with some supernatural elements. WHICH I LIKED. I would try to give a synopsis, but it is much too complicated to try and explain. Even after reading the back of the book multiple times, I still didn't really understand the world and what exactly was going on until page 100 exactly. That was the moment when everything clicked . This isn't to say that the first 100 pages were bad and confusing, of course, but rather that if you start this book and you're enjoying it but you don't really understand what's going on, STICK IT OUT THROUGH PAGE 100. That's when everything starts picking up, and you'll definitely start enjoying it, 100 . Although, I guess I can't really say, "Enjoying it, 100 " when I gave it four out of five stars. I don't know, but something about Rose Hathaway's character didn't sit right with me. I like that she was a strong female character, and she was confident and didn't need some guy to tell her that she was pretty, but at the same time, she was kind of crazy. In the book, it was hard to tell sometimes if she was fighting the mean girls or if she was becoming one. This might have been part of her character development, but when you're reading more than 300 pages of a book in this characters perspective, this side of them can get really irritating, especially when the book is written so that you're inside their head. Still, I really, really enjoyed this book. I will definitely be continuing on with the series.

First things first - it took me almost two weeks to finish this book, and almost a full 24 hours to motivate myself to write this review, because I've been in such a mental funk. So there's no guarantee for how well thought out it's going to be not that my reviews are very well thought out to begin with, but you know what I'm trying to say . This was a re-read! So much of it was the same as it was the first time around. Grand annoyance at Tally at the beginning. Trying to turn it into understanding why she's like that and appreciating an unlikeable character. Feeling like she deserved what she got and has started to make proper amends by the end. Feeling REALLY INTRIGUED by the cliffhanger ending. Noticing that there is just so much social commentary in this book that applies to real life and how society actually is. It's chock full of it and would have my love for it proclaimed at the top of my lungs were it not for a few issues. Those issues being really awkward slang and dialogue, that made me roll my eyes throughout the book's entire length. I understand it was meant to be 200 years in the future, but it was just so hard for me to buy it and take it seriously. And also, the dropped ball on the world building. The lack of explanations - Where do all these automated things come from? How are they produced? Who works in these factories? Who IS the government anyway? Who runs it? Why is politics completely absent? - made my rating drop by an entire star. So many questions went unanswered, and according to two members of my book group who read the entire series, they never do get answered. So that's really just too bad. The potential is there! And so is the interest! It just was apparently entirely skipped over in the writing. My thoughts are, basically, if you can get past the slang and the dialogue, and are able to keep your focus off of the faulty world building, then definitely, give this book a shot if you've found yourself previously interested! The premise is amazing, the social commentary is amazing, and it truly does spark thought about how we're conditioned to treat ourselves and our bodies, in actuality. It makes you think critically about it, especially if you've not really addressed it critically before. And that is something I believe is crucial to living in today's society. The execution of the writing could have been better. But as that is my only major complaint, this book has my recommendation for anyone interested and I truly think you should give it a fair chance!

She is extremely excited and cannot wait to go. She somehow manages to strike up a friendship that leads to more with Chris one of the guys from the band. They talk on the phone nightly and makes plans to meet up. He says all kinds of different things to her, some of them make her happy and others make her extremely sad. She ends up meeting up with them due to one of the other guys in the band that she becomes friends with, and then ends up on tour with them. Things really don't seem to get any better between her and Chris and time goes on. Trust me this is not your typical love story. This one shows you the darker side of loving a rockstar who is on the road all of the time. She knows that she is head over heels in love with Chris and he claims that he feels the same way about her, but he never really seems to make that apparent through this entire book. I will say that I did have a couple of moments where I wanted to cry and there were a lot of moments where I wanted to reach into the book and knock some sense into both of the main characters in this book. But over all I loved this book and I hope that if you take the time to read it that you love it as much as I did.

I was really hesitant about starting this book because I don't really enjoy contemporary YA fiction all that much, but I always like to be involved in the young adult group discussions about the book of the month and Thirteen Reasons Why was the book of the month. I had heard that it was really sad so I prepared myself for a book that was going to make me cry. Even though Thirteen Reasons Why was a roller coaster of emotions for main characters Hannah and Clay, it didn't make me cry. Part of the reason is because I knew from the beginning of the book that Hannah had killed herself so it wasn't a surprise that in every chapter Hannah's state of mind became worse and worse. I did connect with the characters enough that I found myself hoping that Hannah was going to pop up around the corner or from the next room and say, "surprise, I really didn't kill myself." But of course, that didn't happen. What really shocked me the most about the book was the guidance counselor character. As a professional who has worked in the counseling field for a little while now, I know the guidance counselor should have caught on to what was going on with Hannah. It's a big problem in the public school system with all the budget cuts. Guidance counselors are expected to take on classes instead of just focusing on the student body and their mental health. I felt like Hannah went to the guidance counselor knowing that he was too stressed with his classes and grading papers and that he wouldn't see the signs. Towards the end, it just made me so sad to read her going out and finding reasons and people who would take advantage of her. She needed to prove to herself that no one respected her or that she didn't have any true friends. And that's exactly what she did. Thirteen Reasons Why is a very powerful novel that deals with a hard hitting teenage issues bullying and suicide that need to be talked about more.

Mab Prowd doesn't mind that she doesn't have friends her own age, or that she doesn't attend a conventional school. She's more than happy to live with a small group of people on a compound outside of the city, practicing blood magic and keeping the land peaceful. Blood magic is second nature to her, so it's only natural that she is entrusted with the role of deacon when her mentor passes on. But one day a spell goes awry and as she tries to control it, she meets Will, a local high school boy who is inadvertently affected by her spell. This one incident will bring them together and throw them both into a powerful world of danger and romance. Blood Magic was one of my favorite books last year. I loved the story of Silla and Nick. It was the perfect blend of action, horror and romance. I was a little disappointed when I read the synopsis for The Blood Keeper and didn't see any mention of Silla and Nick, but was happy to see that their characters were woven in with this story, they just weren't the main focus. I loved Ms. Gratton's style in the first book, and I thought it was even stronger and more distinct in this one. The book once again alternates between three viewpoints Mab, Will and journal letter style entries from a mystery person who is revealed as the story progresses. Each voice is totally distinct. A lot of authors struggle with this, but Ms. Gratton pulls it off with ease. I loved Mab and Will and their central stories were very engaging. I also loved the connection to Silla and Nick. It was so exciting to see all of the connections slowly fall into place. I especially loved how Silla's brother and his "curse" plays into this story. A beautifully written book about family, magic and love, The Blood Keeper does not disappoint. It is expertly crafted and has the perfect balance of action, romance, deep emotion and horror. I highly recommend it.

I feel like they have just become caricatures of themselves at this point, and it's all just too over-the-top for me. Same goes for Zil and his crew--yawn. And it drove me nuts how unsubtle the Nerezza stuff was. So yeah. Once I finally made it through this I was reminded of the things that I think are great about this series. But also what's not so great. I think things are set up to go in an intriguing direction in the fourth book, so I probably will give it a try at some point. But the series as a whole has most definitely lost a bit of its lustre for me.

Seven Sins. Six innocent people. Five days. Piece of cake... Jessie and her mom come from a long line of Darker's that take care of paranormal problems. He is a hundred or so years older than Jessie but he has been locked away in the box so when he comes out he is really only 18. I often find it creepy when guys that have been around for hundreds of years like teenagers lol but he is a real teenager. Except he isn't exactly caught up on all the new slang and technology. Of course Jessie doesn't listen and goes after the sins. Her mom yells at her not too and then she goes after them again. This part kind of got annoying and repetitive. They only have five days and it sure didn't seem like her mom was making much progress so you would think she would just go ahead and work with Jessie. I am actually even more excited for the next book because this one ends with Jessie in a rather interesting job situation. I also loved that it ends with no cliffhanger. The plot and mystery of this one is all wrapped up but still open for the Darker Agency to get plenty of new and exciting cases. Can't wait to see what is next. --- "It saddens me to bear witness to the decline of the English language." "My entire life, all I wanted was to find something different. Special. I never would have guessed I'd have to sleep for so long to find it." "I waited 147 years to find her."

3.5 stars This is, undeniably, an important book. It's an amazing look into growing up gay in the Bronx where it makes you the victim of hate crimes. But what if there was a way to erase your past? To forget the bullying. Forget your sexuality. Can you really erase part of your identity without consequences? It's an age old 'be careful what you wish for' tale that shows you can't erase who you are. Silvera is sort of a genius with the way he unfolded some things. It's a very well crafted story. However, I personally was attached to less than 50 of the book. I felt like so much time was spent detailing every neighborhood game that I knew the whole neighborhood better than I knew Aaron. It took about 150 pages for it to feel like there was a point to the story. I mean, once everything hit the fan I was REELING, and the book ties up with some very powerful messages. I don't mean to undermine the book's importance at all, but when a synopsis leads with 'memory erasing procedure' and 'gay protagonist' but the book doesn't develop either of those things until halfway in, I feel like I was promised apples and given oranges. I feel like a jerk for saying that though because I do respect Aaron's self discovery and I realize that this story is not written for me, the cis-het adult woman. So, you know, don't judge this book by my viewpoint, but that's my personal review. Time will have to tell where my rating ends up because I do think this might be one where in a few months the messages sticks out to me more than the pacing, so we'll see! But that's my immediate reaction.

In De wereld achter het hek lees je over hoe het er daar aan toe gaat hoe Subhi aan zijn kleren komt, wat ze eten, hoe ze leven en over Subhi's nachtzee. Het gaat over Subhi en over Jimmie, die buiten het hek opgroeit. Waar ze samen met haar vader en haar broer een prima leventje leidt. Wanneer Jimmie zich op een dag verveeld en op avontuur uit gaat, ontdekt ze een gat in een hek. Zo leert ze Subhi kennen. Samen lezen ze in het boek van Jimmies moeder, want Jimmie heeft zelf nooit leren lezen. Wanneer Subhi en Jimmie samen afspreken komen ze er achter dat de dingen die Jimmie als vanzelfsprekend ziet, voor Subhi juist heel speciaal zijn. Of dat hij het niet eens kent. De wereld achter het hek laat de verschillen zien tussen twee werelden, de wereld van een kindje dat nooit buiten een vluchtelingenkamp heeft geleefd en een kind dat geen idee heeft over wat een vluchtelingenkamp is. Het laat je zien en voelen hoe verschillend we leven en wat er eigenlijk allemaal niet klopt aan hoe wij met deze vluchtelingen omgaan. Het verhaal is goed opgebouwd, in het begin had ik zelf het idee dat het wat kinderlijk geschreven werd, maar daar raakte ik op den duur aan gewend. Je zit op den duur zelf in dat vluchtelingenkamp en schaduwt Subhi, terwijl hij op Jimmie wacht en zijn dingen doet. Het is soms wat langdradig, maar dat draagt naar mijn mening wel weer bij aan het verhaal. De personen in het verhaal zijn allemaal levensecht. Ze hebben allemaal hun eigen problemen, naast dat ene grote gezamenlijke probleem. En gaan hier allemaal op hun eigen manier mee om. Daar waar er in het midden naar mijn idee nog niet zo veel gebeurd en het verhaal lekker rustig door kabbelde, gebeurt er op 3 4e van het verhaal opeens ontzettend veel. Draait de hele situatie zich bijna 180 graden om en was ik zo enorm verbaasd over 1 van de personen in dit boek.. het maakte het lezen nog bijzonderder en liet me stiekem wel een beetje huilen. Dit boek is misschien niet heel spannend, heftig op bepaalde manieren of leuk. Maar hij is wel echt heel belangrijk. Wij hebben het zo ontzettend getroffen met hoe wij kunnen opgroeien, de manier waarop onze zaken worden geregeld en ga zo maar door. We hebben allemaal een eigen mening wat betreft vluchtelingen en ik vind dat, als je echt een goede en vooral onderbouwde mening wil hebben over de situatie, dit boek een heel goed begin zou kunnen zijn.

This short story is set in between Past Midnight and One Hundred Candles. When South Carolina experiences heavy flooding and coffins from a graveyard are washed into the street Charlotte's family offer to help restore the remains to the cemetery. As they do this they make a shocking discovery, however, that is not the only strange thing going on. A man can be seen in the graveyard, running into the woods when anyone comes near. What is he doing there and why doesn't he want to be seen? I read this book really quickly. It's short but I really liked it. We actually got to see a lot of the characters like Avery and Jared yep I love that guy , who I really missed when I read the second book in the series. What I liked most was how they came across, it seemed like they were both making progress and trying to move on. We see this a little in One Hundred Candles but it really felt like it when I was reading this. What I did find a little strange was Avery and Jared's relationship. In one Hundred Candles they're definitely becoming more involved, that's clear at the end when Jared is at Avery's house however it's never mentioned all that much in the book. Bearing in mind this short story happens before then it was a little weird that they seemed so close yet their relationship was then played down in the next book. Maybe that's just me but it didn't seem to make sense. I suppose you could argue it's because One Hundred Candles focuses so much on Charlotte, Noah and Harris but I don't know...it just struck me as out of place. I really like their relationship and like I said in my last review I really wanted to see more of both characters which I'm glad happened here. Oh, another weird thing is that the events of this book aren't mentioned in One Hundred Candles, at least I didn't notice they were. Considering this is supposed to have happened before that it just seems...well out of place. The events of the first book are mentioned loads, I know this is sort of book 1.5 in the series but surely it at least deserves a mention in book 2? Perhaps the author wrote it after, I'll have to check the publication date, but even so I find that quite odd from a plot perspective. This isn't a problem I have with this book really, more with One Hundred Candles to be honest.

Originally posted at Marta's Bookshelf SUMMARY AND SPOILER-FREE REVIEW Cadence is a teenager who spends summers with her whole family at an island her grandparents own. She loves it there, and the thing she loves the most is The Liars. The Liars is how Cadence, her cousins Johnny and Mirren, and Gat, Johnny's mother's boyfriend's nepehew, are called. The book is focused on two summers the fifteenth and the seventeenth. The fifteenth summer, when she and Gat fell in love. But also, the summer something terrible happens to Cadence, something that makes her lose the memories of that summer. The seventeenth summer, Cadence -and us- discover what happened during the fifteenth summer. Nothing really is what neither of us thought. We Were Liars is an amazing book for those who love reading a great YA suspense novel that will keep them awake at night and will leave them shocked more than once. Tha main character's feelings are so well defined and described that it is impossible not to feel the same way. This book contains amazing plot twists that will leave you wondering how's it that you didn't realize what was going on. MY THOUGHTS SPOILERS We Were Liars is an amazing book to read within 48 hours, having a night to think about it. I went into this book knowing pretty much nothing, and I am so glad I did. At first, I didn't know what the book was about, I was really confused. E. Lockhart used amazing metaphors that made my heart stop more than once. As the story went on, I felt more and more confused. I really felt as if I didn't understand the language. The fact that I was as lost as Cadence made me grow very attached to the character, and I wasn't too far into the book when I already felt for her. I liked Gat, but I wasn't sure if I should. Same with Johnny and Mirren. I really didn't know who to trust. When I found out about the fire and how it all was a plan of The Liars, I could not believe. I was left in shock. But nothing compares to my face when I read that Gat, Mirren and Johnny had died in their attempt to save their family. Absolutely stunning. I loved the special writing of the author.

Valedictorian and all around perfect daughter Julia couldn't be more different than her volatile older sister Sophie. So when Julia ditches her plans to be a summer intern in favor of helping her sister open a bakery five hours away, her parents are less than thrilled. But the sisters need time to heal from a devastating family secret that Julia just learned. And Julia just might learn to be her own person, rather than the perfect child she was groomed to be. While Julia's narration did keep me interested, the dialogue seemed artificial and contrived. Too often there was more "telling" than "showing" and use of passive verbs. After the secret was revealed 25 into the novel, what ensued was Sophie telling her version of events that transpired before Julia was born and revealing some of her own secrets that were fairly obvious before they were revealed. I had difficulty relating to Julia, who was somewhat whiny and actually likes Sophie better, even though she was sometimes unkind. THE SWEETNESS OF SALT was a mostly forgettable read.

What a marvelous and wonderful collection of peculiar ideas illustrated by peculiar photographs. It does make one wonder which came first. Were the photographs the inspiration for the story or the reverse? Did the change they shape and flow of the tale? Many times one may find oneself inventing histories for the unknown people found in unfamiliar photographs. My sainted father-in-law used to buy picture frames because there were interesting stock photos in them, thinking maybe he would simply adopt those families . Ransom Riggs has combined his passion for the unusual photograph with a gift for expressing himself in writing to make a fascinating tale which also brings to life the half-seen dreams of childhood with the unformed ideas of other worlds to create a very believable Other World of danger and excitement. This book is slated to be released as a movie shortly. No mere movie and understand, I am a movie buff, but a book addict could possibly deliver the incredible possibilities of this book. At the same time, it is certain that this is a book concept which will translate well to the silver screen. The biggest disappointment the book delivers is a problem common to all series the first book is clearly not enough and demands more. It reads quickly and flows so well, it may almost be said to flow violently. There is a veritable white-water experience in turning the pages. It demands that the second and third volumes be read immediately.

I hated this book. I cannot stress that enough. I read these books in early 2012 I think, back when I had hardly read any YA ever. Which is stupid, since it was hardly even 200 pages. It was an easy read, but holy crap was it stressful to read. It actually set me on edge just because of how horrible it was. The characters were annoying as shit. They repeated themselves so many times it was like they were a broken record. It's like those people at work or school where they just don't shut up, and they think that they are the best people in the entire universe. They don't do anything wrong, they loooove nature, they say words like 'handsome', and phrases like 'with all my might'. Literally just shutthefuckup. The writing seemed forced beyond belief. Defy had so much potential to be a great high fantasy read, but the romance overtook it and the rest of the plot took a back-seat. Honestly, I was scared to read this book after the negative reviews I had read. I tried to push those reviews to the back of my mind and I tried to go into this book with a clear head. Overall, it wasn't an awful read. It was still enjoyable, but the negative parts were too negative to be ignored. One of the biggest positives for this book? Sara B. Larson is a stunning writer. Her prose was beautiful and flowed nicely. She was descriptive and vivid and I could see everything perfectly in my mind. I'm not sure if it's possible to like a character's voice, but not like the character. If it is, then that's how I felt with Alexa. I didn't dislike her, necessarily. But I certainly didn't like her. There was nothing about her that stood out, nothing that made me want to cheer for her, to see her succeed. I very rarely felt bad for her. She was VERY repetitive - There was a certain revelation between her, Damian and Rylan. And once that revelation was known, Alexa constantly brought it up. I know that's kind of vague, but it's a big spoiler if I say more. But it was something that she just kept harping on and saying over and over, every time Damian or Rylan did something she didn't like. There's also a LOT of useless inner monologue and thought. I loved Damian. He was an awesome character. I should have hated him, because he was very cocky and slightly full of himself. He even admits at one point that he's a spoiled brat. But there was something about him that drew me to him, especially when he let his guard down. In those moments, we saw the real Damian. I hated Rylan. I just did. He was so unnecessary, it was almost laughable. The love triangle was so forced. This book did NOT need a love triangle. Some books work well with love triangles and some books just DON'T need it. Defy did NOT need it. Rylan didn't even do anything - He was like Damian's shadow - he did the things Damian did AFTER Damian did them - like running after Alexa after she had stormed away. Damian got there first and it took a good 5-10 minutes before Rylan showed up, like it was an after-thought. The deaths in this book were pretty devastating. Two of my favorite characters were killed - one very early on. That definitely made me sad. There were some very powerful moments in Defy, though. Some very touching, some very emotional. Those moments definitely made some of the other things a little more.. tolerable. But not completely. The ways in which we were shown the King's cruelty were.. despicable, overdone and - I'm using this word a lot in this review - unnecessary. There were a lot of revelations near the end, some of which I had a feeling about and some that took me by surprise. One revelation at the very, very end.. Well, I expected more of a reaction from a few people when something was revealed, and we didn't get that reaction. So that was unfortunate. The ending did not need to be left open for a sequel - and there is a sequel, apparently. Everything could have been wrapped up perfectly. This book reads like a stand-alone and would have been perfect as a stand-alone. The only thing left hanging was the love triangle.. Which was unnecessary and annoying.. And that could have been wrapped up in Defy, too. So.. See where I'm going with this? I know some people loved Defy. So I'm not going to say I wouldn't recommend it - I'm sure there are some people who will love what I hated. Especially those who love books that focus on the romance. But I won't be going out of my way to recommend it, either. And I likely won't bother reading the sequel. You can also find more from me on my blog Pandora's Books

Warning There may be spoilers in this review for the first book, Deception. 3.5 stars. Betrayal picks up where Deception left off after Coby's death. Tension between Emma, and Harry and Sara is high, and Coby, now a ghost, is increasingly worried about them. She needs to find a way to help the friends who hate her and defeat Neos and fast, all the while not knowing exactly who she can trust. I had a little trouble enjoying Betrayal. I'm not sure if it was purely because I wasn't in the right mood for it, or if it simply wasn't quite as good as Deception, but it didn't grab quite as much. Harry and Sara's hatred of Emma felt a little too much to me, I didn't believe it. Sure it made sense that they'd blame her and live in misery after the death of their best friend but the way it was portrayed felt a little too much. The fact that Emma blamed both Coby's death, and apparently everything else that goes wrong in her life, on herself only bugged me more. There's just a little too much self pity going on in this book. That being said, it is still a great read and I was excited to see where Nichols would take the story. This series is a real comfort read. One of the big things for me with a series sequel is how repetitive the recaps can get, however, she doesn't overdo them and tells enough so that you know what's going on if you didn't read the books one after the other. I also really liked the idea that they all found comfort in family, whether they're blood related or otherwise. That was a nice message in an otherwise very untrustworthy cast of characters. I also have to mention this, though it's not a criticism at all, but I giggled a little to myself when the British guy said something about the Van Gogh museum and they said, "but he said it like 'van goff'" and I was sat there thinking, "yeah, and?" because that's how I read it in my head. It was a bizarre little moment in Hannah's brain. Surrender, book three in the Haunting Emma series, should be released in December I believe. I for one can't wait to see where the story goes from here.

Average Young Adult romance with a time travel hook. Anna lives in Evanston, Illinois in 1995. She is a runner and attends private school where she is one of the few students from a middle class family. One day she sees a cute boy who mysteriously vanishes in the stands at Northwestern University while she is doing her morning run. A few days later, the cute boy Bennett Cooper shows up at her high school--he is the new boy. Anna soon falls for Bennett and discovers his secret he can travel to anywhere in the world within his own life span simply by willing it. Anna is able to travel with Bennett to Thailand and Italy she has always dreamed of traveling the world but has rarely gone farther from home than the Midwest before complications ensue and the couple is separated. I enjoy time travel books but this book didn't do much for me. Bennett is from 2012 but there is little back and forth between the two time periods--most of the action occurs in 1995. I also felt that the author didn't do much with the 1990s time period other than musical references to Pearl Jam and the fact that the high school students use books to complete research projects for school. The main emphasis of the story was the romance which wasn't very compelling. Bennett and Anna know each other for only a few weeks before they are pulled apart and I didn't care very much if they ended up together. Bennett is too bland--a boring back story about his family and his missing sister she is apparently lost in 1995 where she traveled with him which is why he is in Evanston--he is waiting for her to get home that is abruptly resolved. The travel is more about traveling to exotic locations rather than traveling to different time periods. I enjoy reading time travel novels to see how characters react interact in historical time periods that are vastly different from their own. Bennett adjusts quite easily to 1995 and never tells Anna much about 2012 so the fish out of water wasn't a part of the story. Bennett is handsome and even his flaws are boring and bland he wants to protect Anna and doesn't tell her things . Anna is a standard YA heroine--two defining traits she likes running and wants to travel the world with a best friend and a close relationship with her parents. Nothing memorable about this novel. It was a waste of an intriguing premise. Teen girls who like romance may like this novel.

Right now dystopians are one of my favorite genres so I will read almost anything and everything dystopian. I try to go into them with no expectations, but sometimes I just can't. I have been really excited about Chosen Ones so my expectations were pretty high going into it. It didn't let me down. I enjoyed the setting and that the chosen ones are artificially created beings. All male, because the council believes that women are weak. The chosen ones are made to not have emotions, and be strong and fast. They are built to be soldiers. There are no books or music allowed anymore. The naturals or the actual real humans are living in poverty. The women are essentially slaves. I was totally drawn into this story. I enjoyed the darker feel of this book. There are lots of secrets, some violence, and romance. All balanced really well. I really liked Tess. She is emotionally fragile, but she really keeps strong. She puts up such a solid wall to protect herself. She ends up having to take her sisters place working at Templeton and we get to see her wall breaking down. She starts to do things she knows aren't allowed, and she starts to fall for James who is a Chosen One which is totally not allowed. She starts to discover a lot of secrets that change how she thinks of the world they live in. She begins to realize that it doesn't have to be so black and white. I love the strength that she is able to find within herself. I really didn't know what to think of James. I didn't know whether to trust him or not. He was absolutely swoon worthy, but also being a Chosen One, I didn't know if he could really have emotions and feel the way he did. I really wanted him to be sincere and I wanted for him and Tess to be together. I really wanted to figure him out. Find out why he seemed so different from the other Chosen Ones. I think that the appeal of dystopians for me is that they tend to be darker and have a mentally chilling feel to them. You can really imagine these things happening. This book was so like that to me. I could see the government trying to make artificial people to be better than real humans and phase out all of us. We get sick, we have emotions, we have a conscience. If they could create a perfect new race, I have no doubt they would try to. They already have control over so much so it's not too far fetched to think that they could keep controlling more until it would be similar to what this book is. I was very wrapped up in the whole thing. There were a few surprises thrown in that I was totally not expecting too. This is a fantastic book and I can't wait for more of this series. Tiffany Truitt has written an awesome debut that has me pining for more.

The Grisha series laid a very good foundation which would've been amazing to explore, but it never dared to, it just skimmed the surface to pass on to something else. One concept which I found extremely good was the lack of God only Saints are worshipped in Ravka. That's a lot. That's humanist. If there is no God to answer to, no God to test you, every human can be a Saint. It would be great to explore, the concept that without a God you can aim even higher. But sadly, none of this is ever explained. The whole tsarpunk aesthetic is just an aesthetic 95 of the time. I wish Leigh Bardugo had been braver, I wish she'd gone into the light darkness duality, the humanizing dehumanizing effect of eternity, the real meaning of a name, the meaning of power. The hunger for power, oh my God, I wish we'd gone down that road. Instead what we got with this third act is the frankly terrible moral that if you are strong, if you feel good in your strength as woman, if you are powerful, well... you really should turn all of that down for some boy's love, because he's scared of you when you're powerful. The moral is make yourself little and take up no space, because a boy wants to be more powerful than you. Alina didn't have space to embrace herself because what she wanted was to please Mal, and that is disgusting.

A novel with a fun premise and breezy prose. While I wasn't in love with it, mostly because I got tired of the protagonist and her teenage-isms after awhile, I did enjoy it--especially the latter half, which I felt moved along at a much more appropriate pace for a pulpy sci-fi novel about pregnant teens in space than the beginning. The characters are pretty cookie-cutter bitchy cheerleaders, the weird art kid, and so on and it read like a high school flick in space, which it is, so take that how you will. There's a blurb on the back calling this a mash-up of Juno and Alien, but in book form, which I think is going a little far, but it'll give you an idea of what you've got in your hands with this one. By far, the most impressive thing about this book was how well the authors layered their reveals. They played their cards just right, so that the plot continually thickened without giving the reader information overload at any point. I was impressed with the pacing of the revelations about the aliens. Less impressive were the aliens themselves, who go around impregnating and making barren human women to propagate their species, but justify it because the alien babies contribute to our society with art and politics. And those were the good ones. If you like quick, light sci-fi reads about pregnant teens in space and weird, morally-dubious aliens, this should be right up your alley. And if it turns out that I'm wrong, it shouldn't take you long to finish anyways.

If Guardians of the Galaxy were a romantic comedy, that would be the Starflight universe. It certainly has a lot of cinematic appeal fast pacing, explosive action, and lovable characters. I remember eagerly devouring Starflight over a long weekend, and was so excited to finally get a hold of the sequel. Overall, the sequel features many of the hallmarks from the first book and even alleviated some of my earlier criticisms. Doran and Solara got so much of the limelight in Starflight that their development came at the expense of the other crew members, particularly Kane and Cassia. Landers must have been reading my mind because this time around, Kane and Cassia play the leads in Starfall, which means we get to learn more about the war on Eturia. Or so I thought. While the political upheaval of Eturia is central to the story, I was still surprised at how much off-world adventuring was still taking place. And while most of it was intriguing, there were definitely a lot more threads to follow this time around. So many in fact, that it was a wonder that everything wrapped up so neatly in the end--especially since the crew seemed to have four times the number of enemies, including space rebels, space pirates, space bounty hunters, and the space mafia. Still, I came here for a wild ride through the galaxy, and Landers definitely delivered. Here's hoping that there'll be a spin-off involving dorky-scientist-start-up-entrepeneur, Gage!

The Scorpio Races by Maggie Stiefvater is another YA fantasy. I loved The Raven Boys an ebook ARC from Net Galley , and wanted to try something else by Stiefvater, so I ordered this one for my Kindle. The water horses, capaill uisce, of the small island of Thisby are carnivores--beautiful and terrifying. The annual Scorpio Races, held each November, are thrilling and often deadly, but the ancient tradition continues to be practiced regardless of the risks. Puck Connelly's parents were killed by a capaill uisce, you didn't have to be involved with the races to be killed by the water horses and she and her brothers have difficulties making ends meet. This year's race might present an opportunity for Puck to keep her home and to prevent her brother Gabe from leaving the island. Sean Kendrick, a stoic young veteran of the races, works as a trainer for the largest stable on the island. With several wins under his belt, he sees this year's race as an opportunity to own his beloved water horse, Corr. Both young people have huge investments in the November race, and they move from active dislike to an uneasy friendship as they prepare for the race. Character development and atmosphere are so well done that the reader feels present on the island, and while the plot development is slow, it is not plodding. I liked the fact that Stiefvater took an old myth and altered it to fit the story she wanted to tell, but although there were many elements I admired, I liked The Raven Boys much better.

Ok. So, obviously this isn't the best book I have ever read, but I really enjoyed reading it. In the beginning, I had a really hard time seeing Beau as a boy and not as Bella, but after about 200 pages it got easier. Funny though, because I had no such problem with Edythe. She was a clear image in my mind from the very first time she appeared. I don't think I say this enough, but I owe a lot to this series. Twilight was the book that started it all for me. I wouldn't love books and reading as much as I do without Twilight. And because of that, I could never hate this story. So thank you, Stephenie Meyer, for writing the books that made me who I am today! I first read Twilight back in 5th grade because a really good friend recommended it to me, and because I admired her very much, I decided that if she liked it, then so would I. You see, she was 12 years older than me, but she played with me and was always patient with my annoying younger self. For me, she was like the older sister I had always wanted. And so, naturally, I did what any other 11 year old would do. I asked Santa to bring me the books that Christmas. And he did. He brought me all four books. I remember reading them all in a week during Christmas break. I have never ever seen my mum as surprised as she'd been. You see, I wasn't much of a reader back then even the books I had to read for school, I would find some way to avoid actually reading them. Everything changed when I read Twilight. And because of that, I will always love these books. Stephenie Meyer, words cannot describe how grateful I am to you! Thank you! Despite my love for Twilight, I had a hard time deciding to read this book. Actually, I think that it was because of my love for the original series that I had a hard time with the decision. I was afraid that I wouldn't like this take on Twilight, but I am happy to say I was wrong. I still like the original story better, maybe because of my love for Jacob and Renesmee and the entire original Cullen Clan and Bella. Still, I enjoyed reading this version with its alternate ending. It was very beautifully done. I believe that any fan of Bella and Edward will enjoy reading about Beau and Edythe just as much. On thing I have always wanted to say was that I'd love for people to stop hating on Stephenie Meyer. She is an amazing person and author and she doesn't deserve to be treated that way. If people don't like the books, that's totally fine. Not everyone likes the same things and everyone is entitled to their own opinion. For example, I don't like Fifty Shades of Grey but one of my best friends loved that series, and yet we are still BFFs. In fact, I don't know what I'd do without her. It's a good thing I don't have to find out! . So just because one doesn't like something, that doesn't mean that they can be rude and mean about it. I've also heard a lot of people say that the vampires in this book aren't real vampires. Well let me ask you, what are real vampires? What are they really like? I don't think anyone could answer that question to my satisfaction. There are just so many myths and legends concerning vampires that you don't know what to believe. In the end, we all have our own take on the legends. The vampires in this book were Stephenie Meyer's take on them. And she did a great job too! I know many people don't agree with me. And if you that are reading this are one of them, I'm sorry, this is just my opinion and I am only one person on this immense planet. Please don't hate me for having my opinion, because I don't hate you for having yours. .

I have been looking forward to reading this book for a while, especially so since I saw the cover for the companion novel, The Abandoned Werewolf Support Group. I expected Catherine Jinks to be really funny, and hoped that this would be a good readalike for S. G. Browne's Breathers which deals with zombies . Very much to my disappointment, it was not. The main problem is that Jinks goes too far in her attempt to deromanticize vampires. She wants to make them everything that's unlikable, pretty much. They're lazy, slow, stupid, boring and not attractive. Well, she succeeded in not making them Twilightish, but she also succeeded in making them not at all interesting. I didn't give a damn about any of the characters, except maybe Dave, because they were all of the things previously mentioned. Plus, I did not much appreciate the constant references to guinea pig nomming. I mean, once, fine, but every time someone needs a little pick me up? And, here's some advice, Jinks saying that you'll spare the audience a description of the gory happenings is the same as describing it. This is a perfect example of how something was supposed to be both funny and off-putting, but only managed the latter. The Reformed Vampire Support Group fell completely flat. It was a struggle to read from the first pages to the last. I am not giving up on Jinks yet, but only because I already have copies of two more of her books to read. I hope, for my sake, that the others are better.

I've seen this book around for awhile now, so I finally decided to pick it up and see what it's all about. There are similarities to The Hunger Games, which is what drew me to this book, so of course I am going to compare the two. Whereas Katniss was a character who was strong from the beginning and always despised the Capitol, in Matched, Cassia initially thinks the Officials are good. Her growth is subtle throughout the book, and at the end she has become strong and thinks for herself. The Society determines what food you eat, what your job will be, who you will marry, and when you will die. Everything is decided for you. Your life is not your own. I find this to be very disturbing, but Cassia thinks that the Society is ideal and she is excited to be Matched with the person she will marry. Her doubt about the Officials stems from her confusion on who her Match is, who she is meant to be with. She is conflicted in whether she should be with Xander or Ky. When she saw Ky's face by accident, this is the first time in her life that she realizes that her life is not set in stone according to what the Society tells her. The Officials make all the decisions, but what if she had choices and made her own decisions about her life? This curiosity to understand what is really going on and be able to have control over her own life intensifies as the story progresses. We watch Cassia evolve from someone who blindly trusts the Officials to someone who is aware of the lies and darkness of the Officials and chooses to challenge their power. I found this book and the plot to be intriguing, and I am interested to see what will happen in the next book. Although it is no Hunger Games, this is a good book. This is the first book in the Matched Trilogy Series.

Shannon desenvolve esta versao de historia que eu conhecia como A Princesa Guardadora de Patos com muita humanidade. As personagens, comecando pela princesa Ani e pela sua ligacao a familia, e depois todas as personagens que a acompanham e o reino onde ela se torna guardadora, sao crediveis e com profundidade suficiente para nos ligarmos a elas. Ani tem, como todos nos, virtudes e fragilidades, medo e coragem, o desejo de agradar e o receio de nao conseguir, e passa por um processo credivel de crescimento. Edepois tem o que nenhum de nos tem magia. Nao e a magia que a torna especial, porem, mas a sua forma de encarar as vicissitudes. Ha traicoes e lealdades, desgosto e alegria, odio e amor, pessoas, animais e realidade em doses ideiais. Os reinos sao imaginarios, claro, mas a impressao de Idade Media, que e caracteristica dos contos, parece-me bastante realista. Por vezes, pareceu-me sentir os cheiros e as texturas, imaginar as ruas, as pessoas, os mercados. Gostei da ideia do people, animal e nature speaking, e gostaria de as ter visto ainda mais desenvolvidas. E pareceu-me que a personagem da tia, que traz a Ani o seu lado magico atraves das suas narrativas, depois ter sido tao importante no inicio, acaba por ficar muito esquecida, ate pela propria Ani. E que a ideia da palavra com que nascemos, que e maavilhosa, tambem se perde um pouco na accao. O ritmo da narrativa e bom, com muita accao mas tambem momentos de intimidade e de tranquilidade. Aqui e ali, tanta vigilancia aprendizagem de gansos cansou-me um pouco. Mas a actividade da, afinal, nome ao livro, por isso... A leitura foi um pouco prejudicada pelo facto de a ter feito devagar, o que, ja o tenho dito, dificulta sempre um pouco a minha ligacao ao texto. A escrita da autora e simples mas poetica, e dispensa, felizmente, o tom condescendente e que alguns contos de fadas adquiriram nos ultimos tempos, e e dura quando e preciso. Nao hesita, por exemplo, em 'eliminar' personagens importantes, e nem sempre de forma particularmente doce. Algumas das historias dentro da historia, narradas por Ani ou outras personagens sao maravilhosas. No geral, gostei muito. Achei equilibrada e, aqui e ali, segurei uma lagrima, fosse de pena ou de comocao. Gostei especialmente da historia de 'porque e que as mulheres acompanham os maridos na guerra.' Foi comovente.

So I finally read this book, the subject of an earlier dumpster fire of reviewing and How Not to Respond to Criticism from VOYA. Its review implied a mature rating because of bad language and a bisexual character. Honestly, I'd still give it a mature rating in that it deals with issues more suitable to mature readers--issues like feeling like you'll never get out of your podunk town when you'll probably just get married right out of high school and never leave, issues like being smothered by overprotective parents because of a disability, issues like living in a house with drug use where you keep the police scanner going in case your mother gets arrested so you'll have time to run away instead of being put in a bad foster home . One of the main characters is bisexual, and the extent it has on the story is that, if publicly known, it would be one more thing for people to hold against a girl already deemed a lost cause and a slut by virtue of the no-good family she was born into. If anything, the poverty and accompanying fatalistic worldview that Dickinsons will never amount to anything played a much more significant role in events. In short, it was a YA problem novel--and sexuality wasn't one of them.

Breathe RATING 2 stars. Uninspiring... a bit boring. Couldn't connect with the characters at all shifting POVs didn't help . ------------------------- Portuguese review Ha livros que lemos devagar simplesmente para que durem mais tempo e ha livros que lemos o mais depressa possivel para acabarmos a leitura e podermos passar para outra coisa. Breathe encaixa-se nesta ultima categoria. Quando escolhi este livro para figurar na rubrica Waiting on Wednesday, escrevi que eraficcao cientifica distopica meets romance adolescente e triangulo amoroso, hmm . Tem potencial para ser interessante... ou muito mau. Pois, apesar de nao ter sido muito mau, esta longe de ter sido bom. Vejamos. Breathe passa-se num futuro incerto em que a Humanidade conseguiu dar conta do planeta ao destruir todas as florestas e praticamente todas as plantas, para ja nao falar dos oceanos. Um acontecimento chamado "The Switch" a mudanca parece ter ocorrido de repente ao inves de ser gradual fazendo com que os niveis de oxigenio baixassem imenso e que o planeta se tornasse incapaz de suster vida. Cerca de 100 anos mais tarde deduzo eu, porque muito poucos pormenores nos sao dados , os sobreviventes vivem em redomas onde o ar e constantemente reciclado. Como em qualquer boa distopia, temos uma classe privilegiada de individuos, os "Premiums" ou ricos e o resto auxiliares ou pobres . Sair da redoma significa morrer porque a atmosfera na Terra tem apenas cerca de 3 de oxigenio o que e o suficiente para chover, aparentemente . Previsivelmente, dentro da redoma, tem de se pagar impostos sobre o oxigenio. Seguimos as aventuras de tres personagens a Bea, a Alina e o Quinn. A Bea e a tipica estudante modelo pobre que aspira a uma condicao mais elevada a Alina e a rapariga pseudo-rebelde literalmente e o Quinn e o rapaz privilegiado. O livro vai sendo alternadamente narrado do ponto de vista destas tres personagens, o que me irritou um bocado, confesso. Com esta premissa, este poderia ter sido um livro muito interessante. Mas nao foi. Eis porque 1. O enredo e demasiado tipico ou corriqueiro ou cliche, ou o que lhe quiserem chamar. Havia muito sitio por onde levar esta historia, muitas linhas de accao que poderiam ter sido exploradas, mas a autora decidiu, preguicosamente, tomar o caminho mais facil, com viloes muito maus e previsiveis, uma conspiracao escondida e rebeldes ambientalistas. 2. O triangulo amoroso define a accao. Quase tudo acontece porque a personagem A esta apaixonada pela personagem B que por sua vez gosta da personagem C. O que me pareceu ridiculo, mas la esta, e a formula deste tipo de livros e nao sei porque e que ainda me surpreendo. 3. As personagens bidimensionais. Sao uns paozinhos sem sal, nao me consegui identificar com nenhum deles e nao me interessei minimamente pelas suas historias. As personalidades de Bea, Quinn e Alina sao inconsistentes e as suas vozes indistinguiveis umas das outras. No geral, temos um livro com uma premissa interessante, que podia ter dado origem a uma historia intrigante. Mas o enredo simplista, as personagens apagadas e o foco no drama adolescente va la, estao a tentar sobreviver num mundo sem oxigenio! Podemos ter mais tensao, please tiraram muito do brilho a Breathe. O mundo esta mal explorado e a historia raramente faz grande sentido. Nem o romance me convenceu. Se querem um bom livro de ficcao cientifica com protagonistas jovens, nao peguem emBreathe.

In my eyes, this book by Megan Abbott captures the nature of teenage girls perfectly. Although I myself have not ever been or desire to become a cheerleader, being currently a similar age to Addy, the protagonist, I know from both my own emotions and past experiences with other girls the darkness that can come from those who seem perfect on the outside. What I especially enjoyed about this novel was the writing, in particular the dialogue - Abbott is skilled in writing realistic teenage characters without falling into cliches of how they speak, as so many authors with a number of years between their own age and teenage-hood do. Perhaps it was the fact that the story was told through her eyes, but for me Addy was both the most realistic and relatable character her feelings towards the other girls, though at times dark, were accurate portrayals of the "bitchiness" that is inevitable within teen cliques. Her overwhelming and immediate obsession bordering on crush for Coach as soon as she arrives I first thought was perhaps a little overdone but as I continued with the book I felt it flowed better as the two got to know each other. Beth's jealousy regarding Addy also struck a chord with me, and in some ways felt like the most accurate thing to come from the book - Beth's clear desire to be always in control of people and situations as this is what she has become accustomed to and Addy resisting this for one of the first times was a dynamic I truly enjoyed as I read through the book. Another thing I feel I must comment on, as it is a heavy feature of the book, is the sexual aspect - I have never read a book where every page is saturated with this many suggestive undertones and language. To begin with I was slightly shocked and wasn't sure if it was in keeping with the book style but as I continued reading it become clear that this was a very purposeful move by Abbott and was very well done it fits the situation of Addy between Beth and Coach very well and I felt I could understand Addy more and her thoughts and feelings through this. As for the mystery aspect, this is not a book to pick up if you want a Gone Girl-esque twist of epic proportions, but I did enjoy the small twists as the novel went on all the same. I'll admit I did get this book because I was looking for something with plot twists and a thriller aspect, and I probably wouldn't have chosen it if I knew that this book reads more like a character study - but I'm glad i read it anyway. I only gave this book three stars for this reason as I was expecting something different, but if I had gone into it with a different mindset I may have given it four stars. Somehow this novel is suspenseful and slow burning at the same time which was highly enjoyable, and the insight into the mind of teenage girls from Abbott's perspective certainly forced me to compare myself to the characters and hope to god I was nothing like them! I definitely enjoyed reading this book and at times could not put it down, but I'm not sure it's something I will be reading again in the future.

CLICK HERE TO READ MY FULL REVIEW AT READING, EATING AND DREAMING I WAS BLAIR WALDORF Mia's Heart by Courtney Cole was a great addition to The Paradise Diaries. The Paradise Diaries is a fun, adventurous series that is perfect for young adults. The Paradise Diaries isn't a paranormal series, but there is a magical, other worldly vibe to this companion series. Some of the storyline in Dante's Girls and Mia's Heart is a little farfetched, but everything that happens in this series could potentially happen. Reading this series is like stepping into another world, and in my opinion, that's what makes this series so great. One of the biggest things that makes this series seem other worldly is the setting. This series takes place in Valese, Caberra, which is ruled by a different political hierarchy than the United Staes. Each of the main charcters in this companion series are children of wealthy, influential politicians. While the fame, wealth, and elite social standing sound like the most amazing things in the world, they also come with a heavy price. The main characters in this series must balance what they want with what is expected of them, and trust me, those two things are not always the same thing. Mia, the main character in Mia's Heart, has always rebelled against what is expected of her. She wears a lot of black clothing and she accessories her hair with colorful streaks. It's safe to say that she likes to get a reaction from people, especially her parents. She's tough, ornery, and a little bit of a bad ass. After a tragedy hits Caberra, Mia wakes up without her memory. She no longer recognizes herself or the girl she used to be. To make matters worse, she is extremely attracted to two equally sexy guys and she doesn't know how to pick between them without her memory. I loved the romance in this novel. I also really like how Courtney Cole illustrated Mia's identity crisis. She did a great job explaining how some of her rebelliousness was done for a reaction. I enjoyed watching Mia discover who she was. I also really enjoyed watching her relationship with her mother evolve. I think a lot of teens and young adults will be able to relate to Mia's relationship with her mother. I gave Mia's Heart Paradise Diaries 2 by Courtney Cole 4 STARS 3.5 STARS . I recommend this cute, sweet romance novel to young adults who are looking for a light, fun read. -XOXO READING, EATING AND DREAMING

Nothing is hurried, as the characters and their actions are played out over a span of years. The English vernacular is a bit off-putting at first but once the reader settles in, the language does impede the reading. Dom, Holly, their Mam's and fathers, Vincent, and Jack Law are each so unique--or are they? Is there some of each of them in each of us? Are we all torn by split desires and beliefs? The characters' raw emotions were agonizingly real and, at times, hard to read. Secondary characters, most notable a couple teachers and classmates, add even more depth as the themes of friendship, love, hopes, survival, and religion are explored. Almond's vivid details etch people and events so clearly the scenes and characters will be playing in my head for a long time!

spoiler alert For starters, I do admit that I was hesitant before reading this. I thought it was going to be a difficult read since I don't know a whole lot about Shakespeare plays. I was worried I wouldn't be able to connect to the story because of this. Man, was I wrong. For starters, this is so different from Wicked Lovely. There was great characterization and unique storyline it was hard not to fall in love. Whether you like fairy books or not, you should give this book a try. Kelley and Sonny are our main characters, switching off points of view every chapter. It was easy to follow. You switch between how a human sees the world, and how a changling sees our world. Kelley, is the human, she has moved to New York to start off her passion for acting. So far, it only landed her as an understudy. After the lead has an accident, Kelley takes up the role as Titania in A Midsummer's Night Dream. She struggles with remembering her script, which she goes to Central Park to practice the lines. This is where Sonny comes in. Sonny is a changling, a human that was taken by faeries to live with them. He is trained to be one of thirteen Janus, who protect a gate between the Otherworld and mortal realm. King Auberon has blocked off the gates so no fairy can come to the mortal realm and cause harm. Every nine years, the gate opens for nine nights before Samhein, which Halloween. Sonny and the others have to kill any faeries trying to escape to here. Sonny senses Kelley and tries to cheer her up, because she is struggling. After handing her a flower, he disappears. Later that night, Kelley finds a horse drowning in the lake and saves it. She faints while in the lake and someone saves her. She goes back to her apartment and finds the horse in her bathtub. Sonny, after going back to guard, finds the horse tracks and discovers it's a kelpie. He also sees Kelley's flower and script. This leads them to meeting more, which later on, Kelley is discovered to be something than more. She and Sonny's lives are intertwined more than anyone can suspect. What I like so much about the story, is Kelley and Sonny. Their first couples of meetings are so hilarious and such enjoyable parts to read. I will just finish off with saying... BUY IT! -Ivy

I love a good dystopian and 'The Pledge' was a stand out. As soon as I read the synopsis I knew I would love this book and wanted it desperately. It did not disappoint, it was everything I thought it would be and more. This is my first Kimberly Derting book and after reading The Pledge, I can't wait to read more of her work. Derting has created one of the most well explained, realistic possible futures that I have read in the dystopian genre. In a world where someone could be executed for something as simply as looking someone in a higher class in the eye when they are speaking their native tongue, people are guarded, especially 17 year old Charlie. She has a deadly secret, a secret she must not let anyone know she can speak all languages. When she meets Max, and he speaks a language she has never heard before, she is both frightened and intrigued. She tries to stay away from him, but he keeps appearing everywhere she is. Max is a mystery, he has secrets of his own and Charlie has no idea who he really is. The rebels opposed to the Queen and her regime are moving in on the city, and when Charlie gets swept up in the middle of everything, she'll have to choose who to trust, and the biggest secret of all will be uncovered. I loved Charlie, she was stubborn and level headed, and cared deeply for the ones she loves, doing what it takes to keep them safe. Her best friend Brooke, annoyed me at times, but I loved her other best fried, Aron. He was sweet and protective and chivalrous. And of course I loved Angelina, Charlie's little sister. She was so sweet, and her secret was super cool. And then there is Max. Mysterious, gorgeous, persistent. He vows to do anything to keep Charlie safe. I loved the slow build up of their relationship, how Charlie didn't fall head over heels and declare her love the instant they meet. She kept her head. But I loved the electricity between them and the few stolen, simmering moments they have together. I was worried this was going to be a stand alone, the way this book wrapped up, but then there was a little twist at the very end that made me excited and intrigued, and after investigating online found out yes this is a trilogy and now I can't wait to read book 2 'The Essence', which was released earlier this year. This book is a must read for all lovers of dystopian. It was a compulsive read, hooking me from the start. I highly recommend it.

Having read so much of her non-fiction, I decided to re-read some of L'Engle's novels. Really, I would not recommend this book for children or even teenagers, unless you're ready to read it with them and discuss it. While it handles some issues very well I was frankly appalled by how casually a relationship between an older man mid to late 20s and a 16 year old girl was handled. For one thing that the character's parents allowed her to go out with an adult man, for another that the "love" scene was portrayed as no big deal when it was actually predatory and exploitative, to say nothing of illegal. If my child was reading about it, I would want to be sure he or she understood that a situation like that would NOT be normal, healthy, legal, or moral. It seems out of character for L'Engle to have written it, and the book itself is not as well written as her other books. I really think you could, and probably should, just skip it entirely. Does imagination prove true on the stage? As I read Elizabeth Hand's novel in which high schoolers put on Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, I continuously asked myself if imagination did prove true on the stage. Or is the stage just a more tangible bit of imagination, one that doesn't really ever connect with solid, real things. "Prove true imagination, oh prove true!" is Viola's beginning belief that her brother may be alive in Twelfth Night. And she is wondering if what she is thinking could possibly be true. Could possibly come true. This line hooked me the first time I saw the modern movie version of the play. It has continued to inspire my writing, balanced somewhere next to, on top of, or under the largest window into my imagination. It begs us to ask the question, "What if imagination did prove true?" Hand's novel is short and the ending skips across time, seeming like a simple summary of life events much of the time. But she does find solid ground in the little theater that Rogan and Maddy find in the attic. The theater is one step into the world of imagination, yet it sits behind a wall in the attic. It was found be accident when a piece of the wall fell down. A classic portal into that next, more understanding, yet elusive of worlds. It is the love of the stage that is the central theme in Illyria. A love of that imagined place that turns back time, builds bridges, allows for escape, generates and sustains love, and lets us not be cynical of our hope, faith, and belief in things we cannot see, things we cannot hear, things that we can only feel. Places we must use our minds to visit.

Ignite is the second book in the Defy series and it continues with the action, suspense and romance that I loved about Defy! What did I like about Ignite? The Story You must read the first book to understand the story of events, so my review will be spoiler free. I loved that Ignite picks up where it ended in Defy and how this was fast paced. King Damian is rebuilding the kingdom with Alexa by his side. She continues to be a member of his guard and sacrifices her happiness for the sake of the kingdom. But now a new threat has come and the safety of King Damian is in jeopardy. This book was an emotional ride as I watched Alexa's heartbreak at the thought of losing Damian. She has to make some hard decisions in this book that either way will leave her in pain. The romance between Alexa and Damian continues to be passionate. With the loss they both have had Alexa and Damian really deserve some happiness, so I hope the author ends this series with a HEA for them. The Characters Alexa is still one of my favorite female YA characters. She continues to be a member of the King's guard despite the people's views of the proper role for women. Despite all the whispers and disapproving looks Alexa walks with her head high. She is one of the best fighters in the kingdom and she puts her loyalty to the king above her own happiness. What didn't I like about Ignite? I found nothing wrong with Ignite! The Defy series is fantasy filled with action, suspense and romance. The world that author Sara B. Larson has created is rich in detail but easy to follow. The ending of this book wasn't a dramatic cliffhanger but it leaves a wide range of possibilities for the next book Endure, which releases in January 2016. I can't wait to read the next book and I highly recommend this to fans of YA fantasy.

I wish I could give this 0 stars or negative stars. This one is the most offensive of the entire series and made me feel physically wretched reading it. The prime example I will cite is when Jacob kisses Bella against her wishes. She then punches him and breaks her wrist in the process, then when she gets home, her father the town's Police Chief, no less takes Jacobs side and tells her she should be nicer to him. I'm sorry, at what point did sexual assault - because that's what it is - become entertaining fiction? The message this sends to young girls is appalling! Too bad if you don't want a guy to kiss you. If he wants you, he's gonna take you and there's nothing you can do about it! Just appreciate how he feels about you. Ordinarily fathers would want to beat the crap out of a boy for touching his daughter - if it's against her wishes, he'd be getting his gun. But no, not this guy! Furthermore, it is a complete dereliction of duty for a Police Chief to support a guy kissing a girl against her wishes. He should be removed from his position and thoroughly investigated by Internal Affairs. I REALLY hated this book. I am not the type to advocate the burning or banning of books, but this piece of literary travesty has me seriously reconsidering. Oh and before any Twihards say, "But she did want him to kiss her later!" That's really not the point. He did not have her consent that time, thus it is sexual assault. Besides, can anyone say 'Stockholm Syndrome'?

I seem to be alone in my opinion of this book. I've seen nothing but rave reviews about this book, about how cute and swoonworthy it was, and I'm kind of left wondering "did we read the same book?" because I'm not really sure what I missed here, but I didn't think it was all that adorable. I'm a HUGE fan of the "falling in love online via text via email" trope and I LOVE a good fairy tale retelling and with all the positive things people had to say about this, I was really looking forward to this book. I was kind of disappointed as I was reading it though, and I'll tell you why. For starters, the "falling in love online via text via email" trope didn't really work for me here. One they barely talked to each other before they somehow managed to fall in love. I think they talked for a few weeks, maybe a month at most? So I don't really get how they went from being virtual strangers to calling each other "my heart" in that limited time frame. It just felt too much like instalove via text for me. Two the little bit of their interactions that we do see weren't that swoonworthy to me. I mean, for the most part, we don't even really get to SEE their conversations. Most of the time, we'll see Elle's texts to Darien or Darien's texts to Elle, but there are very few times where we actually see them talking to one another and having a conversation. And the times we do see them, I didn't really feel anything like I usually would if I were swooning over a couple. Their conversations were kind of boring and mostly centered around the show they both liked, so I don't really see how they fell in love with one another. They got so focused on one another so quickly, and I just don't get how or why from what we see in the book. If I fell in love with every person who was as obsessed with my favorite shows and movies and books as I am, then I would probably fall in love with half the people I follow on tumblr. I just really don't see how they got so attached to one another. I'm not sure if that's because they didn't have a long time to talk to one another or because we're never really shown their conversations all that much or both, but it just felt like I was missing the magic that everyone else seemed to love about them. I also just don't really think this fairy tale retelling did very much for me. It was almost too much like the original story for my liking. Everything felt like a copycat of the original story, albeit in a modern setting. I like for my fairy tale retellings to be a little bit more original, and I know that's a personal thing, but that's just how I feel, so someone else might really enjoy this retelling! I also got kind of annoyed with Elle. One of my favorite things about Cinderella is that she doesn't let her bad circumstances and her abusive stepfamily get to her. She perseveres in spite of them and she's just a really incredible character. Elle, however, was not. I found her to be so whiny and annoying. I'm not saying that she doesn't have a right to be that way given her circumstances, but that is not the Cinderella I know and love, so that irked me. Also, I'm still confused about the whole "selling the house" plotline. If the house was Elle's, how could her stepmother sell it without her permission??? I know my review makes it seem like I didn't like anything about it, but I did think it was a cute story overall, and there were some aspects I enjoyed. I liked Sage. She was probably my favorite character and I kind of wish we got to see more of her and Cal. They were really cute and it would've been nice to have seen some more of that relationship and how it developed. I liked Darien too. He seemed nice and I liked that he added some more diversity to the cast as well. The ending was cute and I liked that not everything was entirely predictable. I think my biggest issue with this book is that Cinder Ella is one of my favorite books, and it does a fantastic job of incorporating the "falling in love online via text via email" trope particularly because the relationship between the main characters in that book developed over several years, not weeks , as well as putting a unique spin on a Cinderella retelling. If you liked this book, I would DEFINITELY recommend you read Cinder Ella plus the sequel just came out and it's so heart eyes ! Even if you didn't like this book, you should read Cinder Ella Overall, this book was just okay for me. It was cute, but not worth all the hype in my opinion.
