spoiler alert I haven't read all of Sarah Dessen's books, but those that I have, I've enjoyed. Her novels typically don't have a lot of twists and turns or suspense built in. Instead, they all have a slice o'life quality that makes each novel somewhat relatable and therefore, enjoyable. Dessen typically writes in the coming of age genre just like her latest, Saint Anything. Sydney is the main character in the story, however in Sydney's family the main character is her older brother, Peyton. Peyton has always been the center of attention, but lately it's been for all the wrong things as he continually has gotten in and out of trouble. Up until now, the family has been able to bail Peyton out of his jams, until he makes a mistake he has to pay for...in prison. One would think that with Peyton away, the concern might shift to his younger sister, Sydney, but now more than ever, Sydney finds herself living in the shadow of big brother Peyton. Everything down to her mother's mood is affected by whatever is going on with Peyton. It also doesn't help matters that their mother is in denial about how much Peyton has messed up. This was a source of frustration not only for Sydney, but I'd imagine many readers. In fact their mother's refusal to see anything the way it truly was, and her father's refusal to stand up for anything that matters really, really irked me. But perhaps the most irksome aspect of Saint Anything was how much Peyton's "friend" Ames managed to fool her parents. He was painted as a pretty creepy guy the entire time by anyone who met him, even for a second. Everyone saw his shiftiness, EXCEPT Sydney's parents who- instead- invite him to stay and watch Sydney while they were away!! For how protective her mom was about literally everything else, being so accepting of a recovering addict just didn't add up. I kept hoping for a conversation where the mom admitted and apologized for putting her hopes in Ames since he was more or less a replacement for Peyton while he was gone. Of course the friendships Sydney made and the eventual love story helped keep the Ames situation from entering Lifetime movie territory. I would have liked a little more resolution at the end, but overall Saint Anything was probably a solid 3.5 stars.

I was a bit skeptical towards the theme of angels in this book. I thought it would came out Twilight like romance between two races, this time between human and angel, disguised in a post-apocalyptic theme. Boy, was I ever be more wrong. I instantly like Angelfall since its first few pages. It's intense even from the very start. There's the heroine, Penryn, helping a wingless angel left bleeding in the middle of the street, with the risk of being attacked by street thugs who would kill for angel body parts. Why? Because she thinks the angel can bring her to her little sister who's been snatched by a warrior angel flying to the sky. Penryn would do anything to bring her sister back, even if it means she has to deal with the angel, the creature she despises for turning the world as she knows it into the World After. There is no insta-love in here, mind you. Even though Raffe, the angel with amputated snowy feather wings whom she rescues, was practically an Adonis, she doesn't swoon over him or treat him like a precious lover or something. She isn't scared maybe a little bit to slap him, tie him to a cart, or even step on his injuries just to make a point. Reasons to like this book? 1. Kick-ass heroine who actually knows how to fight, because her crazy mother signed her up for a load of self-defense classes--a realistic reason why a petite young girl has a chance to survive alone in the scary post-apocalyptic world 2. Raffe the angel--yap, angel, but not in the lame kind you might think. This one is of course described as a gorgeous creature, but he is much more than that. My personal favorite is his dry sense of humor. 3. The witty banter between Penryn and Raffe. I couldn't help giggling in the middle of the night because of these two bickering on each other. 4. It is really dark, creepy, and full of gore most of the times but balanced by the interesting dialogues and narrations. Susan Ee really does a good job writing this to be an ultimate page-turner. I could go on but I might have been at lost of words. Except to say that Angelfall is a really good book. And I really, really like it.

The world feels very wrong right now. Between shootings, terrorism, and the horrible people that are governing our country with seemingly no ethics or empathy whatsoever, The Hate U Give is a tough read, but it's also a must read. I hope everyone reads this book. The Hate U Give was incredible, and so very important, and I felt I was changed for having the experience of reading it. Sixteen-year-old Starr Carter lives with her family in a mostly black, low-income neighborhood called Garden Heights. Everyone Starr knows has some connection to the local gangs. Starr's parents enroll her in a mostly white high school with better educational opportunities. She's made some good friends at the school, but they don't know the real Starr. And she's let her childhood friendships lapse because she's not herself with them either. Starr is talked into attending a neighborhood party which takes a frightening turn when shots are fired. Starr gets a ride from her friend Khalil, a boy she's always been close to. When they're stopped by police for a broken taillight, Starr remembers the rules her father has drilled into her... no sudden moves, no arguments, hands in plain sight. Starr learned at an early age to fear being pulled over, and this time her fear is justified. Thomas really helps us to feel everything that Starr goes through, from the horrific experience with the police, to navigating adulthood in her school and community, to coming to terms with who she is and wants to be. It's not just a book about police brutality or racism, although it's both of those. Starr and her family wrestle with what it means to be black, and there are few easy answers. Thomas deftly blends important political statements with a complex and very real story about family, friendship, and the place we call home. There's so much in this book that made me think -- and feel. One thing I've thought a lot about since reading this book is how much I hold back from talking about race because as a white person, I'm sure I'll say the wrong thing. Starr has a good friend who hurts her with racially insensitive comments and actions. When Starr has the courage to confront her friend, she's looking for an apology, but she gets anger and defensiveness instead. I think about being that person say, mixing up two people's names who are the same race, or making a reference to fried chicken, as in this book and how I would feel if I was called on it. Starr's voice felt really authentic to me, to the extent I can judge at least. Sometimes Starr talks the way I remember talking as a teenager, although of course she comes from a different community and a different generation. Thomas manages to make Starr feel sixteen years old without ever sounding childish. This is YA literature that doesn't talk down to its readers. Even if you don't usually read YA fiction, you should read this. Thomas' first novel tells a powerful, important story in a way that's never preachy or oversimplified. Just raw, honest emotion that had me weeping and cheering for Starr again and again. My full review can be found at http thebookstop.wordpress.com.

Kiss of Frost is the second book in Jennifer Estep's Mythos Academy series and it pretty much takes place only a couple weeks later from where Touch of Frost ended. I really liked Touch of Frost, but I enjoyed Kiss of Frost a lot more. I think what I like the most about this series is the relationship between Logan and Gwen. The way it plays out and how at first I want to hate Logan so much, but just can't. I love it! I also really like Gwen's powers. I know there is a down side to it, but who wouldn't want to be able to see the history of everything you touch? Kiss of Frost has just as much ass-kicking as the first book in the series. Someone is out to kill Gwen and she has no idea who. After going through so much already with one reaper, now she has to deal with a new reaper. Of course, Gwen being who she is, decides that she wants to take things into her own hands. She starts to investigate and tries to figure out who her enemy is. By doing this she discovers a lot, not only about herself, but about Logan and some of her friends around her. It was nice this time around to finally learn a bit about Logan and his past. My only issue was that the story was a bit predictable. It didn't take me very long to figure out who was after Gwen and wanted her dead. Not sure if it was supposed to be that easy to figure out, but I would have loved a nice shock. I will say though, what I did not see coming was the whole reason WHY this person wanted her dead and who this person really was, and just how evil they truly were. With her gift, Gwen finds out a lot about this person and all that they've done. I was very happy with the ending and cannot wait for the next book, Dark Frost. 4 out of 5 Stars!

"After I'd fired the gun I'd just run inside. Fight-or-flight response. How about fight then flight response? How about shoot-angel-in-face-and-then-run-away-as-fast-as-you-can-response?" This was a 4.5 star book for me and I would've given this 5 stars quite willingly if only some things were different. Like Gabe being taken away by the angels in the end. Do not judge a book by its cover, ever. Because this books cover is gorgeous, dark, and has beautiful type fonts, but what it contains is nothing but a shallow, deceitful, collection of words and sentences that completely fails to deliver. This story is about Celeana Sardothien, an 18 yr old girl that has been an assassin since the age of 8, and is the most feared of her profession in the kingdom. But she was recently betrayed and captured, and sent to spend the rest of her life in a work camp until the day the Crown Prince removes her to act as his champion in a contest to determine the King's new official assassin. The other contestants are fellow assassins, theirs, and murderers - as in the nastiest people in the kingdom. Only they start dying, one by one, outside of the competition. Interesting right?? HELL NO. This book frustrated the hell out of me and constantly had me going 'What the hell??' I mean seriously how the hell do you screw up such a promising premise? I can tell you exactly how. 1. You host a competition with the meantest, craziest, dangerous people in all of the kingdoms to see who is the best of all to become the king's new official assassin. And then instead of duels and gladiatorial type fights like this... image error instead they have gladiatorial fights like this... image error yeah...cause foot races, climbing challenges, and jogging is what the most the king is expecting from an official assassin. I mean damn...I got over half way thru the book and not a single competitor was killed by another outright. LAME. I get that this book is young adults, but if kids can fucking read Hunger Games then I don't see why Maas felt the need to play the pansy. 2. Write in a damned love triangle - which is quickly becoming known as the laziest and dumbest writing cliche in young adult fiction - and giving the heroine the choice of 2 men, and then having her choose the asshole. First there is Captain of the Guard Choal Westfall who is loyal, witty, smart, strong, and most importantly genuine. Then you have the Crown Prince Dorian Havillard, a womanizing, douche bag who looks at women as playthings for an hour at a time, but claims this is because he is only willing to marry someone he loves and how can he find a woman he loves without meeting and bedding them all? So Celaena, who was imprisoned by the prince's evil father, actually comes to like this man who is the son of the evil king who destroyed her own home country. No he did not actively partake in his father's plans to become dictator of everyone, but he also isn't doing anything to stop him or even slow him down. And then there is the fact that he is a womanizing asshat, but really that pales in comparison to the man's cowardice. 3. You write a 400 page book where nothing freaking happens for the first 225 pages. Yes a couple of competitors die in a mysterious and bloody manner off the page but that's its. The competition is drawn out over months instead of taking place in days supposedly so that they can be trained. But really if they are already assassins, thieves, and murderers what can they be taught that they don't already know?? And frankly if they don't already know it then they won't be the bad ass assassin that they are looking for. And those bodies I mentioned...yeah their deaths have something to do with magic which the king has outlawed, but frankly after reading 1 2 a book where nothing happens how can the author expect to introduce an entire new element to the book's universe and have the reader actually care!? By this point we are all too bored to even try to learn about an entire new aspect to the story, especially when the information is doles out in nothing but hints without any substance or chance for the main character or reader to make anything of them. 4. You only write 2 good characters amidst a sea of mediocre ones. The good ones were hands down Nehemia and Choal. Both were strong, interesting, plotting, conflicted. It amazes me that Maas was able to make 2 secondary characters so freaking interesting but the main character such an idiot. Celaena was a girl who became an assassin at the age of 8. She could explain how she could take down a man in 2 miliseconds, but never actually does anything. She has obviously had a hard and bitter life but never acts like it. She trusts easily, chats with everyone, makes friends, etc. Wouldn't most people in her place be severely distrustful, and damn near broken? Especially after a year in the mines? Plus would a girl who has been as assassin for the past 10 years live a very routine life? Up early, disciplined, and exact? I found her extremely short sighted, conceited, and totally lazy. I swear she should be like a soldier and instead is like a stoner. 5. You write no setting but include a map of the land at the beginning of the book which wasn't useful at all for the first half of the book. Most of the settings were never that richly described and I usually had no idea what made this kingdom any different from any of the other kingdoms. Fantasy books need good settings! Don't skimp on something that basically is another character in your ensemble. So yeah, I am quitting this book. I have found it to be dumb, shallow, and just plain ludicrous. Seriously if you want to read a story like this, but want to actually enjoy it you should check out Poison Study by Maria Snyder. That is a fantastic series with a female assassin lead character that is great.

This book takes a little bit to get into. It is definitely targeted at a more "true" YA audience than an adult one, but once the book got into full swing I found myself enjoying it too. Brief Summary from Goodreads "Dorthea is completely princed out. Sure being the crown princess of Emerald has its perks--like Glenda Original ball gowns and Hans Christian Louboutin heels. But a forced marriage to the brooding prince Kato is so not what Dorthea had in mind for her enchanted future.Talk about unhappily ever after.Trying to fix her prince problem by wishing on a cursed star royally backfires, leaving the kingdom in chaos and her parents stuck in some place called "Kansas."" The story starts out with a main character that is so snobby and full of herself that she is rude to anyone "below her" and only cares about her clothes and shoes. At the beginning, she is hardly an appealing main character. However, there are a ton of funny quips, snarky comments, and inside fairy tale jokes that made it interesting enough for me to want to continue anyway. By the time I got about 1 3 of the way through the story there was a great adventure story, a solid plot, and the princess was quickly becoming not so full of herself. I loved Kato and his backstory, and Dorthea's growth as a character was much appreciated. She went from a loathful annoyance to a character I could actually like. There isn't a ton of depth to either character's development or any of their relationships, but the writing of the book is clearly geared for the young to mid YA audience. As such, it did a great job. The ending was well done for this style of book. It was a satisfying happy ending without a final "happily ever after". There were many plot lines left open to be continued in a sequel, but it was written in a way that didn't feel like an unfinished "to be continued". I found that once it was all said and done, this book was a fun, lighthearted read that I could see myself picking up again in the future. Rating I rate this book a 3 out 5. Young adults would love this book, and adults that don't mind a fun adventure with a low level of character development will likely enjoy it to. I found it to be an easy, enjoyable read.

When it comes to novels, movies, or other forms of entertainment, I'm fairly easy to please. Admittedly, my rating a book a three would be much more telling than if I gave it a five. I'm usually not one to break books or movies down and evaluate every little thing I didn't like. As a reader, I ask myself a few questions 1. Was the story entertaining? 2. Where necessary, was it plausible. What I mean by this is, you can create a fantasy world, and I am happy to accept it. But, within that world, can you convince me that the events could happen? 3. Were there a lot of typos? If those three things happen for me, the book will rate pretty well. I won't usually second guess why the author did something one way or another. I will try to accept that, even if it didn't go the way I wanted it to, if the book met the above criteria, I will be satisfied. To make a short story long, this book and series did that for me, except that there were really way more typos in each of the four than I would expect from a traditionally published novel. Even still, I loved the story enough to overlook it. I enjoyed the ride, and was sorry to see it end. Hopefully, some day Stephenie Meyer will finish the books from Edward's point of view. The portion of Midnight Sun she released on her website was outstanding.

This story is told from multiple points of view about what happens when one day the world goes mad. One Solstice there are major solar flares and all light goes out on earth. No power, no phones, and people you love are dead but still moving and worse, eating people. This is the second zombie apocalypse novel I have read this week and it was not more of the same. This story focuses on the emotional and physical toll this would take on people and the extent to which people will go to save those they love. How many people living in our gadget and computer dependent society could live without electricity, gas stations, supermarkets, and societal defined norms? I have friends who have never slept outside, never started a fire, or had to worry about where the next meal was coming from. Something like this levels the playing field and puts everyone on the same footing regardless of race, wealth, age, educational level or other things we use to judge people. I enjoyed reading this book, although at times the characters seemed emotionally unavailable, that was the point of that portion of the book. I give this book 5 out of 5 clouds. I loved it! Sarah really knows how to do a fairytale retelling. If you like Once Upon a Time then you will love Kill Me Softly and Tear You Apart. Tear You Apart is a modern fairytale that is an actual fairytale. The old stories and the new combine into this amazing story with characters I love. Sarah is such a wonderful writer and the way she describes the scenes you can't help but fall in. With the mix of different fairytales even from different culture and multiple repeating characters will keep you enraptured. Tear You Apart is fabulous, glamorous and magical but it's also dark, gritty and dangerous. You have princesses and princes, fabulous parties, fairies roaming around, magic in plain sight, and fairytales coming to life. However you also have the dark-side like you would see in the original fairytales. There are these curses that come to life and some people don't survive their curses, they actually die. Tear You Apart is a Snow White retelling The Main Characters Viv as Snow White Viv bestfriend boyfriend, Henley, as the Huntsman Regina as the Evil Queen Now characters from Kill Me Softly do make their rounds in this book and there is hints of what happened in the previous book in this one so I suggest reading Kill Me Softly first. Viv is not what you would think Snow White would be like. She lives in modern times and she has know about the curse since she was little. Regina is plotting her death and would one day care out her plans and Henley may be forced to take her heart. So that means that Viv turned into a very cold mean person. She isn't evil but she is harsh and at times you can see who she would have been and also how she still is, soft and caring at times. Henley is a really nice guy and he really cares about Viv. Henley and Viv have such a strong bond however she treats him like crap because she believes in the curse, but he loves her so much that he sticks around. Since curses have the power to change people you can't help but wonder who side is he on. Regina plays her role as the Evil Queen well, but she has this backstory. You find out that she wasn't always like this and I did find myself feeling a bit sorry for her. I love when a story is beautiful and frightening. The descriptions of the scenes, parties and places are glamours and then you see the dark side of this tale and it just makes it better. Tear You Apart had me on the edge of my seat, so many different things was happening, trying to figure out if Viv would survive the murder attempts, trying to solve the mysteries and which fairytales where which. I love this series so much and I really wish that it will continue on.

This is a cautionary tale about how making mistakes can be easier than you might think. Breaking a law may seem like a good way to make a buck, but the consequences might be more than you bargain for. This is a raw, unflinching view of the author making terrible choices and paying for them. I am REALLY not a fan of prison stories, but luckily the bad stuff that happens in prison isn't portrayed too graphically. I loved when he was talking about reading books about smoking weed. That was his only experience with drugs at the time. That reminds me of me. I am often very knowledgeable about things because I read books about them, not because I've actually experienced it. I paced around the cell thinking that I was in some kind of reverse mental institution where I'd only get released once I was totally screwed up. That made me smile, but it is actually a little too true. Lots of times prison can make a minor criminal into a major one or train people to do better in their future criminal lives. And the ill treatment can totally screw people up as well. It's a tough problem.

Unfortunately, this final book is not my favorite of the three. It's always sad when the final book is a bit of a letdown. I did like the book I just didn't love it near as much as the first two. The first two books had very fascinating arena settings that helped move the story along. In this last book, after you get much of the rebellion bits out of the way in the beginning - you get to see the rebellion grow and grow until it's ready to take on the Capital - the characters are thrown into another arena of sorts, in the form of a booby-trapped Capital city. The whole thing seemed contrived and forced and I am not ashamed to say that I skimmed most of it. It was like Collins felt it a requirement to give us that sort of setting but her heart wasn't really in it. It just didn't seem necessary and therefore just seemed to drag the story down. The other parts of the book are definitely more fun. Going along with the rebellion as it plots and plans, particuarly from Katniss' point of view as their grudgingly willing masthead, was really interesting. Not to mention the twists they throw at you at several points - one around the middle regarding Peeta, and one at the very end that truly made me gasp out loud. There was one bit at the very end that I didn't really like - just a bit of dialogue, really, that seemed out of place for the character - but that's just me nitpicking. I also can't really say much more about it as it would give away too much, unfortunately. I'll just have to talk it out with friends who've read the book and see what they thought. This really was a great final entry into the series, even with the annoyingly stupid "arena" action, and I felt that it wrapped things up very nicely. And of course, fans of the romantic aspects of the series won't be left out - never fear, they wrap all that up nicely as well. Or as nice as it could, under the circumstances. I'm very much looking forward to seeing the rest of this series translated to the movies they're sure to be good with the great material Collins has provided.

ARC REVIEW I had the immense luck of being able to attend my first BEA this June and even bigger luck meeting my favorite author, Maggie Stiefvater. The luck kept on building up when I managed to get my hands on a Crooked Saints ARC. Really, I couldnt believe it was finally happening. Im still working on the BEA vlog videos I take forever to edit, ill link the vlogs here and in every other ARC review from BEA. I dont really like writing reviews, I much rather make videos but in these cases Ill be making both. Okay! Now, the review. 4.5 stars but more towards 5 stars Maggie may be my favorite author since I started reading but Im going to be honest with this review. Even though I loved this book, I do have some things I didnt like. I have to admit I was worried when I found out the book would have latinx culture involved. Being latina myself puertorican , I was both excited but hesitant. The first book I picked up from my BEA haul was Crooked, no surprise there. I was so ready for a new Maggie book, I was craving it. I had been suffering a book slump for months, the worst I have ever gotten. I knew this book would help me. I may have taken a long time to finish but its because I left it for most of the month. I took me two nights to read more than half of the book. I could NOT put it down. The book was slow, for the most part. Slow doesnt necessarily mean bad. I didnt expect this book to have much action anyway. I was in it more for the spectacular characters and scenery Maggie always creates. I am a sucker for small town settings, Ive bought books simply because they are set in them bad habbit, I know I was already into this story. A Maggie Stiefvater book? Set in a small desert town? SAY NO MORE. A thing I love so much about Maggies writing is the visuals. She describes places with such outstanding words that im always left speechless. She really outdid herself in this one. Adding the magical aspect to the story really was the icing on the cake. The book felt like magic. I fell in love with the small town, I fell in love with the strange people that lived there, I fell in love with the Soria family. And I fell in love with Pete. I love him. So much. Now, for the things I didnt love as much. At first it was the romance, I felt it came out all of a sudden, I felt like I had missed something, but later on everything made sense. However, I also loved the romance!! Maggie builds a love like no other. Not just romantically but platonic as well A couple may never kiss but the relationship feels more real than other YA love stories out there. I freaking love that. It happend with Blue and Gansey and it happens here too. Its unreal how much I enjoy a love story with no kissing, or in one particular case, no talking. Really, Maggie?? How? What a Talent. This next one isnt really a valid reason. I did fall for the characters, more than I thought I would. Yet, I didnt fully get attached to the extent I have with other Maggie books. It was probably because there were so many characters for just one book, unlike her other series that tend to be four books long, or Scorpio Races which concentrated mainly on two characters. See? This isnt really a valid reason but I wanted to mention it. The book left me wanting more of them. I miss these characters already. Regarding the latinx culture, as I said earlier Im puertorican so I suggest reading a review from a mexican reader for a more accurate view on the cultural aspect of this novel. I personally didnt see anything bad, thats my opinion. The spanish was minimal, the phrases used were real and well applied in context. Overall, I sighed with relief. Some note Some!! american authors have tried to incorporate us in their books but over saturate their story with mediocre spanish and bad stereotypes. More on these topics will be better dicussed in my review video that I will begin filming later in the week. Back to the things I loved, which were plenty. This book is WEIRD. Weirdest book Maggie has written to date, and thats saying a lot. It reminded me so much of my favorite podcast, Welcome to Nightvale. Which if you dont know about you should look it up ASAP If you like WTNV you will love this book. If you love this book, you will love WTNV. WTNV is about a radio show from this small desert town and its various completely odd citizens. Sound familiar? Maggie Stiefvater has such a unique way of telling stories, Ive yet to find a book of hers that doesnt entrance me. All The Crooked Saints may not be my favorite of hers but its definitely one ill recommend. An unusual story about ones darkness and the dangers it can cast upon you and those who you care for the most. Truly spectacular read I wont be forgetting. Actual ARC review video to come

I don't think I've ever read a book about OCD before, but it's something that I'm guilty of using in jest myself - saying that I'm slightly OCD about having my books in strict alphabetical order, or about washing my hands before dinner and bed - without really thinking about the people that are genuinely affected by it. And some OCD sufferers may not like that the author of OCD Love Story doesn't have OCD - and I was a little wary myself - can you really get into the mind of someone with OCD without having experienced it first hand? But Corey Ann Haydu never had me doubting her sincerity for a moment. When the book begins, Bea is a seemingly average teenage girl with a few 'quirks'. She has a tendency to obsess over people in her life, and although in the beginning it's not explicitly explained, there is obviously far more to her story than first impressions would have me believe. Bea is a likable character, if a little naive and not particularly self-aware. She has one close friend and a bunch of peripheral acquaintances, but for the most part she seems quite unremarkable which actually makes her a little more endearing. As a reader I wanted to reach through the pages and either hug her or give her a stern talking to on more than one occasion I enjoyed the blossoming romance between Bea and Beck no insta-love here folks , and I didn't particularly like nor dislike Beck - it was hard to see where the attraction between himself and Bea really came from apart from similar experiences, although perhaps that was the point. One thing I did notice after the first 100 or so pages was the lack of parental involvement, and although Bea herself actually states further on that her mother is completely disinterested and doesn't seem to understand the severity of the situation, it felt like a bit of a cop out to be honest - even a disinterested parent can have a little more involvement in a story, even if it is just being a blatant arsehole. Bea's spiral really starts to ramp up the pace of the story in the second half of the book, and it's almost like a car crash - I knew something bad was going to happen and yet I couldn't look away. Overall I really enjoyed OCD Love Story despite a few small issues and I think Corey Ann Haydu's writing is excellent and really fits the tone of the story. Whoa. Whoa. WHOA. That's pretty much my reaction to Ashfall. From page one, I was utterly hooked, which was too bad, because I started reading it right before bed. An apocalyptic story that starts out with a bang literally that could actually happen? Um, yikes! I've categorized this as science fiction fantasy, even though it's not really - but it fits right in with those great post-apocalyptic YA reads like Cinder, Wither, and When She Woke. This one has a male protagonist, and a realistic one, too - which might get some teen boys to read. Perhaps a few years after they finish the Percy Jackson books? Alex and the girl he meets on his trek, Darla, face danger, death, starvation, and government bureaucracy as they try to travel a three-hour drive on foot to reunite with Alex's family after a freak supervolcano changes the world as we know it. The choices they have to make are not easy ones, especially for teenagers. I found myself wondering what I would do if such chaos descended upon my life, and I only hope I have half the smarts that they did in the book. Ashfall was a great read, and I'm very impressed that it's a debut novel. It's been on my to-read list for a while, and I'm glad I procrastinated a little while to read it - that means I'm that much closer to the sequel's publication Ashen Winter, October !

Solid 3 stars since it wasn't the most exciting book, but it also wasn't bad. Wasn't brilliant, mind blowing, word gushing, but it wasn't terrible, kill me kind of stuff either. I originally picked this series up because I saw the cover of the third book and was like....so prettyyyy I want it! It was very simple--style of writing and plot wise. Though admittedly, the last couple of paragraphs got me. I didn't really see that coming mainly because I already saw the first twist about Jackson. Ari is okay as a character. She wasn't especially annoying, yet at the same time, I really questioned her mental state. In a way, I did compare this with Winner's Curse a little, particular the parallels, like Ari being the daughter of the Commander, and Kestral having been the daughter of the Emperor's trusted General think I got the details right . Where Rutkoski took the time and effort in her writing to give the reader a feel of Kestrel's thinking processes, with Ari, it was more acts based on emotion. I didn't really feel she was much of a Commander's daughter. In saying that however, one must consider the set up of both books. Kestral lives in a historical fantasy society, and from young has been properly brought up, and to some extent schooled. She is spoiled with the finery of her existence, yet she also isn't, having lost a parent, and under the parental guidance of a more than absent father who approves of her strategic ability. In that book, there's a lot of political intrigue going on. In Gravity though, it's much lighter affair. Ari is a very modern child like pretty much contemporary , she's got a sense of privilege about her, and I feel like she accepts things too easily, as opposed to thinking it over, weighing the pros and cons. If someone told her earth was dying and she needed to help, then she would. Kind of like Simon says. It was kind of annoying how willingly she moved to join Jackson's cause. I mean, after all, all we know about Jackson at the beginning of the novel is that he's gorgeous beyond gorgeous, and he's an Ancient aka A L I E N. I would have thought, she might have want to consider what would happen if she got caught, if her father became implicated and so on. But as was the case, within the first 50 pages, Ari has already been recruited to Jackson's cause. And of course, as the story goes on, they fall in love. Well if you could call it falling in love. This book does, admittedly suffer from Instalove. At the same time, the romance, while it could be classified as Instalove, didn't really annoy me this time. Then again, I should note that I haven't really been feeling many books since I read Vicious--that book was amazing--so I don't really blame this book for not living up to expectations of a beautiful cover. I also wasn't too annoyed because I kind of expected the romance heavy plot. I suppose I didn't really expect the Love Pentagon in the middle there, but hey, at least I was mentally prepared for the gooey moments and the 'don't die on me' moments. AS for the setting, it's set in a not too distant future where Ancients have come to earth in peace to offer a compromise. It's a very light science fiction setting. Since I'm not a massive lover of intense sci-fi with weird hard to pronounce names, this was very simple. So simple, it didn't really feel 'different'. This isn't a bad thing, but just don't expect a heavy sci-fi world. Terminology was easy to adapt to, but it was also boringly named I forgot what was what, and also, just didn't really imagine a very futuristic setting. The writing was not very 'great'. It was not particularly emotive, let alone, beautiful. It was very plain and unembellished, getting right to the point. In effect, it doesn't waste any time getting time getting to the action moments. It also makes this whole book a very quick read--don't take my reading time as word on how long it would take to read this, I had many interruptions and wasn't in a very bookish mood over the last week, so reading Gravity was like my last priority. If I had time to sit down consistently, then I could have probably finished this off in one sitting, it was that easy a read. On the downside, because the writing was so simple, it did downgrade the potential of this book, and it also reflects why this book infinitely belongs to the YA category and not the Adult one. I didn't really like the writing on the whole, it was just too plain. But it wasn't boringly written, there aren't any dense and convoluted sentences, and it did get straight to the point. So the writing was okay. Overall, I would suggest this for a simple, quick, scifi instalove read. If you want something more complicated, more sci fi, just more in general, try something else. If you're happy to read something actiony and instalovey, then this is good for it. In a way it reminds me a little of Divergent, only a little less in everything. For Me I am actually considering reading the sequels just to find out what happens. Admittedly, the covers are the only thing that draws me onwards.

Recensione anche sul mio blog http pleaseanotherbook.tumblr.com p... "Nemmeno in paradiso" e uno di quei libri che e entrato nelle mie cose da leggere, solo ed esclusivamente per la cover, di cui mi sono innamorata appena l'ho vista in giro. De Agostini che lo ha portato in Italia il 5 maggio, ha mantenuto la cover originale. Chelsey Philpot ricrea un retelling de "Il Grande Gasby" in chiave moderna e young adult, aggiungendo mistero e amicizia, alimentando dubbi e facendo capire al lettore che l'adolescenza e un periodo difficile, che dietro la perfezione si nasconde sempre qualche problema, che l'amore ha mille sfaccettature. Ammetto che mi e piaciuto, nonostante tutto. Serve una via di fuga per capire che si e in trappola. Diventa fondamentale uscire dalla propria quotidianita o incappare in un evento traumatico per rendersi conto di doversene andare. E un po' quello che succede a Charlotte, la protagonista e narratrice, che si ritrova invischiata in una situazione piu grande di lei. La storia inizia con un incontro, e non sono sempre gli incontri con persone che non immaginiamo che ci cambiano la vita? Conoscere Julia Buchnan e quanto di piu sconvolgente possa capitare a Charlotte. Julia e il mito del collegio femminile che frequenta, la conosceva, come si possono conoscere le persone per sentito dire e alla luce di una popolarita che la avvolge inclemente. Ma Julia e totalmente diversa da quello che tutti pensano, dentro di lei c'e tanto altro che nessuno vede e che nessuno si immagina. Charlotte e la classica brava ragazza, studiosa e diligente, inflessibile, che segue le regole senza mai sgarrare. Julia e un treno in corsa pronto a travolgerla con il suo entusiasmo e con la sua spontaneita. Il loro essere agli antipodi diventa motivo di chiacchiere tra le altre ragazze del collegio, che non capiscono il perche di un'amicizia che diventa epocale. Charlotte e un'artista, e incerta, insicura, incapace di validarsi in un momento, come quello dell'adolescenza, in cui tutto e incerto. La concretezza della struttura del liceo cozza contro la volatilita di un tipo come Julia, che non riesce a stare ferma, che si lascia prendere dall'impulsivita, con moti tanto imprevedibili quanto pericolosi. Charlotte viene completamente ad immergersi nel mondo non solo di Julia, ma di tutti i Buchanan, una famiglia, un mito, un sogno. L'atmosfera che permea questo libro e intensa e allo stesso tempo eterea, dove il lato emozionale e quello che emerge prepotente. I Buchanan sono la gloria dell'apice economico e la profondita di una perdita inimmaginabile, la vetta della gloria, con una casa da sogno su un isola e le occasioni di una precipitosa epopea e il precipizio di una distruzione non solo materiale, ma anche sentimentale. Julia, il fulcro di una vita che brucia, di un segreto che condiziona e consuma, e come una cometa, e Charlotte l'insetto attirato dalla luce. Apparentemente tutto sembra favoloso, con questa patina di accettazione e clamore. Eppure mentre Charlotte conosce meglio la famiglia, e se ne innamora, scopre gli altarini nascosti, quello sforzo continuo di tutta la famiglia di reggere il peso delle apparenze. L'alcool e il migliore amico di Julia e l'ossessione per la sorella, lo stimolo per continuare a non arrendersi. Stare con i Buchanan diventa per Charlotte un giro sulle montagne russe, alti e bassi, fino a che, dopo la salita piu ripida, precipita irrimediabilmente, con la perdita della sua innocenza, e della sua lealta. Tra gli altri personaggi da notare sicuramente il fratello di Julia, Sebastian che ho molto apprezzato, perche non e il classico bello e impossibile, privo di difetti e assolutamente irreprensibile. Sebastian e un ragazzo come tanti, con una guida insicura, imbranato e timido, pieno di difetti e clamorosamente inesperto, eppure tenero, dolce e protettivo nei confronti di una famiglia che sembra elevarsi dalle cime di un lago incantato. L'ambientazione si divide tra il St. Anna il collegio femminile frequentato dalle ragazze e Arcadia, la residenza estiva dei Buchanan, una villa da sogno sull'isola di Nantucket. Il New Hampshire appare come un luogo quasi incantato, coperto da un velo che nasconde le brutture piu inimmaginabili. Ma allo stesso tempo Arcadia e irreale e meravigliosa, l'incarnazione della famiglia Buchanan che vive attraverso la villa e il mare, per perdersi nei meandri di una realta fittizia, protetta e raccolta, lontano dai clamori della vita. Il particolare da non dimenticare? Un sasso bianco... Il mito dei Buchanan si infrange tra le mani di una ragazza che ha cercato con tutta se stessa di crederci. La storia di una famiglia attraverso gli occhi di una ragazza come tante che prova a mettercela tutta ad aiutare la sua migliore amica. Un libro intenso ed emozionale, tra amore e amicizia, viaggi e gloria, nei meandri oscuri di una tragedia gia scritta. Buona lettura guys!

It was the last book and this is when everything can be cleaned up and all questions are answered, but I finished this feeling like it was incomplete and empty. I will say that I felt this was probably the most original book of the whole series and that's only because of the twist near the end. That twist was something I wasn't expecting and that was exciting to read especially since the first 3 4 of the book I was bored and that's what I want when I read this supernatural fantasy YA books - exciting new twists and ideas you've never heard of before. The majority of this book from the beginning was just so slow and I was bored. I honestly didn't know if I could be bothered to read until the end. The whole journey was too still even when they were progressing, it still felt like they were still at the start. Ultimately, it was the last 100 pages again! were all the action and excitement was. However the ending - I hated. After all they and everyone else readers went through to have that as their happily ever after - was disappointing for me. After the thousands of years Luce and Daniel went through that's the way it ended? That's just sad. Even the ending for the other characters just... depressed me, because they just faded into the background and were lost. It was pointless to have even included them in the end. I did like Luce in this more than the others. I felt at times Daniel had changed and was a completely new character but I liked him in this book the most. My bigger issue is the whole Cam thing. I didn't get how or why Luce started to love him. Like when did that happen ? Because he's hardly been around these past few books for her to even know him. And Cam had changed in this book, he was nicer but I just didn't get why he went from wanting to kill her, then helping her, then actually killing her but it wasn't her and then he's helping her again. But the worst thing is, at the end when someone mentions where's Cam and theres no reply and then the conversation moves on. Why mention him and then add nothing more. I'd like to know what happened to Cam! He was introduced as a second love interest, then as an enemy, then as a helper and then as a love interest again but he wasn't fully used to his potential. He could have been a far more interesting character - which would have made the books far more interesting to read. We still know very little about him in the end, so really was he a necessary character that needed to be written into this series. No. Also, when I finished the book I felt sorry for Lucifer. Which may seem strange and I don't like feeling sorry for him, but I think it's because he stopped his plan which I didn't get because he didn't even put up a fight, he just stopped because the throne said so ? Which was weird and in the end he got nothing. He suffered the same, if not more than Daniel by not being with Luce , because she was in love with Daniel and not him. He loved her too, even if she didn't love him the same way back, and for him to just walk away - that was an unsatisfactory ending. But he does come back in the end with the coin flipping thing, which made no sense at all - what did it mean ? It's not explained so was it necessary ? I presume he was checking up on her and that be probably still loves her but he just lets her walk away - to me that makes no sense. I feel like we need a complete history guide for the full story on all the characters because nothing was ever fully explained. The penultimate chapter started off so well and exciting and then just ended so poorly. I was so upset and I didn't think it could any worse and then it did. That was just so disappointing because the potential was there and it wasn't used. For Luce and Daniel to end up as human was predictable and not original at all. What would have been different is if the throne had let them back into heaven and allowed love to come before everything else because is that really a bad thing , along with the other fallen angels, even those who switched over to the other side that wanted to go back to heaven because they deserved to be rewarded as well. That would have been a different ending and made everything they went through worthwhile. Instead they have to suffer through other 17 years or so before they meet again - which was a really pathetic first encounter. So, I finished this book feeling unsatisfied. The hope near the end was taken away, leaving a sorry excuse of an end. P.S I can't imagine this series being made into films or a tv series unless it is heavily edited and re written. P.P.S. I still don't understand why the girls on the covers have long hair unless they are Luce from the past. It feels like they were just chosen because they look pretty.

I got this as an audiobook, so I'll just mention that the narrator was great. The character's were not as diverse as some other narrators, but in general his voice was uniquely smooth and raspy which lent a mysterious edge to the atmosphere, and he clearly rehearsed the part very well. Overall this was a fun, short read. I was a little nervous it would be Twilight-esque, but it's not at all. I suppose the high school characters act like what you may have thought Twilight MIGHT be like, when you first heard about it and were halfway willing to give it a chance. Young and impulsive and flirty and nervous. Not obsessive and melodramatic. Friendship is the spotlight here, romance just an unavoidable possibility. The supernatural level is a bit all over the place. At first it seems like a rare but established thing. Then all of the sudden it's very much all over the place in a big way. Yet the characters mostly accept these things in stride, which kind of took me out of it. I would not stop talking about some of the discoveries they came across! Then again, Gansey's living situation for a teenager endlessly rich and independent--apparently travelling the world on his whim by age 16 while still attending schools is probably more out-of-this-world than anything they come across. The protagonists' ultimate goal, and the antagonist in general, are not adequately fleshed out by the end. And the ending was quite abrupt because of these things. Even so, I rate this at least a 3.5. It never felt like a chore, and I wasn't rolling my eyes at characters or screaming at them or cringing. I had a lot of fun and I feel like I got to know the gang. I'd definitely pick the sequel, especially with the same narrator.

Meh. A Little Wanting Song is told from alternating points of view. There is sixteen year old Charlie, a socially awkward, sensitive, musically talented girl with few friends. And there is also Rose, a sixteen year old, socially awkward, mean girl who is also quite interested in science and has few friends. Do they sound a little similar here? They do in the book, too. Their voices aren't that different from each other. This book relies heavily on dialogue between not just Charlie and Rose, but also their friends Dave and Luke, as well as Charlie's dad, granddad, and the ghost voices of Charlie's mom and gran. It might have worked better had this story only been from Charlie's point of view, or displayed less dialogue. But as it is written, all of these unique characters came out sounding so very much alike. The plot here had little surprises. Read the synopsis, what do you think is going to end up happening? It happens. Happily ever afters all around, hooray! Between the undistinguishable characters and the obvious plot, A Little Wanting Song is missing that Aussie magic. This story had potential, but as it is, it doesn't really bring anything new to YA lit.

Yep you heard me. "She's been trying to potty train them for weeks now, but they refuse to be tamed. Essie and Libby were bribed with sticker charts and new toys, which was good for my parents' diaper budget. I just hope it doesn't mean they'll grow up to be slutty girls who give it away to any cute boys who buy them dinner." I almost set the book down right then and there. Not to mention that Eva is a complete snob with her high and mighty attitude. It's no surprise that she only has one friend. Though in one little snippet this is what she says about her best friend "I only have so much sympathy for girls who could find a boyfriend if they wanted to, but instead keep liking unattainable guys above their social station." Yikes! I wouldn't want her as my best friend! So to be honest, I was sending all these terrible quotes to my friend as I read. So wait, does this mean that she is in fact "like most girls"? So sorry to be so harsh, this attitude is just not acceptable, and I'm hoping that the author grows in her views of acceptance and friendship as she continues her career.

Jael is tired of moving around so often. Every time she gets settled in one Catholic school her father whisks them away to yet another, in another out-of-the-way place. Jael understands, really. After all, the demon Baliel has been hunting her since before she was born. He hates halfbreeds, and he really hated Jael's demon mother, so if he finds Jael he'll kill her. But Jael's uncle, Dagon, believes that Jael may have the untapped potential to destroy Baliel and bring back the era of the gods. If, that is, Jael can learn to harness her power before Baliel destroys her and everything that she loves. I found this novel difficult to read. The omniscient narrative created an emotional barrier, keeping me from truly caring about Jael and her worries. The dialog was also problematic, sometimes spot-on teen and other times rather stilted and dryly academic. The flashback scenes of the relationship between Jael's parents was much more touching and realistic. The story has potential, though. Many aspects of the plot are unique and original, which can be difficult to find in today's teen lit. And somewhere around the last third of the novel it began to really catch my interest, though it was primarily the secondary characters who sparked my interest. Hopefully any sequel will develop Jael to the same level. Finally, as with many series openers, the climax wrapped up very easily, belying the drama of the buildup and the worries of Jael and those around her. The book will move because of the plot description, but readers will need to be determined to keep reading. This review refers to the NetGalley digital advanced readers version of the novel.

Lauren Oliver took a risk when changing writing styles from Delirium to Pandemonium and then again in Requiem. The first book was all from Lenas point of view. Things were shook up when the second book used the past and present in equal parts to tell the story. Finally in this third and final book in the series things changed again when we got to read the story from both Lenas point of view and Hanas. Changing writing styles like this can be risky but surprisingly it worked. Not only was it done well but if anything I think the way these books were written enhanced the story using the best possible tools available to Instil emotion and connection. When I started Requiem I was again shocked and unsure. I found my self however drawn in within a few pages and unable to put this book down. If I have anything to criticise on it would be the ending. I understand the message and concept Lauren was trying to portray in the ending. Turning the meaning of the book into a metaphor to connect with our lives. I however don't think this was needed. As a reader I would have preferred more of an ending with wrapped up characters and relationships than a lesson. That being said I truly loved this book and will definitely be reading more of Lauren Oliver's books as, in my opinion, she has established herself as a fantastic writer.

I received this book from the publisher in exchange for an honest review I had a LOT of issues with this book. Most of which stem from people's reviews giving me an entirely wrong idea of what this book would be. Let me start out by saying that this is not a 100 body positive book. Yes the main character is plus size. Yes she enters a beauty pageant to show everyone that bigger girls can be and are beautiful. But she also body-shames EVERYONE she comes across, from the other fat girl in her class whom she makes fun of, the skinny girls who are friends with her best friend also skinny whom she calls "twiggy-bitches", to one point where she starts talking about the worst features of the guy she fancies. I can't remember it exactly but she does something like say how nice he his but then deliberately tries to find a flaw and points out his nose is too big or something not to him but like an internal monologue . Like sorry? How is that body positive? I hated the main character. Mostly for the reason above. I was going to rate it 1 star as it just did not live up to expectations. But then I realised that the book doesn't state to be 100 body-shaming free. The reviewers did. Once I got over that and told myself to forget what I thought this book would be and just take it as it is it got better. It's definitely overhyped but it wasn't awful. But please, if you get a book for review, absolutely do not lie or hold back your real thoughts. A publisher won't refuse to ever send you another proof because you HATED that one book one time. Reviews are there to encourage people to read a book or give something a shot, if they go into it believing it's a masterpiece because all the reviewers upped it, they may never read that author again. If they go into it knowing half the reviewers hated it, they won't have high hopes and may be more inclined to try the authors other stuff. Everyone has different opinions. I didn't like this book but felt it was worthy of two stars but gave it three as my judgement was impaired because of anger at feeling betrayed by reviews. Some people would think I've done this book and injustice by only giving it three. I've just recently bought Julie's new book 'Side Effects May Vary'. We'll see how that goes!

First of all 'More Happy Than Not' is a highly deceiving title, there is about 1 happiness in this young adult novel that includes suicides, homicides and several attempts at both I suppose than on the title's optimistic note, there wasn't any rape? . IDEK where to begin, I do see the attraction and it's highly readable with its rather circular structure even if it's on the clumsier side of narrative tricks For a real mindblowing take on subjectivity unreliable narrators that destabilize the story itself go for Justine Larbalestier's 'Liar' BUT the ending was just tacked on, as if the author's houses of cards had started to crumble and he decided to follow everything to the worst possible conclusion for the hell of it metanarratively one of the character's comments on how ridiculously unfortunate the main character is, but this, of course, does not make it any more believable or meaningful. Life sucks, sure, but in fiction suckage has to mean something, I do NOT need to read any books to know life is unfair and people unlucky, trapped in situations in which they have very little control or choice and in which out of desperation they will do really dumb things that will have even worse consequences. There's some stylistic problems, too, like the protagonist's tendency towards grandiloquent language that makes one feel like the author lost control of the character's voice for a moment or two the kid who's super into comic books and running around in the park probably doesn't have any reason to know what 'meta' is, for eg., although feel free to correct me! . The repetition phrase 'no homo' was frankly irritating, although the point that it was increasingly meaningless was interesting even if I'm not all that sure it was intended. Perhaps yes, considering the MC points out that he can't no longer say if he admits he has guyliker feelings . The 'guyliker' label was sweet and interesting and I could almost buy two creative teens would come up with it, even. I also enjoyed the novelty of a character going 'I know HE is gay. Poor guy, I hope nobody gives him a hard time" in a projection so obviously denial that it was both sweet and beliavable... until 2 pages later Aaron claims 'he cannot no longer deny the truth about himself.' The transition was so sudden I went back to check I hadn't skipped a few pages by accident. I finished this book feeling truly horrible, not like I wanted to have a good cry either which I did but like I wanted to throw up. A similar effect to watching those films where hundreds of dolphins are violently murdered for sport. I did care for the main character and I liked the cast, even if I found the mum and brother quite bland and uninvolved for all they claimed to care. But I truly really did not see the point the story was meant to make at all. Well written, but honestly, from my heart, hate it.

What happens when the cameras stop rolling? Justine has lived her life in front of the camera since the age of six, signed up, along with five other kids to participate in a series of documentaries that would follow her life in installments until the age of twenty one. Six year old Justine was a natural in front of the camera. At eleven, her quick tongue and edgy style made her the break-out star of the movies. While centering the lives of three young girls growing up in Queens Jacqueline Woodson weaves in Tupac's story as way to look outward at the larger picture. She writes about wrongful imprisonment, gay identity, police presence in black communities and about the deepest parts of relationship with such grace and skill it will break your heart open. She writes edges around what has no words so that it has a space to exist, so it can be contained the way a hug can contain the pain so it does not engulf you. She writes about the deep knowing of childhood, something we can easily forget as adults. She reminds us that we have been learning these lessons all of our lives loneliness, loss, friendship, change, what is left when someone has gone. Maybe we will never make sense of them, but they are our shared human history, part of the thread connecting us all. "You know a lot of other kids?" The narrator asks D on their first meeting. "Not really..... I meet a lot of kids, but I don't know a lot of kids." D is about to leave and Neeka says "The trees'll be waiting for you....You got a rope?" "Well next time you come bring it, all right?" In just a few sentences Woodson tells us with such nuance how easily we can be lost. How easily we can be found.

Title Outcast Author Aileen Fish Rating 2 5 Warning review might contain slight spoilers. First off, let me start with the synopsis copied from Goodreads "When the world collapses, the only person who comes looking for Niki Mathers is the loser who made fun of her in high school. JC Phillips saves her life, so she can't really tell him to get lost. And he is keeping her from being alone at the end of the world... JC will never forgive himself for choices he made the night before the earthquake. Rescuing the girl he's been crushing on for the past year doesn't bring atonement. Maybe making the world safe for Niki will take away his guilt. The world they know is dying. All they want is to find their place in it before it does." Now, let me write my own version of the synopsis this Young Adult novel begins when Niki's apartment crumbles after a quake and she is immediately found by JC Philips. Within the next few chapters she switches between chewing him out and kissing him while they stumble from one place to another, trying to find stability in an apocalyptic world. Thankfully, they each develop supernatural powers in this terrible time to help them through the crisis. I think what ticked me off was how the book's synopsis led me away from what the book actually was. If I had known that this book had visions of dead people, aliens from other planets, and a protagonist and two supporting characters with suddenly-developed superpowers, then I wouldn't have picked it up. The synopsis is literally the first chapter or two of the entire novel. I expected a lot of angst and struggle and a slow progression of love, if you will... But it all came too abruptly for my taste. Even the relationship was rushed, developing all of a sudden and becoming very emotionally charged much too rapidly. However, I found the concept of Aileen Fish's end of the world really nice. It's the book's saving grace. I appreciated that it wasn't, all of a sudden, the total end of the world. The synopsis seems to imply that Niki and JC are alone in the world, but what the synopsis means is that their family is not with them I won't spoil anything here! . They are followed by Antwon, a friend of JC's, and there are many refugees and survivors out there, so don't expect a "Niki and JC against the elements" type of novel. I liked that the authorities and stores got together and helped the survivors - there isn't as much crime and extreme panic as your typical apocalypse novel. I absolutely loved the part where JC and Niki work in the refugee camp. That was well-thought of and very realistic, which counters the fantasy feeling of perpetual earthquakes and creates a lovely balance for the middle part of the book. A big problem in the novel is the utter lack of time management. At one point, a character claims that electricity should've been brought back months ago, and my reading stopped completely. To me, all these had happened within the span of a few days, a month at most... I wish the author had worked a bit more to create a timeline of events in her prose so the readers could follow along. JC and Niki were fine characters. I really liked JC Niki was average. I have nothing great to say or nothing bad to say. I was ready to move on from them at the end of the book I'm not really interested in knowing what happens after the strangeness of the last few chapters. The book does foreshadow that conclusion, but it wasn't an ending I would've chosen for it at all. To be honest, unless the book especially the synopsis! goes under revision, I wouldn't recommend this book. I doubt I'll keep reading into the series. Overall, it wasn't a terrible story, but the above reasons just made it forgettable to me. I would like to thank Aspendawn Books, as well as Netgalley, for the free copy of this novel in exchange for an honest review.

In the Labyrinth, we had a saying keep silent, keep still, keep safe. In a city of walls and secrets, where only one man is supposed to possess magic, seventeen year-old Kai struggles to keep hidden her own secret--she can manipulate the threads of time. When Kai was eight, she was found by Reev on the riverbank, and her "brother" has taken care of her ever since. Kai doesn't know where her ability comes from--or where she came from. All that matters is that she and Reev stay together, and maybe one day move out of the freight container they call home, away from the metal walls of the Labyrinth. Kai's only friend is Avan, the shopkeeper's son with the scandalous reputation that both frightens and intrigues her. Then Reev disappears. When keeping silent and safe means losing him forever, Kai vows to do what ever it takes to find him. She will leave the only homes she's ever known and risk getting caught up in a revolution centuries in the making. But to save Reev, Kai must unravel the threads of her past and face shocking truths about her brother, her friendship with Avan, and her unique power. I'm not really sure why so many people are asking why this doesn't have any Greek Mythology save for the Labyrinth. You do know that labyrinth is essentially another way to say maze, right? Which I think is an adequate description of Kai's home a bunch of freight containers laid out in such a way that could be confusing if you don't know your path. I do have to say that this book kind of pulled me in multiple directions. I wavered between being slightly disconnected from everything and wanting to devour the pages and see what happened next. The world that Kai inhabits seems like it could be intriguing, but I could have done with a little more description. There were times when I felt like I didn't really know what was going on how things were supposed to be. I did like who the Infinite all turned out to be. That was interesting and they all had their own little quirks. I really like Irra, and I can stand Kalla based on what happens here, I'm thinking she's going to have a bigger role to come. I'm hoping she can grow on me . I felt like Kronos was a big jerk, and Ninu just struck me as a spoiled child. That being said, I'm interested to meet the rest of the Infinite to see if they all have just as varied personalities. Kai was a breath of fresh air in the YAheroine mix that is books today. Yes, at the beginning, I was sort of leaning towards seeing her as just kind of there, but as the story went on, she really grew on me. I liked that she could stand up for herself and willingly defended herself and she was determined to find Reev no matter what. Although there were a couple times when she started to get a little whiny and I was worried I was going to want someone to smack her. Luckily, she turned that thought process around quickly so I didn't want to smack her. At least for being whiny. I did want to smack her a couple times after her interactions with Avan. Speaking of which...Avan was totally worthy as a book boyfriend!! Completely swoony! The way he so readily agreed to going with Kai made me slightly suspicious of him to be honest. However I was not expecting the curve ball that I got. Plus, I'm not really sure why Kronos sped up his time...technically Avan didn't tell her. At least not on his own. Kronos spilled the beans and left Avan to pick them up. It's not completely fair for him to kill Avan at that point. Wasn't there some way for him to just make it so that going forward his time was normal? I'm also a little worried about his ending. Something tells me that the road for he and Kai is going to be a rough one... I wanted to like Reev. And what we got of Reev, I really liked except for him playing Kai and then turning around and trying to kill her. However, that I blame on Ninu . I mean, it's clear he cares for Kai and will do whatever he has to in order to keep her safe without even knowing exactly why . I just felt that he wasn't there enough for me to really care one way or the other. I liked learning a little about his past and how he ended up finding Kai by the river. Hopefully there's a little more of him to come. The secondary characters were awesome. Mason was great, although I feel bad for him because I don't think he's going to get who he wants. I hope that Grene and Tariza come to help Kai, something tells me they could be a great help.

POSSIBLE SPOILERS but maybe not too bad "The world seems so clean if you only look up." Wither. Chapter 25, page 333. To give the set up of the story, in an effort to create a world without illness by altering genetics but this meddling causes people's life span to shorten drastically, women die at 20 and men at 25. So, of course, world goes awry. There are many more orphans, girls get kidnapped and or married off at ridiculously young ages, and marriages are usually polygamous. So I'll go head and say the shock factor of teenaged sister-wives really got me when I first started reading Wither. I mean, really? Ew. But I kept reading because I had heard good things about the book. The main character is Rhine Ellery, age sixteen. At first, I didn't really understand her and motives but the author did a good job of giving me just enough to keep me intrigued at integral moments. I also felt it was a sign of good story telling that in the beginning I hated Governor Linden but by the end I understood he was a victim as well, though not to the same extent. I was almost feeling sorry for him, almost. I will say that I liked the way the book ended. I knew Wither is part of a series. but yet DeStefano was able to conclude the book where I felt satisfied and also wanting more. Which is good for me because book two Fever came out earlier this year and the front cover of book three Sever was revealed earlier this week and the book comes out February 2013. My final thoughts I give the book a 4 5 stars because I reserve 5 stars for life changing reads. I really liked the story Wither provided. It is considered YA young adult but because of some of the overtones I'd recommend this book to older teens adults but I would definitely recommend it to those interested in this dystopian type genre.

If people didn't act like this book was the Book to End All Good Books, maybe I would give it three stars. So, there you go. The hype ruined it. Plus some other questionable stuff! One of those is Tris. It sounds horrible, doesn't it? Tris is this hardcore heroine that is supposed to be the epitome of feminism. Not. She's rude and brash especially in the second book and her mind revolves around one thing Four. From the moment she meets him, that's all. That's actually another problem I have, but more on that later. The things that Tris said were so arrogant. She could have never been Abnegation, thank God she switched! I mean, listen to this comment she made regarding a "strong looking" boy crying I should comfort him--I should want to comfort him, because I was raised that way. Instead I feel disgust. Someone who looks so strong shouldn't act so weak. Hey, Tris. Remember two seconds ago when you were complaining that people underestimate you because a you're a girl and b you're small and c you're a Stiff? Why are you judging this guy off of looks? Makes you sound like a hypocrite. The romance between Tris and Four is just a waste of time. It can be predicted from the minute they lay eyes on one another. The chemistry is there immediately and in the worst way possible. It's...insta-love. Shudders. Some of the time I thought they were good for each other in the way that they helped each other through their fears and problems but for the most part I can only remember how they were in Insurgent absolutely atrocious. I don't think I felt warm because of them once in that book. They were fighting constantly and were always breaking each other's promises. If this book had better characters and didn't spend as much time building this supposedly "swoon-worthy" couple, this book could actual be brilliant. I mean, the idea in itself is sort of ingenious. If you ignore the fact that Roth pulled ideas from every single dystopian out there at the time. It deals with factions, and I just realized this today the factions kind of resemble our political parties. The Abnegation Tris' original faction is all for helping the factionless the lower class . However, the Euridite is angry because the Abnegation are wasting supplies and money on these people that don't contribute to society in the way that Euridite so desires. Sound similar? That's why I'm torn between giving this two or three stars. There's also just a lot of plot holes and unanswered questions that I don't think even get answered in the rest of the series. All books have them, especially books like dystopians and high fantasy, but some of the things that happened in this just didn't add up. The world felt very high-technology but then at the same time low-technology. Events contradicted themselves, and it was hard for me to easily picture this world in my mind. So there you have it. A lot of people have asked me why Divergent is one of those series that I just didn't really like. Here it is. I will continue the series but if I recall correctly, it's a downhill slope from here.

I'm not sure I have ever felt so conflicted over what to say about a book. I wanted to love The Raven Boys so much, but it just fell short for me. I didn't hate it, but I didn't love it either. I kept waiting for it to pick up for me and it just didn't until about 70 through, and unfortunately that's a long way into a book. I will say the writing was done very well, which is what kept me going. The concept too of psychics and "treasuring hunting" I guess you could call it peeked my interest, but unfortunately the story just lacked what I was looking for. I have to say my two favorite characters were the ones who I think weren't intended to be the front and foremost, and those were Ronan and Noah. Noah was broken, and adorable and funny and my heart just ached for him. Then, Ronan... I love his fierceness, how he's straight up with everyone, and yet he has secrets of his own and I just wanted to know them. With Gansey and Blue, I wanted so much more from them and unfortunately I just didn't get what I was looking for. Finally Adam... Adam was just Adam to me. I felt for him and wanted to hug him and then other times I wanted to kick him. I absolutely loved everything about Maggie Stiefvater's Shiver series, so many people raved no pun intended over The Raven Boys, and I admit the synopsis sounded so darn interesting, but the story just didn't do it for me. I just kept hoping it would pick up but it didn't until the very end and even then I found myself slightly confused. Unfortunately, and this is just my opinion, I feel like the story spent too much in a back story then actual action. Please, please remember this is just how I felt about the book. It in no way means I think it's a terrible book, because so many people did love it. The story just didn't peek my interest and I always want to be honest in my reviews. With that being said, I'm not sure I'll pick up the second book, but you never know! Originally posted at Shortie Says
