Review I don't like bashing books unless they're really bad and I can't form anything that I can say without either sounding overly offensive or sarcastic. So the rant goes in. I tried really hard with this book. I really really did. I first tried it one day and at some point, I got so fed up with it that I chucked it into my bag and didn't look at it for weeks. Then I fished it out and tried to pick up where I left off yes I have good memory I could remember . And again I stopped. And I gave it one. Last. Try. And right now it's lying at the foot of my bed so that I won't tear the spine in half. I mean, the premise of it was simple enough. A girl with poisonous touch, meets guy, is manipulated by other guy, runs away with first guy, falls in love, all that. Simple. And Tahereh Mafi did try to make the writing style different, by blending the raw voice from Chaos Walking with the typical YA novel first person commentary. Great. And the world building was typical YA dystopia--violent, weird and more than a bit unnecessary. Let's elaborate on that, shall we? So this will be a walkthrough of the plot until I threw the book out. The plot was simple. I mean, a lot of books get away with simple plots. It's fine. The idea of a girl having poisonous touch is fine. I mean, it's biologically possible. But the whole "rush of exhilaration" thing doesn't make sense. Like scientifically. That was just a more than slightly lame plot point to add more of that angsty teenage conflict. And then, boom. Out of nowhere, we get our lovely hot guy Adam, joining Juliette in her cell. After some predictable banter and "hate", the warm up to each other. And then BAM Juliette's taken from her cell, Adam's supposedly evil and she's being controlled by superhot other guy, Warner. I'll take a minute to praise Tahereh Mafi for being creative with Warner. it's not all the time that our "other" guy is totally screamingly evil. That was pretty original. slow claps His evil plots were impressive and pretty well thought out. Okay, back to my rant. Turns out Adam isn't evil at all, but instead is totally good and oh, did I mention? He's in love with Juliette. Apparently had a crush on her for years before she was thrown in a jail cell. And he's the only one who can touch her without getting hurt. Wonderful. And so the hot makeout scenes continue. Love, love, love, angst, angst, angst, but Warner's evil plots in between, displaying Juliette's powers while she spends the whole time whining about it and trying to "rebel". And then BAM she decide's she's in love with Adam and they run away together. Far too easy, if you ask me. And turns out, Warner can touch her too. And they run away to Adam's house and mushymushymushy and he has a brother who's perfect and adorable and they pass their lives perfectly and wonderfully and- And I slam the book shut. And there it lies. At the foot of my bed. Okay, I'm going to review the main characters here Juliette Well excuuuse me, but I didn't know that being locked in a cell with no sunlight for a few years with practically no food would leave you looking like a perfect beautiful supermodel. I should try that sometime. And I know you've been scorned and treated badly your whole life, but you shouldn't be whining and complaining and moping all the time. slams head in frustration . And if hot guy who likes you tells you that there are no cameras in the bathroom and brings you in there, what the hell?! What the hell would make you think that he's going to rape you? When did you even learn what rape is? And I'm sorry, making out a few times in a shower isn't love. It's called hormones. And I know you haven't had eye candy for a while, but you don't have to oogle every single guy that you see. Seriously. The psychopath who's forcing himself on you and using you to strike fear in people, no matter how handsome, is not oogling material. Just no. Adam Dear Adam, you have no chemistry with Juliette whatsoever. Your declaration of love was sappy and completely ridiculous, and you really didn't have any time to actually fall in love with her. Also, what made you think that escaping was a good idea? Really? And stop angsting. Just. Stop. Warner You redeem this book. You're different from other guy characters. You might be sick, sadistic and psychopathic but you make me happy. Last thing I feel the need to comment on is the writing style. Tahereh Mafi tries to mix it up by using Juliette's internal dialogue, by cancelling words and writing in thoughts. But please, be consistent. It seems to randomly switch between Bella Swan-style commentary and Todd Hewitt's broken thoughts. It was distracting and annoying. Stoppit. So yeah. I might try and finish this sometime. Sometime. Grade C Go away, Juliette.

My copy was provided by Netgalley. Cora lives with an overprotective dad who doesn't leave her alone because her mother disappeared in Ireland. Now Cora is forbidden from going to Ireland and she doesn't know why. She has this whole heritage she doesn't know about and isn't allowed to experience. If she knew the legends of her native country, she might learn what the colors she sees around people mean. Cora could learn what the silver color is that only surrounds herself. When Finn comes to town, originally from Ireland, Cora might find the answers to her numerous questions. Yet Cora's father forbids Cora from seeing Finn and Finn's mother banishes Cora back to Ireland. To figure out the answers, Cora travels to Ireland to finally unlock the secrets, but some secrets are meant to be hidden. This book moved very quickly. I got caught in the story the instant I started reading it and I couldn't stop until I finished it. The chapters were short and filled with action. Even some of the boring moments were still kinda entertaining and went by pretty fast. There were some awesome one-liners that made me want to laugh out loud. I enjoyed Cora's humor and how this book wasn't heavy with the plot. The twists and turns in this story really made it come to life. There wasn't a point where you could just rest your eyes. You just had to keep reading to know what happens next, to know what Cora discovers that will change her whole life forever. Cora seemed real and relatable. She knew she was different, just like everyone else in the world. She didn't like her looks which makes her relatable to teenage girls. There's always something wrong with our looks, no matter how insignificant it is. Teenage girls will love the magic, the insta-love, and the beautiful writing. What I didn't like was how this book is not really original. I mean, the whole concept with auras and Ireland is definitely original, but the forbidden romance and the insta-love happens all the times in books. In most young adult novels, the main female is different and she finds a guy that knows about her. And just like other books, Scintillate happened in the exact same way. Also, I did not like how deeply Cora fell in love with a guy she knows nothing about. She travels all the way to a different continent to be with the guy she loves and she's only in high school! This part didn't seem believable and I can't imagine a girl ever doing this for a guy, even if she is in "love". But this book was entertaining and fun. I definitely want to read the next book and learn what happens next with Cora.

Meg's a wild, rebellious girl who has panic attacks at being confined by as much as a seat belt. Her mother still cries over her and her father has washed his hands of her and her currently blue hair. She has just a few months left of high school to go and then she can escape the small town and move to the city to go to uni. And the one thing she's looking forward to before that can happen is the March Break trip to Mexico. Which is ruined by one night's stupid decision. Along with her pot-addled "boyfriend" Eric and two friends from school, Tiffany and Brian, Meg is arrested for trespassing on a train bridge - which killed two kids several years ago. While Eric's hot-shot lawyer father gets him off, the other three are made to spend the March Break week with the ambulance, fire brigade and police - and guess which one Meg gets. Not only does she have to spend five nights on the graveyard shift riding around in a cop car, but she has to spend them with the very same cop who arrested them John After. John with the "Matt Damon" body, who turns out to be nowhere near as old as Meg had assumed. He chose to stay in the town, to serve and protect and save teenagers from stupid choices, but Meg pushes him to question the things he abides by - and he pushes back. As they both confront each other the chemistry coalesces and thickens, and something new is forged. "Chemistry" is the Big Word for this novel. It has shovel-fuls of it. Meg is a spunky, smart, inherently vulnerable girl with a sharp, hard exterior. John is more complicated than he seems, and the character development is beautifully explored as layers are revealed and they both become very real in your mind. The plot is a simple premise to get these two together, and it has that small-town ring of truth to it it's the people who are complicated. Narrated by Meg, her voice has that same hard, spiky exterior behind which she hides her compassion and interest in others - you get to know her and yet she keeps you at a distance at the same time. It's John who breaks through that exterior, and him we follow as Meg learns to accept herself. Nothing's easy, of course, and the revelation one of two the last one at the end - while hinted at, or something you could guess - had a similar impact on me as it did on Meg. I have to draw your attention back to the romance and chemistry again. If you, like me, loved Twilight and similar books for the chemistry between the two main characters, and you'd like more of that intense thrill, then you absolutely have to read this. It's not the same, but it has that same quality that breathes off the page. Somewhere out there, John and Meg are living their lives. Sweet and charming, heart-warming and sexy, Going Too Far is a book to read in one sitting not just because it's a fast read, but because you won't want to put it down.

The book started off strong, but I lost interest pretty quickly. My two major problems with the book were that there was too much going on, and things happened too quickly. Too much going on... So New Orleans has been basically destroyed by a hurricane, and there's this post-apocalyptic thing going on. Fine. But wait, there's also all these paranormal creatures running around witches, vamps . Okay. THEN there's also some mythological creatures and gods goddesses. That's where the story lost me. It felt like the author had so many good ideas and ended up throwing them all together in this story. Using just one maybe two of those elements would have been fine, but putting them all together resulted in a mish-mash that didn't work for me. Things happened too quickly... There's a bit of insta-love happening here, with Ari and Sebastian. Less than 24 hours after they've met and after only a few hours of hanging out they're making out and Ari's thinking how crazy she is about him. Sebastian apparently reciprocates these feelings, since he chooses to stay with Ari rather than his father who has been missing for ten years. Definitely not the most believable moment in the story. Then there's the part where Ari walks into what she knows is probably a trap to rescue her "friends" who she's known for, oh, about 1.5 days. And she's developing all these motherly feelings for one of the kids, and buying them presents. I just couldn't buy into all of that happening so quickly. I knew from the first chapter what Ari's deal was in terms of being a Medusa-like creature...the whole thing about her crazy hair and eyes, and her mother thinking she had snakes trying to claw their way out of her hair were really, really obvious signs to me . It took a bit of the mystery out of it for me, and I was surprised that the author made it so easy to figure out. Look, the book isn't horrible. It's not poorly written. It just wasn't for me, and I didn't enjoy it.

It is not a book for everyone, but I feel like it can find a very strong, appreciative audience. Full review On a whole, mermaids don't seem to get a lot of attention in the YA genre. You definitely have notable books like Of Poseidon and Lost Voices by Sarah Porter, but it just seems like these books don't necessarily get the attention that books with angels vampires etc. seem to get. Also, for reference's sake, here's a list of 80-something odd YA books featuring mermaids http www.goodreads.com list show 78... So when I realized that Bennett Madison's September Girls would be featuring the elusive mermaids, knew it was something I had to check out. Plot overview After his mom leaves to find herself, Sam's father has a mid-life crisis, and decides to take him and his brother off to vacation in North Carolina. Not long after they arrive, Sam realizes there's something extremely odd about the town they're holed up in. Not only does time seem to slow down, all of the girls that Sam encounters are extremely beautiful. And more surprising yet, they all seem to want him. Sam's intrigued by all of the girls that he encounters, but he's especially intrigue by DeeDee. She's unlike anyone he's ever met, and he feels an immediate connection to her. However, she pulls away after meeting him, and it's up to him to figure out why... Full review Ok. I'm going to state outright that I liked this book, but it wasn't for me. I definitely get what Bennett Madison was trying to accomplish when writing this book, but neither the plotline nor the writing style appealed to me. However, I think that there are people this book will appeal to, and I hope that my review helps point them in the right direction. Things that worked Characterization. Madison does an excellent job of capturing Sam's feeling of restlessness and confusion, just as he's on the cusp of adulthood. I think the fact that he knows he's looking for something - but he isn't quite sure what! - is something that anyone can relate to. Sam's relationship with his brother and his parents are also very realistic. They're rude to each other. They have quirks. Sam's brother isn't shy about giving him a hard time, but he's also the first to step up to protect his brother as well. Ultimately, the family dynamics were extremely screwed up, but also one of my favorite parts to read. The mythology I'll be honest I still don't think I fully understand the mythology of the Girls. This may have to do with the fact that I skimmed a couple of their chapters . However, I liked the idea that they essentially are the ocean, and have to mold themselves to fit into their new bodies. It's incredibly unique, and unlike most of the mythological sea creature stories out there. The setting. It feels like most of the YA books I read these days tend to take place in larger cities, so I appreciated the fact that this book took place in North Carolina. Madison does an excellent job of describing the feeling of living in a small tourist town that's primarily driven by the summer season. The pacing. As other reviewers have mentioned - the book is very, very slow. Time does seem to blend together, but I liked this about the book. Madison definitely captures that feeling that summer should last forever. The writing. Madison is an indisputable pro at writing beautiful, long lyrical sentences which invoke imagery in feelings in creative, a-typical ways. Things that didn't work Showing vs. telling for Sam's character arc. We're told that Sam feels like he learned a lot from his experiences during that summer, and he feels changed. And while I agree that Sam's definitely gone through a lot, but I also feel like Bennett Madison never really shows us how Sam goes back into his real life being impacted by these changes, and whether they've changed his world view at all. I don't know - maybe that's the point. Maybe Madison's trying to show that sometimes, life experiences aren't always going to give you that big eureka moment. But if that's the case, it didn't come through very well for me. The POV chapters from the Girls. They were beautiful and well-written, but I felt like they suffered from the same showing vs. telling problem as Sam's character arc. We're given a lot of information about why they've arrived in this town, and how they're surviving, but it started to feel like a continuous info-dump by their third chapter. Sam being objectified. I wasn't the biggest fan of the fact that all of these gorgeous girls were throwing themselves at Sam, for a very specific reason. I felt like their decision to chase after seduce entice Sam, was Madison's way of incorporating what is basically every teenage boy's fantasy, and loosely disguising it as a plot point. The Girls. We're told that the Girls - including DeeDee - are gorgeous, unique ethereal creatures. And while they're physically attractive, I never got much of a personality from any of them. Instead, I tended to think of them as a collective - a la the Borg from Star Trek. Yes, I just outed myself as a giant Trekkie. While the collective nature of the Girls make sense in the context of the novel - especially once you get to know more about their origins - it doesn't necessarily make for compelling reading. It also makes it hard to get invested in DeeDee and Sam's relationship, especially when you barely know anything about her. I've written some pretty blunt criticisms of September Girls, but I feel the need to reiterate this is just my opinion. I didn't especially like the book, because I felt like it was more focused on imagery and an uncertain mythology, rather than a concrete character arc and developments. HOWEVER! I still believe that September Girls will find an appreciative audience. There are people who will appreciate the book's writing and plotting, and the unique love story that Madison was trying to tell. And who knows? Maybe after some time, I might give this book another try, and like it better myself. Final verdict Bennett Madison has written a lyrically beautiful love story, with very unusual mythology. While not everyone will like this book, I also think that it's still worth it for readers to give the book a try. Recommend for readers who enjoy reading books with complex, beautiful sentences, e.g. fans of The God of Small Things.

spoiler alert 5 5 My disease is as rare as it is famous. Basically, I'm allergic to the world. I don't leave my house, have not left my house in seventeen years. The only people I ever see are my mom and my nurse, Carla. But then one day, a moving truck arrives next door. I look out my window, and I see him. He's tall, lean and wearing all black--black T-shirt, black jeans, black sneakers, and a black knit cap that covers his hair completely. He catches me looking and stares at me. I stare right back. His name is Olly. Maybe we can't predict the future, but we can predict some things. For example, I am certainly going to fall in love with Olly. It's almost certainly going to be a disaster. ------------------------------------------- Okay, I want to make a quick announcement that because this was so heavily praised on booktube and because everyone was hyping this book up, I was not going to read it. But then I had to choose a book for the letter E in my group's Mega Month Challenge Hangman. I chose this one because why not? The reason why I stepped away from the hype was because I have been let down time and time again to books that are either mediocre or just flat out boring. To start things off, the cover is beautiful. Omg. I have the ebook and I'm definitely going to Barnes Noble to get myself the physical copy in order to highlight and mark all the quotes and the moments that made me SCREAM so if I ever let anyone else read it they can read along with me. D There were a few things in this book that won me over. How it was written. It was written beautifully and I could picture everything. From Olly's all black ensemble to the Bundt cake chronicles to Maddy's huge curly hair. It was amazing. Also, the fact that Maddy was a POC. The minute she established that to Olly, I was like, yup I need to finish this book. The characters were fucking complex. Excuse my French, but I love a book with good characters and these characters were damn good! Maddy was content with her life of being locked away until she met Olly and she wanted to explore and to see the world! I received a copy of the ARC at BEA 2014. The Jewel introduces us to a world where the wealthy elites have become so obsessed with the purity of their bloodlines that they are now unable to conceive their own children. To overcome this obstacle, they take children from the poorer areas and train them to be surrogates. Once she reaches puberty, each girl must submit to the testing or be executed. Those who pass the test are taken to containment facility where they are taught Auguries magic? best I can figure and various other talents. At age 16 they are sold at auction to the highest bidder and brought to the Jewel, the opulent inner circle, where they are paraded around like trophies and treated like pets. Our heroine is Violet, who is likeable enough. There is a sense of "chosen one" about her as she has scored the first perfect growth Augury score in decades. This uniqueness makes her desirable, and she is finally won by the Duchess of the Lake. Violet's life with the Duchess teeters back and forth -- sometimes the Duchess is violent cruel and sometimes she is kind, even attentive. But Violet does not see surrogacy as the honor the ruling class seems to think it is. All she wants is to be back at home with her family. It is hard to describe the process of world-building in The Jewel. On the one hand, we learn very little about what I presume is the Lone City seeing as how it's the name of the series for which this is the first book . As is my understanding, the city is laid out in a circle, and at the edge of the circle is a giant wall which holds back the ocean. Violet is from the outer rim of the city, called the Marsh. The Jewel is home to the affluent families and sits at the center. In addition to surrogates, we learn about companions -- who seem to all be good-looking boys forced into what amounts to a life of prostitution -- and ladies in waiting, some of whom are castrated men. What we see of the wealthy comes to us through the Duchess of the Lake and her interactions. Violet, as her surrogate, is nearly always at her side and manages to overhear several conversations that give us a glimpse of what kind of government exists in this world. We also learn that there is quite a lot about surrogacy that the surrogates are not told. There also seems to be some sort of resistence, which we learn about through Lucien. Lucien is a "lady" in waiting, servant to the Electress, and is resolved to secret Violet out of the Jewel before she becomes pregnant. Because this is a YA novel, there is a romance. It's in the description on the back of the book, and I was expecting it to happen much earlier than it did. Violet accidentally meets Ash, the boy who is to be the companion of the Duchess's niece, and immediately becomes infatuated with him. In true YA style, the insta-love is reciprocated. Violet and Ash have very few interactions before they are kissing, and not many more by the time they declare their love for each other. Because surrogates and companions are forbidden to form their own attachments, they must sneak around to see each other, because if they are discovered, Ash will be executed. I was much more interested in the world of The Jewel than the romance. Violet and Ash's relationship felt shoe-horned in, the obligatory star-crossed romance that must exist in a YA novel, and I was not particularly a fan of it. I like the idea, but I feel that Ash was introduced too late in the story to fully develop the relationship before the end of the book. The world, however, is fascinating. I was disgusted the entire way through, of course, because the idea of these teenagers being forced to give up their homes, their families, their names, their bodies, and even their lives in order to carry children for other people made me sick to my stomach. I was frustrated all the while, feeling nothing but hatred for these rich women who treat these girls like brood mares. I anxiously awaited for Lucien to show up, for news of the resistance. The political intrigue was extremely compelling. No one seems to have any sort of affection for anyone, not even parents for their own children. Granted, the only parent child interaction we see is the Duchess with her son, Garnet, and he is too unpredictable to be a valuable enough asset. Late in the novel, Violet wails at the Duchess about how love does not seem to exist in the Jewel. I am unsure how many books there are to be in this series but this is a YA series, so probably three , but I sincerely hope that the others focus on the politics and the world itself rather than the ridiculous romance. It was by far the more interesting of the two.

Waiting on the Sidelines was Ginger Scott's debut novel. I've read all of her recent books, and I thought it was time to go back to the beginning. I was not disappointed. Waiting on the Sidelines is quintessential Young Adult. If ever there was a book that would bring you back to the best and worst of high school, Waiting on the Sidelines is it. The title Waiting on the Sidelines captures not only the football theme, but it is also a reference to the heroine, Nolan Lennox. She is smart and athletic, but she is socially insecure. While she loves her close-knit family deeply, she feels her lower-middle class upbringing is a brand she wears identifying her as a target for the jabs and jokes of the cool, wealthy, and popular kids. Nolan's insecurities keep her on the sidelines, feeling like an outsider most of the time. Even though Waiting on the Sidelines is YA, there are some rather mature themes for this genre--underage drinking, sex just eluded to , and bullying. Scott handles these themes realistically. From the Nerds to the Jocks to the Queen Bees, Scott has nailed the high school social structure and common behaviors of the various groups. The angst and drama in this book know no bounds. The peaks and valleys of hormones, crushes, on-off romances, and mean-girl pranks kept my heart racing and my stomach in knots. I went through it all with Nolan and Reed. Their near-misses and false starts as well as the solid friends who bolstered them through their toughest trials made Waiting on the Sidelines an emotional read. Nolan and Reed's self-discovery, life lessons and first loves would be a great book club discussion material or could provide a meaningful start to a conversation with your own young adult. Waiting on the Sidelines is a little bit Friday Night Lights and a little bit My So Called Life. You'll pray for Nolan and Reed to make the right choices, you'll thank their great friends for their support, and you'll cheer when Nolan figures out that a happy ending sometimes means the girl gets self respect instead of the cute guy who doesn't always have her back. Most of all, you'll do a happy dance at having discovered indie-author Ginger Scott. Visit Book Junkie Reviews for more book recommendations https abookjunkiereviews.wordpress.com

Even though dystopian novels are everywhere right now - especially in the YA aisle - I have to admire the creativity of the authors when they are faced with the task of creating their own world. During the first few chapters, I wasn't a huge of the world Peterfreund created for Elliot - it was too rough, too harsh for me. When Elliot began to talk about her farming and her passion to create something to better those under her care, For the Darkness Shows the Stars changed from a Jane Austen retelling to a YA dystopian novel set in the South. I imagined huge old plantations, and that familiarity made me began to enjoy the book. As I kept reading, I liked that Peterfreund didn't struggle to put images in her readers' mind she gave the basic outlines and didn't keep reminding me that a certain character had blue eyes, another green. Instead, the setting focused on the differences between the classes, emphasizing not only what they didn't share, but what they had in common. Besides all that, I really want to know what that ship the Cloud Fleet made looks like. There were elements of the Reduction that confused me at first, and I almost didn't finish the novel because of them. I wish that Peterfreund had included information like that at the beginning, to help the confused readers like me fight thier way through the story. I had some issues with the differences between Posts and freed Posts. Those who were free wanted to shake free the shackles of their old life understandably but those who weren't didn't seem to mind. Maybe I missed a big chunk of the novel where it explains this. Kai and his younger companions had an element of pride about them that those working for Elliot didn't. Those characters had an element of loyalty. It was an interesting contrast. The story flowed fairly well for me, after some hiccups in the beginning. I felt that initially Elliot's farming nature was overemphasized, almost to the point of irritating me. I got it. After I passed that point, the rhythm of the story grew on me, and I enjoyed Peterfreund's fairly straightforward narration. The decision to keep the novel first person was good - I feel otherwise I would have been too confused, trying to decipher all of the emotions circling that particular group of characters. I will admit, I didn't particularly like Elliot initially. It probably bounces back to that narration hiccup, but she, like the story, grew on me. I had to admire her tenaciousness, especially when she finally discovered her own strength. I couldn't imagine being in the position she was - an old lost love returning, new people on her land, class barriers everywhere, and a girl trying to keep her family together after the loss of her mother. That's more than one person should have deal with in a lifetime, and Elliot handled it with class. I enjoyed reading her inner thoughts, which, if said aloud, wouldn't have been called classy, but I would have still admired her. There's some debate in the blog world on whether or not this book is too based on Jane Austen's Persuasion. I don't really want to enter that debate. Although there were some blatant references to the original inspiration, I enjoyed the story on its own. It's not Austen novel, by any means, but the tension between Elliot and Kai were enough to keep me up reading late at night when I had to work early in the morning. Their relationship had a little pride, miscommunication, and general stubbornness, all of which made it a really fun element of the novel. I liked the plot. It didn't give me a book hangover. It was well-written and thought out. I enjoyed the plot twists near the end, but I never quite had that feeling that everything would would not work out. If that emotion had been added somewhere into the story, I would have gobbled this book up like Thanksgiving turkey. Final Thoughts I liked For the Darkness Shows the Stars. It was deliciously dark, with a strong female lead and a intriguing romance. I felt it was a little predictable at times, but nonetheless, still an good story.

Like many reviewers here, the gorgeous cover pulled me in. I've had quite a few students say they kind of, sort of liked the book but that it was slow. Still, I had to read it. Personally, I enjoyed the book very much. The Society fascinated me and the energy and spirit of Cassia inspired me as well. The concept of choices and being led to believe that your life is ideal when you don't have to make them is curious. How many times have we all felt that way when we were overwhelmed and exasperated? Condie's use of that feeling to build a Society where you get exactly that is unique and well done. In the beginning, I was so upset with Casia's grandfather for planting the seed of doubt about the Society in her happy, young mind. What really makes him any different from the Society--manipulating her thoughts and feelings through suggestion? When you step back and look at the interactions between all the characters and Cassia, you begin to think about our own society--how "free" are we really? Are our thoughts and actions truly a result of free will, or are we all unknowingly "going gently"? The love triangle is compelling using a bit of the law of "bad boy" attraction that so many women understand . I haven't yet decided if I'm team Ky or team Xander. Well done Ally Condie. You have definitely made me think while entertaining me as well!!

The Girl of Fire and Thorns is an excellent fantasy adventure story. I say story, it reads more like an epic than it does your typical YA fiction tale. There is a historic Spanish backdrop to this tale which Carson details so intricately I found it very easy to place myself in the countries that she describes, both in terms of the landscape, the buildings, the clothes, the people and the food Oh the food!! . The main character is Elisa who, at the beginning of the story, begrudgingly finds herself being married off to the King of Joya d'Arena on her 16th birthday. Whilst her older sister is to ascend the throne in Orovalle, it is decreed that Elisa has been chosen to go into service. This is because of the appearance of the godstone, a living gem, which resides in her navel and which is given to her by god during her naming ceremony. Service we soon learn is a commitment to humanity and it is expected the Elisa will carry out an act in the future which will benefit mankind. It is also something that requires knowledge and courage and at the start of the story it becomes apparent that Elisa does not appear to have a great deal of the latter. Rather she sees herself as lazy, fat and useless in comparison to her sister. With her new husband by her side she arrives in Joya d'Arena to find out that her marriage is a secret and soon discovers that not everyone is as trustworthy as they first appear. As she tries to determine her purpose as bearer of the godstone she is kidnapped and suddenly finds herself immersed in a dangerous world where she as the bearer is coveted and where only she is able to save those caught up in a bitter war which threatens her country as well as those she loves. Magic, sorcery and good old fashioned battles all have their place in this book and they make for an exciting read! By the time I finished this book I felt as though I had gone on the journey with Elisa. I had seen her struggle with and beat her neuroses mainly to do with her weight and her lack of self worth and watched as her and her friends struggle in the war against the Inviernos. Her transformation through the book is wonderful to read and you find yourself cheering her on as she realises how strong she is. There are some fantastic characters in this book, most notably Alejandro, the husband who is not as strong as first thought Rosario, his son from his first marriage Cosme who becomes a good friend to Elisa, Humberto, Cosme's brother and Hector, Alejandro's personal guard. Each character is more complex than first appears and I love the way that their plotlines develop as well as they way they interact with Elisa, which isn't always pleasant. There is of course a dash of romance but this is by no means a romantic YA story, far from it. There are bigger plotlines that run through this book that make for a thrilling read and one I found hard to put down. The story is tied up quite nicely at the end of book one so you do feel a certain sense of closure when you reach the final page. I'll be interested to see where book two picks up. I now also have a soft spot for certain characters in this series and I do harbour hopes for a romance in the next book. Fingers crossed! Original review at http themidnightreaders.blogspot.co...

I don't know what happened with this book. I was hooked enough and I liked how the Marina and Em storylines tangled up, but after a point the story just fell through. For one, I didn't feel like there was much action going on, there were little scenes that were more intense, but the rest ended up being dull. As for the big twists I kept on waiting to happen... let's just say that if James killing himself in order not to become evil in the future was supposed to be one, I saw it coming a mile away and I wasn't impressed or shocked or anything. Another thing that made me lose interest were the characters and my complete lack of regard for them. I didn't dislike them per se, but I wasn't invested in them either. I feel like they weren't fleshed out enough for me to care for them, for example Em was supposed to have been tortured for months and yet the writing didn't manage to make me feel sorry or pretty much anything for her. It's just that, everyone is easily forgettable and in the end I didn't particularly care about whether they lived or died. And then there was that ending. I gather the author intended to write a sequel but then decided this would be a standalone. Well, that ending wasn't good enough for a standalone novel. Apart from the fact that the final confrontation was anticlimactic at best, the attempt at having sort of an open ending without giving any specifics felt like a trick poorly executed. I mean, I wasn't that big on how the Delirium series ended, but the open ending there felt right, whereas here it just felt like the book was incomplete. So, the book had a great idea behind it, but it just wasn't used to its full potential.

As a simple minded teenage girl with raging hormones, no real goals or ambition, who have just discovered that her life BELONGED to some boy, this is the book for you.

At first, I was incredibly skeptical of her validity, but by the end, there's nothing to question. Western views of Islam are challenged, too. There's a lot of good here. There's even this wonderful moment where characters are saying "Come to America. You can have everything there, everything you ever need," and others say no, they belong in Afghanistan. America can't give them what they truly want. But, the ending is so abrupt with no indication of any outcome be it positive or negative. Is there a sequel? It just... drops off. We know that everyone's decisions are very difficult, but come naturally. I just feel like there's something missing all around here.

I may be the only one in the world that does not love this series. Many people that I know keep telling me that this is a great series. This is really rare for me to find a female in fiction that I love. But slowly her character has went downhill. It really started in the last book, but in this book my love for her turned into hate. I just really hate her now. I wanted to slap her most for most of the book. I wanted her to shut up many times! And she also became really stupid in this book. Moroi were coming up injured, and Rose could not figure out what was going on. I don't understand why. It was very clear that Jesse and the other royals were fighting each other. They even told Rose that they had a group, but she still could not figure it out. It was actually painful to read Rose trying to figure it out. Dimitri - I don't love him, but I don't hate him either. I just like him. Lissa - And the award for the most annoying character goes to? LISSA DRAGOMIR! She killed me at the end! Not everything is about you, Lissa! Adrian - Same as Dimitri. Eddie - I love Eddie! Mason - I was heartbroken when Mason died in last book. I was happy to have his ghost in this book. Christian - My love! He is why I keep on reading. I must also comment on the writing in this book. Wow was it bad! I loved Richelle Mead's writing in the first two books, but this was just crap. I rolled my eyes many times when reading the book. I hope her writing goes back to the way that it was for the rest of the series. I also have to talk about all the typos in this book. I understand that it is not uncommon to have typos in a published book. I have read books with typos before. The book was written by a human, so of course there will be errors. But I couldn't help but wonder if anyone read this before it was published. There was some mistakes in the book that it is hard to believe that someone did not notice them. I think that I'm going to continue with this series. I made it halfway. Why stop now? I am sure that there will be at least a few boring parts in the next three books, and I can always skip the boring parts. So it should take me no time to read the next three!

rolls eyes Realistic fiction book about a smart, misunderstood teen named Garrett who is sent to a behavior modification boot camp by his parents for several months for having an affair with a teacher. For a YA book it's pretty violent stuff--details of the beatings, verbal abuse, and torture of the teenaged detainees were all throughout. It's obvious that the author did his research on these kinds of places, but it's like he took every horror story from every source he came across and put it in this book for shock value. I understand the point the author was trying to make but Garrett's experience seemed so overdone, almost to a point of making him a caricature. With the amount of mistreatment that Garrett received it was hard for me to believe he was still alive at the end, or that places this bad with staff this sadistic really do exist. Also..there was a lot of skipping in the narrative. A few days, a few weeks, a few months...all of it runs together and the time line of events was unclear. The ending was a bit of a shocker, and it was a stretch for me to believe that Garrett went from one extreme to the other within the literal span of a few pages. Unbelievable.

Make no mistake, this is a heart-wrenching story. But there are no extraneous characters in this story, and no weak plot points. Every character and every event is perfectly meaningful and necessary. "My attention is constantly homed in on her like I'm a compass and she's my North." - Holder You should definitely read Hopeless first because it is amazing story. With that being said, you will love Losing Hope if you are a fan of Hopeless because it is a passionate, fresh and lyrical story. Enjoy.

I started crying in the most unexpected part of this book, and upon analyzing my feelings on the matter, I can understand why I did, but so much of this book was incredibly sad, and incredibly provoking. Valerie and her boyfriend Nick are bullied, teased and picked on at school. Both seem to have pretty terrible home lives, although we find out more about Valerie. Her father in one particular scene screams that she had a perfect life and he can't understand why she did what she did, why she felt like she did. For me, that was the biggest moment of the book. It just proves to me how much her own father didn't understand her, and how he could think that fighting constantly with her mother was somehow normal and a healthy family unit. Yet he was out having an affair the whole time, a thing his family was clueless about! How he maintained his narrow view on the world just astounded me. The whole 'Hate list' seemed to me to be all too true to life. You hear about similar lists in similar situations. I think all people note people, and not children who are bullied wish something would happen so that the people hurting them stop and see what they're doing. Of course, most people leave it there and don't react like Nick did. If you look in my own teenage diary, you will see angry letters asking why people wouldn't leave me alone. Why do people pick on the stupidest things? For me, I was picked on because I always wore my hair out in a wild, just brushed look I thought was nice, but girls would trip me, threaten to 'bash' me, shriek 'Pixie!' any time I got near. I never got to the stage of mind Nick ended up in, but somehow, I can see in a small way why he did what he did. My situation ended abruptly I did the whole 'ignore it and it will go away' and the girls moved onto new targets. But it remains in my mind even now, five years after school, as one of the loneliest times of my life. They always, like with Valerie, picked a time like on the bus when I wasn't surrounded by friends. When I was with friends, I felt like an idiot for not defending myself. How could I be a fun, laughing person around them but not when alone? Reading about the battling feelings for Nick experienced by Valerie was another part of the book I felt made the story real. She had all the memories of a good Nick, a romantic boy and a friend. When someone does something 'bad' or 'evil' you can't just switch off all your good feelings or memories, and you shouldn't. The slow build up of understanding Nick takes time, and understanding Valerie just as long. I wish at some point, like the last assembly, she had said more about not wanting anyone dead. We the readers know that what she wrote was a way to vent against people who hurt her, but it seems like too many of the characters end the novel without this knowledge. Too many characters have loose ends, like her brother, and the boy Jeremy? Nick had been hanging around with. I guess my fingers just kept looking for pages that weren't there. I guess what I'm trying to say with this novel is I felt pieces of myself there, read bits of my life in the character's experiences. There was stuff there I'd never felt, situations I've never experienced, but this book draws you in and keeps you there. I think this book will be in my thoughts for a long time.

I absolutely adored 'The Scorpio Races', so there was no question about whether or not I would check out Maggie's new series. The concept was so interesting sounding, and after reading 'The Raven Boys' there's also no question in my mind about how intriguing this book is. When thinking of how to express my feelings for this book "intrigued" is the word I keep coming back to and using over and over again. I really don't know of any other book like it, which makes it stand out all the more. The fusion of history, legend, treasure hunting, and the occult make for an irresistible combination. One reason why I appreciated 'The Raven Boys' so much is because I love history and historical mysteries I could identify with Gansey's obsession in that way. The characters are another huge aspect of what make this book so fabulous. The aforementioned Gansey is rich, eccentric, and completely socially awkward, but he is such a fabulous character, primarily because of how much he cares about his friends. I adored all the Raven Boys and the friendship they had, and also I loved how Blue fit into their group. Blue and her family of psychics add another interesting dynamic to the book. 'The Raven Boys' is a bit meandering and slower paced at some moments, so I can see how it might not be for everyone. However, I was so enchanted by the characters that I loved every moment I could spend with them. Don't get me wrong, the book isn't all slow. There are plot-twists that have the potential to leave you shocked, and moments of higher intensity when you can't read quickly enough to find out what's going to happen next. Overall I was wholly impressed with 'The Raven Boys', and it confirmed to me that I am a fan of Maggie Stiefvater's writing potentially enough so to make me go back and give 'Shiver' another chance . 'The Raven Boys' is an enchanting read, one that will stick with you long after you've finished the last page.

Audiobook performed by Nick Podehl ZERO stars In New World things are different. Animals can talk. Men can hear each other's "NOISE." Todd Hewitt is just a month from his 13th birthday, when he'll become a man, and share the secret of the odd, isolated settlement - Prentisstown - he calls home. But a chance discovery results in his fleeing for his life, accompanied only by his dog, Manchee. Todd is many ways a typical young teen - full of anxiety about growing up, certain he knows much more than he actually does, prone to rash actions, and lacking impulse control. My stars, but he got on my nerves. Add the dystopian post-apocalyptic scenario, the religious megalomaniacs, and a scenario that has kept Todd ignorant of the basics of reading and writing and I'm about to scream. I disliked his use of vulgar language right left and "effing" sideways, not to mention his or any adult's total inability to speak in anything remotely resembling grammatical English. I kept exclaiming aloud as I listened, and wanted to just shake him and tell him to shut up and listen for a change, rather than continually running off half-cocked. Nick Podehl gives virtually everyone, except Viola, the same backwoods, hill-billy accent, differentiated only by how deeply he growled for the adult males , or how loudly he yelled for Todd . I actually did like his voice for the dog, Manchee, however. One of my big pet peeves is cliff-hangers which try to force the reader to buy read the next book. THAT alone would have lost this book a star or two ... if there were any left to lose. Can I give negative stars? Well, at least I could listen at double speed on my MP3. Save yourself and don't bother with this claptrap.

Growing up with twin sister Wren meant that Cath always had a built-in best friend, roommate, and even fanfiction writing partner for her Simon Snow stories. Cath isn't just a Simon Snow fan who shows up for book release parties Simon Snow is her life, and she has fans in the tens of thousands in all parts of the US and Japan waiting for her to write her own ending to the last book. Offline, she's shy and reserved, only going out with friends who see her and her sister as part of a package deal and dating a boring neighborhood boy she never liked much in the first place. Wren, on the other hand, wants to experience all that real life has to offer and isn't interested in doing it with a tag-along twin. When the two girls go off to college at the University of Nebraska, Wren decides they need to live apart. College is a frightening world for Cath. New people are everywhere, and she's worried about her dad who is home alone and a little mentally unstable. Her roommate Reagan is like another species, going out with different boys every night and seldomly spending a night in their dorm. Cath is relieved that they don't have to talk much. One of Reagan's most frequent visitors, however, is another story. He's always talking to Cath--hanging out in her room, sprawled across Reagan's bed, waiting in the hall to be let in when Cath comes home, needling her to go out with them. It's no wonder that she feels the need to retreat to the world of fanfiction. When her fiction professor asks her students why they write, most respond with statements, such as, "Because we like the sound of our own voices!" and "To set ourselves free." Cath sits silently, thinking that she writes to become free of herself. Fangirl is the third novel I've read by Rainbow Rowell, and I know I'll be placing a hold on the next one the moment the library orders it. I'm impressed by the way she manages to cover "serious issues" in this novel without making it feel like an "issues book." Cath's father is bipolar and has trouble living on his own without his daughters' watchful eyes, while Wren starts to drink more and more as she's trying to make the most of her college experience. Still, Fangirl is more of a picture of Cath's day-to-day life, showing her perspective as an onlooker to her family's struggles, and her involvement in them is much the same as I would imagine it to be for the friend of an alcoholic or bipolar person in real life. In addition to this, I can't help but say that I'm astounded by the sheer variety of boys Rowell creates in her novels and the fact that I love all of them, in spite of how different they are. In Fangirl, Levi is a tall, gangly, and sociable barista, offering a smile to everyone he meets. Lincoln from Attachments is an IT guy who is as shy as Cath. Park from Eleanor Park is a pretty ordinary teenage boy, but he's exactly who I'd want to hold my hand on the bus if I was the new kid who was bound to be ostracized. I even fell in love with Cath's writing partner Nick for a few pages of this book, as she watched the back of his angled hairline hunched over the page. In short, Fangirl is the perfect read for those who love fantasy but are willing to read something realistic or for shy girls who get what it's like to be scared to sit alone in the cafeteria. I loved this book, and Cath's fangirling made me into a Rainbow Rowell fan for life.

I needed something to kick me out of a recent book rut so I thought this would do the trick. I'll say right now that the thing that drew me to this book is my deep abiding love for my favorite apartment in science fiction, Republica. That's right, that shining tower spanning thousands of floors with every mod con and all the interesting, fashionable political people of Galactic City living, loving, plotting, conniving also going generally off the rails occasionally. The place had everything from entertainment to medical facilities it's said that there were residents who never left the place from birth to death. This whole idea fascinates me so, The Thousandth Floor had me because of the promise of something similar. If anything, I wanted more world-building. The Tower was fairly well laid out described but ultimately, there's no context on how this place fits in with the rest of the outside world. I did like the mention that there were other similar towers in other locations around the world it's made me think there could be interesting stories to be told from those who reside in them. Are these towers constructed by one architectural group or is there a Dubai situation going on where these great constructs are the work will of a very wealthy visionary individual or family? It's not explained why those eking out a living of strife toil on the lower levels chose to live this way inside the Tower. Is life outside the tower worse, more dangerous. even less desirable? Perhaps this will be covered in the next book. I did love the future tech and all things Nadia. While I'm still contemplating my comfort with ingesting gummy candy with RFID chips in them, the screaming wiggling Gummy Buddies candy has my interest. Now to the characters. Rylin had my interest the whole way through. She finished as she began, a favorite. Watt too was worth every word devoted to him he started off finished as a well done character. I look forward to more from both. Leda was one of the most interesting characters and while I enjoyed her having an actual arc and personality, she devolved into a drug-maddened unsympathetic shell by the end. Here's to hoping for a bit of character redemption in the next book. Eris began basic but by book's end had become one of the best characters. Fifty pages in, I was already hoping Avery was the girl in the prologue who takes the plunge to her death off The Tower. Alas, I reached the final page disappointed. All that money spent on genetically engineering her into being and her parents didn't bother to get her an enhanced personality. Apparently the only things you can manipulate genetically in the future is still physicality. Pity. Her brother, Atlas, flirted with being interesting but that unfortunately fizzled. Cord became tolerable but only because of his connection to Rylin. In general, the monied males need a lot of work. Their personalities gender attitudes were like they stepped out of modern day America from any teen show from 1990 to now. One hundred years on they're stuck in our modern day rich teen boy trope? It just felt dated, much like a lot of the slang being the same as that of today. Spoilers follow About the sib-cest situation... not rooting for it won't because the author didn't sell it. One hundred years in the future apparently siblings hooking up is still wrong not just frowned upon which explains Avery's shameful secret lust for Atlas. At times it seemed the writer wanted the reader to root for Avery "getting her man" because... twu wuv but who can invest when the characters are themselves hesitant because they know sleeping with the kin folk is not cute? I'm not sure where the writer is trying to go with this. If it's "only adopted" the siblings aren't related by blood while having been raised as such from a very young age , the familial bonds don't count the hook up is on? Does only blood matter? Adopteds aren't "real" family members? I needed the author to pick a lane ride it to the end here. She's going to need to do more to sell Aves At as rootable because I'm still side-eyeing their vibe like they're channelling Woody Soon-Yi. Not cute. Some weird similarities to another series struck me. Avery felt very like Glass from The 100 to me. Not good. In other things Very Like The 100 here, there's a familial connection that was so similar to Wells Bellamy I balked. I know these two series are written by different authors but this made me wonder if The Thousandth Floor is also under the Alloy Entertainment multi-platform umbrella going for YA sci-fi setting drama. I read this in a day so I give points for being a page turner. It's a good, quick read I'm fairly sure I'll read the next in the series. Recommended as it definitely got me out of my slump.

spoiler alert I was disappointed by this book on multiple levels. Taking the characters of Sherlock and Watson and using them as inspiration for a heterosexual romance felt off to me from the start. It only got worse as the book wore on. Sherlock has some serious issues, which is true to his character, but even though this book takes place in modern times Watson not only enables all these behaviors but claims at one point that doing anything to address his mental health would take away his genius and turn him into a different, lesser person. I find this message deeply troubling. There is enough stigma around mental health and it's so difficult to get help at all, let alone in a combination that works. Adding to that stigma and scaring people away from getting help with claims that it will take away what makes them special is just irresponsible, especially in a novel aimed at teens. On top of that their relationship, which is incredibly unhealthy, is painted as romantic and even as a possible solution to Sherlock's troubles. Take a deep breath and repeat it with me "Love does not magically cure mental illness." Of course there is no magical cure for mental illness, but getting into a relationship without working on your own issues is a recipe for disaster. All of that aside, the plot just didn't make sense. The villain was meticulous in his plotting when the author needed a difficult mystery to solve, but when a dramatic climax was called for he takes two teens, in a zoo full of cameras, and drags them to an exhibit and forces them to crawl in then walks away, trusting that they'll be killed. At that point I'm almost surprised he didn't haul them to an aquarium so that the could tie them to a rope with a candle slowly burning through it above a shark tank. There are many great adaptations of Sherlock out there. This is not one of them.

Samantha Ruiz has a freak gene that makes her turn invisible, or ripple. She can't control it, and it's getting worse. Afraid of becoming a lab-rat, Sam keeps her ability secret, until fellow runner Will Baker sees her vanish into thin air. Will promises secrecy and help, and Sam begins to fall in love. Together, the two discover there are worse things than being a scientific curiosity. Someone's been killing people who possess Sam's gene. A mysterious man from France sends letters that offer hope for safety, but also reveal a sinister connection with Nazi experiments. The more time Sam spends with Will, the less she can imagine life without him. When Sam uncovers secrets from her past, she must choose between keeping Will in her life or keeping Will safe. This is the first book in the series Ripple by Cidney Swanson. It was a good book I must say though there are a few points I am going to talk about. Some things I disliked about the book. Will and Sam's relationship I feel like it progressed a little too fast. It was a bit to coincidental that Sam's best friend was the one with the gene. Maybe if they had not known each other and met each other I would have liked it better but as the story went on it did not matter all that much because I liked their relationship and the author did slow it down during the middle of the book The ending It was a bit abrupt. This is only my opinion. You might argue and say this is because it is part of the series. But, even if it is a part of a series, there is a way you write a cliffhanger. I am not saying it was bad but, it could have been better. I mean Will disappearing like that and then suddenly appearing and then everything being fine. I mean as fine as it could be in their situation Some of the action scenes I don't know they seemed a bit unbelievable. The way Samantha managed to follow that man. Only to become captured by someone who we had never seen before. That was it about the things I did not like as much as the other parts of the book. Now I can talk about the things I actually liked about this book. The way the plot developed was really good. I loved the story line and how it related back to Hitler's time. The diary which we were slowly piecing together. I really liked that. It was nice trying to figure out the mystery by ourselves as well and not just finding it out as the characters found it out. I always have loved books like that. Another thing which I really liked about this book was Will and Mickie's relationship. I think Cidney got the sibling or rather the brother sister relationship down to a T. I have a younger brother and I know exactly why Mickie was so protective and I just loved their banter. It was hilarious. It was sad that Sam and her best friend's relationship got strained because of Will but, I could understand why it happened. I could understand Sam's best friend's point of view too because she was not getting the whole truth and she was just piecing together the information she knew. Hopefully, their relationship would get better. All in all, the book was well paced. The plot was good and kept you hooked and I did not put the book down once. Cidney Swanson wrote another book. I love her Saving Mars series and this is another series which I think I am going to like. Time to move on to the next book. I would recommend this book to all you readers because despite there being some things I didn't like, overall the book was great!

Todd Hewitt is the only boy left in a town filled with men on an otherwise abandoned alien planet. There were once women in Prentisstown, but they were killed by the native race called the "Spackle" , when Todd was just an infant. The remaining men were infected with a germ which caused even their most private thoughts to be heard as plainly as if they were spoken aloud. Todd knows that in just thirty short days, he will thirteen and considered a man. But before he can get to that day, he discovers something in the swamp that causes him to question everything he's ever known. The Knife of Never Letting Go is the March selection for calico_reaction 's bookclub, and it's a novel that I've been meaning to read for a few years now. Like many young adult releases these days, it's a dystopia, although at first it doesn't really feel like one. Life in Prentisstown is almost void of any advanced technology. In fact the character's lives feels a little rustic in comparison to today's western lifestyle. I found this to be refreshing. The novel reads like a thriller tale of survival, with plenty of twists, turns and intense moments. I don't want to give too much away about the story, but I do want to mention that it's quite dark for a young adult novel. Although there are plenty of young adult novels out there that explore dark themes, there are certain lines that most will not cross. The Knife of Never Letting Go waltzes right past one without looking back. It can also be a very sad novel. I found myself getting attached to certain characters early on, and was very sad when one of them died. The Knife of Never Letting Go is a strong novel with great characters, but it also worth noting that it embraces some of my biggest pet peeves. One of those pet peeves is how characters seem to do a lot of standing around and talking, when they really need to be running forward in a chase scene for example . There's just something about that that makes me want to tear out my hair, and this book does it frequently. Another pet peeve of mine is when so much tension is based on delayed information. An example of this is when characters stand around and talk about important information that must be revealed to a character but as there's "no time now," we don't end up learning anything although we do get a lengthy scene where people talk about how there's "no time now." I'm sorry! It just drives me nuts . I've always felt that this was kind of a cheap way to build tension, and by the time you get to the big reveal at the end, you've pretty much already guessed what it is. The book also ends on a cliffhanger, which is not one of my pet peeves in fact, I thought it was well done , but I know a lot of people dislike cliffhangers. I'm not going to deny that I had a few issues with The Knife of Never Letting Go, but the majority of the time, I quite liked it. I experienced this book as an audiobook, narrated by Nick Podehl. It's been a long time since I've seen someone narrate an audiobook so passionately. I do hope that they got Podehl to narrate the rest of the series. I plan on reading the last two books in the trilogy, and will probably experience them both as audiobooks as well.

I was looking forward to reading this story ever since I heard about it, and it was worth the read. The characters were believable, with great personalities and interactions, particularly between Fletcher and Othello. I liked the way the author portrayed racial differences abuse tensions in this story. In most fantasy stories I've read with orcs, elves and dwarves, there is always tension between the races with each considering themselves superior to the other, but this story tackled the issue on a whole new level. Humans very clearly consider themselves the superior species, freely attacking dwarves in the street, abusing and trying to execute elves out in the open, and so forth. Yet there was hope in open-minded people like Fletcher, who found that the more he learnt about the dwarves, the more he respected them. It gives a message that ignorance is what causes hatred, and if people took the time to actually look past race and get to know each other as people, we'd find a lot to respect in each other.

To start, I was bombarded with love for this book by my sister, her friend, and Julius Caesar through this one quote "The fault, dear Brutus, in not in our stars but in ourselves." Like An Imperial Affliction when read by Augustus Waters, I feel as if I need a few days to mull it over to realize its immense grandeur. Taking into account this sheer awesomeness I could hardly go without writing a review, which undoubtedly I would have forgotten to do unless I did so upon finishing the book. The characters are wonderful, the plot is great, the dialogue hilarious and just about everything about the book makes it worth being read at least 7 times over 7 Harry Potter books-you know that's a good number . It was anticipated to be so good that I started reading it the moment I got it from the holds at the library and despite a mandatory 3 hour break for dinner and a class, and tried to read through the night to finish. But, alas I fell asleep and was forced to finish in the morning after the second mandated ungodly morning exercise. It was beyond magnificent and I often found myself repeating the words and sentences because they flowed so smoothly and sounded so poetic and I couldn't help but see how they sounded coming from my mouth. This books only hamartia that I saw was the similarity of the characters. They all seemed to talk the same except the lovely 25-year old British socialite trapped in a 16-year old body Kaitlyn. But even that aside, while they were all very fun and great to read about, there was a certain blandness where it felt like it was the same person talking to different physical versions of themselves with slight variations here and there. However, by the end I couldn't bear to repeat words, or grin at the poetic fluency because I was crying so hard because it is such a beautiful story. The only books that made my cry this much before were Bridge to Teribithia by Katherine Patterson and Black Box by Julie Schumacher. That is exactly why this cannot be my favorite book. I for one don't exactly enjoy crying, but rather the feeling that causes crying which is why if any other book can invoke the same strong feeling I would be content. "The Fault in Our Stars" is pretty damn close though. It is a wonderful book a magical wonderful book a book that let you know that "Apparently the world is not a wish-granting factory." a book that delved into the common things we take for granted, and the terrifying ideas that so many choose to ignore claiming the bliss of ignorance. It is a book that I think helps us a members of the human race to accept one another more readily. When you meet the characters of Van Houten and Kaitlyn, and Augustus, and Monica, and Isaac, all the parents, and everyone else you see their different personalities and how when the world wrecks havoc upon them they take it out differently, but no matter what it is not truly them you are angry at but the cold-hearted universe that laughs from above. Maybe I didn't phrase any of that very well, but at least I know what I mean. Well, it's a bit choppy, but also probably the longest review I've ever written D

This review also appears on my blog alexreadsboooks Contains spoilers! ___________________ I do not like this book. I'm saying that now as a warning for anyone who doesn't want to read about how much I don't like this book. Enough warning? Good then let's go ahead. I had a really hard time getting into this book, because i was just a few pages in when I thought 'Huh, I read this story before, haven't I?' and realised that I was essentially reading Hunger Games with superpowers. Of course it's not exactly the same story, but the basic elements are there. A somewhat reluctant heroine who becomes the symbol of a revolution? Check. The best friend who could be a love interest? Check. The guy she falls in love with but it's also complicated? Check. A rebellion that's essentially not any better than the existing system? Check. I could go on, but if you've read the novel it's not too hard to find more parallels, if not, you'll have to believe me that there are more. Maybe some people don't feel like that but for me it was a massive problem while trying to get into the story. it took me about the first half to finally move on from the Hunger Games similarities and feel like this is a different story. And this is the point where the second reason why it took me a lot longer than planned to finally finish this book comes into play Mare Barrow. I always thought Katniss annoyed me a little because of how much she worried about herself instead of thinking about others, but she has nothing at all on Mare Barrow. I know she has a lot going on in her life, but the amount to which she doesn't care about other people and their very real problems is unbelievable. If Aveyard wanted me to hate Mare she did a great job, because that's exactly what I'm doing. And it doesn't stop there, on top of being so wrapped up in her own problems, Mare has a serious attitude problem. She keeps talking about how she wants to free the Reds, just to turn around and talk about how they can't do anything and need her protection because they're weak and powerless. She herself has been a part of this group for most of her short life, but she keeps looking down on them like they're lesser than her. And when someone calls her out on it, she reacts entirely unreasonable and completely dismisses any concerns others have. Whether it's Cal, calling her out on becoming the very kind of person they are trying to destroy, or Cameron telling her how it is, Mare dismisses their concerns and just goes on doing what she has been doing before. Something else that takes away from what could be a decent and maybe even a good plot, is the continuous reiteration of the phrase "Anyone can betray anyone" and its variations. In the first moment it just got on my nerves to read it over and over again. In fact, it feels like it appears at least once a paragraph. But as I kept reading and thought a bit more about it I realised that it actually took away from the plot. Because at some point it starts to affect the reader's perception of the characters.Mare's distrust becomes our own. There comes a point in the novel where I just couldn't stop myself from doubting motivations. It just feels really weird to not trust any of the other characters. Even more, it just feels really weird from a personal point of view. Not trusting anyone at all just feels incredibly lonely, and unreasonable. Yes, in theory anyone can betray anyone, but can you imagine doubting everyone around you because of that? Including people you have trusted all your life? I'm sorry but I can't. And maybe Aveyard is trying to make a point in the long run, but if she is, it doesn't translate at all for me. Less reiteration of the same point over and over again, please, we got it the first five times. Then there is the death of the queen. She has been built up to be this great, fearsome villain, and then this? Its so very anticlimatic and completely wasted by its absence. Her death is reduced to be one death of many. And hers is not the only wasted death or character. Shade's death would have a lot more impact if he had had any significant relationship with Mare. And along with this one practically every relationship in Mare's life that is not with Cal and maybe Kilorn, is severely underdeveloped. She could be friends with Farley, but she's so completely focused on herself and her own misery that she doesn't even try to build a friendship. Last but not least, I do have things I like about this book. The world building continues to be interesting even though it does feel more and more rooted in the real world instead of a fictional one . Also Cal and Maven are probably my favourite characters in the entire series. Cal is just too good for Mare and I would have loved it if we got to see more of his inner conflict I also really loved how he was able to make decisions Mare was unable to make, thanks to his military training. Cal is definitely a character I could root for. Meanwhile, Maven has partly become my favourite because I just want to see everything burn. I don't usually like characters who betray others, but Mare has made me dislike her so much that I'd be fine with Maven burning everything to the ground. In fact, the two things I'd most like to see are Mare going full dark and becoming the tyrant queen Maven currently is, or Mare and Maven becoming some sort of dark tyrant duo.

To make things worse, Tyler couldn't stay forever, eventually, he would be called back and the Tyler that she knew would go back to being the boy that he lived inside. That day came sooner than she thought though, when he helped her save her dad from a fire at his office and was hurt pretty badly. Then not only did she loose her Tyler to a Tyler that didn't even know she existed, but she also lost her dog Sam when the building after him to save him. With this strain of loosing her watcher and her beloved dog, and the distance between her and her friends, things became hard for her. Hey ex boyfriend was back in her life, and was trying hard to keep a watch on her for her watcher, but it was very stressful for him. Billie was starting to fight against evil forces and terrible creatures would come up out of nowhere. She only knew they were around when her necklace grew cold. She needed her watcher. She needed her protector that she knew was supposed to come. How will she learn to use her gifts if she doesn't have anyone to show her how? All she really wants is a normal life.
