Shortly after she moves in with Delia, she's provided the offer of researching the Manson girls for money. Here's the thing I nearly DNFed this. The first chapter is an ode to Charles Manson oh, how I wish I were kidding and I do. not. give. a. shit. I feel like when you're involving something real-time in your book, it could go either way. This is half of Anna Delia's story, half of Charles Manson's and his followers. If you've ever watched an E! Special and or read Wikipedia on them, you might already know everything this book contains. A Study In Charlotte was the same way, except with the story of Sherlock and Watson. If I wanted to learn thousands of unnecessary Snapple facts, I would've ran to Google. We also receive stupidity, such as this "Ass pox?" "At least, that sounds edgy," Delia said. "Herpes' sounds like something a really dirty Muppet would get." ... "Okay, they had choices, but Susan Atkins said that he could see right through her when he met her. And she wasn't the only one." "Anna," Dex said. "Never underestimate the power of telling a person exactly what she wants to hear." He was talking to me like I was an idiot. And he was missing the point. I don't know who would pay a fifteen-year old to research Charles Manson in the first place. I don't think someone that young could grasp the importance of something so gruesome. She kept comparing herself to a "Manson girl" as if she were one? In her author's note, Umminger even said she didn't enjoy the research for this book. Understandably. Also Anna's mother is a horrible person. Later in the novel, she is revealed to have cancer and Anna insists to return home, but Anna's mother literally says "No, you might make the cancer worse." What the actual hell, woman?! Delia reminded me of my own sister in a few ways. For those who may've been annoyed by her, obviously don't have an occasionally annoying sister. How LA wasn't viewed as a place filled with brainless blonde idiots i.e. Tell Me Three Things, L.A. Candy was a relief as well. "So I had a breakthrough," he said, and he took my sister's face between his hands, like he was going to make out with her or snap her neck in one swift move. "I know. I know who you are." "That's reassuring," I said. "You did live together for five years." My sister glared and Roger ignored me. Just like old times. I had no idea American Girls and My Favorite Manson Girl were the same book, actually. It's a The Anatomical Shape of A Heart Night Owls situation. I requested this for the cover, really. In the thirteenth book of Rachel's series, you can feel it's slowly winding down. This book, like some of the previous ones have a couple of different POVS. This book is unlike the others we have read. Things have changed between Claire and Amelie. Even Amelie and Oliver.. and many other relationships. The stakes are raised, and things are even more intense now that Michael and Eve have gotten married, which was against all the laws there are. Along with the action, as there is plenty of that, this book is more focused on the relationships of our core characters. We have Michael and Eve, as they go through the typical things of a married couple, less alone a marriage between a vampire and a human. Claire and Shane seem to have their own share of problems, and issues they have to deal with... and then we have Oliver and Amelie. That relationship is always something I wanted to see, even though they were always in competition of one another, and in this book... we get a glimpse of how they feel about one another. I really felt bad for Oliver at a point in this book. It seems almost everyone was being used in one way or another. Oliver, Amelie and then our beloved characters as well. Manipulation by someone they can't control or stop. I think both Amelie and Oliver are very similar, and maybe that was what have bonded them together over the centuries they have known one another. The ending of this book... opens up a new beginning, and I can see the light of the end, I think. It was a ending which I probably thought wouldn't happen until the end. I look forward to see what happens now. It kind of brings a whole new range of options for the characters. Verdict 4.5 5

I received this book through the goodreads giveaways. THE FOLLOWING CONTAINS SPOILERS I think this an important book. There isn't nearly enough literature about intersex individuals. However, I do think readers should stop comparing Golden Boy and Middlesex this is a debut novel that delves into the character of its protagonist, while Middlesex is more high-brow and utilizes more themes, symbols, motifs, etc. The good Tarttelin hits some key points so beautifully you just want to read through her writing as fast as you can so you can re-read it. There are some thought-provoking passages, as when Max points out how difficult the mundane can be for him choosing bathrooms, filling out forms . There is some great dialogue between Max and Daniel I really loved the fraternal relationship. I also liked the first person multi-narrator format. The most interesting viewpoint besides Max's was Daniel's, and seeing the discovery of his brother's condition through his eyes. He also brought some much needed comic relief. As a whole, this book brings up some great points the continued stigma surrounding certain groups despite leaps and bounds with others like LGBT , nature vs. nurture, the benefits and detriments of a medical approach, and family secrets. It does make you think. The bad I can hardly blame Tarttelin for the length of this book all authors' works are, and should be, cut down. This should have been better scrutinized by the editor. Golden Boy could do with some artful cutting down. It's difficult to slash contextual narrative because of the amount of events this book contains a rape scene, a pregnancy, a school scandal, an abortion, a coming-out, a suicide attempt, an arrest. But there are certainly a lot of repetitive dialogues and inner monologues, especially because some of the characters are so one-dimensional. Karen is predictable, and I don't know how many more times I could have read her complaining about her husband's campaign, or about how much she cared for her children. Furthermore, Sylvie as a character was just irritating. We get it, she is "alternative" but struggles because she likes the gorgeous, mainstream, popular guy. The dialogue between her and Max was mostly pointless there are way too many ellipses. And I didn't find that the descriptions of her poetry were really necessary. To mention it once would have been enough I could have done without the 'I just absorb the poetry around me' bit. The most infuriating line of the whole book was when she said she "wished for best friend that got her ." Perhaps it's because Tarttelin nails the teenage voice so well that I found these parts so annoying I can't tolerate melodramatic teenagers in the real world either. I understand that her presence precipitates the conflict in the book, as Max has to deal with new feelings and more exposure. I just wanted less of her. I applaud the author's tackling a tricky subject, particularly in her debut novel. I think there is a little too much going on in the book to just tie up the ends so nicely. I don't like how Max's suicide attempt is brushed off because he was drunk it doesn't really work that way. The end is so quick but just as dramatic as the rest of the book it's almost too quick for the events that happen in its last 50 pages... the arrest just seemed like a sidenote. It's hard to classify this book. It is a YA novel because it's all plot-driven and most of the story is shared through the voice of teenagers or in language that is pretty comprehensible. However, it begins with a graphic rape scene and it can clearly be classified as mature content. In conclusion the writing caliber does not always suit the important subject matter, and there are certainly passages that could be cut. However, it is a good first novel, and I look forward to more of Tarttelin's work, once she has refined her style a bit more.

Esperaba que The Boyfriend App fuera una novela simple sobre relaciones de instituto que no me hiciera pensar mucho. Y al principio lo fue. La primera parte nos presenta una historia tipica de chica semipopular caida en desgracia con bastante humor, personajes interesantes aunque un poco estereotipados y el toque anadido de la cuestion de clase economica como parte del enfrentamiento entre la reina de la colmena y nuestra protagonista. Tambien tenemos la relacion entre la protagonista y su prima, un acierto, un triangulo amoroso totalmente desaprovechado y la inverosimil posibilidad de solucionarlo todo con el premio de un concurso. Hasta ahi nada novedoso pero entretenido. Es cierto que la parte tecnologica esta metida con calzador y que algunos eventos necesitan una suspension de la incredulidad bastante alta, pero en general, era hasta disfrutable. Sin embargo, en la segunda parte llegan los problemas. Audrey necesita mejorar su app y decide utilizarla para hacerle la competencia al GHB. Usando una tecnologia ilegal incorporada en los telefonos que la compania usaba para empujar al consumo a traves de ultrasonidos, Audrey consigue que esos mismos ultrasonidos, a mayor potencia, tengan el efecto de provocar un enamoramiento instantaneo. Esto provoca que el "enamorado" no sea consciente de sus acciones, generalmente de caracter fisico sexual, hasta despues que se desactiva el ultrasonido. ?Lo mejor? Que no pasa nada porque Audrey ha programado la app para que solo mujeres puedan utilizarla, y por tanto, no importa. ?Que son un par de morreos y tocamientos no consensuados con un hombre? A los hombres, con tal de pillar cacho, no les importa nada mas. ?A quien le preocupa su libertad o su derecho a relaciones fisicas o emocionales consensuales? Segun este libro, a nadie. Aunque el comportamiento y la app de Audrey me parecio moralmente reprensible, segui leyendo esperando que en algun momento alguien criticaria o haria ver a la protagonista porque su comportamiento era erroneo. Sin embargo, ninguno de los personajes involucrados se quejo y ningun adulto cuestiono lo ocurrido. Todos trataron el tema como si fuera una gracia de adolescentes. No lo es, es la perpetuacion de la cultura de la violacion.

Under normal circumstances, Clementine wouldn't want to spend all summer on a boat with her parents and younger sister. She's just gotten her license, after all! But these are not normal circumstances. Her best friend Amanda hates her, and she's kind of right to. Clem's fallen in smit with Amanda's boyfriend, Ethan. And now Amanda knows. So maybe a summer in exile is just what the doctor ordered. But almost immediately, Clem meets James, who's also spending the summer at sea. And...well, sparks. I love this book beyond all measure or reason. I love Clem and her parents and especially her sister, Olive. And oh, do I love James. He has his own reasons for wanting to hide, and the two of them together are magic. Clem's not perfect. It's an awful thing, what she did to Amanda. And to her credit, she gets that. She doesn't try to rationalize it or make Amanda the bad one. Nope, it's all on Clem and she plans to spend the summer punishing herself for it. Except James won't let her do that. And again, sweetest couple since Etienne and Anna. This is only the second book of Melissa Walker's that I've read after Small Town Sinners and I think it's now safe to say that she's one of my must-read authors. I'm excited to read her backlist, and all future books. While on Twitter, she said that her books are different, there's also a common thread well, at least of the two I've read so far of trying to figure out who you are. In STS, it's about challenging your belief system and growing. In this, it's about figuring out how to go on after betraying who you thought you were. Because I don't think anyone would consider themselves the kind of girl who would go after her best friend's boyfriend, right? But Clem did. And in her eyes, that makes her a horrible, horrible person. This book is sweet and laugh-out-loud funny. You'll definitely want to bring it along on vacation, preferably someplace near water. Highly recommended.

I was looking through my Want To Read list and I was reminded of this novel, which I'd read about in a magazine when it first came out, but had never been able to physically find in a shop. I bought a used copy on Amazon for a penny, and I'm sad to say that I didn't love it as much as I was hoping to. The novel definitely grows on you - I felt like the beginning was slower, and once I got past the halfway mark I really did feel more compelled to finish the book and find out what would happen. But even so, there are some questions that I'm left with, that make me think like the storytelling wasn't the greatest. I realise that it might have been the author's intention not to answer these questions, or simply that she did but I wanted more than I was given. For example, Heather staying friends with all the 'mean girls' crowd was something that didn't make huge sense to me, and it wasn't really addressed whether as she began a new relationship this would help her free herself from these friendships which she knew full well had never been very good. I'm also a little irritated that by the final scenes Cass really does refer to Julia as her "dead girlfriend", and I think that this kind of depreciates what this book could have been about - a great friendship, a genuine friendship without a one-sided crush from either of them. The fact that right at the end Cass seems to acknowledge loving Julia as more than just a friend is just going to feed the ego of all the straight girls who, as soon as their friends come out, ask "but do you fancy ME though?" like it's a given. Additionally I don't feel that it's fair to use the term 'girlfriend' when the two had never been together, it's not the same as having a "confusing undefined" relationship like you sometimes have in your teens where you're not sure what to call it - there is no shadow of a doubt that the relationship between Cass and Julia was just friendship, not romantic or sexual. Also I felt that, like it often happens with made-up songs and rhymes, the songs from the musical the characters are putting together and even the plot did not feel clear or relatable from the reader's perspective. It's not the same as reading lyrics on a page that you know the melody to and that you can hum in your head. These were original songs, and they just looked like, well... words on a page, with no reference whatsoever that would help them come to life. For me, they fell a little bit flat. I enjoyed the flashback chapters of the book a lot more towards the end and I especially enjoyed the sub-plot involving Maggie, somehow feeling that this side character was the most fleshed out, I could picture her clearly in my head. I didn't love how that sub-plot was resolved, but I can accept it. I wish we could have seen more of Heather's reaction, though, when Cass tells her the story. I wish she could have been told in detail rather than in one throwaway sentence. Overall, it wasn't terrible by any means, but it wasn't deep enough. I like finding quotes that resonate with me in novels, and with this one, it only really happened once.

" The Cleansing didn't end violence. The Cleansing didn't bring peace. When free to find their own way, women are just as destructive." A young adult dystopian novel with a different twist. Years ago, a disease wiped out the entire male population, and a lot of the women. Now only women survive and reproduce through genetic engineering. They live in Sectors, abandoned hospitals, schools and other large buildings. The women follow a strict set of rules including not touching that were designed to bring peace, end war and stop the spread of the disease, which men were blamed for even though the women fight and believe themselves to be in a war with the women who choose to live outside, the Earthers. The enforcers of the rules for each Sector is the Matriarch. Mary lives in Section 1 with a very strict Matriarch. She has never even seen a boy, not even in her biology textbooks, they've been cut out. When Section 7 is bombed, a new person comes to sector one. Taylor has hidden his identity his whole life, but when he meets Mary, he feels...different. This story is told from the alternating points of view of Mary and Taylor. This makes for a quick-paced read. The plot, for a YA dystopian story was unique. The world and how it works was explained well, I usually have a lot of questions about these questionable worlds, but the disease, reproduction and the hierarchy of the society was explained fairly well. My favorite character was actually Taylor, he grew up hiding who he was his entire life and at seventeen that will start to become more and more difficult. At Section 1, coming out as a boy is extremely dangerous, so it was very interesting to see Taylor's decision making process and this time and how he finds his role in the matriarchal society. The Earthers were another interesting part, living off the Earth and keeping their secrets buried underground. The plot twist with the Matriarch was great! I do wish that the immunity with the disease was explained at the end, but that's it. This book was received for free return for an honest review.

At first I gave this 4 stars, but I had to be honest with myself because I really feel that this book is a 3.5 There's not going to be anymore Percy books... I'm okay. I'm okay crawls into fetal position and cries for the rest of eternity WARNING SPOILERS AHEAD Please beware that it may seem like I'm ranting but I really did love this book overall it but I felt like the solution at the climax was way to quick and easy. I didn't necessarily hate the ending but I wished for an epilogue. The more I think about it, the more I'm beginning to think about the parts I really disliked. Like I felt Rick had built up so much with the past four books and the climax was like three pages. Defeating the Giants felt waaayyy too easy like I'm pretty sure it lasted for like 3 minutes. Also the defeat of Gaea was unbelievable in my eyes. I hoped that the entire seven would have a part in taking down the Earth Mother who is suppose to be "all powerful" but all we get is Jason, Leo, and Piper, who hold Gaea up and charm speak her to sleep. I wanted to scream ARE YOU SERIOUS IT WAS THAT SIMPLE??! Some stuff needed to be explain such as the physicians cure, which came out of nowhere and was an excuse to make them go on mini quest. There of course are parts that I love such as Reyna and Piper. Even though Reyna and Nico's POV with the Parthenos took too much from the story I really grown to love Reyna by the end. I loved seeing Nico become more warm towards people and let Reyna in. You also get to see Piper be all awesome and badass. But I felt Hazel as a character was very glossed over, at times I forgot she was even part of the seven. She is one of my favorite characters in this series and I felt this book gave her no justice. Did we ever get resolution about her curse? This book needed more Percy moments too, sigh. Percabeth felt like side characters in this book which extremely disappointed me. In past books Percy is viewed as the most powerful demigod. He can summon hurricanes and huge waves, but in this book they made him seem like he was like everyone else. I miss that epicness of the PJO books. I was hoping we would get a POV from at least one of them, but no we had to get one too many Jason chapters. Every 10 seconds we get a Jason chapter There are parts in this book where you get to see Percabeth through someone else's eyes but what I really want to see is through theirs. Annabeth's feud with her mother is never really resolved, you don't get to see her talk to her mother after finding the ATHENA PARTHENOS. Can we also talk about the fact that NOBODY DIED. This felt like in City of Heavenly Fire when we were promised s i x characters that we know by name will die, and how so much hype was blown around that but it ended up being people we didn't even care about. I felt it was a cop out as I do now. It's the final battle with Giants and freaking Mother Earth herself but nobody died. No I do not count Octavian or the random people who don't even have names. We've been alluded to how one of the seven was gonna die, but they didn't. I didn't even believe for a second that Leo died when everyone thought he did because it was way too obvious how they were always pointing it out. I felt as if I've been cheated. At least in PJO, Luke redeems himself and ends up dying but here we have none of that. Also Percy's fatal flaw was never delved into. We built so much tension around how Percy would make have to make an impossible decision and how he would "let the world burn to save his friends." But then we get nothing... Nada Zilch Diddly squat. Wow okay then. The ending felt a bit rushed too. It was never explained how Leo even found Ogygia again which was confusing and then the story just cut off. There was no reunion with the others which I made me sad. Also, I hoped that we would get to see Percy reunite with his mom, whom we haven't seen in ages, but no we get a brief spew of their future plans and whatnot. I do not hate this book, everything I said above I say because I love this character with my whole heart. No one will understand the amount of love and loyalty I have to Percy Jackson and all of Rick's work. I say this as a loyal fan who stuck behind the past nine books only to be a bit disappointed in the end. I feel as if I didn't get to really say goodbye to my favorite male character. I'm gonna go into denial that I won't be getting anymore Percy adventures...

I put off reading this for the first few months that I knew it was out there. I always get nervous that the sequel won't live up to the original. But, alas, I was wrong. This book is just, if not, as endearing as Stargirl. Here, you get to see Stargirl inside out. Instead of just being a prairie skirted, ukelele playing object of Leo's eye, you see her point of view and the year that she spends after Leo. The characters are amazingly original and I grew to love Stargirl even more. A definite read.

spoiler alert This is a sad love story of two young people, Hazel Augustus, and deals with the difficult issue of terminal cancer in children teenagers. Teenager Hazel has terminal cancer it has spread to her lungs and her life is likely to finish almost before it has begun. She meets Augustus "Gus" at the cancer support group he has lost a leg to cancer but his chances of survival seem good. Gus's friend Isaac also has cancer faces the tragic knowledge that he is about to lose his sight as a result of an essential surgical procedure his girlfriend Monica cannot deal with the prospect ends the relationship. Hazel Gus fall in love and decide to travel to Amsterdam to meet the author Peter Van Houton who has written about the death of a child from cancer. Van Houton has many problems of his own and the reason for them becomes clear later in the novel. This is a brave subject for an author to tackle and not an easy one to read about but John Green pulls it off well.

I still really enjoy this book. It has some of my favorite passages in it. The character development of the MCs is a little weaker than in the first book, focusing more on the danger Fablehaven is in. It does have some true to sibling arguments though

Hold Me Closer, Necromancer RATING 3.5 stars. There are books that stay longer than they deserve on our shelves. Hold Me Closer, Necromancer was one of those books. I'd read a few glowing reviews so I bought it last year, but then I "kind of" forgot about it. Thankfully it was brought to my attention I really should start my very own "because Wendy said so" shelf , by a review of book 2,Necromancing the Stone. I decided to read it... and I was left wondering why it had taken me so long to pick this up. I was constantly reminded of the TV series Reaper while I was reading this book. It's a good thing, I thought that series was hilarious. Maybe because the protagonists of both the book and the tv series are named Sam. Or because they are both college dropouts who work at a store and are really the most normal of guys. They just happen to have superpowers... sort of. Anyways, back to the book. Sam is a college dropout. One day he has a very random and unfortunate encounter with Douglas who is a... necromancer. Douglas is as mean as they come he is a psychopath. And he forces poor Sam to be his apprentice because Sam is also a... necromancer. Here's what I liked about Hold me Closer, Necromancer it had that kind of no-nonsense narrative that most YA books lack. There are no flourishes. No highly intelligent and mysterious males. No extreme unpopular protagonists, who turn out to be again highly intelligent or simply attracting the most popular guy girl in school. There was only Sam, semi-loser, very little prospects and his friends. They suddenly find themselves in a world of trouble. Mayhem and genuinely funny humor ensue. Severed heads talk. Harbingers of death and Egyptian deities pop up. Sure some things could have been better explained the Council comes to mind and the action seemed a bit rushed in places, but overall this was a funny, entertaining read. The cast of characters is diverse and represents stereotypes the "mwahaha" villain, the henchman but somehow still maintains some individuality and personality. Other things you won't find in this book insta-love, love triangles and a male protagonist that is super dark and tortured. You will find strong female characters and fairy hounds who can resist that. Overall it was, as stated before, a nice read. I loved the cast of characters, especially Mrs W., Ashley and Brid. Recommended.
I spent the entire time reading this wondering if I've outgrown YA or Sarah Dessen. It's the latter.

I was so close to giving this one 4.5 stars because the relationships between a few of the characters annoyed me a lot and seemed rather pointless Chaol and Aelin mostly but the ending chapters yanked it back to 5 stars! I flew through the last 200 pages and thought the whole book came together really well. Every one of the books in this series have gotten a 5 stars off me so far so I think Ms. Maas can do no wrong!!

I thought this book will be really good but I didn't like it that much. The story was boring, and the only moments I enjoied were the Zoey-Doug moments, apart from that the book was really boring. I really thought it will be better.

This was just fine - a girl moves from India to Iowa with her immediate family, misses home, adjusts to life in a new country, and deals with a mean girl in her class. I was hoping for a little more depth and originality, and maybe something about Iowa City to set it apart from every town since I've lived there, and it has lots of great things about it . I liked the sections set in India more than the parts in the U.S. Decent suggestion for upper-elementary multicultural assignments.

Before reading this book, I had a conversation with someone about Paper Towns one of my favorite books. I had only read Paper Towns and The Fault in our Stars, and said that Paper Towns was my favorite. The person I was talking to said something along the lines of "Paper Towns is the second best book by John Green" and of course I asked what was the first, and when they replied Looking for Alaska and told me I really should read it, I finally picked it up. This is actually my least favorite book of John Greens, which I have a feeling is an unpopular opinion. A lot of people compare his books and say that "the characters are all basically the same" and things of that nature but I don't see how that's true. For one thing, I didn't really like Pudge very much. I found him a little self centered in a weird way, and I don't actually think he is like other male protagonists that I've read. For example I loved reading from Q's POV in Paper Towns, but Pudge wasn't great to me. Similarly, Alaska and Margo are entirely not the same person. I didn't really like Alaska. I didn't WANT her to die, but I wasn't very happy with her. I did like the Colonel in some ways, but overall the book was just not my favorite.

If I was hoping for a return to adventure after the second book, I was sadly disappointed. The potential was there, but instead the author continued down the path of serving up angst topped with angst sauce and a serving of angst on the side. Really, this book could have been half the number of pages and told the same story. In fact, the first three books probably could have been condensed into one book, if all of the over-emoting was left out. As for the characters, they were all a bunch of self centered jerks. Oh, and they are pretty stupid, too. Unless it makes total sense for warrior beings created to fight demons will cow tow to the threats of a lunatic who uses demons to attack them. Yeah, I didn't so, either. One thing that did play out well was that I thought Ms. Clare closed most of the significant plot arcs, providing a solid conclusion for this trilogy. Wait . . . there are more books? Are you sure? Um, I really hope this is not a case of a series meant to be a trilogy, but the author can't seem to leave it alone. Sigh. Maybe I should just leave it as a trilogy.
Probably one of the most annoying and irritating books I've ever read. Coming in third next to Beautiful Disaster and Lux.

This novel deals with very difficult issues such as depression, suicide and death that may be difficult for some readers "Sometimes I wonder if my heart is like a black hole--it's so dense that there's no room for light, but that doesn't mean it can't still suck me in." WOW... I am so blown away by this novel. It was raw, heart breaking, real and inspirational. I am still reeling from all of the emotions and I finished this over a week ago! Aysel pronounced Azel is a 17 year old girl with deep depression and no will to live. As stated in the synopsis, she wants to take her own life and finds a website where you can find a "suicide partner" to do it with. She chooses this in hopes that her partner will ensure that she does not flake our fail. She finds Frozen Robot Roman, a boy her age and they decide to commit suicide together. My heart absolutely was shattered by Aysel and Roman, the depression that they endure, the horrible experiences each has suffered in their lives and their perceived isolation were beyond what most humans could cope with. Although they are both dealing with different issues, as a reader I felt their pain and understood their reasons for the deep depression they each suffered from. "Depression is like a heaviness that you can't ever escape. It crushes down on you, making even the smallest things like tying your shoes or chewing on toast seem like a twenty-mile hike uphill. Depression is a part of you it's in your bones and your blood." Aysel was an outcast in her entire life, she was bullied at school and even her family did not understand her or even try to help her. She was alone, afraid and felt there was only one way out. After a tragic family event rocks Roman's family, his guilt begins to eat him alive. He becomes horribly depressed, closed off and gives up on everyone and everything that he loves. The way that Jasmine Warga wrote these characters, I only felt empathy and sorrow and I just wanted to help them. It takes talent in my opinion to write a book like this and have the reader empathize with your characters instead of feeling that they are noting more than a self absorbed "victim." Warga did this exactly the right way, and in doing so brought to light a very serious topic of depression and suicide, especially in young people. "Maybe the sadness comes just before the insanity" While reading this, I was so unsure how it would end. I had cried so many times throughout the novel and really worried myself over how it was going to end the entire time. I felt as though I was really a part of Aysel and Roman's lives and I cared so much about them and prayed they would get to have a future. Having dealt first hand with depression and seeing a family member suffer through it, My Heart and Other Black Holes really hit home for me. This book inspired me and left me hopeful that there is help and people can change. If they have the right people around to love and support them... anything is possible. "I will be stronger than my sadness." This is Jasmine Warga's debut novel, and she has absolutely impressed with her writing, her phrasing and her ability to evoke so many emotions. She wrote a book about a topic that needs to be heard and she gave a voice and a name to depression and suicide and did an amazing job! One thing I was missing though was an Epilogue, I really wanted a glimps of the future. But that is just a tiny complaint. This novel was absolutely beautiful and Warga completely pulled me into the lives of her characters and made me believe their stories. This novel has had such an emotional impact on me in such a positive way. If you have not read this novel, trust me when I tell you DO IT! "He's no longer the person I want to die with he's the person I want to be alive with." This was the first time that I have heard Rebecca Lowman narrate. I though she did an amazing job with this. She really captured the depression and angst of these characters. She did them and this story justice! I will definitely be on the look out for more narrations by her.

Umm... No thanks. What the heck did I just read? The plot was ALL OVER THE PLACE and omg instalove at it's finest ladies and gents..... This book is like it had more than one plot. The only reason why this isnt a one star review is because it is in verse. I love verse, but even the verses were awkward and choppy... Sorry just not my cup of tea.

Another recommendation, this time from a huge FNAF fan in my classroom. This book circulated through the fandom in the 5th grade and wound up on my back table with the statement that I was to keep it until I had read it, because they wanted me to know what their obsession was about. I can definitely see why middle grade readers that like horror and suspense would be enthralled with this book. I mean, I read it in one sitting! I've never been into horror, myself, but I just couldn't put it down! I know little to nothing about FNAF, but was able to follow everything just fine. It was engaging, for sure. It was written in such a way that it was easy to construct mental images that would send chills down one's spine. I do want to attach a warning label here, though. As I said, it IS part of the horror genre, and with good reason. At 10-11 like these kids, I would NOT have been ready to handle the content of this story. I would have had nightmares for weeks. The violent scenes have quite a level of detail in them that I rarely see in the suspense that I normally read. I feel like a lot of kids these days are more desensitized than I was and am, but still, I wouldn't recommend this for younger middle grade readers without their parents previewing it first and determining if they have the maturity to handle it. 3.5 stars rounded up to 4 due to the hearty recommendation that was given by my fifth graders. They would give it 5.

Someone please save me from the nightmare that is this moment. I am so disappointed. I have been waiting for this book for months now. Even preordered it. And the cover, how beautiful. THE COVER TRICKED ME. I so hardcore wanted this to be amazing. But it wasn't. Okay first of all- the plot. It's a story about a girl who dresses like a boy to achieve her goals while slinging a gun like a champ. This is a fine idea, and I personally like it, but I've seen so many like it lately. And this particular version did nothing to wow me or bring anything new to the table. For a large portion of the story the two main, hot, young hetero characters are venturing across the desert. Sidenote How do so many situations find a hot guy and girl adventuring together? Like why are seventeen-year-olds so special? And why are they always paired this way? Anyways, I honestly found myself skimming this pointless traveling majority of the book. Nothing happens that is even remotely important and it is so darn boring. This boringness includes the semblance of a romance intertwined in the plot, because that whole thing was just a huge fail. I didn't even care about the two main hot people kissing or anything. I would have preferred to just skip that altogether, which is really weird for me because I love romance in stories. There was literally no chemistry between them and barely any buildup to what I guess was intended to be the glue to the whole story. The main girl character Amani has been wanting to escape her desert homeland for basically her entire life and go to this mystical city she's heard about. But then she meets this handsome dude and she suddenly would follow him anywhere? The only part of this story that I liked was when we got to the magic part THAT THE BLURB PROMISED that was allllll the way at the end! GAHHHHH.. But! All of these annoying qualities would have ultimately been okay if not for the writing. That's where it died. Because the balance here between action and internal monologuing was too vast. And within that internal monologuing there was entirely too much pointless detail. To conjure up an example of my own so I don't have to type out what the book says because I'm feeling lazy As I walked down the dark dreary alley, that once I danced through on the night of the Dance. I thought about how my mother would never reach the world of her own thoughts. How love would never grace the lowly precedence set my her forefathers. Suddenly I heard a click at my temple. There was a .05 rifle slighshooter rifle notched easily against my cranium. "Time to die," said my assailant. I took in the situation and thought about what my great-great-grandfather would do. Oh how he loves dolphins. Where do you think dolphins even come from? Like we're in the desert here. Haha, I'm so funny. Sigh, I wonder what my best friend is doing right now. I have to give him back his lamp that I borrowed. Not sure why I had to borrow that but yeah. It's a yellow lamp that helps guide the way through the darkness. In my land, after the sun goes away, things become dark. We have begun to call that "Night." Suddenly my thoughts flashed back to the gun at my head. "Not today bitch," I screamed and grew a gun out of my own arm to shoot him. Logic doesn't matter here. Neither does time. Okay so there's an example. Like something would happen and then there would be this endless time in between the action and the reaction for thoughts and even sometimes conversations. It made no sense. One time they were getting attacked in the desert by magic creatures and suddenly they find out Amani is a girl and they have this whole argument about whether to trust her now ????????? Like what????? Are the ghouls coming after you????????????? I am lost. Basically the writing was too uneven and soiled what action the book did have. Plus with all the descriptions and random names, I got lost in the middle of action sequences. It was actually pretty impressive how confused I got. Anyways, if you want, you should try this book out. I didn't particularly like it though.

Remember the novel, 1984. Now imagine if teenagers had been in charge of the resistance. That's pretty much the essence of the story set in modern day America. I've always had a fondness for "false utopia" stories, particularly because I have such a fear of being told what I can and cannot read. This one has two things that set it apart from the others a great sense of humor and optimism. The author has obviously done extensive research into the technology of which he writes and is able to explain it in a way that non-computerphiles can understand. His characters are very well fleshed out. Basically, it's a great read. I also think it's an important read for this time in our country. When it looks as though people will be allowed to snoop on our telephone calls whenever they feel like it without fear of repercussion, it behooves us to be very aware of what is happening and what we can do to stop it.

OK this book was good made me cry in all the right spots and laugh at inappropriate times but there is just something about the book that makes me say 'eh it was OK'

To me this book was, in turns, boring and annoying. Nothing much happens. The book opens with a girl's dead body being found and that's about all the excitement there is. The main characters are 1 a weak-willed girl who lies about half the time she is actually speaking and 2 a crazy girl who needs some serious counseling. Unfortunately, this does not make it interesting, just sad and not much fun to read. There is no big moral of the story so at the end I just felt kind of annoyed that I'd continued to read the book waiting for something good or surprising to happen. There were no characters to relate to, no real mystery to solve because in the end you find out the guy who killed Zabet wasn't even a secondary character in the book. No one has a good relationship with anyone. It was just one big drag. I might not have disliked the book so much if the description on the back cover had not made it sound more exciting and interesting, more sleuthy, than it actually was. I feel misled. Product Description In this haunting tale, quirky loner Evie is in the wrong place at the wrong time when her sometime friend and total crush, Jonah, discovers a body in the woods - a body that turns out to be that of her childhood playmate. At the funeral, a fateful lie leads Evie into a complicated relationship with the dead girl's father and best friend. Before she realizes what is happening, Evie is on the hunt for a killer, spinning more lies along the way and putting herself in serious danger.

In the first book, protagonist Lily gave up being a mermaid a mermaid Princess to be exact in order to be with her human boyfriend and to live on land. What she didn't tell boyfriend Quince though is that by doing all of that, she would be giving up her right to be the Princess of Thalassinia. A large amount of the first book was set underwater but in this one, Lily is going to high school, preparing for SATs and thinking about her future and college. I really liked the difference in setting as it helped to show what a big decision Lily had made. Fins are Forever had quite a few plot twists which I really liked. Not only does Lily have to deal with everything that comes with being human, but her cousin Dosinia Doe turns up after being exiled. Doe has a strong hatred for humans and has been forced to live in the same world as them instead of her happy home under the sea. Lily is furious and doesn't want to be the one to deal with her but that's exactly what she gets. It is Lily who has to show Doe that she is wrong and to learn to love humans. Doe is all kinds of crazy and I loved the drama she brought to the story. She is the complete opposite of Lily so it was great to see the contrast between the two. Something very unexpected was that Doe ends up forming a bond of her very own with a human... Lily's ex-crush Brody to be exact. While this did bring out different emotions and characteristics in both Lily and Brody, it also forced the story to head back to the water for a while. It was nice to see familiar characters again and also for the world to be explained more. In this book, we get to know quite a bit about how the underwater world works and their political agendas. There was some quite serious stuff going on but I really enjoyed these aspects of the book. It made it something more than a cute mermaid romance story and gave it added depth. I really enjoyed Fins and Forever and considering the ending of the story, I cannot wait to see what happens with Lily next. The end was a big shock for me but I loved every word. If you're wanting a cute, easy read that's a bit difference then I recommend this series.
First half of the book is great....it keeps the reader wanting to read more. Once Luke gets out of his house, it gets harder to stay interested. The ending was rushed. Ultimately I was disappointed.

I randomly picked this one up from the library recently, but it was an okay listen for me. One I wasn't expecting Isabelle to be so young- granted, she's 13, but I assumed that she would be a lot older. Still, it's nice to see a book focused on a middle school character, instead of one in high school, which seems to be a lot more common. Two I didn't feel like Isabelle moved up the social ladder at all. Sitting at the popular for all of two weeks...we don't see much change in Isabelle's social status as result, and she's more on the periphery than anything else. Three At one point Ashley is bleeding from her mouth after we see both girls purge. Nothing happens with this, and it seemed like a random thing to bring up, only for Ashley to be perfectly fine. It's explained away as "it happens sometimes, it's no big deal." I really expected Ashley to end up in the hospital or something. Four I did like seeing how Isabelle changed over the course of the book. By the end of the book, she was starting to deal with the death of her father, and she got to the point where she went over a day without throwing up, and I like seeing that change in her. Five Danielle Ferland seem to narrate a teenage girl pretty well, but there was nothing about her performance that really stood out to me. I wouldn't avoid any books narrated by her, but I'm also not running out to see what else she's narrated. Six This has more to do with the actual CD's I checked out with the library, but there were a couple tracks on the last disk that were a little funky, and went super fast, so there are a few minutes I ended up missing...including the very end. I should probably say something when I return it. Seven Isabelle goes to group therapy, and Trish wants to see her individually...but it seems like no one ever mentions anything to Isabelle's mom. Really? You want to see her more, and yet you only ask Isabelle, a 13-year-old girl, about it? That seems a little weird to me. Eight It seemed pretty open-ended, with not a lot of resolution, which is fine, but...I don't know. I think I wanted more of a conclusion. Or even a longer book, because it wasn't much over 4 hours, and maybe things could have been a little more resolved then they were in the book. Nine Her dad's death was super-vague. She only mentioned he died unexpectedly, and that he was sick but they didn't know about it, so that was really weird. Did the mom know, and not give her kids more information, or did everyone just get taken off-guard. There was just something off about his death. Ten How she treated her little sister. I'm an only child so sibling relationships are completely foreign to me, but I thought Isabelle treated her younger sister by three years sort of mean. Eleven The fact that a 13 year-old and ten-year-old are making themselves pizza from scratch and mac and cheese and have to feed themselves because their mom still cries herself to sleep at night and randomly sleeps during the day...they weren't completely on their own, and their mom didn't completely check out. But they were still on their own a lot, which is weird because their mom is a college professor teaching a couple classes. The mom also seems to constantly grading papers understandable, given it's English she teaches . And I'm sure the mom has meetings and office hours, but there was something off about the mom too. Besides grieving, something didn't fit quite right. My Rating 2 stars. I wanted to like it more, but it was just okay.

It was nice to know a little bit more about the series' background the playlist was a nice bonus too... I received this book from netgalley in exchange for an honest review, which will also be posted on my blog thisisjustabookblog.tumblr.com I found that this book started off with quite a lot of potential, but quickly went downhill. The female protagonist, Kate, has been diagnosed with diabetes for over a year, but is struggling to deal with it. Aiden, the male protagonist, lost an arm while serving in the army, and is struggling to assimilate to life back home. The novel's written in alternating first person point of view, so you get both Kate and Aiden equally, and I have to say that I enjoyed his chapters and his story a little bit more. Kate was immature, and selfish, and I felt that Perry's depiction of her struggle with diabetes was a little bit superficial. I was offended by her talk of the insulin pump as disgusting or strange - my sister has one, and it's neither. It makes life a lot easier for a lot of people struggling with a horrible condition, and I felt that the way Kate talked about the condition was actually pretty insulting. She doesn't see the consequences of her actions - things that are actually life threatening - until Aiden shouts at her, and then she suddenly sees it, which is a bit weird. I just didn't understand. Aiden was slightly better, though not amazing. He's struggling to come to terms with the loss of his arm, and Kate is really the only one that treats him like normal. At the beginning of the novel, their interaction was interesting, and fun, and it had so much potential. But I feel like the author only really scratched the surface in the novel. She could have developed both of their struggles further in a much better way, when it comes to Kate , and also their relationship, which seemed to kind of plateau for the second half of the novel, until it came to a far too easy and simple resolution at the end. Though not terrible by any means, I wouldn't call the writing 'good'. There were a couple of editing mistakes, and I found that the writing could be sloppy - prepositions were missing when they should be, so that the prose read more like speech than anything, as well as some comma splices and sentences that just weren't grammatically correct. It wasn't a big thing, as I wouldn't say it was that detrimental to the reading of the novel, but I'm a but picky, and as I noticed it, it did affect my reading experience.

spoiler alert Every now and then, that little bug nips at my skin. A popular book that I can't stop hearing about, constantly being recommended to me. Popularity tends to rank on the "hit or miss" scale with me. For example, I loved The Secret History by Donna Tartt. I don't even remember how long that book was, only that I had to keep coming back to it. Featuring characters who were so incredibly unlikable that they were strangely likable and incredibly beautiful, lyrical prose that called to mind the very classics that these college students were studying. I loved Jeffrey Eugenides' The Virgin Suicides, with prose that infused the novel with an unsettling, eerie atmosphere. On the other hand, I kind of hated Will Grayson, Will Grayson, Her Fearful Symmetry, The Ocean at the End of the Lane, and A Darker Shade of Magic. Thus, Cassandra Clare's City of Bones. Recommended to me by several people. Massively popular. Made into a movie franchise that ultimately trickled away into the dark recesses of development hell . A TV show, even! I knew of Clare and her dealings on the internet, as well as the claims of plagiarism. But hey, I'm an adult. I can read a work without considering the dealings of an author. And initially, I thought, "I can do this! This isn't so bad! There's a light at the end of this tunnel!" You see, for as much as I didn't like the previous popular novels mentioned above, the least I can say for them is that they were written professionally. Edited. Showcased sentences of varying length and word usage. And as much as I disliked how bisexuality was portrayed in A Darker Shade of Magic, well . . . I will be upfront with you and admit right now that I'm not particularly fond of dialogue that follows the "witty-witty-bang-bang" volley of "intellectual" minds. For that matter, I don't think sass or sarcasm infers intelligence. I think it just implies immaturity. It's that game of, "I'm so much smarter than you." For this reason, I never cared for Buffy the Vampire Slayer in its television incarnation. Sarcasm can be a defining characteristic. When all of your characters act this way though, it makes it seem as though they are not so much characters as walking, talking expies of a writer's supposed wit. For that matter, when a character makes a sarcastic comment about child abuse that is meant to lighten the mood, it makes me a little sick to my stomach. As I said, I was willing to give this book credit where it was due. I don't read books in the hope that I'm going to hate them. I read popular books because I want to be surprised. Initially, I started to think that City of Bones might be a Wizard of Earthsea case for me, a book that ended up amusing me greatly and bringing me joy while I was very ill. This is not the same case. In fact, this is a far worse case, considering that the book is littered with quotes from John Milton and Arthur Rimbaud. City of Bones opens with one Clary Fray, 15, somehow managing to get into a popular night club with her childhood friend Simon Lewis. She witnesses the murder of a young man by a group of teenagers, people her friend Simon is incapable of seeing. And when the young man dies, he dissipates into thin air. This is Clary's first instance that leads her into the world of Shadowhunters and seeing the world as it really is, filled with vampires, werewolves, demons, mermaids, and angels. "All the stories are true," Jace Wayland, a Shadowhunter Clary grows particularly close to, tells her. Every single mythological creature possible really does exist in the world. And Shadowhunters exist as a police force against demons who would ruin the world for "mundanes" humans and "downworlders" werewolves, vampires, the like . Clary is eventually brought to the Institute where Hodge resides, who trains Shadowhunters Jace and siblings Alec and Isabelle Lightwood. It is revealed to her that she is capable of seeing past the glamor of the world because Clary herself has Shadowhunter blood within her, from her mother Jocelyn. Things are complicated when said mother who has all the answers to Clary's questions is kidnapped, which slowly pulls Clary further and further down the Shadowhunter rabbit hole. Clary serves as our female protagonist du jour. She can draw, but isn't as good as her artist mother. She's cute, but not as beautiful as the tall and curvy Isabelle. Her defining trait is how stubborn she is, insistent on saving her mother from the hands of big bad Valentine. And yet, she's not really a character. Everything that happens to her is because it has to happen to her for the progression of the story. More time is spent forcing her to end up in a relationship with Jace than with exploring her fascination with a world that was hidden to her the entirety of her life. This would make her name all the more fun to play with, considering that "Clary" reminds one of the word "clarity." To contrast her forgettable quality, Clary is often transformed into a shrill, slapping shrewd and treated with disregard by the other Shadowhunters for caring about her mother and the well being of Simon. There is one slap that is warranted, administered to Jace after he puts her life in danger. And her banter with Jace, which is meant to be cute and flirty, is often confusing. "You're driveling," she tells Jace at one point. Can anyone tell me of one teenager who would actually say that instead of, "Shut up"? That is not so fetch, Clare. However, the animosity of this novel becomes more apparent with Simon. As the lone human, and a self-described "geek," Simon is often treated exactly as how he labels himself. The Shadowhunters, despite the fact that their very existence is to protect mankind, seem to care nothing about Simon's life. When he's transformed into a rat and kidnapped by the vampires, their reaction is akin to "oh well." Um. I don't think I want to trust my life in the hands of these hunters. The only reason why Jace follows Clary is because she's going to go save her friend no matter what he thinks. My boiling point came when Simon witnessed a kiss between Jace and Clary. For you see, Simon has been eternally friend-zoned by Clary. Never mind the fact that he has never told her of his attraction. Never mind the fact that he salivates over Isabelle and wants to be by her side at Magnus' party. Simon is infuriated by Clary when he sees her with another man and tells her then that everything he's done has been to gain her interest. And Clary is meant to feel bad about this?! What the hell! She can decide who she wants to date. She doesn't have to date Simon just because he's accrued enough brownie points and now wants to cash in. Just because he loves her doesn't mean she has to love him back. That is unfair and mean and is entirely intended to either cast Clary or Simon in a bad light. No. No. No. This is something that has taken me a long time to accept myself and I feel as though more women need to be told this. Just because a man loves you doesn't mean you have to be nice to him. It doesn't mean you need to date him just to make him feel better. If you don't love someone, that's it. You're not in love. You do not owe them anything. And if they're upset with continuing to have a role as your friend, maybe they don't deserve to be your friend. Simon really couldn't redeem himself though after Clary asked him if he was gay and his response was, "I'd dress much better if I was." Jace is a sass machine who was programmed with the saddest past possible. He is every possible cliche of a "bad boy" even down to the black clothes and rune tattoos. But at least Jace is laughable, perhaps not with Clare's original intention. His entire change around Valentine is akin to Buzz Lightyear discovering his relationship with Zurg in Toy Story 2, as they play frisbee with each other. "Thanks, dad!" Much like Clary, Jace doesn't really have a character and flip flops about simply for the plot's sake. This is mostly evident in the last few chapters as the writing attempts to make a character out of this sack of cliches and fails. In fact, those last few chapters are just terrible. They are boring in the worst possible way, not including the sad attempts to take these characters seriously. Isabelle exists simply to be the other woman. Her only purpose in the entire story is to make Clary jealous about her body and to tempt Simon. In fact, it's said constantly that Isabelle lures men. Then, at the end, Clary and Isabelle are magically friends who hug it out. Show me these two becoming friends. I want to see how Isabelle and Clary start to grow fond of each other. The scene in which Isabelle dresses up Clary doesn't even come close, as it's entirely meant to show how Clary is so different from the privileged and beautiful Isabelle. We're getting into warmer territory now. Oh, Alec. Where to begin? I will say that I think Alec is a needed component in this group of Shadowhunters simply because he doesn't snark all the time and often takes Jace's sarcasm seriously. My positive thoughts end there, though. Because, for you see, Alec is not a character. He's a sexuality. That's the entire reason for his existence in this book. Rather than, you know, develop him and slowly reveal his fears about coming out, Clary just asks Isabelle out of the blue, "Is Alec gay?" And it's like, yeah, how did you know? I don't know, maybe because he dresses so well. What information ever gave Clary that inclination? We're never shown Alec being attracted to anyone at that point. He seems far more aloof around Clary but what reason has she given him to trust her? She's placing his childhood friend in danger. Oh, but it gets better. Alec is not wary of Clary because she's placing Jace in danger or that she's trying to edge into his circle of trusted people he's known all his life. No. Alec is mean and distrustful of her because Alec is in love with Jace. She's moving in on his man. I do not have the words for how angry this makes me. I do not. It gets better. So of course the only character that Alec can hook up with is bisexual warlock Magnus Bane. Have I mentioned he's bisexual? Because he's bisexual. He wears glitter. Never mind the fact that Magnus is a 400 year old warlock and Alec is 17? 18? And yet this whole relationship is treated as cute by Isabelle. I am all for taking a relationship like this and treating it seriously. But the fact that it's meant to be cute is really unsettling to me. Far more unsettling than the brother-sister relationship thing, which is obviously not true. If it were true, this book would be far more interesting. And I've heard of so many other stories that Clare takes from in this series, but I had very strong Tokyo Babylon feelings around Magnus, Alec, and Isabelle. I also felt very strong Persona 3 vibes in this as well, which is how I knew Hodge would betray them from the beginning, because Ikutsuki-san did! The worst aspect of this is that I think the author confused character depth with love triangles. Everyone's in one. Simon's in a love triangle with Isabelle and Clary, Clary's in a love triangle with Simon and Jace, Jace's in a love triangle with Clary and Alec, Alec's in a love triangle with Jace and Magnus, and Magnus is in a love triangle with Alec and indolence. The other characters are all pretty routine. Valentine is the villain because somebody has to be the villain of this story. He never actually does anything villainous and never actually appears in the story until the end, but villain he is. If you were hoping he had extremely cliched villain speeches, guess what! Hodge is so obvious in his ambiguity. And Luke is boring, boring, boring. His inclusion in the novel is when it drags the most. Especially the unnecessary werewolf pack that is only needed for extraneous bodies to be killed. It's cool, I didn't care about them either. The writing features absolutely no variety and this entire story is exposition. I don't remember how many times I called characters "walking-talking exposition" in my notes. The entire world of Shadowhunters is dumped upon you by everyone. In no way are you allowed to experience this world through the writer's talent. Everything is told. Nothing is shown. I think the worst aspect of this was when Alec was close to dying and we don't even get to see how he's saved. It all happens off-screen and we're told later what happened. I would have been far more interested in that than what happened in the last two chapters. In case you need it, here is a whole list of my "thanks for telling" thanks for telling me those aren't real police officers, thanks for so obviously changing the subject with Isabelle, thanks for telling me this is foreboding, thanks for telling us about Jocelyn, yes Jace, let's tell her some more, tell her how EVERYTHING happened, thanks for telling me Alec is gay, thanks for telling us exactly what happened to you Magnus, thanks for telling us he wants to hurt Clary, thanks for even telling us about yourself Abaddon, thanks for everyone TELLING us about a villain who has had little to no importance in this story so far. Not to mention, there are some very troubling sentences. "A shriek tore itself out of Clary's throat." "He grinned the ghost of a grin." "The weapons room looked exactly the way something called 'the weapons room' sounded like it would look." There are "fragrant tangles" and Isabelle's hair which is always described as "sticky," which sounds like a problem she should go see a doctor for. The only moment in which I liked this book was when Dorothea was taken over by a demon and Clary hears a clattering sound, thinking its Dorothea's bracelets. She looks down to realize it's her teeth, falling out of her mouth. I love that. I think it's fantastic. But it's ruined by an entire novel that insists on forcing this world down your throat, a world that the author doesn't even fully realize in the novel. What exactly does this "stele" do? It seems like it's just a plot-hole saving device. Is there really any necessity to having the downworlders as part of this story? If you're telling me that every mythological creature possible exists, then show that to me. Don't just mention one and be like, "Oh, hey, they all exist here!" How can you take Nephilim, creatures that are so monstrous, amorphous, and bizarre, and make them so ordinary? This makes me miss Madeline L'Engle's incredibly bizarre take on theological creatures. I've been thinking of returning to Progo Ultimately this is an incredibly lazy novel. And it's infuriating because the building blocks exist. I keep thinking about how this would be such a better novel if Clary were left to her own devices for the majority of the novel. Or if she really couldn't trust the Shadowhunters or the Clave. Or if she was thrown into every demon encounter with just her and Simon. But this novel never wants to go into murkier territory. It stays true to its predictable young-adult path and never wavers.

Even though I just finished the book, I still feel way too confused. The story is all over the place and at times seems ridiculous and improbable even for a fantasy book. I had no idea what was happening throughout it. None of the mysteries were solved, almost everything was left unexplained. I understand that the point of the first book was to introduce us to the characters, the world and the dark powers that lurk within, but even that was poorly done. Nick was a character I couldn't identify with. He was too weird. Despite the fact that there were so many bizarre things happening, he refused to believe that there were supernatural beings. He firmly believed that he was right and was oblivious of everything. Then he meets Acheron, who happens to be a god, and he immediately accepts that as a fact. All of a sudden he starts believing in gods, immortality, zombies and all sort of things, which didn't seem likely due to the nature of his character. Oh yeah, and he's not afraid of a god at all. Instead he talks to him as if they are childhood friends and even calls him Ash. Another thing I didn't like about Nick is that he didn't want to believe there were vampires. Oh, but there are zombies, demons and gods. Vampires, however, don't exist for him. No matter how others tried to reason with him, he didn't buy it. Plus, it was obvious that Kyrian, his guardian, was a vampire. There were hints here and there that he was but nope, Nick, of course, didn't get it. Moreover, Nick pretends to be a very cautious guy. He wouldn't trust a stranger no matter what. Or that's how he appears to be. The truth, however, is that he immediately starts trusting Kyrian when offered money. Yeah, because if a stranger suddenly gives money to a very poor boy and pay him 1000 a month for doing nothing that will make him a generous and reliable person. No, that's not how life works, Nick. I had a problem with the Peters who looked down on Nick just because he was poor. I mean, what kind of a teacher does that? And then insult him by calling him a 'hoodlum' and say that he is inferior to the 'honour students'. The hell was that all about? I can't accept this as normal. The rest of the characters were way too generic and not worth mentioning. Honestly, I expected much more from this book given the high rating it has here on goodreads. But anyways, onto the next book.

Es un retelling del cuento de las "Doce princesas bailarinas". Tras la muerte de su madre, el Rey les ordena guardar el luto durante doce meses sin bailes y sin jugar en los jardines. Mientras su pais y su padre esta en guerra, las chicas solo quieren divertirse. Despues de que todo se resuelve, en vez de ganar en aplomo, se dedican a la tarea de enganchar un marido 15, 16 y 17 anos, las mayores con mas voracidad de la necesaria. Los romances fueron un poco desabridos y las chicas propensas a las rabietas y a responder de mal modo, realmente, no me termina de cerrar. Lo siento, creo que "Mujercitas" de M.Alcott, trata el tema de la guerra, el sentido de permanecer a una familia, ayudar a los demas en tiempo de necesidad, perdida de familia ante enfermedades, sacrificios por amor y romances de epoca de una forma elegante, algo que este retelling, con toda la magia y complot no puede llegar a reflejar una parte positiva de toda esta aventura. You know you've found a great book when you find that upon laying it down for the night, the book takes hold of all your dreams. When you find yourself dreaming about all that has already occured in the book along with the potential of what is yet to come, it's at that point you know you have a new favorite book and series on your hands. For the first time in a long time, this is exactly what happened to me when I first read Suzanne Collins's "The Hunger Games". Note spoilers ahead . "The Hunger Games" takes place in a future distopic, totalitarian United States. The United States of America as we know it has ceased to exist and is now a country which has initially broken up into 13 districts, with a Capital City. Each distric is responsible for cultivating a certain material, native to its region, which is then harvested in large quantity for those who live in the Capital with the residents of that district benefiting from their work last. As quite often happens in societies where the government takes advantage of its people, the districts rise-up against the governement. Unfortunately the uprising fails and Distric 13 is destroyed. Jumping 74 years into what is present day for the books heroine, Katniss Everdeen, the reader learns that following the failed uprising the Captial instigated the Hunger Games, a televised fight to the death among 24 teenaged boys and girls. Every year on the day of what is known as "the reaping", each district's occupants gather in the town's main square where the names of one young boy and one young girl are drawn. As District 12 gathers in the town square for the current year's reaping, the citizens find themselves witnessing the drawing of Peeta Mellark, son of the baker and Primrose Everdeen, Katniss's youngers sister. In order to protect her sister, Katniss volunteers to take Prim's place. With Katniss and Peeta being the new tributes for the coal mining District 12, the two say farewell to their family and friends, well aware they will in all probability never see them again, and head to the Capital and the Hunger Games arena. On their course to the arena, Katniss finds herself being portrayed as part of a "star-crossed" lovers pair with Peeta, who has professed his secret love for her on national tv. With the knowledge that she and Peeta must present themselves in love and heartbroken over the fact they may have to kill one another, Katniss and the rest of the tributes enter the arena and begin a fight to the death. During Katniss's time in the arena, she finds herself making alliances only to lose them, facing possible betrayals, confronting her fears and bearing witness to monstrosities to horrible to have ever dreamed possible. In the end, Katniss and Peeta find themselves to be the two remaining tributes and they make the mutual choice to end their lives simultaneously, rather than fight one another to the death. Seeing this, what comes to be viewed as an act of rebellion, the Capital steps in and declares them both winners. Peeta and Katniss are then free to return to their home as victors. My thoughts I cannot even begin to praise this book enough, that's how much I loved it. It consumed both my waking and sleeping thoughts. Even now, after having finished reading it over a month ago, I still find myself experiencing the occasional dream, reliving the action of the book. Needless to say, it has made its way onto my listo f favorite books and is one of my new favorite series. I think one of the things I enjoyed most about this book, aside from the plot and the empowering heroine Katniss, was that elements of it reminded me of other pieces of literature and even film that I enjoy. While reading the reaping scene, when the tributes are chosen, I found myself recalling Shirley Jackson's "The Lottery". The fighting in the arena reminded me of the movie "The Running Man", while the segment of the story where Katniss sets out to destroy the careers and makes them the hunted instead of the hunters, I found to be reminiscent of the short story "The Most Dangerous Game". In the end, I know this is a book I will not only read more than once, but one I will suggest to all of my friends. Now if only the opening of the film adaptation weren't so far off.
