When eighteen-year-old Levi returned from Denver City with his latest scavenged finds, he never imagined he'd find his village of Glenrock decimated, loved ones killed, and many--including his fiancee, Jem-taken captive. Levi is determined to rescue what remains of his people, even if it means entering the Safe Lands, a walled city that seems anything but safe. Omar knows he betrayed his brother by sending him away, but helping the enforcers was necessary. Living off the land and clinging to an outdated religion holds his village back. The Safe Land has protected people since the plague decimated the world generations ago ... and its rulers have promised power and wealth beyond Omar's dreams. Meanwhile, their brother Mason has been granted a position inside the Safe Lands, and may be able to use his captivity to save not only his people, but also find a cure for the virus that threatens everyone inside the Safe Lands. Can Mason uncover the truth hidden behind the Safe Land's facade before it's too late? What I Loved... The inspiration for this book is great and opened my mind to dig deeper into the lives and people that shaped the bible. It is clever! I loved Mason! I felt myself drawn most to him. The book is a great mix of adventure, hilarity, love and suspense. Jordan! He was a riot. I warmed up to him once in the Safe Lands. What I Liked... The creativity of the Sim Art and other technology. The small details like the slang...it helped me feel like I was there. While some may think that the use of vapor and promiscuity may have seemed surprising, I didn't. We live in that world now and it would only make sense that the future would hold more of the same but in a "new" way. Again very creative. Other... I don't like Ciddah. There! I said it. I just can't help it. I am not a Dystopian reader usually, BUT Jill has opened up my mind to branch out in my reading selections. I love how this book idea was derived from a bible study and am looking into using this book for my bible study class. More at who YA reading? This book has one of the most beautiful writing I've ever seen. I'd go as far as to say it's on par with Laini Taylor. It's magic. Wicked like a wildfire is a novel about twin sisters who have the ability to manipulate beauty. They live quiet lives with their mother, Jasmina, who has the ability to make pastry that transports people and evokes beautiful imagery of places in their minds. She is fierce, insanely protective and a bit paranoid. She forbids her daughters from ever "gleaming" in public and from ever falling in love. Iris has the ability to see flowers as fractals and can turn her kaleidoscope visions into glass-work. She is as fierce as Jasmina and is quite a rebel, often fighting with her mother. Malina can interpret moods as music and has the ability to entrance people with her musical abilities. She's the sweet, cinnamon-roll twin who'd never hurt a fly. The sisters' sheltered life is abruptly turned upside down when their mother is attacked. To save her, the girls set off in search of answers, accompanied by two of their close friends. Slowly they start to unravel their mother's mysterious past and discover a curse that looms over their family line. I haven't seen anyone point this out but I feel it's incredibly important to mention that Wicked like a wildfire has some diversity. The book is set in Montenegro and the twins are half-Japanese. There's also a F F romance and it is the purest, most adorable thing ever. Also, the twins' close friends are Romani. This is a book that so perfectly explores the relationships between sisters and mothers and daughters. It was especially beautiful to witness the relationship between Iris and Malina it brought me near tears several times throughout. The characters felt so real and incredibly complex. There was a lot of girl power the women introduced in this book are all beautiful and deadly in their own ways. The magical aspects of this book are truly original and everything has an almost circus-like witchy vibe, which I adored. The writing is absolutely gorgeous lush, magical and out-of-this-world. One of the most unique books I've ever read. It did take me some time to get into the story and I wanted some of the side characters to be more fleshed-out, but aside from that, I really recommend this book! Check out more reviews at my blog

Nope. Let me start off by saying that I did not rate this book low because I'm an uber fan who is disappointed in the ending. I have always been wary of this series. I do have issues with the ending, moreso with how it happened, and how pointless it was, but the whole death of a certain character did not upset me. And no, I don't mean that I hated that person and was glad they died. I do like it when authors can be bold enough to kill characters and do it in a honorable way. So, I'm not just some fan here having a tantrum over who died. Throughout the series I have felt that all of the characters were under developed. Especially with the minor characters, none were distinct. This continued in Allegiant. Worse, was that small characters I had not seen since book 1, which I read over a year ago, were brought up and were supposed to have an emotional impact on me because they were hurt, or dying, or whatever. But I had no idea who these people were. A simple one sentence recap about the roles they played in past books may have helped, but overall I think this was a fault of the characters lacking depth. For instance, Christina and Cara felt identical to me at times. Uriah and Caleb, the same. I was not a fan of the duo narration. Tobias did not have a distinct voice. Many times I was taken out of the story because I thought I was reading as Tris only to realize it was Tobias narrating. And then literally one line later he says something so Tris-like I had to backtrack all the dialogue to double check who in fact was narrating. This was really distracting. As for the story itself, it was simply not for me. Insurgent left with a good cliffhanger, which I was eager to discover the truth behind. But Allegiant's big reveal was rather bland. Most importantly, it was revealed too soon, around the 100 page mark in a 500 page book . Everything was info dumped right up front and then repeated or expanded upon for 300 more pages. All of this new information about the outside world became the final conflict, and I just was not vested in these new issues. Spending so much time on the truth behind this society would have worked better if it had been original world building in the first book. Instead, it feels hastily thrown in at the end, like she just now came up with a reason behind her world. It was added too late for me to form attachment to this backstory. Meanwhile, all the people and the city we HAVE come to care about got dropped only to be used in ways uncharacteristic of what they used to be. The bottom line is that I had to force myself to keep reading. Roth proved herself to be a good storyteller with Insurgent, and then just dropped the ball. The plot of Allegiant is a total mess. My biggest issue was with how little any of it made sense. Spoilers from here out... I did like the idea of the genetic problems, but I found some faults with the plot. According to the book, scientists eliminated the genes that made people evil, but then that messed us up more and there were wars, and then the government established these experiments hoping that our genes would fix themselves. I believe Chicago was in the 8th generation of people. So, if a generation is roughly, 20 years, that is 160 years. I believe I have since seen it said that it was actually 80 years. It's been 160 years! Has science not advanced at all?? And furthermore, if all the good genes were eliminated, how were the good genes coming back? That is genetically impossible, someone has to pass them down!!! That is science! And what about other countries? This was the history of the USA but no other countries were ever mentioned. Did we mess up the whole world's genes too? Has the rest of the world died out? Or is the future USA so bigoted that they won't repopulate with the pure genes of other races? Nope, this whole theory that the book is entirely based on did not fly with me. So narrow and forced. Either take the time to explain your world, or come up with something more simple. Then Tris comes along and thinks that her 16 year old self who has been in the real world for about 2 days knows better than the Bureau who has been studying genetics for over 100 years. She has this "brilliant" plan, which actually sucks. Except that Roth would have you think it doesn't suck at all because all the faults are just brushed over. She succeeded in wiping the memories of all everyone working at the Bureau, but it was mentioned several times that they had superiors that they reported to. Would the rest of the government just not notice that an entire branch suddenly forgot its job? Apparently so. Not to mention that Tris died for nothing. If her mission was to stop the Bureau from resetting the memories of all of Chicago, her actions and subsequent death weren't useful because Tobias stopped the war inside the city already, which was the whole reason for her suicide mission. If her mission was simply to end the genetic prejudices that people had, she really didn't affect it on a large scale. As stated above, there is a government higher than the Bureau, there are Genetically Pure soldiers working for said government, and Genetically Damaged people living in the slums, all of whom were unaffected and still have the prejudices. NOTHING WAS ACCOMPLISHED! Not only did Tris die for NOTHING, but the entire trilogy has accomplished NOTHING. The victory is limited ONLY to the city of Chicago. The city that got brushed aside this entire book. I don't mind that Tris died, but I didn't think it was noble. Yes, I have read Veronica Roth's blog, and I still don't agree with her reasons for killing Tris. She mentions how Tris was sacrificing herself for Caleb. It was mentioned over and over again how she was immune to the truth serum and simulation serum, so she had a high chance of being immune to the death serum. She actually had the thought going into the room with the airborne death serum that 'I will survive this.' And she did. So, with her, and the reader KNOWING she would survive it, HOW IS THIS A SACRIFICE?! So what happens after Tris survives the impossible to survive death serum? Does she become a super hero and donate her genes to fixing people? Does she stand up to the government since she can't be manipulated by them and make a change? No, she gets shot and dies. So anticlimactic after this amazing feat. Whyyyyyy did we go through this whole serum thing? Why even state over and over that she could survive it?! It did not matter in the end, so why was it hammered into the brain of the reader? False hope? Shotty writing? Just... nothing about her death felt satisfying at all. She may have died in the end, but that was just coincidence, not her going into it with a sacrificial mindset, so we need to STOP calling this heroic. And then as I am reeling from her death, and the nothingness that it accomplished, I had to sit through a dang 20 page epilogue about freaking Shauna and her sad legs, who I don't even remember!! Why was this random character given such center stage at the end? She did nothing in this book. And Tobias is sad and cannot overcome his fears. Not a satisfying ending at all. Sorry. I do want to disclaim that I don't think that Roth is a poor writer, I have read her blog and think she addresses her audience very well there. It's just that they way this story was told did not draw me in, or make me care about the characters or events happening. This is a personal preference. I am an avid reader, so I think that I am able to discern what types of stories are well developed and told in ways that suit me, and this was simply not for me. The bottom line for me is that even if I were the most die hard fan of the series, I would still have seen the above flaws in the plot and with the motives. I can't put blinders on and pretend like this was a decent story. This is the worst series finale I have ever read, and Allegiant was my worst read of 2013. Unless you are a diehard fan of this series and can put those blinders on and see everything as being rosy, then I wouldn't recommend this series to anyone.

I have a secret fondness for selkies. They aren't deadly, like some mythological creatures, and they're most well known for being kidnapped and stuck with horrible men, which is not a great fate. But there's something about the folklore that resonates with me. The two young people at the center of TIDES are Noah and Mara. Noah is working as an intern at the Marine Science Research his last summer before college and living with his grandmother the lighthouse keeper and younger sister who needed to get away from their parents . He can't wait to move on and go to college in the fall. Mara is a selkie whose sister Aine was kidnapped years ago. Now, the Elder of her group is afraid to let the youngest selkies grow and Mara and her brother are stuck perpetually babysitting. She wants to be a leader and is chafing under the rules that keep her close and powerless. Then they meet. TIDES is a quiet, lovely novel that builds to an action-packed finish. It's morality is fairly simple, but explored in interesting ways. It shows the ways that people can hurt each other, accidentally and on purpose, as well as how they can forge new connections and become stronger. I liked TIDES had a plot that came together neatly, even though the focus was on character. Almost every character in TIDES has their own motivations and goals. Even the grandmother Gemm has a lovely lesbian romance that's given a fair amount of detail. There are also differences between the humans and selkies, culturally as well as physically. Perhaps my favorite moment that illustrated the difference was when Mara first meets Lo and muses about how she does and doesn't look like Noah and decides that they do look enough alike to be siblings. Then a human immediately mistakes them for not-siblings since Lo is adopted and Chinese. I did feel that Lo's eating disorder was overcome somewhat quickly, but I liked that it never completely disappeared from the story despite not being the focus. It's not a disease that shows up much outside of issue books. I think TIDES will appeal to fans of classic fantasy novels like A RING OF ENDLESS LIGHT by Madeleine L'Engle. It has that quiet, intimate appeal. It's also a good choice for YA fans looking for a slightly older protagonist. Noah definitely doesn't have high school worries. I thoroughly enjoyed TIDES, and think I would've even if I weren't fond of selkies.

As someone who isn't really into video games, particularly first person shooters, I feel like a lot of this book was lost on me. That being said, I think even if I absolutely loved video games I would not have loved this. The amount of suspension of disbelief this book requires is just too much. The premise is so flimsy. The author does at least try to fill in the gaps and provide some kind of justification for the way things are, but there are still entirely too many holes in the plot to make it believable. This was frustrating for me as a reader because I love getting lost in the story and I just couldn't do it with this one. Not only is the plot full of holes, but I never felt like the story was moving toward any real point. The sense of urgency is completely lost. Yeah, there are aliens attacking earth, and the characters worry about it, but the larger focus is on the arguments between Miki and her friends, and the budding romance between Miki and Jackson. The hot and cold, back and forth crap between Miki and Jackson drove me nuts. They don't have any connection to begin with, and then to top it all off they alternate between spewing cheesy crap to one another that feels so fake it's almost painful to read and bickering at one another. As people died throughout the story, I felt no remorse because I didn't feel like I really knew a thing about them. I wish there had been more focus on the world building in this novel, and that the author had paid more mind to ensuring that the reasoning provided for things was believable. Between the lackluster world building and the poorly developed characters, this book was not my thing at all. That being said, I think if you are a reader who adores first person shooter games and aliens, you will love this book.

I received this from NetGalley in exchange for an honest review. Andy suddenly finds herself in a white room with six strangers. None of them have any idea where they are, how they got there, or what they are doing there. They are forced to participate in various scenarios, each of which ends with a fade to black and one of the kids gone. It turns out that they have been brought to the Place of Dreams to confront whatever fear is holding them back from following their dreams. John Dreamer has such a promising premise. Too bad that is all it has going for it. The writing was basic, and while "basic" isn't necessarily a bad thing, in this case it was. The prose is juvenile and reads like a school assignment written by someone who doesn't particularly care about their grade. I kind of feel bad saying this, but I legitimately rolled my eyes almost the entire time I read this, which thankfully was not that long. The characters are one-dimensional. The book is largely told from Andy's point of view except for one random chapter told from Roy's perspective which makes absolutely no sense , and she makes judgments about the others based on what she observes. We are meant to take these judgments as absolute fact despite never learning much about any of them. Each character is given a stereotype and fulfills it to the best of their ability. None of the characters have any meaningful interactions or any depth at all. Later, when only Andy and John remain, she talks about missing the friendships they had and I found myself wondering if I had maybe skipped six or seven chapters because they all barely spoke to each other yet she considered them friends. What is absolutely appalling is the romance. Andy claims that she knew she was in love with John after 8.5 seconds, after looking in his eyes. Much of the time they are in the Place of Dreams, she shies away from both holding his hand and looking him in the eye, despite how much she claims to want to. The reason she's afraid has to do with an event in her past that isn't mentioned until the very, very end, if you care enough to get that far into this drivel. I mean, the book is called John Dreamer, so you think that John is going to be important, but he really isn't. No one in this book is important. Even the premise, which is so, so intriguing, isn't explored all that much. The scenarios to help them conquer their fears range from accidentally killing someone to having an appointment with a therapist, and even though they know what's going on after the first one, they still fall for it every single time. At one point they discover a room of videos, which may or may not be real, and one of them has John's name on it. I believe it's supposed to add mystery, but we never learn the importance of this, and the kids don't even know if it's real. Not to mention, it's very unclear as to where the kids go when they leave the Place of Dreams. Presumably they are returned to their lives, but at what point? The ringmaster or whoever will bring proof that after leaving, the kids went off and achieved their dreams, becoming philanthropists and actors and what have you, but is that proof from the future? How long are the kids in the Place of Dreams, or does it exist outside of and independent from time? These are questions that are apparently not important enough to answer. Every conflict is resolved too quickly and unrealistically. The longest time the author spent on anything is the original description of the room and the chairs it contains. We can't learn anything about the characters, or learn any background on the Place of Dreams, or find out what happens after the kids leave, but we can learn all we need to know about the damn chairs. Basically, what was the point? What did any of it mean? Just...WHY?

Read The Sapphire Flute before starting this book. The number of people introduced in the first three chapters is mind boggling if you're not already familiar with the story, and besides, The Armor of Light begins where The Sapphire Flute left off. I started book 2 thinking the author would describe the continuing settings and characters and explain the backstory basics. She didn't, so I had to go back and read the series from the beginning to get a mental picture of book 2's beginning. I loved book one even though it came to a stopping place as opposed to a real end. It wasn't meant as a standalone. I have to admit I wanted to dislike the second book for not being a standalone. That lasted all of three chapters. Then the author began introducing new situations and new magical phenomena as she ramped up the tension. All the color and detail of the first book wove itself into the second tapestry. One storyline features romance with competing suitors, heart-breaking betrayal, magical battles, death and hopelessness. I cried through certain chapters. Evil gets its due in this book with a storyline fleshing out the antagonists and making one of them seem sympathetic--in a twisted way. The main story focuses on learning, friendship, trust and free-will in a case of nature versus nurture. When hidden evil undermines the good influences, conflicted characters must run or face-off with betrayers. With exception of some well-deserved dread at expectation the three stories will come together in a disastrous way, little feels formulaic about evil's bid to gain control of the magic keystones that created Rasann. When the storylines come together with a crash, the elements combine with dark magic to rage against the magic academy that serves to protect the world. A battle ensues that could end in the death of the only person able to mend the fraying magic holding Rasann together. As trials, joy and sorrow transform the characters in the book, so you will be transformed in the reading. If not for the lack of adequate descriptions in the beginning, I would give The Armor of Light 5 stars. The ending resolves most of the conflicts in a way that feels satisfying to the reader even though the characters suffer great loss and face a terrible challenge, setting a difficult path for future books in the series. I look forward to the journey.

As for the story - I really, really enjoy YA fantasy and I thought the author did a fabulous job at fleshing out the world of Hytanica and the characters to make it seem like a real kingdom. And I loved the prophecy and the backstory, and all the secrecy surrounding Narian's identity and why Narian came to Hytanica, etc. Overall, I loved Legacy, despite the fact that some of it was a bit over described. I actually teared up a little bit at the ending and I cannot wait for the second book in the series. I definitely recommend it to fans of fantasy and anyone who loves a princess story.

Charlie's friends aren't talking to her ever since she told on two boys who started a fire. Her twin Sammie thinks this is for the best since mean-girl and leader of the pack Lauren isn't nice at all. Charlie just wants to be part of the in-crowd though. When Lauren decided to form The Junior Waves club she needs Charlie to increase their chances of getting approved. Charlie is excited to be back in the group and will do pretty much anything even if it means going against what she knows is right. This book was pretty cliched with no likable characters. I know it has a nice message about not giving in to peer pressure and bullying and being true to yourself but the delivery had the subtlety of a sledge hammer. Pretty much any cliche you can think of was in this book and you knew how the story was going to play out from the beginning. There are much better books out there that deal with these topics.

"I'll tell them how I survive it. I'll tell them that on bad mornings, it feels impossible to take pleasure in things because I'm afraid it could be taken away. Overall, the writing is silly and cliched seriously, the word "boobies" was actually used on several occasions . The audiobook narrator was horrible and annoying. I'm giving this book 4 stars because even though I did truly enjoy this book it's didn't "wow" me. It was refreshing however to have the main male character actually stand up and be true to his love. Even when opportunities arose he did not faultier in his love. That in itself made the story different from others I have read. Liam was a stand up male character and for that I respect this author. It was a sweet story line, with sadness weaved in. Over all, I'm happy I had the opportunity to read this story. It was a feel good with some tragedy within it.

This was a great finale to the epic Mortal Instruments series. I cried, I laughed, and I got closure and I thank Cassandra Clare for being so amazing at writing and not killing off all of my favorite characters. The beginning didn't hold up to my 2-year-long-wait expectations, but halfway through, it really picked up pace, and kept me reading well past midnight. I can't believe the series is finally over I'm still in shock, I think. Although I'm sad that it is over, and have shed many tears, I love the way Cassandra Clare wrapped up the series. It was perfect, and I can't think of any other way she could have done it. In the end, the book held up to my high expectations, and gave me the ending I needed.
Okay, but when is Leigh Bardugo going to write a book of fairytales? I need that in my life.

Write an action-packed thriller Check. Be "inspired" by other YA series like The Selection and The X-Men Check. Create unique and rich characters Nope, not at all. Hold my interest enough to purchase Book 2 of the Trilogy Fail. Red Queen was a disappointment. The storyline is a Frankenstein of a plot, with elements of The Selection Queenstrial, anyone? the relationship between Mare, her Prince Cal and hometown love interest Kilorn is pretty similar to America, Prince Maxon and Aspen , Marvel's The X-Men mutant teenagers with extraordinary abilities , Game of Thrones elite families vying for position and power , and many, many more. All of that I could have accepted IF the characters had drawn me in. But, a day after I finished the book I had to look up the MC's name before writing this review. Each character is sketched on paper so thin and insubstantial that it could float away. Mare has absolutely nothing going for her, and there is no reason why she should be the central love interest of Cal, Maven and Kilorn - she is sarcastic, self-centered, stupid, and has no sense of humor. Every single character is as predictable as Christmas. They are "classic characters" given names and ripped out of a thousand fantasy novels Farley, the leader of the revolutionaries Kilorn, the stubborn, scared hometown boy Queen Elara, the evil, manipulative snake etc. IF the writing had stood out it is at the same level as any first-time writer, and though it has been edited didn't stand out for any beautiful or interesting metaphors, turns-of-phrase, syntax, etc. , or IF I had loved any of the characters, this might be a different review. But as it stands, this just didn't make the cut for me. I finished Book 1, but I won't invest further time or money in the Red Queen trilogy.

original can be found Books Swoons 3.5 out of 5 stars After being disappointed by The Elite, I was hoping for a better outcome for The One. Like always she only thought of herself when it came to her situation with Aspen, never thinking that he might have moved on or have another love interest. The pacing of the book was quick and the story transitions well from one moment to the next. There are sections that are filled with suspense but in the end I knew America would end up with Maxon. Don't get me wrong that is what I wanted, but there was so much unnecessary drama between them before they finally decided to be together, which was a turn off for me. Although the outside revolution played a bigger role in The One, it was just kind of back ground noise to the drama of what was happening in the selection. I would have liked for it to play a bigger role. There were certain reveals that were supposed to be shocking but really kind of fell short. It is so not that! The book is very much like a choose your own adventure where you read every single scenario. Some I liked much better than others. The first few seemed a little lengthy and more tedious than the more interesting segments later on. The stories got more and more outlandish as the book went on, and that's probably why I liked it more and more as I read it. I can see realistic fiction fans liking it less and less the further down the rabbit hole you go.

The Coldest Girl in Coldtown wasn't the first time I'd read anything by Holly Black. I knew going into this book what her style was like, and she's been a favorite since I started reading more YA in my early 20s having read the Modern Fae books first and absolutely fell in love with them . Nonetheless, I also knew that it's been hard to attach the word "original" next to vampire anything in recent years, so this made me curious. I hadn't read the short story and didn't know anything about it before going into it. I was still insanely excited to pick it up and it'd been one of my most anticipated reads of the year. I'm happy to say that it didn't disappoint me at all. In fact, it went above my expectations. I stayed up well into the night on the edge of my seat because I couldn't put this one down, and for days after I couldn't stop thinking about it. Ms. Black crafted a dark, unique world full of excitement and horror, twists and gasp-out-loud cover-your-mouth OMG moments. The Coldest Girl in Coldtown won me over from the first scene--a frightening heart-racing beginning that started off with a bang--and I wasn't able to let go of this addictive story or its characters from that moment on. This book blew my mind. I am mind blown . I am still practically speechless and flustered and I don't know how I'm able to even write this review properly. I found Gavriel just as forbidden and charming and mysterious as Tana had. Gavriel is my new favorite hero. Anti-hero? He's not all fluffy bunnies and flower hearts, that's for sure. But he does know how to certainly charm some. And while Tana had had it rough through the years since vampires revealed their existence, her character showed so much determination and strength that I just had to love her and hope nothing but the best by the end for her. These characters had spunk and a realistic appeal to them. Though the blurb may make it feel there's a possible love triangle, there's not. An awkward ex-boyfriend friendship, yes, and for that I was like "thank you!" Because really, how often do we see that? The romance overall was exciting and different. And I adored it. I'm curious though Is this a stand-alone or a series? The ending left off a bit open-ended, though could have been considered pretty well wrapped up at the same time. As much as I love stand-alones and we all know we probably could use more of them , I'm sincerely hoping this is going to be a series because I want MORE. There are so many feels . And just gah... I need to know what's happening to Gavriel and Tana and Pearl, and what's going to go on next in this crazy-imaginative world. Please?! The Coldest Girl in Coldtown is hands down one of my favorite reads, not just for 2013, but in years. Not hard to make that decision. Holly Black has once again delivered a unique cast and imaginative, fresh world not to be missed! 3 Pixie The Bookaholic

This book tells a story of two characters that live in a different world. Elias was born to be a Martial, or maybe you can say, an army, a fighter or anything along that line. While, Laia is just a girl who lived with her grandparents and her brother. Everything changed when Laia lost everyone in her family to the Martial. Simple and easy. I bet most of you know how this story is going to be. All the inevitable romance and stuff. The storyline is a bit predictable, I have to admit that. I'm so sorry it doesn't make its way to my 2016 favorite list although it is actually published in 2015 . First of all, this book will teach you a lot about the middle east culture which is impressive. Not so many authors had ventured to that part of the world. I bet there is, but I'm talking about young adult fantasy books. I haven't read anything that works around the desert. The mention of supernatural creatures that are very popular in the middle east is also amazing. I forgot that the middle east their own unique tales too. However, a lot of people seem to think that the story must be better if the romance is better than it already is. I'm not certainly sure what that supposed to mean, but, to me, the romance part is perfectly done. According to the age of the characters, I think, the romance part is very much relatable and logical. It is amazing to see how Sabaa Tahir managed to get the romance real and convincing since not so many authors managed to create a lovely romance element in a fantasy book. Oh! I love the small chapters. It makes the reading easier and Sabaa knows exactly where to stop to keep the readers reading. It's not easy to create the best stop but Sabaa did it pretty well and I loved the book for that. Not just that, Sabaa Tahir also writes everything beautifully. This is not just some empty compliment. I really mean it. There are a lot of amazing quotes you can find in the book. It will draw your heart closer to the characters, forcing you to understand everything they did when it is hard to do so. Even so, I do have some disagreements with the ending. It is obviously not enough. I need it to be done and settling but no, it doesn't happen that way. There are so many unanswered questions and I don't like it because I need answers. I need to know why some characters did what they did. Talking about the characters, I personally couldn't relate much to them. Most of them are weak but, they try to appear stronger. Most of them undergo such rapid changes throughout the book and I totally understand why. Just, I don't think it makes sense. There were so many questions in my head and I hope the next book will have all the answers because I truly need it to not turn me off. Nevertheless, I still actually think that I might not forget Laia and Elias that easy. Their stories are unique and refreshing. And their names are just so unbelievably close to my heart. Maybe that's why I gonna remember them regardless of how much misunderstanding we are having right now. So, let's sum it up! I do not suggest anyone with dislike towards cliffhangers to read this book. But if you love some rebellions and darkness, this might be the right book for you. I got to say that it is a very dark book. And some of you might find it satisfying.

Voy a empezar este comentario con los puntos buenos A pesar de ser una novela muy corta, tanto los personajes como la trama estan bien estructurados. A lo largo de las pocas paginas que la conforman, los dialogos funcionan de manera correcta para que toda la historia tenga fluidez y ritmo. Salvo por el final, ninguna otra escena presenta la informacion de manera forzada, y es el principal acierto del texto. El lenguaje que utilizan los personajes sus dialogos son una perfecta combinacion entre el lenguaje coloquial y el literario, por lo cual la novela, si bien cumple la funcion de acercar al lector a un universo mas "real", si tiene la suficiente literacidad para ser considerado literatura. El recurso de estar escrita toda mediante mensajes de texto es original si bien no es pionero, pues desde el siglo pasado existieron novelas escritas en puros dialogos y esto es lo mismo, pero con la novedad tecnologica y, sobre todo, SE JUSTIFICA. Hay escenas que, por obvias razones, no se muestran al lector, pero los autores han sabido construirla a modo de que ni un solo detalle de la trama pasara por alto. Pero, y es aqui donde vienen los puntos negativos, el fondo de la novela es poco profundo. Primero la historia es muy previsible desde el primer dia hasta el ultimo. No hubo momento en el que algo me sorprendiera o me hiciera cuestionarme. Segundo el enamoramiento de la protagonista se siente poco real puesto que, a diferencia de la segunda entrega y ya hablare de ella despues , el lector no tiene oportunidad de ver como va naciendo el amor entre ellos todo lo cuenta la muchacha de repente y despues de haberlo recordado asi porque si. Tercero los motivos de Phoenix para esconder su verdadera personalidad creo no son lo suficientemente poderosos para soportar el peso de una novela y al final parecen casi, casi ridiculos con las de veces que vemos ya leido y visto esto . Cuarto la trama en general es muy infantil. Es decir, a pesar de que es una novela dirigida a los jovenes, podrian haber tratado temas mas profundos, de interes social. Sin embargo, todo se reduce a una historia de amor que, a mi parecer es muy, muy tibia. La ventaja es que se lee de un tiron, en una sentada, y no te da tiempo para sentir aburrimiento o pesadez. Simplemente la terminas y te quedas con la sensacion de querer mucho, mucho mas. Mi calificacion es de 6.5 10, pero me ensenaron que el .5 se redonda, por lo cual es un 7, que traducido al lenguaje de las estrellas es 2 5.

While the idea behind this series is interesting the Greek gods, dying in various slow and gruesome ways, go to war , this book felt both slow and disjointed. Much of the emotional content feels unearned. Why does Cassandra hate and despise Athena so much? Yes, her life has been disrupted and she's mourning Aidan, but the degree of her anger stops making sense rather quickly. Why does almost everyone like Calypso? No idea, we barely see her as a character and she does almost nothing. Why do Andie and Henry distrust Achilles? They don't have any memories of him killing Hector in a past life, so why would they react that way? It took me a long time to get around to this book after the first one, and it lacked a lot of the striking and original imagery which made me want to keep going with the series.

DNF at 70 This is my first ever 1-star review of a book by Ellen Hopkins. I've given her, at the lowest, 3 stars, or 2.5 if we want to be technical. I've had a rough time with her lately. I didn't like Collateral. I thought she fell way short of the mark. However, that was an adult novel by her, so I thought maybe I just didn't like her adult stuff. The only problem was, I really enjoyed Triangles, an adult book that I really connected with. Last summer, I was privileged enough to get an ARC ofLove Lies Beneath. Boy, that one fell short, too. It was one where there were high points where I thought "Yes! Here it comes! The Ellen Hopkins twist where it leaves me breathless and terrified!" But, pages later it went down to the mind-numbingly boring information that I just didn't like. Again, I thought that I wasn't the target audience. I'm not a middle aged, white, cisgender woman. So, I brushed it off, just thinking that I'm not interested in her woman's fiction stab, which is fine by me. Then this one came around. I've literally owned this book from the publishing day. Ellen Hopkins is one of the only YA authors I trust not to lead me wrong into something I don't like. Again... I was wrong. And I'm so, so sad that I was. Matt, our MC, was... I'm going to put it bluntly. He was a whiny 18 year old boy who needs to make peace with the fact that his brother killed himself and stop blaming God because, that's who he was blaming ultimately, let's face it for something that God couldn't control. You don't have to believe in the Christian God to say this. He's an angry atheist. I am annoyed by angry atheists. I like friendly atheists, and when I identified as an atheist, I was definitely a friendly one. You keep with your beliefs, I'll keep with mine. Don't force yours on me. If I've said it once to angry atheists, I've said it a million times. Religions, most of the time, don't cause the problems. They preach for the masses and want to gather people into their fold. It's the people who do the interpretations that cause the problems. So, there. Matt annoyed the hell out of me. From his whiny self to his faux-deep thought about religion that just came out as, again, whiny. Now, I understand Matt's angst. I get it. Really, I do. His little brother was gay and was mercilessly bullied by people at school, people he thought was his friends, his damned parents even. And, he imploded instead of exploded. He killed himself. Their family is falling apart worse than before. Matt is the only one left to hold together the pieces, all while he deals with his grief and the fear of losing his girlfriend, Hayden, who, quite frankly, seemed quite distant from him before the huge twist that happened. It was a good twist, but not too shocking. I didn't like her. Nor did I like Matt. All right, that's not really a spoiler, but this is. When he cheated on Hayden with Alexa, that's where I really hit my limit of being okay with what he did. I don't condone cheating. It's an asshole thing to do, even if you're in a failing relationship. There was that. I hated the MC. It happens a bit for me, but I typically give a book higher than 1-star. More like, 2 to 2.5 stars. But, I didn't like the pacing. Literally, taken from the Goodreads description But when a horrific event plunges Matt into a dark, silent place, he hears a rumble...a rumble that wakes him up, calling everything he's ever disbelieved into question. I LITERALLY GOT 70 INTO THE BOOK AND NO RUMBLE? Where the fuck was the aforementioned rumble? No where. None at all. That is the worst description ever. It should have been titled something else since the "rumble" never came. I kept waiting and waiting and waiting for it. But, nothing. That description -- and the whole description in general -- is the most misleading thing I've ever read. Bad MC. Horrible pacing. Yet, again, I'm putting some of the blame on myself. I decided to listen to this book instead of read it. I know it shouldn't make a difference, but this is poetry. I always feel a bit of power, all tingly, when I read Ellen Hopkin's poetry. Her use of language and the way it's formatted on the page makes me feel in awe and constantly speculating what she meant by things. And, I lost that magic since this was read straight like a book. No cadence of poetry to it at all, not in the way I read her books. I may not preorder another book from her, but I'm going to continue reading her things. Specifically read the only book I own by her that I haven't read, Traffick. And I need to reread Tricks to do that.

I also hated the duel points of views alternating between the past and present, with news reports emails photos blog posts thrown in. Messy.

I'll be very surprised if you haven't heard of 'How I Live Now' because the film of it was out a couple of years ago, so it got quite a lot of attention then. I didn't hear as much hype about this book, but I thought I'd try it out anyway because I was very interested in watching the movie. 'How I Live Now' tells the story of Daisy, a fifteen year old American girl who moves to England to live with her cousins, Piper, Edmond, Isaac and Osbert, right before a war breaks out. Daisy and Edmond fall in love, which is quite inappropriate because they are cousins - and even Daisy herself can admit this - but because her Aunt Penn, the cousins mother, has gone to Oslo to give a speech about the imminent threat of war, there is no one to control the cousins behaviour. However, when the war breaks out the cousins get split up, Piper and Daisy going one way, Edmond and Isaac going another way and Osbert becoming involved in the war effort. Piper and Daisy seem to settle down with their foster family quite quickly, but they can't stop thinking about the family that they've been separated from. I read my first Meg Rosoff book back in October, and I had a massive issue with her writing style, which I had hoped was just contained to the one novel. However, as soon as I started 'How I Live Now', I knew the writing style must be across all of Meg Rosoff's books, because this novel was also written in reported speech, without any speech marks differentiating the description from the talking. For the majority of the novel it wasn't so much of an issue, but there were still areas in which the talking and the thinking about what someone had said afterwards all blurred in together and was hard to separate. 5 stars I'm going to try to be coherent, but I just finished this novel and am totally running on a book high right now. This is a book that, at it's heart, is about how there's good in everyone. Oliver just nails character development - REALLY nails it in the most unexpected ways. Yes, there's the main character, who goes through the required change. And the progress of that change is chronicled very well . But what really got me was the expert portrayals of Sam's friends. It would be so easy to make her mean girl clique just straight up bad people. That's how most YA-novels handle stories about mean girls who suddenly turn good. But Oliver ignores that trope and shows that even though Ally, Elody, and especially Lindsay have done very awful things, there's also some good in them. They're real people driven by their irrational fears. And then the ending. It's the kind of ending that I absolutely hate but also love. I want that happy ending. I want Sam to magically fix everything and lead a better life with Kent. And when that doesn't happen, my heart hurt. But it's also a powerful ending, and it shows that Sam has actually changed and isn't just trying to solve problems to help herself. Of course, it's not a perfect novel. The male characters, like Kent and Rob, are pretty one-dimensional. Rob is a jerk the entire way through, and Kent is a little too perfect. I also don't feel like the changes in Juliet on the last day are super well explained. But overall it's an excellent book. I could not put it down.

Sigh. Another fairytale retelling bites the dust. Oh, dear me. I was so hoping this to be good. The promise it had. Sorry for sounding like an ancient old lady but really. Just look at that cover. Sparkly, red-silver heels - ooooohhhhhhhh, aaaaaaaaahhhh - which are appropriately named Hans Christian Louboutins. I mean, really. Can it get any better than that? Obviously, I was enraptured by the cover alone. So when I dove into the book, I was soon turned off by the impression Dorthea gave. She was annoying, whiny, and had every single sore trait of Eadlyn from The Heir. Dorthea has everything - I repeat, everything - she could ever ask for, well, except for freedom. After the previous Emerald Princess cursed the kingdom, Dorthea's parents have kept her on lockdown until the night of the Muse Ball. And since this is a cute lil Wizard of Oz retellin', there's a spin on the original story. Dorthea's parents rule the nation and are trying to marry her off to the highest bidder ASAP. Dorthea wasn't having any of this, though. She huffed and puffed, stomped her feet, found faults in every boy, and flatout refused. So after a literal wish upon a star for a better life and a prince with cleaner fingernails , Dorthea's world is upturned. The kingdom is in chaos. Beauty becomes a Beast, Rapunzel goes bald, and her parents have disappeared to a mystical place called Kansas. Ha! And now Dorthea, the prince she was almost forced to marry, Kato, who has now become a chimera, and a mouthy little maid named Rexi, set off on a journey to reverse the curse. This should've been titled Dorthea's Mediocre Misadventures. If so, I would've probably not picked it up. The fairytale puns were cute, at first, but after awhile, they grinded at my nerves. Dorthea is far too obnoxious for me to like. I saw that a few reviewers said she grew from beginning to end but I don't see it. Well, maybe a little. But for the most part, she remained the same inane brat. If I wanted to read about a girl whining about her Louboutins, I would stick to my Gossip Girl books. Anyway, I hate to talk bad about a fairytale retelling. Although, I have yet to find myself a good one, I'm still hoping.

Oh, what do I say about this one? I was desperately hoping that this one would be better than Go Ask Alice, but it is really just a modern-day version of it, maybe the tiniest bit better. Tiniest bit! I could go off on this book see my review for Go Ask Alice but it has been a few weeks since I finished it and I've mostly forgotten what made me angry about it voyeuristic, glorification of drugs, ridiculous situations the girl finds herself in, the way she says things like "I had to boogie with the monster"....okay I guess I CAN remember a lot of what I didn't like . I defended YA lit-including this book-to a teachers aide during a recent high school visit. She asked me why I was there promoting such "dark" books and wasn't there any "uplifting books about inspiring real-life people?" YEAH RIGHT LADY. I told her that I was there, as the teachers requested, to show the students what is new and popular among teen readers at our library, and that although the young adult books are often ostensibly about these dark subjects like drugs, the books manage to transcend these subjects and give the readers something wonderful and to take away. Well, Crank is absolutely NOT one of these books. It 100 glorifies the use of methamphetamines and other drugs in a I-totally-shouldn't-my-family-and-school-life-sucks-and-I-got-raped-and-everything-because-of-drugs-but-it's still-worth-it! type way. The ONLY good thing, and I am so ashamed to admit this, is that I could not put this book down in a train wreck you can't look away from kind of way. The free-form poetry format is sort of lame, but I couldn't stop reading this awful book--and I hated myself for it. It is really awful. I really tend to not judge people for what they come to the library to get to read, but I seriously have to do my best acting to not cringe when a teen comes and asks for these books!!!!! And it happens almost every day to my horror. I'm still looking for the appealing drug-related YA book I can give to teens at the library and not feel sad about what they are going to read.

THE RULE OF THREE is action-packed, filled with heart pounding adventure, and clearly the first book in a series. It is a post-apocalyptic survival story. Adam Daley is a typical teenager with a snarky best friend and a crush on a sweet girl when the world changes. In the blink of an eye, everything with a computer goes dark. No computers, no cell phones, no cars. Luckily, Adam drives an '81 Omega which has no computers. He picks up his young twin brother and sister from their elementary school and takes his friend Todd and crush Lori home. Adam's mom is the a police captain his father is a commercial pilot. When everything goes dark, his father is on the ground in Chicago and has no way to communicate with the family or get home. Luckily, the Daleys have a next door neighbor named Herb who is a retired spy and who has been in situations where life has gotten very difficult before. He is a major pessimist who is very good at planning for all possibilities. Adam also has an ultralight plane and the skills to fly it. When it becomes apparent that the lack of computers isn't a short term problem, Herb and Adam's mother gather some influential people from the neighborhood to try to figure out a way to survive. The also convince Lori and her parents that they aren't safe on their farm and bring them and all their belongings - animals and equipment - to the neighborhood. However, it is dangerous being an outpost of civilization in a world that is growing more and more chaotic. The story is filled with action, battles on land and in the air, and is very exciting. There is even a little bit of romance as Adam and Lori get to know each other. The story ends with a very unresolved ending. I can't wait for more books to find out what happens to our group of survivors.

Con meno di 200 pagine certo non ci si puo aspettare grandi cose. Di solito un prequel - in ogni genere letterario - non vuole scimmiottare i suoi fratelli piu grandi, ma vuol stuzzicare, anticipare, regalare qualcosa di extra, qualcosa che ti fa venire voglia di attaccarti alla sua serie di appartenenza e divorarla senza indugio. Non so perche - perche sono stordita? - ho trascurato la serie Lux pur sapendo che l'autrice e quella santa donna della Armentrout Lynn. Io, che la venero con i lucciconi negli occhi, avrei dovuto trasformarmi in una piovra e risucchiare questi libricini uno dietro l'altro. Non l'ho fatto, ma sto rimediando. Shadows e il prequel di Obsidian e assolve piu che egregiamente il suo compito. It got me hooked, questo e sicuro, e mi ha anche divertita. Sara forse il genere paranormale, con gli alieni luminosi e l'ambientazione montanara, che ha ispirato l'autrice ad essere piu ironica del suo solito, sta di fatto che in meno di 200 pagine ha saputo coprire un range di emozioni molto vasto con una dimestichezza sorprendente. Dawson e Bethany sono molto piacevoli da leggere, sono spigliati, hanno brio e insieme riescono a creare dialoghi frizzanti e coerenti con il target liceale della storia. La Armentrout, pero, non ci fa mancare anche qualche scena sexy perche Dawson e un personaggio troppo interessante da leggersi fantagnocco per non venire sfruttato nel giusto modo. Non mi aspettavo, invece, la drammatica svolta finale - anche se snaso un cambio di rotta piu avanti nella serie - che stronca in pieno l'allegria della lettura e che regala un tono piu serio e commovente al prequel. Considerando l'esiguo numero di pagine l'autrice ha fatto un ottimo lavoro perche, oltre a divertire e commuovere, non ha caricato troppo la trama limitandosi a presentare alcune cose, alcuni personaggi e a lasciare aperto il finale in modo da instillare nel lettore la smania di proseguire.

Soon she learns that hiding things from Patch is about as useless as trying to see the back of your head. Yet she tries to conceal her feelings to no avail and dwell on his past. Her hunch says that Patch is the phantom she has always felt stalking her after her father's death, but her heart tells her Patch can never do something like that. More of a 3.5 star rating! I didn't realize until recently that each Glittering Court book would be from a different girl's point of view, but from the start I was most interested in Mira's story. In this book, Mira struggles to find her brother in the new colonies and find a way to free him from this work contract. Yet as crimes mount in the colony's Cape Triumph, Mira can't help but try to assist the targeted, poor. While there is some overlap in scenes between this book and the Glittering Court, I am relieved that the plot and direction of this book is decidedly different. I really liked to see some of the prominent scenes from the previous book rewritten from Mira's point of view. Midnight Jewel predominantly takes place in Adoria the new colonies still in the developmental stages though. I really liked that we got to see the workings and hierarchy system of the Adoria as well as the dark underbelly of the city. This book has a vigilante and espionage twist that made this story really addictive once the plot took off. I loved all of the missions and the trickery and fighting. Throw in some social justice fighters and a charming crew, and readers are in for a fun time. Mira was such an admirable character, and she really made this book enjoyable for me. Her unfailing loyalty to her friends and her brother are touching. She was such a strong lead. So many people and obstacles came in the way of her goals and her future, yet she still prevailed and never let the stress get to her. I also really like her inexhaustible sense of morality and right and wrong. She has a line that she never dares cross no matter the reward or desire. But her compassion does give her a bit of wild streak, recklessly throwing herself into danger for those she cares about and those who can't defend themselves. Unfortunately I wasn't onboard with the romance for most of this book, mainly because I wasn't a huge fan of the love interest, Grant. He is a spy with a harsh background, but his unemotional countenance and behavior and scathing words were so infuriating. Mira deserved better! Near the end of the book though, I developed a begrudging respect for the guy... Overall I really enjoyed the second book in the Glittering Court series, and I can't wait for Tamsin's book!

Aristotle is an angry teen with a brother in prison. Dante is a know-it-all who has an unusual way of looking at the world. When the two meet at the swimming pool, they seem to have nothing in common. But as the loners start spending time together, they discover that they share a special friendship, the kind that changes lives and lasts a lifetime. And it is through this friendship that Ari and Dante will learn the most important truths about themselves and the kind of people they want to be. Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe is a sweet, complex, poignant story of two fifteen-year-old boys and their connection to each other. This is a coming of age that highlights the questions we all had when we were growing up, questions about people and our parents, about words and actions, about family and love. Ari and Dante work so well in this book, as characters and as friends, as searchers for answers. They both have their quirks and their questions, their way of seeing the world and wondering why it works like that. It's more that Ari is more street smart while Dante is more book smart. It's not that they have close to nothing in common. It's that they both have questions, questions about the world, why parents don't talk about certain things and why people act the way they do, and it's the way they search the world they know for answers that defines who they will become. The summer in which they meet becomes a summer of discovery, of growth, but what about when the summer ends? What about the rest of the year? How much more will they both discover about the world and how complicated it is? What are the secrets of the universe? I imagine you could study for decades upon decades and barely scratch the surface of what makes us tick. What makes us human, what makes our parents our parents, what makes sparrows and dogs, what makes dreams and stars. What makes everything. The prose is so simple but so powerful and completely without artifice. This is the guileless voice of a boy and his unusual friend hoping to understand the world and where they fit into it, and the journey they go on is one not to be missed.

Good wow. This book is so much better than the first one! The action is intense and relentless, the plot is fantastic and the story line is terrifying. A group of high-school students is accidentally transported back in time to 65 million years BC. They have to find a way to leave a message for the Time Riders, letting them know when they are so they can be rescued - all the while fighting for the lives against a horrific and extremely intelligent species of dinosaur. Now we've all ready Crichton's book, right? Well any time you mix humans and dinosaurs you're going to have some story cross-over. You can't really write too much original content from that single plot device. So no, I didn't feel like Mr. Scarrow borrowed anything from Mr. Crichton's Park. It just is what it is. If I wrote about some dudes fighting some dinosaurs I'd have to use some of the same narrative teeth, claws, attack, humans are prey, et cetera. However, this one was completely original for other reasons as well. These are mostly all children stuck in the distant past. Not on some dinosaur resort. And they have to come up with a way to leave a message they know will be found by their peers - but not chance falling into the wrong hands. This was very well executed, and the action and suspense rolled hard right up to the very last chapter. I don't think this book - or this series, for that matter - is perfect. I would love to give it five stars, in fact. And maybe I will change it. But I find some flaws in it occasionally. And maybe that's because of the YA genre within which it is written. This is not, however, something that should keep anyone from reading the series. Don't let the YA letters scare you off. If you like time-travel, give this and these a shot. Seriously. It's really, really good.

First let me say that I did not like the writing style of this author. She does a lot of telling instead of showing. Also, she constantly has her terrible protagonist, Aurora, repeat herself both aloud and within her own inner dialogue. When I first started reading I was sympathetic toward Aurora. She's an orphan, her adoptive parents have died and now she's staying with her adoptive parents relatives - who hate her. She has no friends at school, her cousin is making her life hell, and she's barely passing her classes. Well, I found out very soon why she was barely passing. She's dumb. Like she fell out of the stupid tree and hit every single branch on the way down. So she gets kidnapped. And keeps asking this guy where he's taking her. Even though she overheard him say he's taking her to the queen, and has had him tell her directly that he's taking her to the queen as well. Aurora.. You're going to see a queen. You just went through a magical tapestry.. So do you really think that anything this guy says is going to make sense to you? He could say he's taking you to Sesame Place in Langhorn, PA and it would still mean nothing to you. You imbecile. And this.. "No, princess, not yet. My mother's house is on the top most branch," he said with a hint of pride in his voice. "It has the best view, you know." "Please call me Aurora," I said absentmindedly, "all this 'my princess' stuff sounds silly." This was literally the first time anyone had called her princess, let alone "my princess".. I really had some problems with her by now. Which only intensified more with this.. "Run, Aurora, now!" He said again. His sword glistened in the moonlight as he drew it from its sheath and prepared to meet the Shadow Guard. I was about to turn and run, but I couldn't help watching him for a few seconds more.." Are you kidding me? You're life is in danger. Every single second counts and you just .. Watch this guy? Because you think he's cute? You're pathetic. Later, Aurora was sent to learn more about her Mage magic by her Greatuncle Gabriel. And he informs her that since her life is in danger, for her protection, she'll be given a new identity. insert hissy fit here She is told to keep her identity a secret, to keep a low profile and never take off her amulet. And just like she was told not to leave her uncles property without guards.. What does she do? Well she does the very opposite of what she's asked. This is a reoccurring theme. Don't leave the academy grounds after dark. You'll get expelled and it's not safe. And what does she do? She leaves with people who hate her and her family. And when things go wrong - shocker - she thinks, "how could I have been so stupid?" She asks herself this question throughout the novel. I'm not exaggerating. You'd think she'd learn. During the 22nd chapter I thought maybe she was finally starting to get herself together. She was studying and practicing physically and magically and get better and stronger. But then she does something so incredibly stupid that I almost threw in the towel on this book for the 100th time. She takes off her amulet during a duel with Damien. And oops now everyone knows who and what she is. And her reaction when it was gone was, "what could I say? My ego got the better of me? I shouldn't have done it but I did?" By this point I just had no hope left for her character. And I was right not to. The ending.. Honestly, I was so full of hatred for Aurora by this point that nothing surprised me. But for all you people out there thinking of maybe reading this? Guess what.. You think maybe she's going to be great but then she just fucks up. Yeah, screw that dire warning. Great idea. She's unapologetic about it. She freaks out and has a hissy fit. Her uncle explains to her how and why what she's saying isn't logical.. And then she's like screw you guys I'm doing it anyway and sneaks off in the dead of night with her not so lover boy and her fae bud. It pained me to finish reading this novel.. And not because I'm upset to see it end. It's because I subjected myself to such garbage and was left with one monster headache. All I can say is, thank god it was free. Nantucket Blue has been one of my most dodged books. I was afraid that I would be left disapointed due to its excessive praise, which I take as a caution in most cases. Ironically though, I decided that this contemporary YA novel would be able to lift me back into reading because I thought it would be a light, summer read. It definitely transported me to a beach, but it was not that light. Mostly occuring on a luxurious island Nantucket , Nantucket Blue tells a story of a summer that can change one's life. For Cricket Thompson, the ambitious protaganist, this cliche resounds through the book as she experiences loss and love, isolation and independence in various forms. When her best friend, Jule suffers a tradgey that makes their friendship distant and questionable, Cricket has to find her own way to travel and to manage in Nantucket without the lodging security of Jule's guest house - without even knowing her way around. Cricket's independent attitude aids her a lot throughout the novel, especially when a minor scandal hovers over her. Rather than staying home with her mother, Cricket determines her own destiny by taking up a chambermaid job at Nantucket that will supply the income and housing she needs during her stay. I really admired this decision of hers because it revealed just how determined she was. She has to grapple with the thought of losing her best friend Jules, but she does not let this decaying friendship dictate her decisions, whether they are the short and snappy decsions or the ones that require a little more brooding. Many claim Nantucket Blue is a great piece of realistic fiction, and I too agree with that sentiment. This is especially seen in the manner of Howland's relationship building. Readers see the complexity of human relationships through Cricket. For instance, the relationship between her and her divorced parents is noteworthy, as readers see her reaction to her father's new family and her mother's shrunken personality. The romance is also well-developed, especially since it follows the backstory of her own mother's teenaged love via epistolary. There's Jay, her high school crush that she has always dreamt of, and there's Zack, Jules brother who is 'off limits'. Through these various relationships, readers actively see how messy can life be - no matter how hard you try to avoid things, they can have a way at coming at you. Sexuality is not presented daintily either. Instead, Howland presents the realness of physical progression between two young people and how it affects their choices. She leaves no room for perfection in Cricket's character or relationships. She is definitely real, and I loved how Howland made Cricket dominate this novel. While the story's content was engaging, I was not too excited about the writing. The writing is definitely perfect for the general air of Nantucket Blue with its conversational narrative, multitude of pop culture references, and directness. It also brings about serious themes without overwhelming readers. However, it was not memorable to me, but Cricket's Nantucket story sure managed to stay with me somehow. I guess the writing style was a perfect fit though not my favorite type.

Obwohl sich die Geschichte aufgrund der leichten Sprache recht schnell liest, muss ich doch sagen, dass es auch stellenweise seine Langen hatte, die absolut nicht notig waren und die mich mehr genervt als unterhalten haben. So wird u.a. in aller Ausfuhrlichkeit beschrieben, dass Sophie zu ihren Keksen gerne Milch trinkt und wie sie ein Glas aus dem Schrank nimmt, sich dieses einschuttet und austrinkt. Da frage ich mich ganz ehrlich was das soll, da es so gar nichts mit dem eigentlichen Inhalt zu tun hat. Dafur bleiben wichtige Fragen lange Zeit offen und wurden kaum beantwortet. Daruber hinaus gibt es unglaublich viele Klischees in diesem Buch, die alles andere als gut sind. So wird immer und immer wieder betont, wie reich und gut aussehend Wes doch ware und Sophie absolut nicht verstehen konnte, wieso er sich ausgerechnet fur sie interessieren wurde. Standig wird darauf hingewiesen, wie sexy und unwiderstehlich Sophie ihn findet und er ja so wunderbar sei, gleichzeitig wird aber auch immer wieder erwahnt, dass sie ihn eigentlich gar nicht kennen wurde. Dieses Buch ist wirklich zum Mause melken und ich hatte wirklich keinen Spass dabei, erst recht, wenn ich an die Charaktere denke, bei denen mir stellenweise fast schlecht wurde. Sophie ist eine typische Mary-Sue, wie sie im Buche steht Zuruckgezogenen, schuchtern, haufig umgezogen, ohne Vater aufgewachsen und verliebt sich in den erstbesten Typen, den sie naturlich sofort bis an ihr Lebensende lieben und ehren will. Obwohl immer wieder erwahnt wird, dass sie weder naiv, noch leicht zu beeindrucken sei, geht sie immer wieder nur auf das Geld und das Aussehen von Wes ein und stellenweise machte sie mir den Eindruck, als wolle sie seinen Charakter gar nicht mal kennen lernen. Wes ist ebenfalls so eine Type, die man nicht unbedingt in seiner privaten Umgebung braucht. Egal, was Sophie macht - und sei es noch so damlich - er ist immer an ihrer Seite, weicht nicht von ihr, verzeiht ihr alles und verwohnt sie an allen Ecken und Enden. Er ist zu selbstlos und betrachtet auch sehr vieles sehr naiv. Und ja, auch wenn ich solche Vergleiche eher ungern mache Sophie und Wes schreien quasi schon nach Twilight, denn dort konnte man bereits samtliche Eigenschaften in gleicher Form schon erleben. Der einzige wirkliche Unterschied besteht lediglich dadrin, dass es in "Zeitenlos Der Anfang" keine Vampire gibt. Bei dem Titel "Zeitenlos Der Anfang" dachte ich zunachst an Zeitreisen, aber Pustekuchen. Die Auflosung ist so dermassen an den Haaren herbeigezogen und unlogisch, dass ich das Buch am liebsten mehrfach gegen die Wand geworfen hatte. Da muss man sich als Leser plotzlich mit der Wissenschaft und Reptilien auseinandersetzen und ich war oftmals uber die Wendung der ganzen Handlung mehr als irritiert. Ich habe mir eine nette Liebesgeschichte uber Zeitreisen gewunscht und kein Buch, dass sich plotzlich mit Themen wie Blut, Reptilien und der Wissenschaft beschaftigt. Sicherlich ist dies nicht ganz uninteressant, nur leider gar nicht das, was ich mir bei diesem Werk gewunscht habe. Die Covergestaltung ist auch so eine Sache. An sich finde ich es wunderschon, nur leider passt es, wenn man weiss, worum es wirklich geht, nicht mehr so ganz zur Thematik. Schade, aber dennoch sehr schon anzusehen. Die Kurzbeschreibung ist dagegen super, verleitet nur durch den Buchtitel und dem Text zu falschen Erwartungen - Stichwort "Zeitreisen"! "Zeitenlos Der Anfang" hat mir leider gar nicht gefallen. Die ersten zwanzig Seiten waren noch toll, aber danach konnte ich leider weder mit den naiven und stellenweise sehr oberflachlichen Charakteren, noch mit der Thematik grossartig was anfangen. Vielleicht gibt es Leute, die von der Thematik begeistert sind, nur gehore ich da nicht zu. Wenn ich mir andere, ebenfalls negative, Rezensionen durchlese, kann ich mir nicht vorstellen, dass die anderen Teile ins Deutsche ubersetzt werden.

Plus he gives yummy hot kisses and you can't pass that stuff up. Violet and Jay are completely adorable and when they get together it is completely epic and adorable too. They both get each other and I can tell their relationship is going to get very interesting and hot pretty quick. You do not want to pass up this good stuff, The Body Finder is a completely original story in my book. I have yet to read anything like it. Full review on my blog, holes In my brain. My Thoughts There was quite a bit going on with the novel, there were the two trials, family tension, and Danny's internal and external conflicts, but I thought most of this worked well together. The pacing and the plot was a bit off for my tastes, I thought the "first trial" the father's conviction was both a bit preachy and a bit slow. It took forever to get to the predictable verdict, and the jargon used could be odd at times. I think it was designed to act as a "set up" to the second trial, but it didn't work as well as planned. It did sound very realistic and official though from what I know from watching too much TV . One comparison would be it is very John Grisham-y. I thought that the characterization of Danny and his family was very well done, his love for his father despite his shortcomings felt realistic, along with his resentment for his mother relocating them. It was very like a 13 year old boy to rebel like he did, especially for reasons he doesn't fully understand yet. The sibling relationship was okay for me, but it was understandable because Danny was his father's favourite, and his sister was just "there", something that's foreign to him. The overall plot was solid, I thought the 'witness protection' thing, the family income troubles, and the other personal issues Danny had were well represented and portrayed. It was a very unique storyline that I was happy to read about. Boll expertly unravels the horrors that a single abusive family member can cause have on a family the fear and the hope molds into one as a courageous mother fights for her life and the lives of her children. I think that The Second Trial deals with tough, and extremely important issues with a sturdy hand, not afraid to shy away from difficult truths. Rating in HP Terms Acceptable 7.5 10- because I thought that although the plot being pretty strong, characterization got on my nerves along with the narration. There were some parts that I was really annoyed with, along with some really realistic parts. Overall, I enjoyed this type of novel which was reminiscent of a few John Grisham novels. I found Danny to be an okay character, I wanted a bit more from him though. Would recommend to people who would like to read about a boy main character, legal-stuff like Grisham for YA , social issues, and family and personal relations.

Stupid was an enjoyable book that helped me understand a little more of the difficulties a student with a disability might face. As I read through this book I would shudder every time Martin's dad called him stupid or lazy. I thought back on my own experiences in the classroom and I truly hope I never told a student with a learning disorder to simply "try harder". I will admit that I had a hard time when working closely with students with disabilities because I felt I just didn't understand them sometimes. I know it has been frustrating for me but I can't imagine how frustrating it must be for the student. Martin has been diagnosed with ADHD but his still has to work incredibly hard to "break even" as he put it, but he keeps going. He has to keep trying even while his dad continually tells him he is stupid, yelling and punishing him to improve his grades. He feels that he has been diagnosed incorrectly and he keeps trying to explain this to his parents but they just think he is making excuses. There is one thing that Martin is good at and that is movie making. He loves being behind his camera and finds himself making a video for some new friends doing parkour. He films their free-running, flips, jumps, and fast moving tricks and finds that he can relate to what they are doing. It's like his brain is doing the same fast moving tricks as he processes the world around him. Now Martin hopes to use his movie making skills to show his dad what it is like in his head. By making this movie and with the help of one of his new friends he works to find out his actual disability. I liked how much this book explained the disorder and also what Martin was doing to help himself. I would love to have some of my students read this book and like I said before even some teachers. It's not that I think some teachers are unaware of students with disabilities but it is hard to understand something you don't have and this book described it so well. I like this book for students in middle school who have a learning disorder although even those without will enjoy and learn as well . These students might sometimes feel they are losers or too stupid to try anymore and this book might help them when they see someone else struggle and learn to work with their disability. This book shows how stressful a learning disability can be but also how that same disability can spur creativity in people. At one point in the book Martin is talking about his disability and he is listing famous people who also have dyslexia. You might be surprised to hear some of the names. This book might help some students see that everyone has the ability to learn it's just that not everyone learns in the same way.
