For Roth fans feeling disappointed, I completely understand. Allegiant, if anything, was inconsistent with the first two books of the series, and to put it simply, a massive let down. I can't be sure if it was the introduction of dual perspective absent of authentic voice, the angsty teenage relationship between Tris and Four, or the removal from pure escapism by setting Book 3 in the real world that detached this book from the remainder of the trilogy. Regardless, it felt rushed and under-edited. The plot of the novel was not a flaw. Nor, contrary to the Internet tears being shed, was Roth's brave ending. However, these were undermined by the way the text was presented. The characters felt over-exaggerated an unauthentic, the suspense if you actually experienced it was orchestrated. And this was such a shame. This book could have explored discrimination, urban development, innate human characteristics, family vs relationship love and acceptance, but this was overshadowed by two parallel monologues of angst. Roth had a quality plot the only reason I persisted to the end , however, it's delivery was poor. I know it's tough to write a novel, particularly under this much fan pressure, but Divergent Insurgent lovers deserved better.

Twilight Tenth Anniversary Life and Death Dual Edition is basically half of the book is the original Twilight and the other half is a Twilight parody where all the characters have switched genders. The new version with new genders follows along with the story with a little bit of change here and there to account for the swap until the ending which is different. All I want to say when done reading this really is please save your money, this is just so not worth it. It makes me sad that so many people will probably still run out and buy a copy, luckily I just picked it up at the library and didn't waste a dime. I really really try to never write anything overly negative even when I've really disliked a book but this is just stupid, I'm sorry but yes I said it, stupid. The gender switching just so does not work on so many levels and the entire thing had me wondering why I was even bothering but morbid curiosity won out so I had to keep reading. Truly you start off with things like when Beau experiences the first snowfall and the teenage girls start tossing snowballs at each other and having a snowball fight... Really?? What teenage girl is going to be ok with being hit in the head with a snowball and not start a cat fight over it? Or how about Beau fainting from the blood in biology? A teen girl struggles to help him along until Edythe comes and puts Beau's arm over her shoulder and half drags him to the nurse.... this so does not work the same visual as Edward picking Bella up. Scene after scene of things that just don't work with the gender swap all throughout the book. And then some are so hard to gender swap and make sense that they get bigger rewrites which loses all the power that the original version held for those of us that actually loved this series just the way it was.. For example Bella Beau getting attacked and Edward Edythe saving the day, didn't work, hated it. In the end I just kept thinking why did Meyer's do this?? I know the answer had to be money, but in that case why not finish up the version from Edwards point of view instead?? That version I was actually enjoying reading but she just dropped it and never put a finished copy of it out. This seems like someone purposely set out just to make fun of the story that so many people loved and defended. Sad that it was the actual author that made me see all the flaws that others had pointed out for years in a much brighter light by writing this version. Overall, I can't recommend this at all.... run far away from it. And if you feel the need to read it anyway like I did then just pick up a library copy.

I am not a huge fan of Jane Eyre gasp! shock! dismay , but I am a huge fan of authenticity, romance and good writing. And this book was seriously lacking. Oddly enough, I couldn't put it down. The desire to see what new horror would be conjured to reflect the original overcame my sense of self-preservation. What drove me nuts about the story was the Nico Rathburn treatment of Mr. Rochester. I don't know anyone who would fall in love with Nico, anyone who would talk to each other in the way Nico and Jane do, or anyone who would act like any of the characters do in real life. Hmm, sort of reminds me of Wuthering Heights. I kid! I kid! But honestly, Jane Eyre deserved better. I'm not against modern retellings of our beloved literary classics, but I think the whole point is to show how universal the stories are. And this one just doesn't.

As usual the teams meet with many monsters along the way, defeat everyone and many rainbows are puked and daisies are sprouted. Ops did I spoil the book for anyone? The end was a pretty neat and bittersweet tie up for everyone's arc in the story though, especially Nico's. SO CUTE. I wanted to hug my book and give him and AHEM a happy, motherly kiss...even though I'm still only a student. Single and ready to mingle. Harhar. There were a few things that really irked me in this book tho 1 Last installment, so I thought it was only a fitting end to have the story be told through Percy or Annabeth, or maybe even the whole crew getting their own show time individually. Percy was literally useless in more than a few fights getting knocked unconscious, swimming directly into poisonous waters and thus out of commission, you get the point , and Annabeth was paralyzed in fear useless in quite a few instances too. I'm not exaggerating when I say paralyzed. Don't have to. It's even worse cause Riordan makes them stupid so that Jason and Piper could really shine through. And it's the final insult to make it so blazingly obvious. I finished reading When We Collided a while ago but needed some time to process my thoughts. I wanted to love this book SO badly because of the stunning cover why does this keep happening to me? but I didn't. When We Collided splits between Jonah and Vivi's perspectives as they fumble about life. Jonah is dealing with the relatively recent loss of his father and its aftermath, which has left his mother in depression, and Vivi is new to town with her backpack of drama. I appreciated that this book addressed topics such as depression and bipolar disorder but it pissed me right off that this wasn't mentioned in the book description. Vivi has bipolar disorder guys that's what her deal is, and it causes some SERIOUS problems for not only herself but other characters in the book too. If you don't know what bipolar disorder is, you might want to do a bit of googling before you read this book. Why? Well, because if you don't, you're probably going to rip the book in half and throw it at the wall because Vivi's character is so damn exhausting to read. If I had gone into this book without an inkling of what bipolar disorder is, I would never have finished reading it. When We Collided is not a particularly long read, it's about 345 pages, but it took me almost two weeks to finish because every time I finished reading Vivi's entry, I needed a break. Vivi's entries were tiring enough when she was experiencing mania, but the writer didn't help by throwing in unnecessary metaphors 'his dark eyes the color of a filled-up coffee mug when you stare into it - deep and brown and fading into black.' What's the point of saying his eyes are the colour of coffee when you're going to go ahead and describe the colours anyway? I'm not even going to bother going into detail about the number of adjectives... Although she did try to butt into Jonah's life and sparkle it up a bit, Vivi was way too selfish and mean at times. I didn't like how it felt like this aspect of her personality was somehow tied to her disorder. People with bipolar disorder are not inherently selfish or horrible, so this nagged me quite a bit and prevented me from liking her. There were moments where she was utterly incapable of understanding the people around her and how her actions may affect them she pretty much treated her mother and Ellie - Jonah's friend - like mats. I find it so annoying when a character supposedly has their life 'transformed' by another character who does abso-freaking-lutely NOTHING for them. It frustrates me when the reader is basically told that someone wonderful is going to waltz into their lives and sort it out for them. Yeah, let's all wake up now. Jonah was troubled, but he did not need Vivi to fix anything for him. Everything he was experiencing was normal, considering his circumstances it would have all worked out for him without her interference. I would have preferred a story on Jonah with more focus on his personality. His character could have been better developed in a story dedicated to just him, especially with the whole story about his father's death and the restaurant business. It was sweet how he'd resort to cooking to make someone feel better. Jonah's that guy who would leave homemade cookies and a fresh pie at your doorstep when you're having a shit day. The world needs more people like him. The whole romance fluff with Vivi was meh. They didn't 'fit'. I appreciate that opposites can and do sometimes mix wonderfully together, but this was just bizarre. I felt like Lord overdid it by trying to throw two characters addressing such huge topics as depression and bipolar into one book. The consequence of this was that Vivi's bipolarity overshadowed everything in the book, and Jonah's mother's depression was something mentioned in passing. We only saw her depression through Jonah and his siblings, which I found problematic. While Vivi does have some moments where she says some important things about the nature of depression to help Jonah understand what his mother is going through, ultimately, I felt like the way the topic was handled wasn't very effective or helpful. It made her seem like a bad mother for not being able to pick herself up after her husband's death, leaving her eldest teenage children to take care of the family while she locked herself up in her room. However, that made the book very very very real. Very very much so like the high school experience I have survived and never ever wish to have to live through ever again. It took me a while to get through the book because to be honest, it was like looking back in a mirror at that time in my life, and I really don't like doing that. However, if you are at that time in your life, this book might just be that lifesaver for you. The idea of the Duff - all girls are the duff at some point. I came to that realization sort of vaguely in grade school, that I should stay friends with this one girl because it made me look cool in comparison, because normally I was the outcast who was forever picked on. I know that sounds harsh of me, but I remember that day that realization occurred to me. That friendship was an awkward one and ultimately did not last. But anyways the book. Lifesaver if you are at that point in time of your life were you need to know you aren't the only one and that you will get through that whole sucky experience. I got why the pro-tag is kind of miserable and a skeptic. But having to read that the whole time really dragged the book out for me. Final Thoughts What it comes down to is this book wasn't for me. I can see the value in it, and appreciate the writing. But I like my world a little shinier. I read for escapism. Unfortunately for me this book brought back too much reality for me. My own luggage mind you, but because of it I kept this book at a distance from my heart and did not fall in love with it. Would I recommend it to teens, absolutely. They need this kind of book. For adults, not so much. Unless you forgot what high school was about and those raging hormones and you need a swift wake up call in order to relate to a teenage daughter -that is if you forget the entire experience. For me I really don't think that will happen. But when I have a teenage daughter. This book will definitely be one that finds it way on to her shelves. My theoretically teenage daughter - yes. Rating I can't really fairly rate this book. From a personal standpoint and my own reaction to is 5 10 maybe 6 10. From a standpoint of who this book might better relate to 7 10 maybe 8 10.

I felt the finale of the series to be rather weak - JP's betrayal felt like a copout just so Mia would end up with Michael. And too much time had passed between 9 and 10 - almost two full years, and I felt like I didn't know the characters as well anymore. ETA 7 years later Having binged the series this time, and being older and wiser, this finale still didn't quite do it for me. It didn't do it for me the first time around, and that was reading them as they came out so there was passage of time between installments . When reading the books one after the other, this book just ends up too jarring and different from the rest of the series to be a good finale. Meg Cabot said at Book Expo America 2015 that Princess Diaries was originally going to be 16 books, but no publisher would commit to 16 books, so she settled on ten. Well, this makes a lot of sense, because it feels like there are about five books missing between Princess Mia and Forever Princess. The entire premise of Princess "Diaries" is that we are privy to Mia's story day-to-day. And that was largely true for the series - we got to read about pretty much the entirety of Mia's freshman year, got the important bits in sophomore year, and Princess on the Brink Princess Mia gave us the start of junior year in vivid detail with 9 picking up literally the evening 8 left off . To that end, a flashforward to the end of senior year - skipping half of Mia's high school years - feels almost like a betrayal of trust. Forever Princess is a very indulgent finale. Prom, colleges, graduations, happily-ever-afters - it's pretty much every salient point of an end-of-high-school book. The problem is, this book feels like the finale to a story I haven't read yet. Mia and her friends change dramatically very frequently - both their characters and their relationships - so missing out on two years of that is not something that can be glossed over the way Meg Cabot tried. For example, why are all of Mia's friends suddenly Team Michael instead of Team JP? Logic would dictate they be Team JP the perfect-on-paper boyfriend who's been around for two years and is part of the friend circle . Yet none of them seem to be fans of JP, even if they were gung-ho about him in the last book. That's because we missed out on two years of the dynamics between JP and Tina Boris etc. The book is also supposed to present this whole love triangle between Mia, Michael, and JP - but we haven't seen any of Mia and JP's relationship. So it's very hard to know the dynamics of that especially given that Mia's a notoriously unreliable narrator . And because of the lack of foreshadowing, JP becoming the villain still does seem a bit of a copout. Having reread the series, I didn't really pick up on all that much that would paint JP this way. I hate what's happened to Mia's character, because she is a Grade-A bitch in this book. Sure, I could buy Mia becoming a tad more cynical over the years again, if only we'd seen it! . But the whole hipster, totally-over-it attitude really rubs me the wrong way. Mia being too cool for prom and not wanting to go because it's lame? Mia constantly lamenting her need for new friends? Mia treating choosing a college as an annoying minor chore? I'm sorry, but I couldn't stand her in this book - if Mia were like this at the beginning, I never would have continued reading. Even her whole "I hate high school" shtick seemed overdone, considering how all her good friends were made there. The book's ending is dreadful - Mia spending pages reflecting on What It All Means, on How She's Grown, on What She's Learned, on the meaning of Princessdom and how totally awesome but, like, meaningfully awesome being a Princess is. The last few pages of this book are straight out of an ABC Family show. As the old adage goes, Show Don't Tell - let Mia reflect a little on how her life is pretty good now, and fade out on a happy scene, instead of beating the reader over the head with the message. If I am being overly critical of this book, it's because I hold it to the very high standard of what came before. And there is lots about this book that I loved - certainly, I breezed through it in three days, as if I were reading for the first time. It's really romantic, it's really funny, the writing is compelling, the characters are mostly delightful... it's really the ultimate in fluffy feel-good YA. And to be fair, I have read finales fucked up way more epicly that this one, which just made some serious missteps at worst. POSTSCRIPT Even though this review is already way too long, I want to reflect on the entire Princess Diaries series now that I've finished my reread. When I read it the first time, I was slightly younger than Mia, reading them as they came out, and thought the series was kinda the best thing ever. With about a decade more books and life experience under my belt, I have to say the series holds up impressively well. The series is the purest example of fluff I think I've ever read, but damn if it isn't a good time. I still found myself laughing hysterically and sometimes snorting as I read. What Cabot so deftly did is make Mia and her friends totally believable teenagers. When I read as a teen, I thought most of what they did made perfect sense. When I reread in my twenties, I kept shaking my head and muttering, "Teenagers!" The fact that their actions are plausible both to a teen and an adult means Cabot got it right. The series is also a wonderfully feminist series that's ahead of its time. There are some great points that come up in this series, making it ideal for a gender studies course. For example, at one point Mia laments that while she's a feminist and all, she likes it when Michael is bossy - a microcosm of women's struggle to be progressive yet sometimes not minding gender roles. The series embraces sex positivity in an intelligent way, again before it was cool to do so - the overarching message is that sex is not the be-all-end-all of one's life, but differing viewpoints on it are presented, and all treated as legitimate. There are LGBT characters presented from the beginning, in a series that debuted in 2000! Lilly is a Social Justice Warrior before that became mainstream, and it's incredible how accurately Cabot portrayed her. To be sure, the middle section of the series is not especially strong, where Cabot is treading water while Mia and Michael are together, searching for ever more convoluted conflicts to fabricate around them. But it's worth it to get to 8 and 9, and it's always entertaining to read no matter how much plot momentum there is. So I stand by my original assessment Princess Diaries is one of the best YA series out there, and everyone should read it if they want a good time.

Rating 1.5 5 Minor spoilers I hadn't even heard of this book before I saw that it won the 2014 Goodreads Teen Fiction award. After that, I thought that if so many people loved it, I'd better read it since it must be good. Now I'm sitting here thinking why so many people liked it. A lot of my friends on GR gave it 3 stars or less, and had major problems with it. I'm just really disappointed about this book. We Were Liars is told by Cadence "Cady" who is part of the "All-American," rich, white Sinclair family. Her family goes to an island that her grandparents own every summer with the rest of the perfect Sinclair family. She hangs out with the other eldest children. They call their group "the Liars" but we never really have any explanation why. During their 15th summer on the island, some sort of "accident" takes place where Cady has no recollection of what happened and forgets nearly all of what happened during Summer 15. The rest of the book is spent trying to discover what really happened during Summer 15. The first thing I noticed about this book is how different the writing style is. A lot of the time, I didn't mind. But I did have a couple of problems with it. Cady likes to personify her emotions, for example, when her dad left her and her mother, she described the grief and pain as being shot in the chest, and bleeding through her ears, eyes, etc. When another tragic thing happens, she describes the pain as melting. With this sort of thing, sometimes I found it difficult to discern what was real and what wasn't. The second thing is that for some points of the book, it was sort of written in verse, where there were only 2 or 3 words per line. I'm okay with novels written in verse, but when it's randomly inserted into one that isn't, I feel like it interrupts the flow. Gat was my favourite character because he recognized that almost everyone on that island was a rich spoiled brat. Gat was the only person there who wasn't white he's Indian, and is Aunt Carrie's boyfriend's son. I loved that he realized things for what they were. He told Cady to her face that she is lucky as hell, and shouldn't be complaining because she was in some accident. She's on an island that her family OWNS, she spent a summer in Europe, and she gets nearly everything she could want. Gat basically gets bullied by Cady's grandfather because he's close to Cady but he isn't white. But of course Cady turns her back to that because obviously it doesn't matter that her family is bullying the person she "loves" based on race. Long story short, Gat was the only likeable character because everyone else besides the maids cooks are privileged but still complain about things that don't matter. Cady was such an irritating character. She was childish, annoying, and dull. She still calls her mother "mummy" at 17 years old. I don't know a single person that does that, but hopefully I'm not offending anyone by saying that it sounds pretty ridiculous while you're reading. Lastly, this book is a whole lot of boring. The whole book we're wondering what the hell happened, and we only get something interesting, AKA the answers, for like 10 pages. I didn't expect what the twist was, but I also didn't really think about it much, although I probably should have. I just wish that more could've been revealed earlier, or that the book was shorter so I didn't have to struggle through 200 pages to get to something remotely interesting. Overall, this book is about 95 boring and 5 interesting. I probably would've enjoyed it more if I connected more with the characters, but I just found it so difficult to find something I could relate to. Honestly, I don't really recommend this to anybody because it's so boring and takes way too long for anything to happen. You're left with questions at the end with no way to get answers. If you're going to read this, I just hope you enjoy it more than I did.

The Rebel Series by Lance Erlick is a curious examination of society after the Second World War which divides men and women into separate communities. Each with their own government, religion, morals and values. What I Liked Most About the Series The grey area. There are some obvious plus sides to a society made up of a single sex. And there are some obvious down sides. Erlick, through the characters, presents many of these views, but doesn't push the reader in either direction. Annabelle. She fits right up there with Katniss and Tris, but Erlick takes her a bit further than Collins took Katniss and Roth took Tris. There's a complexity to Annabelle as she discovers the dark side of an all female society and starts to actively fight against it. She's stronger, in my opinion, physically and mentally. The obstacles that break her down do not paralyze her or scare her. You can feel her fighting every inch of the way. What I Liked Least About the Series The order of the books. If you read them in publication order, I am almost certain you will be confused because I certainly was! Annabelle is given a mission at the end of book one which is not mentioned in Rebels Divided. The Rebel Trap explores that mission. Now that all three books have been released, I hope that GoodReads will change the series order. The many voices in The Rebel Trap. While there was good formatting to show you the different voices speaking to Annabelle, it got frustrating to follow what was going on. With so any competing voices--both internal and external--I wasn't sure which side I should be rooting for. Overall, I would give The Rebel series by Lance Erlick a thumbs up. The unique single sex societies along with a strong female lead drove the story forward. If the books are read in chronological order The Rebel Within, The Rebel Trap and Rebels Divided I believe the reader will find the series reaches a satisfying conclusion.

Penelope "Lo" Marin has severe OCD and hoarding kleptomanianc tendencies, and a recently dead brother. She becomes obsessed with the murder of a stripper known as "Sapphire." Lo decides she's Veronica Mars but does it wrong - instead of being a snarky badass marshmallow, she starts bumblingly solving the murder, being rude to everyone who is nice to her, and throwing herself into danger. Lo's voice, filled with tap, tap, tapping and a fixation on syllables and other compulsive rituals is a nice break from the usual YA heroine. It's different and it's interesting and I think Ellison wrote it heartbreakingly well. Lo was also nicely "shown" and not "told" as being extremely booksmart - like when Lo did extremely quick mental math when her treacher tried to trip her up on a calculus problem. Lo is a clever girl, trapped in the rituals she created to enforce order on a chaotic and frightening world. Unfortunately, she is street-dumb in an incredible way and absolutely the worst teen detective ever. I think the Olsen twins were slicker and more saavy in The Adventures of Mary Kate Ashley series than Lo was. Lo leaves a note for Flynt, her street kid love interest, saying literally "I think I might know who killed Sapphire now. I'm going back to Tens. I have to speak to the girls again. I know it's not safe, but I have to do this" and then not telling him who she thinks the murderer is. Brilliant, Lo. You KNOW you are going to get kidnapped threatened in this scenario because that always happens when you go to uncover the murderer but you don't want to share your information because...? Lo also had a police officer who had offered to help her and believed her and Lo totally just blew her off instead of, you know, letting her know her hunches about the clues she had. Because Lo thought she could do it on her own. Even though she failed miserably and only survives through luck and plot contrivance. Lo also uses the ol' TV show bit of going undercover as a stripper to get information about the mystery. I always thought this was an excuse for TV writers to get their actresses into skimpy, sexy outfits. I don't know what Ellison's reason is then. Lo is the WORST STRIPPER EVER - as in, she doesn't even pretend to work. She goes to the strip club three times and the only thing she does is pump the girls there for information. She never actually strips or performs at "amateur night" like she is supposed to. Why did management keep letting her in instead of getting pissy that she was such a lazy worker? Lo was also just plain rude to everyone who tried to be nice to her. I know she is prickly and tragic, but girl that is still not okay. Lo must be the prettiest thing around because despite her inability to be a decent human being, she has not one but two boys fall hard for her. There's an unnecessary subplot about a nice track team boy at school leaving her notes and asking to be her study buddy and asking her to prom and bringing her homework when she skipped - that was so unbelievable because she was so cold to him and was entirely pointless because he couldn't even make it into a love triangle. It was obvious that Flynt was Lo's true love interest. The villain didn't make any sense either. Most of the things he did seemed to be for the evulz rather than because of any realistic character motivation or logic. I mean, why did he threaten Lo several times instead of killing her outright? It's not like anyone would ever connect the murder of Lo to either Sapphire's death or to himself. Leaving a dead cat on Lo's front porch to try to "scare her away" seems incredibly needless. It would've been a lot easier to deal with Lo by just having someone shoot her in a drive-by while she was hanging out in the bad part of town. Ellison is a debut author, so I'm cutting her some slack. She has promise - Lo's narration really was well done, even if her decisions weren't - and I'm going to read Ellison's next book.

If you can explain to me how this is functionally different than roofie-ing someone... oh, wait, you can't, because it isn't. What's truly horrific is that this little HA! ethical dilemma never seems to come up because the victims are exclusively male. Had the situation been written in the reverse, I suspect Harpercollins would have passed on this at best, or possibly sent Sise for some mandatory sexual harassment training. No means no, regardless of the chromosomal makeup of the person saying it. Skip this, unless you for some reason need some blinding rage to release your inner Hulk.

Jeep Trembley is a freshman who took off a couple of years after high school before starting college. He's extremely self-deprecating, his conscience is constantly deriding him, he was a big loser in high school and he apparently has huge no pun intended issues trying to control the "visual result" of his almost non-stop lustful inner monologue. Quite the, uh, package, eh? A runner, Jeep always meets up with Gage at the track and tries to race him. Though he runs his absolute fastest, Gage always seems to beat him with ease. Jeep's also smart., which means he has rivals off of the track as well. He has a huge crush on Melody, a gorgeous girl that he has been asked to tutor. How can he concentrate on studying when some of his body parts won't let him? Then the unexplainable happens. Jeep hooks up with a hot girl named April perpetual virgin status denied! . Then the god-like star of the college football team tells him that he needs to try out for the team because he runs so fast and would be a great receiver. So he does, hoping to get Melody's attention. Or is it April's? When everything starts to fall apart, who can Jeep trust to tell him the truth? There is so much happening in this book. Jeep's father left when he was young. His oldest brother died. His mom dies. His remaining older brother took care of him. He can run really fast. He's a virgin. He's really smart. He has an odd name. He was a loser in high school. He has academic rivals in college. He is sought out to play receiver for the college football team. His diet consists of candy, porn and wanking. He thinks about his peen A LOT. As well as breasts not his . Normally, when there is so much going on in a story, it gets overwhelming. In this case, though, many of these topics were barely touched other than a mention, so the opposite happened there wasn't enough whelming. These places were where the depth to Jeep should have come from, but didn't. The theme of this book is how to stand up and be your own man, which we discover nearish the end. Jeep learns from some cryptic conversations with Chase, the football star, that no one should tell him what to do, etc. Jeep is supposed to be this huge loser. I couldn't picture him that way at all. He's apparently handsome enough, since the girls all talk to him. He's smart enough, since he's got some rivals in class. He can run super fast, so he has to be in good shape. And, when he finds out who is behind his sudden inclusion on the football team, uh, OK? Since the coach knows nothing about it, and Jeep had to try out, so what? The anger Jeep works up after some things are revealed to him seems very out of place. Not that he shouldn't be upset how it happened, but it was surprising that he cared so much. He showed more emotion over smashing his computer hard drive than anything else. Look, college is the great equalizer. All that crap that happens in high school is left in your home town. Yes, you can reinvent yourself. There are more nerds, weirdos, jocks, goths and people who experiment with all categories that the categories don't matter any more. People actually speak in class without repercussions. This is not to say that the jerks from high school turned angelic over the summer and everyone holds hands and sings Kumbaya, but differences are way more accepted in college. This story just felt like a high school tale in a college setting. It may have made more sense set in high school instead, actually. For the most part, the book was somewhat engaging, but there was zero depth to the characters. As said before, there were a lot of opportunities to have depth, especially with some of the subject matter, but it was not there. There is some odd person named Tate whose purpose in the story is unclear. Comic relief? Then the ending...it seemed completely out of character. Though I can live with unfulfilling, this was beyond that. Mean, really. And toward the end, where the self-evaluation and deep thoughts start, there are a couple of of paragraphs that are going for the profound, but miss the mark. Considering the tone in the rest of the book, they not only were in the wrong novel, they didn't make much sense, either. Her once lively eyes, now departed from innocence, appear languid, lost within a vessel of darkness, as if desperate for some form of rescue. and For that split second our eyes meet, a million allocations of thoughts brush throughout the car, giving birth to a certain convoluted life. I just finished this book ten minutes ago and I'm uncertain of what to write. This series has come so far since the first book. Of course, Adam and Noah are still my little munchkins, but Ronan has also found a way to my heart. Perhaps I can make a little bit more room for Blue and Gansey too. But just a little. I have no clue how to describe this feeling of being completely enraptured with these characters, but still dissatisfied with the overall execution of the book. The thing is, no matter how much I try, I just can't figure out what the heck is going on with the magical elements throughout the books. Is it supposed to be aggravatingly confusing? Because every time a scene in which something terrifying happens, I have to read over the paragraphs a few more times to get a good grasp of what's going on. I really do hate feeling stupid and I really do hate trying so hard to understand something in a story. But enough of that. I've already talked about that sort of stuff in my previous reviews for this series. Let's get on with the good things in this book - Colin and Piper. They are our new villains in the book, and boy, are they entertaining. This couple's bickering made me laugh a few times. - Pynch. It's so subtle, and barely there at all, but man, the feeeeels. Matched by Ally Condie was one of the most hyped up books at 2010's Book Expo America. It's the first in a planned trilogy about a dystopian society where the government matches people up with who they are to marry, what jobs they'll hold, etc. Except, for Cassia, the main character in this book, it all goes terribly wrong when something malfunctions and, while viewing the micro-chip that holds all the information about the boy she is matched with, she sees a second person's face for a split second. I've seen some wonderful reviews for this, including being listed on many "best of" lists, but it just really didn't do it for me. Learning about the rules and functioning of this society was pretty interesting, but ultimately I didn't feel like there was really a whole lot to it. I did think the author did a good job of depicting how one small event or glimpse can cause someone to obsess over another and for feelings to build when they might not otherwise have. I could think back to my teen years and relate to this dynamic. But other than that this was just an okay read for me. I finished reading it a couple weeks ago and my memory about it is already fairly vague. I will say I didn't think the ending was a cliffhanger like some reviewers said. I do agree with some reviewers, though, that some parts dragged slightly. I think I would have liked this book more if it had been maybe 75-100 pages shorter and more action packed. I would think this might be a better book for younger young adult readers except that I've read some good reviews by adults. I may read the second book to see where it goes, but I'm not dying to read it. I was wondering, though... are we choosing teams for this one? Because if so, I'm Team Xander!! Perhaps "These dimensions aren't off in faraway outer space." would be a simpler explanation. NO. I read to relax. Not to Google concepts about dimensions and complicated science experiments. Sigh. I'm also confused about how the book is written since it has flashbacks in the middle of reading about what is currently happening. There are times that I can't even tell if I'm still reading about some flashbacks or not. The book started on a sad note, but I'm wondering at first why I can't connect with it. The grief that's supposed to affect me didn't register at all because I'm forced to think about the jargons being presented. That's why. The world building is fascinating. Yes. Yeah. Okay. I did like it, but who write a book branding it with a Sci-Fi genre just because it involves science experiments and dimension traveling only for the plot to be about love and something else I didn't care at all? I was so excited to get an eARC of Panic Lauren Oliver is by far one of my favorite authors and after Requiem being my most anticipated book of 2013, I was itching to get wrapped up in another one of her stories. My first impression of Panic was surprise honestly. I have no idea why I thought this, but I was shocked that this was a contemporary! For some reason I thought it was another dystopian so I was actually pleasantly surprised to find out it was a contemporary! Panic is a game that seniors play the summer after they graduate. It's risky, scary and basically all about what it says ... Panic. The story is told in dual point of views, Heather's and Dodge's. They are both competing in Panic and both for very different reasons. I had a very, very hard time with these characters. It took me a long time to warm up to Heather, I didn't find her unlikable exactly but I found her bland and boring. I eventually did start to like her and her relationship with her younger sister was endearing and lovely. Her decision-making was completely askew although I supposed that could be accounted for her terrible home life. Dodge, I didn't like, and I didn't ever end up liking him. He was completely warped. Because he was so messed up, even when he did somewhat nice things, I couldn't warm up to him at all. Natalie, Heather's best friend was selfish and Bishop, her other best friend was probably the most likeable character of all. He wasn't a favorite of mine, and I will most likely forget I liked him in the future but while I was reading I did enjoy him. I think one of the most difficult things about these characters is that they all had an incredibly poor moral compass. Every single one of them had such poor judgement, the decisions and situations they were in unbelievable. I won't go into detail because a lot of it had to do with Panic but honestly, I found it extremely hard to believe that you would put yourself into some of these life threatening situations for money. The story itself however drew me in immediately. I can't even pinpoint what it was other than pure curiosity to see how the story would end. I was entirely into this story until the very last page, the game Panic, while absolutely ridiculous was also equally thrilling. On of my main dislikes about the book though was the predictability. I could see where the story was going before it got there, and only the final few pages had me unsure of what would happen. Another aspect that turned me off from loving this book, and this is upon reflection the following days, is the memorability. Unfortunatly for me Panic, and the thrill that I felt when reading it, especially in the last few chapters... went away. It is almost forgettable. I actually could not remember if there were two POV's or three POV's, I had to go back to my Kindle to doublecheck! When I finished Panic, I knew this was going to be one that I would have to mull over before writing my review or rating it and ultimately, after my excitement died down, I didn't love it as much as I expected to. I find this is a trend for Lauren Oliver books with me I get so entirely swept up with her writing, her prose and her stories that when I finish, it's like I'm mixed up. I thought I hated Delirium when I finished it, then after a bit of reflection, I realized I was in LOVE with it... that's how strong the emotion was. Before I Fall, I finished and was an emotional wreck but thought I loved it... and then days later I found a lot of things I didn't love. Now obviously this practice didn't go entirely in Panic's favor however it does attest to Oliver's writing. She's a beautiful writer and her stories are captivating when your reading them. Despite my issues with Panic, it was a really good story. It was thrilling when it needed to be, had an interesting and unique concept and had me clinging onto the story until the very last word.

Where The Rock Splits The Sky definitely has a unique and intriguing premise there has been alien invasion which destroyed the moon and altered life on earth forever. Some areas are more affected than others. There is "the zone" where anything and everything can happen no natural rules or laws apply. This "zone" is in the new-old west. Yes, this science fiction has a very western feel to it. Outlaws and sheriffs. Horses and Stagecoaches. Of course, modern technology does not work in the zone. The good news, and this novel desperately needs good news, is that the heroine discovers that ALIENS are just as vulnerable INSIDE the zone as un-invaded humans. She doesn't know why, she doesn't particularly care about the why. Megan, Luis, and Kelly set off into the zone. Technically, Kelly is a friend they pick up in the zone after their official mission has started. But. Kelly is probably the most intriguing character in the novel. I'm not sure she's meant to be. All three join together, but, all three have their own personal agenda. Luis wants revenge, in other words, he wants to kill some aliens. Kelly is looking for answers. Twenty years of her life is missing. She wants to know if any of her family or friends have survived. And Megan, the heroine, wants to find her father. Megan is the leader of the three, she is the one most in-touch with the zone, most sensitive to its strangeness. Where The Rock Splits the Sky is not my kind of book. I'm allergic to westerns even if there are aliens it seems. I was hoping the science-fiction would overcome that. It didn't quite work for me, but, it might work for you.

It's been a long time since I read a Star Wars book probably about 10 years or more . I gave up on them as I often found new authors and stories lacking and overly long for delivering very little to enjoy. After the new release of several books to coincide with the new movie I thought I'd give one of them a read while on holiday. The reviews suggested the best one to try was Lost Stars. The reviews are not wrong. At it's core, Lost Stars tells a basic story of two close friends and later partners who are split up by galactic civil war. It's not a long book and that works well for it. The book's characters are not major heroes or those with super powers, just highly skilled pilots that make their way in the world. Possibly the worst part of the story is how the two main leads end up going through each pivotal moment in the original Star Wars movies. It feels a little forced, but this is a relatively minor issue as it doesn't really detract much from the enjoyment and other parts more than make up for this. Being a fan of the films, I'm not sure what the impact would be if you haven't seen the movies and read this book secretly I think you might find it more enjoyable by not knowing what to expect . I particularly enjoyed the moments when the two characters were together something quite common at the start and then, understandably, less often as the story progresses . They believably fall in love, although one's loyalty to the Empire seemed to last a bit longer than I would think realistic given the trials she goes through. I give props to the idea of one character sticking with the Empire for so long though. I thought that was a cool idea to see the war from the other side and it was a good contrast between the character and others who were obviously fanatical and couldn't see the evil around them. I thoroughly enjoyed the book. I would have liked more pilot dog-fighting between space fighters they always seemed really good moments , but they weren't the main purpose of the story. The author is apparently writing another story with different characters . I'll be picking that up when written. If you're a parent and thinking of getting your teenager this book, I'd recommend it. It's one of the better 'young adult' Star Wars stories I've read and I spent a lot of time in high school reading them . It's also a good book for anyone older -which is more than you can say for a lot of similar genre books. Lastly, the female lead plays an equal role to the male lead chapters alternate between point of view . So if you're wanting a more independent female lead in the genre, this isn't a bad pick -certainly not something to worry about if you're concerned about young romance novels with wishy washy leads. 5 5 Stars.

Tough, brainy Alchemist Sydney and doe-eyed vampire princess Jill are still hiding out in Palm Springs at a human boarding school. Their fellow students, spoiled children of the wealthy and powerful elite, carry on in ignorance as Sydney, Jill, Eddie, and Adrian do everything they can to keep their secret hidden. That Jill's a vampire princess hidden away to keep her alive. But with some forbidden relationships and dangerous threats, keeping a secret is harder than expected. This time around, Sydney's got even more on her plate, like questioning the motives of the Alchemists, like dealing with a possible new threat to everyone's safety, like maybe figuring out what to do when a guy asks you out. Second in the series, The Golden Lily doesn't fail to disappoint for loyal fans of both this and the previous Vampire Academy series. Readers will be tossed straight back into Sydney's story, complete with all her issues and neuroses, her uneasiness over her Moroi friends drinking blood, her gradual acceptance that perhaps not all vampires shouldn't be trusted. What makes reading this series so much is Sydney. She's smart, she's interesting, she's got morals. Apart from the Alchemist knowledge, she's rather plain, there's nothing super about her, she's not fashionable or outgoing, but it's the other aspects of her character that make her enjoyable. It's the multiple internal and external conflicts that she's mixed up in, the fact that the Alchemists want to use her to keep tabs on the vampires, the fact that she's liking Jill and Eddie and Adrian more than the Alchemists, the fact that the Alchemists are keeping secrets from her that might get her killed. It's all about instinct now, which feelings to trust, which people to trust. The biggest surprise in this new installment is the prospect of Sydney getting a boyfriend. Considering the fact that she's more focused on schoolwork and the job at hand, you know she'll be flustered and ever so confused when she doesn't know how to proceed with a guy that likes her. The side characters like Jill and Eddie and all the others are so fleshed out and flawed, and such a contrast to Sydney's practicality. It's the vampire's ability to control the elements, to use magic, that's at odds with Sydney's Alchemist nature to only believe in something when she sees it. This is what I expect from Richelle Mead interesting and outrageously complicated characters, something insidious hiding in the shadows, conflict upon conflict upon conflict, revenge and betrayal, loyalties stretched to the breaking point, romantic entanglements and love rectangles and polygons. Fan will relish this new story, and also be left clamoring for more.

Originally posted at The Scribbling Sprite Why was this book so hard to rate? After all, I flew through it. The world building was spectacular. And the story's delightfully morbid. I kid! I kid! For being a book about an assassin it was pretty low-key. Except for the whole gushing entrails thing. So. Why do I settle on only 3 stars? Because I've become this stupid analytical reader, that's why Is this what editors feel like? . All of the problems with this book wouldn't stop glaring at me. I glared back at them I told them to leave me be and let me enjoy my book in peace! They didn't listen. Bother! On the upside, for everything I didn't like about the book, there was something else to praise. For example The writing was beautiful and the descriptions were well done. Maas does a good job of really transporting you into the setting of the story. BUT--the info dumps scattered about the book and the frequent lack of showing was a major turnoff. As for the characters? I LIKE them, and I like how they were portrayed. Celaena isn't a favorite character of mine, by any means, but I like that she wants to be known for something other than killing. I like that she's not some unfeeling killing machine. I like that, despite her job and her past and her circumstances, she can be girly. She can love dresses and balls and care about how she looks. Oh, and she loves books. She's quite the well-rounded assassin . I like Chaol and that, through all his gruffness, he's shown himself to be noble and generous. I like Dorian in that he wants to show that he's more than the crown. And that he wants a wife equal to him in mind and spirit. I like how Kaltain wasn't just portrayed as the simpering, catty girl who hungered after the crown but rather an intelligent, complex character who hungered after the crown . I like a lot of things, okay? BUT I know, I'm so mean. Another 'but'. while I liked them, I didn't feel this TRUE connection I was supposed to feel, I TRIED to feel. Where were all the FEELS?? It was also hard to get on board with the whole love triangle thing. First of all, WHERE WAS THE LOVE? I get that our two main guys both like Celaena, but the romance felt really flat. It was like the author put the characters together and gave them these weird mushy feelings for each other so we expect SOMETHING to happen and then... Yup. I mean, there WAS romance, but it was pretty lame. The tension was lacking, which is the whole point of a love triangle. But it really wasn't all bad. It was refreshing, really, reading a Young Adult Fantasy with an emphasis on the actual fantasy and less ooey gooey stuff . DNF Okay, so this book had all the kind of themes that I usually love to read about. Cute teen romance? Yay! Problematic mental health filled storyline? YAAY! Little bit of suspense full of cute anecdotes? YAAAAAAAY! So why oh why OH WHY didn't I like it? I wanted to like it, I tried to like it, BUT I JUST DIDN'T LIKE IT! And I love these kind of books! I mean, All the Bright Places? Check! Five stars! Twenty Boy Summer? LOVED! Five stars again! The Fault in Our Stars? I'M IN LOVE! ALL THE STARS! But no. This book just didn't do it for me. I even struggled to finish it, and I rarely leave a book unfinished BECAUSE IT WAS JUST SO BAD! I mean, mental health problems such as depression are difficult to write about at the best of times, and I fully appreciate that.. But to me the author seemed to have no idea about mental health. This book therefore completely fails to capture depression in my opinion, because falling in love is not a magical cure for being depressed! One more time.. FALLING IN LOVE IS NOT A MAGICAL CURE FOR BEING DEPRESSED! There, I said it. And I'm sure many other readers will disagree with me whole heartedly. And that's fine too. But overall, this book was a big let down for me. The plot seemed somewhat okay, very rushed, and could've been improved by slowing down a little or extending the book. The characters weren't that likeable, yet alone realistic. And i'm sorry, but the story itself could've been so, so good. And yet was so boring, so fickle, and so crap. AVOID

Una historia con la que mas de una se sentira identificada. Un grupo de chicas hartas de ser el objetivo de los chicos, hacer ilusiones y despues tirarlas como si fueran juguetes rotos. Se rebelan de tal manera que llega a oidos del director, cosa que me parece excesiva, y por eso la nota es menor. En si, es una historia de amistad mas que de amor y me encanta ver como el grupo cada vez se unifica mas y se convierte en un gran pilar en la pila de muchas chicas. Yo, si existiera un club asi, me uniria fijo. Mejor aun, ?por que no crearlo ahora? Tambien es algo negativo el cliche de Los Beatles. Ultimamente hay muchos libros que sus historias estan fundadas a partir de canciones o componentes de esta banda. Por lo demas, un libro muy agil con un tema muy juvenil y que a pesar de entrar en algunos topicos de la romantica juvenil, da lugar una historia basada en la amistad y de una forma muy original.

I liked the premise of this book three young ladies who work as assistants to a scientist inventor, a magician, and a fencing teacher. The girls team up to solve murders and save all of steampunk Victorian London, proving that they are just as capable and intelligent as their bosses. It's just good fun! The plot moved a little too slowly for me. This 440 page book could have been told in 200 pages. It dragged on a bit in places, setting up relationships, setting up dialogue, explaining this and that. I liked the characters of the girls, but I didn't love them. They are spunky and sweet and sassy and intelligent and independent, but somehow.... I wasn't particularly impressed. Of course, the author killed off the ONE supporting character that I actually loved! And then there was the S-word, which popped up about 10 times, and annoyed me every time. The chapter titles are boring. This shows a lack of creativity. meh. The villains and henchmen were decidedly unoriginal and one-dimensional the sort that twirl their mustaches and laugh in deep baritones. double meh. The one really good thing was Michiko, a Japanese girl living and working in London, trying to learn to speak English and feeling very out of place in a new and strange society. Her culture shock was well-described, and I loved her dignified attempts to learn a new language. She's a treasure!

So I've read this book in about two hours - just further proves my point of how easy of a read this whole series is - and I have to say, I am fairly disappointed. I was actually a bit surprised that more of the people in the book weren't rebelling against this, and this is putting it mildly, screwed up system that they seem to have in Illea. I mean people divided into and born into groups that is vital to their survival and decides the value of their life for them? That is insane. Of course I can't help myself when comparing their system to the one they had in The Hunger Games, with the 'Ones' being the new Capitol. They have many of the same problems, people in the higher ranks not really caring about the people in the lower ranks, because they are just happy to be there. Inglorious and ignorant powerful men, who choose to turn a blind eye to the suffering of their people. This is actually quite a heavy topic Cass has going on, but she chooses to portray it in the most mind numbingly way - through the eyes of a seventeen year old girl, whom her biggest problem is choosing between what guy to be with. I don't really even know what to say about this book, really.. There were times where I just wanted to slap every single person in this book apart from the maids and Marlee, they are all very nice or just sit down and have an intervention. Where I found the first book light-hearted in all it's simple-mindedness and basic nativity, this one was sometimes just plain up annoying. All the characters don't seem to evolve at all, they just go round and round, like the clothes in a washer, in their little circles of ignorance, without even trying to come up with plans on how to make everything better. And ah, this for me just turned into an episode of "The Bachelor", really. But for some reason I also feel like I shouldn't expect that much from a series where I could finish the first two books within the period of a few hours..

In 1940s Lord of the Rings was written by Tolkein detailing an epic journey, and the massive amount of traveling the characters have done through it. I wasn't a fan of the dry parts of the story, but a teacher explained that the walking sections allowed the context of the book to come in. It allowed the adventure in the Mines of Moria to get a proper exposition, it allowed the characters to react to the loss of a character with out having to do it in the middle of the act of losing the character. It allowed revelations to sink in and the quest to be fully examined. I still wasn't a fan. Then I read The Titan's Curse and I realize I appreciated The Lord of the Rings that much more. The problem is a systemic problem of the Percy Jackson series but it really shines through on this book. An example can be gained from this. The band of heroes jump on a train in Washington DC, get off it for some unmentioned reason in a mountain village in New mexico a ski resort? there of all places? They get down the hill quickly and then the next chapter they are in Arizona, and then after that they're in San Francisco. How do they get between these two places? In odd ways, but how much traveling is done? None. Three lines of exposition and the characters have arrived where ever they are going. Hell them getting off a train is just ignored as if it just happens and he was on to his next set piece. Riordan is so in love with his "epic moments" I use quotations because I don't know if that's what he calls them, but they are pretty cool that he doesn't allow his characters to experience them or give them any context. When Gandalf falls in the fight with the Balrog the characters mourn him for a very long time, you can even feel their movement through the world is slowed down because they overcome with the sadness of losing a traveling companion that they have spent months with. Percy loses companions but he's only been with them for 3 days, he meets two companions in this book so they don't have time to bond with Percy, but Riordan wants that sadness, but doesn't want to devote the precious page space to fully experiencing it. And the shortness of the journey does no favors of that. The legnth of mourning Gandalf as the band walks to Lothlorien probably is a longer span than any of the three Percy Jackson books, and that makes for a very different journey. But the issue is Riorden is taking the hero's journey for the third time but not allowing it to build, he misses the size of the story for the excitement of the moments of the story. Do you need a 3 day mourning period on a journey. No, but some serious acknowledgement that the character is going through a change is crucial to the hero's journey. The hero's journey requires a revelation. It then requires reflection and requires atonement. And it's not like Percy Jackson isn't using and abusing the hero's journey. But without the reflection and atonement the revelation is weak. The character's reaction to the revelation is what puts it in context, and Riorden just doesn't even attempt that. It's a shame because after two books that I could enjoy Riorden just pushes the story a bit too far and a bit too fast on this book. In book two I knew something was missing, and the story was going too fast, but there was some moments for reflection. In The Titan's Curse, those small moments are gone and we are on to a book that moves entirely too fast for the situations to be fully explored, and overall it weakens the book. I am undecided between a 3 because I enjoyed the book, or a 4 because yet again we fall back on the "this was written for kids". I'm leaving this a 4 because to be honest, if you enjoy the first two books, you'll enjoy this book, the flaws of the writing do leave much to be desired, but this book was better than Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix that just let me down. It's a good book that could be better, not a bad book that could be good. And then there's the big spoilers that helped the score Characters die!!!! Thank you Rick Riordan. You're on huge adventures with large groups of people and no one dies? Bullshit! You're fighting gods and you don't even get a scratch? What? Riordan not only kills one but TWO characters. It took Harry Potter four books and even then it was a bit weak. In this book two characters die, and no they don't come back. They're dead. Granted one character should have died and somehow "survived" but overall Riordan takes a huge chance with these deaths and actually made me nod my head and applaud the commitment. Can a major character die? Well not yet, but at least these two characters have passed away. The only problem is neither of these characters are mourned. Hell hours after one dies, the band of adventurers are at a party to end the book. Umm wut? But at least the recently deceased didn't appear in the middle of the party.

I didn't guess the killer, but I guessed the motive. Mild spoilers ensue. This book starts off as a cookie cutter slasher story. In fact, for the first 130 pages it's plagiarized scream. Scream is a series I watched when I was 6 and ignited my love of serial killers and horror movies. I was a little annoyed to see how blatant this was at ripping it off, but then halfway through the book we get the killer reveal. That changed a lot for me. Getting the killer reveal halfway through was an interesting tactic. I wondered if there were other killers, it puts you on edge and makes you wonder why. I think the motive was pretty obvious so I guessed it early on, but I think it was a really unique way to pull the slasher genre into and I applaud Perkins for it. I liked the characters and plot too. I actually didn't hate any characters which was nice. I will say, there's a deep dark secret in the main characters past and i thought it ended up being pretty anti climatic. But honestly everything else was well done. I also experienced something I never have before where the last page of the book ended up being a full page so I flipped the page expecting more and got acknowledgments. I just wanted even more, so that was a nice feeling. Lastly, don't expect too much. This isn't scary. It's not even spooky. It's YA slasher so it's rated PG and relatively plain. If you just expect to have fun with this novel, it won't disappoint as much as I think it has others.

I was intrigued by the premise of Arclight by Josin L. McQuein, and was excited to read this YA horror story. Unfortunately, it was a disappointment for me. I'll do my best to explain. Summary The Arclight is the last refuge in a post-apocalyptic world consumed by terrifying creatures called the Fade. No one crosses the wall of light that keeps the last human survivors safe. There's nothing else left and nowhere to go. Or so they thought, until Marina, a lone teenage girl, stumbles out of the Dark. Marina doesn't remember who she is, where she came from, or how she survived. And the Fade want her back. When one of them infiltrates the compound and recognizes Marina, she begins to unlock secrets she didn't even know she had. Marina knows she's an outsider, but she'll do anything to protect those who saved her. Whether they want her help or not. The description leads you to believe it's going to be an action-packed sci-fi horror story, but it really isn't. In short, I thought the book was a bit vague and slow-moving. The Arclight, which protects the surviving citizens of the world from the Fade, sounded like an incredible story-world. However, the setting was difficult to picture and so I wasn't very impressed. I didn't connect with the characters as I'd hoped to, and even the romance was a bit too sudden and predictable. The big reveal of the novel wasn't predictable, at least, so there's that. However, it didn't excite me or move me. I won't be reading the sequel. I really don't relish writing reviews for books I disliked. I don't believe in bashing authors, or forcing my opinions on others, but in this case I wanted to share my reasoning for giving the book 2 stars. And honestly, I'd probably give it 2.5 stars, but Goodreads doesn't allow half star ratings. And possibly I feel this way about Arclight because I'm not the greatest fan of sci-fi. That said, I don't usually give genre a second thought when I fall for a book's premise, and don't believe my feelings for sci-fi are what ultimately led me to dislike the novel.

Find this review and more fantastical things at The Leaning Tower of Tomes. The review The Cage is a pretty tough sci-fi story to swallow. It brings up some heavy psychological questions and dilemmas. It's dark, it's grim, it's disturbing at times. We are reminded that humans, and any human-like species, can really be disgusting and despicable when circumstances get ugly and people get desperate. The premise is actually fascinating, if downright creepy Humans held in captivity by aliens. Basically, a human zoo. Where the aliens study and experiment on them. The book is narrated by six characters, which is five characters too many. The main-main protagonist is Cora, but we get chapters through the eyes of Lucky, Nok, Rolf, Leon, and Mali. Perhaps The Cage's biggest downfall is its unlikable and cliche characters. Although racially diverse and from very different backgrounds, these teens showed some terrible true colors. I might go even so far as to say I hated a few of them. I really disliked Cora for much of the book, although I admired the fight in her and the unwavering hope she could escape and go home to Earth. I really wasn't a fan of Lucky he come off as a douche sometimes and while I understood his desperation to survive via Cora's cooperation, I still didn't like him. I started off liking Nok very much... but then she totally fell off the rails and I couldn't believe how much of a personality change she had. Rolf was actually very promising early on, but he, like Nok, became stupid and suspicious and close-minded as the book went on. Leon, although the group's bully at the start, shaped up to be mildly interesting, but I didn't like him much, either. Mali, however, really grew on me and became my favorite character, although she didn't have much to do except drop some info-bombs on the others and begin to doubt what she'd been told. I liked Mali, she could really kick butt, but she couldn't save this story. Then there was Cassian, the Caretaker. A gorgeous alien. Who Cora was immediately attracted to and captivated by, despite knowing he was her captor. I knew it was coming, it says it in the book's description, but I was all like, Girl, don't you fall in love with your captor! But, alas, she did, and he with her, and it was both not too terrible but also terrible because Stockholm syndrome. Shudder. I did think Cassian was a somewhat interesting character. He was a mystery, he wanted to understand humanity, he sometimes viewed Cora and the others though mostly Cora as real people. I mean, of course he viewed them as animals intelligent ones, but still beings lesser than his kind , he was their Caretaker, and he didn't do anything about the researchers performing their experiments on the teenagers and messing with their heads to see how they'd react. I don't mind the trope of two people from completely different worlds falling in love, and I don't mind human-alien pairing, as ridiculous as it is, so I was curious to see where Cora and Cassian's bizarre relationship would go... I didn't hate Cassian, but what he did to Cora especially is pretty tough to come back from. The world building was actually pretty interesting and well-done. "The Cage" was very detailed and expansive and just downright creepy. It was really like a home for lab rats, complete with puzzles that would award tokens to exchange for prizes. Even the glimpses of alien life outside the Cage was pretty depressing, if a much-needed break from the hell going on among the human characters. Cora's story-line was the only one I modestly cared about, and I still got sick of it at times. I also don't think there needed to be six narratives going on. I just didn't like anyone, and didn't care about the "dark secrets" they were all hiding. The teens were unhappy, suspicious, and played one another. They were going crazy in their environment and it was messing with my head, too. In the end, The Cage wasn't a bad book at all. It's just not a happy book, and the characters are far from compelling. The concept is great, and Megan Shepherd's writing is great, and the book's atmosphere hits perfectly. But it's a tough story to swallow, and there are many lulls in the plot when characters you don't give a crap about take turns giving their take on events. I also wasn't surprised by the big reveal at the end even though I didn't guess it. It definitely complicated things, that's for sure, and hit all the characters and myself at an emotional level. No one likes being deceived! The Cage is a strange, dark, twisted story that I both liked and didn't like. So tell me... Have you read The Cage? If you haven't, would you be interested to? What's the last book you read about aliens? What's a book you've read that you might describe as "disturbing"? Comment below letting me know! And, as always, happy reading! L'ho finito... praticamente divorato. L'unico difetto che posso trovargli e che e troppo corto e quindi dura troppo poco. Per il resto... wow, mi ha completamente stregata. Un'eroina del tipo che preferisco, la ragazza combattiva che sfida le regole di un mondo che le va troppo stretto, un eroe intrigante e misterioso, che dietro il sorriso malandrino nasconde enormi segreti, un'ambientazione veramente magica e originale, una narrazione incalzante ma esaustiva, un buon equilibrio tra azione, dialoghi e descrizioni. E tutto ridotto all'osso, non c'e una parola di piu di quelle che servono, forse anche per questo e corto, ma l'autrice e veramente brava a farti percepire il calore del deserto e non solo di quello! , il profumo delle spezie, l'impeto della sabbia e del vento e la magia di leggende esotiche in poche parole. E dietro la narrazione cinematografica sembra proprio di veder scorrere la pellicola di un film nella testa , ci sono anche nascosti temi toccanti e di una brutale attualita la discriminazione per le donne, una lotta religiosa che nasconde invece interessi economici e di potere, l'odio per lo straniero, per il diverso, lo sfruttamento di risorse che stravolge l'ordine della natura. Tutto e trattato in maniera molto superficiale siamo pur sempre davanti a un romanzo di avventura per ragazzi scritto da un'autrice giovanissima , ma questi echi di un mondo reale contribuiscono a rendere piu vivo il mondo creato dall'autrice. Il finale e aperto, ma per tranquillizzare futuri lettori, posso dire che comunque c'e una sorta di conclusione, non si resta del tutto con il fiato sospeso in attesa di un seguito che non e ancora stato scritto. Un seguito che pero spero vivamente che non tardi, perche voglio troppo sapere come proseguira la ribellione seeeee, a chi la racconto? In realta voglio vedere di nuovo Jin a petto nudo... e gia che ci siamo, pure Ahmed! Insomma, davvero un romanzo originale che non posso che consigliare a chi ama ambientazioni esotiche, principi del deserto ed eroine guerriere.

This was a very confused and confusing book. I'm wondering if two stars is a little generous, but there are parts that are actually quite good, they just don't add up to a decent whole. It's an Alice in Wonderland retelling origin story, and I believe the first of a trilogy. The majority of this book was taken up by lengthy, lavish descriptions of Dinah's the princess of Wonderland and future Queen of Hearts everyday life in the palace, her all-consuming crush on her childhood friend, the palace itself, and how horrible her father is. For the first third or so, that's literally all there was. It's pretty well written, but after a certain amount of time it becomes dull. After that, it's interspersed by episodes of seemingly random action. I mean, really, I'm still wondering how the various plot elements fit together. And this book has a real problem with tone. It's like there were two books being shoved together to make a single story. Or maybe someone recognised there was no real tension, no impetus driving the story forward, and so an episode of ALL THE DARK, ALL THE MENACING, ALL THE EVIL was shoved in the middle. The frustrating thing was, that particular section was really good! It was creepy and horrifying and... belonged in a different book. And then we went back to the airy, descriptive royal palace life. The main conflict is between Dinah and her father, but I have no idea why. What's driving it. He seems to be horrible for the sake of horribleness - I'd go so far as to call him a pantomime villain, but with none of the anarchic charm of the Queen of Hearts in the original Alice. I mean, for goodness sake, of course families can hide all sorts of dislikes and divisions and skeletons, but there has to be something at the root of it. No matter how mean he might be, a king doesn't decide to frame his eldest daughter and heir for murder and have her killed without some actual reason! And about that ending! What? Where did that come from? It wasn't built up at all, nothing in all Dinah's "bad feelings" even hinted at such a dramatic turn of events - I'm all for a plot twist, but there has to be some sort of foreshadowing. And some of her decisions had me tearing my hair out who the hell decides to run away on the word of a masked stranger who turns up in their bedroom in the middle of the night? - they stink of plot convenience rather than being true to the character or story. I didn't feel Dinah had any real character development, she sometimes fell into the too-stupid-to-live mould, most of the secondary characters and walk-ons were cardboard cutouts. Oh, and right at the end, after all the Happenings have Happened? She stops to admire the view. For what seemed like five pages I was listening on audiobook, so I can't prove that. It was a Long. Time. Lengthy descriptions of how many shades of blue a flower can be. Kill me now. Also, I would not recommend the audiobook. I was initially happy to have a British reader it's my native accent, so I always find it easier to listen to, my personal preference but when every character bar the royal family was voiced as some sort of idiot yokel... No.

There is a reason that this is my 13th book of Rick Riordan's that I've read. This guy just knows how to write a fantastic YA fantasy book. Sure, is it basically the same formula in every book? Yes. But where Riordan shines is in his characters. No world is more diverse than that of Percy Jackson, Jason Grace, and Magnus Chase sorry I haven't read the Kane series . This book was so much fun and had me on the edge of my seat every moment. I loved the first book in this series but I loved this one even more. I am excited where the series is headed in the upcoming finale huge sigh that I have to wait until next year . After the last book where Magnus finds himself as an einherji in Vahalla and his friends Sam, Blitz, and Hearth stop the Fenris Wolf from being released... yep , we pick up with a new quest Thor's Hammer is gone! But didn't it get lost last time? Yes. Thor is very clumsy. Magnus and friends embark on more adventures to recover Thor's hammer and to stop evil Loki from getting himself unchained gasp . We get to visit Hearth's "hometown" and meet his dad, which was a heart breaking part of the book. I'm glad we got to see more character development with Hearth like we did with Blitz in the the last book. We hang out with more giants in such a fun scene that has to be one of my favorites so far and I'll just leave it at that. We see more of Loki this book and man that guy is evil. Also, poor Randolph. I think. I haven't decided if I feel empathy or not yet. We hang out with Thor some more and his "lovely" wife. It was nice to see that the gods actually came through for the demigods in the end. Sometimes the gods are portrayed as obnoxious and uncaring and sometimes even very dumb. Thor helping out Magnus and his friends in the end was great. Lastly, and most importantly, we get to meet a new character. Another child of Loki Alex Fierro, a shapeshifting gender-fluid teenager. I wanted to fist pump the air when Riordan first introduced the character. Having a gender-fluid teen in a HUGELY popular young adult book is such a massive step forward for books everywhere. I hope there is a teen out there that reads this and feels important and not alone and can find inspiration from Alex. She I'll use this pronoun as that was the most common gender she identified with during this book is super spunky and strong willed. What I loved even more about her character was how Magnus treated her with respect. Even though he didn't understand her sometimes, he respected her. Overall, another fantastic book by Riordan. I cannot wait for the next book.

Kestrel is the general's daughter and within three years, she is expected to either marry or join the military. Kestrel often wanders the markets without an escort but things change after a slave auction. Without thinking, Kestrel bids and wins the slave who the auctioneer claims to be a blacksmith and a singer. Kestrel is drawn to him and develops feelings for him but she eventually finds out how doomed her love for him becomes. I had high hopes for this fantasy book and the beginning was promising and succeeded in drawing me in. Kestrel seemed to be a sheltered person with not much of an idea of the world around her and it was great to see how the slave Arin helped her opened her eyes and look at things in a different perspective. The blurb mentioned a romance and I was looking forward to how this would blossom. With the progression of the romance, I felt like both parties showed signs of Stockholm Syndrome. I lost a little interest and became bored when Arin became less mysterious and his motives became clear, which was about half way into the book. I suppose I found the whole war between the Valorians and Herrani dull because the book didn't really delve into the politics or raging battles. The war essentially served as a backdrop for the Romeo-and-Juliet-esque love story of Kestrel and Arin. The book was anti-climatic because there was very little action and Kestrel and Arin spent a great deal of page time thinking about their feelings... Overall, The Winner's Curse was an OK read. Just expect it to focus heavily on romance!
