Io capisco che l'autrice vuole incentrare il libro su loro e sui loro sentimenti reciproci capaci di aiutare i protagonisti a superare persino le situazioni piu avverse, ma cosi e davvero troppo e soprattutto inappropriato in determinati momenti. A deludermi anche la figura di Bianca che appare una ragazzina senza spina dorsale e che ha bisogno di appoggiarsi a Lucas per ogni motivo, serio o stupido che possa essere. Diamine, sei una mezza vampira, potresti avere tutti i poteri che vuoi, non hai bisogno di un cavalier servente! Per non parlare del finale. Se avessi letto questo libro e avessi dovuto aspettare non so quanto per il successivo avrei ucciso la Gray. In poche parole un finale alla Lisa J. Smith, finisce che non finisce e ti lascia li a dire E quindi? Hai intenzione di lasciarmi cosi fino al prossimo? Sadica! In piu mi aspettavo una presenza maggiore e piu fondamentale di Charity, giusto per dare quel pizzico di movimento in piu alla narrazione, ma anche in quelle sporadiche apparizioni resta come una figura marginale e non rilevante. Grosso errore, a mio parere. In sostanza, un inaspettato flop. Spero che almeno nell'ultimo ci sia quel qualcosa in piu che e mancato nei primi tre.

slams head on desk Someday I will get my awesome dark badass Little Red Riding Hood retelling, but today is not that day I was so excited for this book. SO. EXCITED. This book was calling my name. I mean, it's Littler Red Riding Hood! But sexy! And in Versailles . Cruel Beauty had such promise and was such a solid story, that to add a sophomore novel from the same author with my favorite of all fairy tales to play with, and I was so ready to be blown away. Cruel Beauty was so quick and fun and sexy I was dying for this one. And it was just... too much of that same book yet not enough. There were a lot of plates in the air for this one. The same prophecy, evil boyfriend, evil god, three-pronged romance, mysterious quest thing going. But it was so complicated. Cruel Beauty was mostly two people, in a room, trying to get something from the other. This worked, it was a complicated relationship. They wanted different things. They used each other. They grew to like each other when they mirrored each other's monstrosity. There were definitely relationships like this in the book but coming from all sides. It was a little overcomplicated. Erec was too despicable to be redeemed within the first half of the book, but she keeps trusting and letting herself be used by him. Armand was too sanctimonious and principled. A morally grey character like Rachelle needs her equally ambiguous match, instead both love interests were very black and white, good and bad. One preying on her dark side, the other calling for her to seek absolution. Yes Armand's faith and principles are challenged by the end, but they are unshaken enough for him to really do what he said he was going to do before they fell in love. He chooses what you know he's going to choose. And it seems like his goodness fixes Rachelle- an offense that after something as deviant and morally gray as Cruel Beauty, I'm not sure I can forgive. There's a lot of morality in this book, CB definitely had it too, but it was a little more preachy this time around. While I thought it added some depth to Rachelle, she was still a relatively flat character, or at least in how she came across as a carbon copy of Nyx. and she loses all of her godly powers in the end. That was the fun part. That pissed me off. I know it shouldn't have but...just... there are things I like to see in books, and her as a great reckoning was one of them. There was just too much going on in this book. It felt too dense and complicated. I wanted this simple, reeling seduction temptation story that Little Red Riding Hood could be. It was still a worthwhile read, but it wasn't what I'd expected or wanted. Disappointed but still pleased enough, I suppose was the final verdict.

I just did not like this that much on either a regular or a Newbery level. I didn't think the dynamics of the school were very believable most of the kids read too old to me, and the way it all worked out in the end was just TOO warm-n-fuzzy --I think that was my main problem--and while this is way, way better than most guidance-counselor fiction, the writing did creep that way too often for my tastes. The big action scene near the end didn't work for me. I'm assuming there really are environmental education schools in New York where one of the evening activities is getting together to watch a movie in a park, so while I thought that was really strange and it didn't make sense to me, I give that a pass. But... logistically... there were a bunch of things in there that puzzled me. Perhaps most of all, the ending was both too feel-good and a little creepy. I was really uncomfortable with how we're supposed to think a school full of kids calling Auggie "Hey, little dude"--including kids his own age--was a great thing. Better than before? For sure. But so icky and condescending. All the kids thinking it's so great that Auggie won this school award? I mean, I don't think kids care about awards like that all that much, and even if they did, I would have expected more grumbling "they only gave it to him because" than admiration. I liked that Julian never came around. That felt real to me. But I didn't like that he just won't be in school next year, problem solved. My favorite narrator, and the one that felt most real and natural to me, was Via's boyfriend Justin. I love that guy. I would like to say that I wish we'd gotten more of him, but I think it was probably a wise choice to give us just a taste and leave me wanting to know more. Likewise with Miranda. The scene at school that felt the MOST real to me was the one where Auggie is in his Halloween costume and hears his so-called friend talking about him. The kids' voices in that seemed spot-on, and I took what Jack said quite seriously and alarmedly. But then it was never really dealt with. The scene was, sure. But it seemed to me like it was kind of passed off as "I didn't really mean it" when at the time Auggie notes that he sounds very serious. I mean, Jack says he thought a lot about what he would do if he was in Auggie's situation, and I think that IS the kind of thing a kid would think about. I don't think he made that up on the spur of the moment. Perhaps further talk about suicide would have made the book too dark for its audience, but I felt like it left me hanging with something very serious. Overall I think this has too many holes to make it a Newbery. And "Mom, thanks for making me go to school" not an exact quote sums up my philosophical problems.

Y'all I really hated this book, but I couldn't tell if it was me or the writing. This is a YA version of Middlesex that attempts the most saccharine, insincere brand of magical realism I've ever read. I might have been able to stomach a short story written in this style, but all 300 pages of this was too much of a gigantic eyeroll. And I tried! I really did! I may be a cynic with no heart, but sometimes I can stuff that part of my brain into a little box and let myself be absorbed in the story, whatever its inconsistencies. But it honestly feels like this book was written in this kitchen and I just could not get past the fact that, at its core, this book has an inauthentic heart that's full of cliches about "love." It uses magical realism not to enhance the story but to draw attention away from the fact that THIS BOOK HAS NO CENTRAL STORY. I utterly reject the idea that the central story is love's redeeming power. In the context of the ending, that's horrible. To be fair, Leslye Walton completely commits to her world, and she's not afraid to pull her magic into the macabre a character in the first chapter carves out her still-beating heart to offer it up for her wrongdoing. There's real sadness and pain here, but it's overshadowed by how tritely it's written and how flat the characters are. Now that I'm thinking of it, this actually reminds me of a less successful Pushing Daisies In a story set in the late 1950s where the peripheral characters are named things like Ignatius Lux, Cardigan Cooper ! , and Laura Lovelorn - guess what her main character arc is - it's hard not to see the parallels. Except that I hated all the characters, especially the cartoonish, unsatisfying relationship between Viviane and Jack, and I especially hated Rowe Cooper, though throwing in a stutter as a cute characteristic is a surefire way to win my enmity I'm looking at you, too, Glee! . AND THE ENDING First of all, Nathaniel Sorrows? You are kidding me, right? Second of all, the main theme of this book - which the older Ava Lavender hammers home again and again - is that love makes fools of us all. Saying that someone like Nathaniel Sorrows, who is a psychopathic, mentally unhinged man who perpetrates a horrific and violent sexual assault, "suffers from love" just as the Roux family did is disgusting. Whatever Nathaniel Sorrows felt - unrequited lust, longing, whatever - it's not love. Couldn't it be twisted love? No, it can't be. I'm extraordinarily uncomfortable with a world in which Rene's murderer "suffers from love" the same way Rene does. Sad, fantastical, and slightly twisted is Pierette turning into a canary. It's not Rene Roux being shot in the face. There are many different kinds of love, Walton seems to say, and they all affect us differently at points in our lives. Well and good, until you get to a story that's predicated on Ava "accepting" the love of a man to get past her traumatic assault. Ava is cut open to remove her individuality, and the Roux family all finally sees that as a catalyst for change in their own lives. NOPE NOPE NOPE NOPE NOPE. So yes, I think this book will do very well on Tumblr direct quote "broken hearts smelled surprisingly sweet" , and Leslye Walton will be a successful YA author, and we shall all probably have to suffer through future books that come out of her middle-school creative writing workshops, and I will continue to be puzzled by all of the reviewers who are "dazzled" by this book. Ava Lavender, I am NOT sorry to see you go.

3.5 stars Once dubbed America's Fattest Teen, Libby decides to go back to high school after years of homeschooling. She'd hidden herself away from the outside world after having to be cut out of her house and lifted BY A CRANE due to her spectacular weight. A boy, her neighbour, had watched her rescue from across the street and once her house was left abandoned, he went inside to explore and find out more about her. He ended up pinching a copy of the girls favourite book and a fridge magnet. He then sent her a note telling her he was rooting for her which he slipped into the book and sent it off anonymously. Libby receives the book and note amongst a countless pile of hate mail. Years later, the boy, Jack, and Libby meet at school under pretty hilarious mortifying circumstances and Jack decides not to tell her he knows her from her horrific past. This is Libby's chance to fall in love for the first time and live life as a normal school girl... but Jack comes with his own 'weight.' He's got Prosopagnasia AKA face blindness... Brad Pitt has it! Look it up.. This means that the poor boy can never remember what people look like, including his very own family. There's something about Libby, though, that seems to be permanently ingrained in his mind and he, unlike everyone else, seems to be able to see past her size and gets to know the 'real' her. Libbys character is inspiring. She knows who she is, she's ballsy, brave, witty as FUCK For example..on the first day back at school this is one piece of dialogue "Hey," he says. "Hey." "Is it true fat girls give better blow jobs?" "I don't know. I've never gotten a blow job from a fat girl.". I smiled and laughed at all of her comebacks and a part of me wishes I could be that quick. She's strong... and she knows what she wants. Jack's character on the other hand didn't do much for me. Yeah, he was sweet. He looked past the weight of Libby and was pretty romantic - but he was also a bit of a douche as most school boys are, no? . He has this big problem of not being able to recognize faces and pins it down to being because of a fall he had as a child. For as long as he's known he has kept his problem a secret and the only other person he tells is Libby. But why??? What's the big deal about keeping it a secret?? I don't know - that part of the story just fell flat for me. This book definitely doesn't compare to All The Bright Places... but I think if you've ever suffered or are suffering from weight issues, this book could really inspire you. Also I just want to say here.... a lot of people have problems with books that 'romanticise mental illness.' WHAT. D'Fuck????? I think it is so important to learn about mental illnesses, to speak about it and make it normal so that the millions of people out there that actually suffer from something can have something to relate to. Something to hopefully help them. On another note, having a love story intertwined with teaching us about that illness makes it wonderful for everyone to read and easier for those of us who don't know anything about those illnesses - EVERYONE deserves love. Everyone deserves to have their story told. Everyone in some way or another is wanted, needed and loved - and that's the overall message this book gives to us all!

I was given a copy of this book in exchange for an honest review. To read more reviews like this one, check out Obsessive Book Nerd! First Impressions I quickly noticed that the chapters in Chasing Spring were really short, making it hard to really get into the story before switching POVs there were three, two first-person present and one third-person . And at the start of the book, I liked the narrators. I want to state here, for the record that I have loved every R.S. Grey book I've read so far, so my expectations were high for Chasing Spring. Then I really got into the book...and things did not get better. Only worse. After awhile I really didn't like the narrators. Mostly Ricco Fajardo. Which bums me out, I think, though, his Texas draw isn't his strong suite and should be avoided in future books. When he wasn't voicing the character's friends in this draw, he was fine. With all of the narrators, their Texas twang just felt forced. But what got me the most, was how infuriating the main character, Lilah was. You know those books where the character just makes dumb decisions and assumptions after another? That was this book. Take Lilah for example..."My kinda-sorta-boyfriend just left school with one of his best friends who he also used to date. He gave her a hug and that means he must still be into her, so I'm gonna go hang out with this bad-news guy and spend hours with him, even though I don't know what my kinda sorta boyfriend's reason was for leaving me to walk home by myself. What? I'm totally NOT gonna call or text him to find out why. I'm just gonna think the worse and do something really, really stupid." Yeah. That kind of character. That was Lilah. And she drove me NUTS. Final thoughts This book...this book bummed me out. I wanted so much more from it. But it just fell flat for me.

http openbooksociety.com article av... Brought to you by OBS Reviewer Scott Fast forward to the future - the Second Civil War between the States is well underway. The Liberty Union Democracy the North clings to outmoded, ancient traditions, placing value on material worth rather than the human condition Avantica the South provides for the people who are genetically engineered, from birth, to do tasks they are most suited for the productivity they provide the state. Thus begins the rollercoaster ride through a myriad of plot turns and twists and plenty of food for thought on the way things are headed in society today. As most fine speculative fiction, Avant Nation proffers a delightful spin on the world as we knew it, and from threads, weaves the extremes of both sides of these rather poignant topics. The writing, deceptively simple, plays up the various themes and the overall story arc. The citizens of the L.U.D. are an extreme of capitalism and the horrors that merit brought on by material acquisition entail. Higher crime rates, increased poverty, a division between the haves and have-nots and increased violence because of this. By way of comparison, Avantica seems idyllic, except that its citizens are sterilized and "vat-grown" embryos are the norm, save that they are genetically engineered to be the perfect cogs in the machine that feed the state - however, since the entire population can be controlled, nobody really wants for anything - but everyone lives in fear of discovering they're "defective" i.e. not fit to carry out their duties . At no point in the story does the reader converge on one side or the other, as the blacks and whites portrayed are mired in shades of grey. The prose flows from chapter to chapter, trickling from the viewpoint of the lives of Avants from Avantica, to what a skillfully written plot, and gushing into high adrenaline pumping action adventure. The main protagonist, Claire, is from the "Compassionate" class and it is through her compassion that the force propels the story. Although others appear in the novel, they aren't as fully fleshed out as Claire. With Claire, the reader is given a sounding board and the people passing through her life serve as reflectors of her current state of mind. She is a fully fleshed out character that exudes compassion as she's supposed to and a deep three dimensional understanding of how things work in the setting. Sadly the other members of the cast are two-dimensional in flavor and her Academy classmate Hawk from the Rugged class , is the only other individual we get to know, somewhat well. Overall, Avant Nation is a joy to read, right up to the climatic ending. Well executed in plot and setting and the theme of genetic engineering vs. rampant capitalism should earn this a spot on any Alternative History or Science Fiction fans shelf. Had there been a little bit more character development, this easily would have received 5 stars. However, the story itself is sound and should keep readers guessing until the very end.

Meh. It was okay. What a way to start the year lol. One of the things that I really enjoyed about this story was the world-building that Sasha and Lindsay wrote about. I got both a Star Wars and a Star Trek vibe to it, with the different planet systems and jumps into hyperspace. I liked the idea of the plot, where it was heading. I sensed an unusual, but good, love triangle between Valen, Andi, and Dex? . One aspect I did not enjoy was Andi herself. Yes, we can call her the Bloody Baroness - it suits her fairly well with all the blood she spilled in the sixty or so pages I read. But I thought she was far from ruthless, and quite honestly, a little boring. Like, she splayed her insides for all readers to digest from the get-go. There was no mystery, no intrigue as to her motives. There would be a sentence about how she called herself merciless, and then the next sentence would be her almost bursting into tears at the thought of her crew being injured. I just don't put ruthless and open emotions in the same category I absolutely adored Nor, this supposed evil queen on Xen Pterra. Now she was characterized as ruthless. She loved the smell of blood and couldn't wait to kill more people. Do I sense that the weapon she is building to be like a Death Star? Hell yeah! I think Nor adds a great layer of complexity to the cast of characters in Zenith Someone I also liked was Lira. She's cool and blue, and so loyal to Andi and the crew of the Marauder. I'd want her on my team any day! And then there's Dex. He's complex and characterized in a way that all we would get from him is that he's always hated Andi, and that he's always going after the money, like a Han Solo type of guy. You can tell that the author that characterized Nor and Dex was not the same one who characterized the crew of the Marauder. I honestly can't tell which one is which but I have my suspicions. Final Verdict 7 10 I would have given this 8.5 but Andi and her over-openness about her character made me feel less motivated to want to continue ...circumstances of characterization. I LOVED the world and the direction in which the story is headed. Hopefully, with loads more editing, this can be a story that will keep you on the edge of your seat!

While this wasn't my favorite short story in the bunch, it is definitely up on my list simply because it was not what I was expecting - in a good way. Lemme be straight with you guys I don't like Kami Garcia's writing Or Margaret Stohl and I haven't since I read the disaster that was Beautiful Creatures. DON'T HATE ME! I couldn't bring myself to like it, and the same goes for this story. While I enjoyed the plot and what it was trying to do... it was simply meh in every other aspect. Therefore, it fell flat and that's all I have to say about that. Yes, I am biased. Deal with it. Things About Love by Jackson Pearce This was so cool. Plain and simple. I still liked it, don't get me wrong - I just don't like missing things. Oops. Merely Mortal by Melissa Marr FINALLY! One connection to something else that I've actually read! Despite all that, though, this fell flat for me. It was sort of just underwhelming, and therefore disappointing. I had some pretty high expectations because I enjoyed Wicked Lovely and its interpretation of faeries. This just didn't hit the bar for me. Should I feel bad? Also, be warned - if you haven't read Wicked Lovely, this little tale is spoiler central. Facing Facts by Kelley Armstrong Spoilery but soothed my fangirl heart - and that's all I have to say about that. mic drop Let's Get This Undead Show On The Road by Sarah Rees Brennan While I appreciate the constant satire on vampire stereotypes and the like, the lore and everything else about this sort story required some serious suspending of disbelief and common sense. It was just lacking that little bit of.... sparkle See what I did there? DID YOU SEE IT!?!? I'm serious, though, despite the Twilight joke. This story was just another bout of meh. Bridge by Jeri Smith-Ready This one... wow. Just wow. If you read this, and when you read this - get some tissues and therapy lined up. This is sad, compelling, and needed. It is about family, about learning to let go, and trying to decide when everything becomes too much. It had a very fitting format, it was the perfect mode to tell the perfect story. This one might take the cake, as it were. Skin Contact by Kimberly Derting Leaving by Ally Condie Why all the feels? Honestly, these last couple killed me, why did you have to join in? Ugh... this one cuts deep, and I mean deep. There is a lot in a little space, once again. This story really has something to say though, it has a purpose and it completely nails it on the head. At The Late Night, Double Feature, Picture Show by Jessica Verday Just close your eyes for a second and picture this Flesh eating, zombie girl scouts and vampires dressed in so much drag they belong on Rue Paul's Drag Race. This story is pleasantly surprising, entertaining, and everything else in-between. IV League by Margaret Stohl Gargouille by Mary E. Pearson This short story was perfection. Just... agh! The Third Kind by Jennifer Lynn Barnes Bows down to the queen Automatic by Rachel Caine Rachel Caine.... happy sigh Morganville makes an appearance and my life is made. It is just that simple. I would've liked more cues from the characters themselves, as it was hard to feel anything for characters who shrug off everything that was happening. The characters themselves, I found, were underdeveloped. The narrator keeps the reader at arm's length, and though this was initially interesting, it made it extremely difficult to sympathize with the characters and grow to cheer for them. After one hundred and fifty pages of feeling nothing for the characters, I grew apathetic and I no longer cared about the story. The writing in Possession was blunt, to say the least. While I don't mind blunt writing, I don't feel it worked for this story. Not to mention her action scenes were very poorly written and I had to go back multiple times and reread the passages just to figure out what was going on. This was one of the my favorite reads this year. The story was amazing, the writing wonderful, the characters were unforgettable. Heartbreaking, memorable, a powerful read. I think it will be qutie a while before I recover from this book, just in time to read it again. Its years after the fresh water source has diminished and Lynn and her mother live on their own out in the middle of nowhere on a pond. Lynn's entire life has been a lesson to protect the pond on their land. As soon as she could hold a gun she was taught to shoot. Lynn's mother trusts no one and helps no one. Shoot first ask questions later.... or not... just make sure too shoot. Lynn suddenly finds herself in need of the help of strangers when there are new and dangerous people living south of her pound. She finds out that shooting first isn't always the way to go and she isn't the only one just trying to survive. This was a very slow building book but it very intense slow. I was never bored and even though it was not full of thrills, the story still kept me on the edge of my seat. I didn't want to stop listening and I never wanted the story to end. I think I could have stayed in Lynn's scary world for a quite a bit of time. I loved the characters and I was completely pulled into their lives and their world. I absolutely adored Lynn. I found her her heartless nature understandable and I found it easy to soften out when she did. It was in her nature to be caring but she was always taught to be ruthless. For good reason, survival. The relationship between Lynn and her mother was strong and endearing. They were the only ones in each other's lives and they meant the world to one another. I loved their relationships and their interactions with each other. Lynn held all her mother taught to her dear and as truth. It was a hard road for Lynn to learn and accept that her mother's way may not have been the only way. It was quite a journey to watch Lynn grow and learn about other relationships... first love, friendship, and family with no blood relation. She learned responsibility came in all forms. I loved her sense of duty, her loyalty, and her integrity. She was by far one of my all time favorite characters. The book was full of awesome characters... Lucy, a 5 year old that completely stole my heart. I loved her voice, her innocence, and her loving heart. Stebbs was just the best. A true survivor with a heart of gold. I also loved Eli... Sweet and sincere through in through.. not a mean bone in his body. Just so so so sweet. blush and swoon worthy. Each character brought something fresh and new to the story and held their own. The relationships between each were beautiful and heartbreaking at the same time. The characters made the story for sure. One of my favorite things about this story was the tone. It almost had a western feel but was completely modern oh and of course the feel of desolation. All of it together was just amazing and I could feel the atmosphere perfectly. The tone held strong throughout the entire book and made the story that more haunting, exciting, and intense. I love post apocalyptic stories, especially when they are done well and stand on their own. Its hard to really make one unique and one that can stand out against all others out there on the market. This one was done supremely well and it made all others I have read recently disappear into the background. It was completely engrossing and trapped me til the end... by the way the end was pretty darn awesome. I don't generally mention narrators and I know I should... they can make or break the read. The narrator for this book completely rocked and I would read anything she narrated. Loved it and will love it over and over again. A Must have in my shelf collection.

Never finished. Got to 34 I thought the premise and the world interesting. A bit teen angsty but that's to be expected for a young adult book I'd think. I felt it rather predictable. I'm in love with Poison Study, and just dying for the next two to arrive in my hands see... we're not just 'book sellers', we really are readers! ...A few underlying romantic themes, a little bit of mild nastiness more implied or glossed over, rather than being the focus of many chapters , some wonderful escape scenes and great mental dialogue. I can see why this gets bumped into the Youth Fantasy section - other than trying to ride on the coat tails of Twilight of which this book is NOTHING like by the way... although might appeal to those you liked the general themes of the Twilight series but weren't hung up about the romantic relationships - it's just 'light'. There isn't really a lot of darkness. Don't misunderstand me, it's not an 'after school special' - it is after all a book about a murderer who becomes the food taster and is hounded by lots of nasty people wanting to kill her in a variety of unsavoury ways, but it does have that overall happy ending feeling. Oh, but some 'nice' twists that came totally out of the blue. Poison Study was a debut novel for Maria V. Snyder, and is even more exceptional because of that. The next in the series "Magic Study" was in the finals for the RITA awards hence getting popped over to romance and "Fire Study" number three in the series spent two weeks on the New York Times bestsellers list - so I am expecting good things when I finally get a chance to read these. Here is what I was expecting from this book a story about suicide, a murder mystery, coherent psycological thriller maybe. Nothing of this is what I got in the end. Suicide Notes from Beautiful Girls is a mess of a story. The pacing was off, plot twists happened all at the wrong time and there was not enough thought given to any of the characters. June could be just a cardboard instead of a person and it would not make a difference, Delia is a poor attempt of a fucked up girl that never comes across as really dangerous. So many things made me roll my eyes while I read, because it just makes no sense that a bunch of young teenagers would be able to do what they did. That's why so many times writers leave gaps for the readers to invent their own theories, giving us the wrong details makes the story unrealistic. Just as giving us an ending that feels like another of thousands of things made for shock value. The amount of gross things these characters say for shock values, to seem like they are all 'fucked up' and 'not normal at all' never came out the right way, it just made me uncomfortable again, not in the right way . This story was just trying to be a copy of many others we've seen done it better before, it read like a first draft of a half written story. If you want to read a good book about toxic friendships and that does 'fucked up' characters right, you can try Dangerous Girls by Abigail Haas.

Ugh, I hated this book! I was excited to find it at a garage sale for 0.50. I mean, it was a great bargain for what I'd heard was a phenomenal novel. I wish I would've saved myself the 0.50. Thirteen Reasons Why is the story of how 13 people "caused" Hannah Baker's suicide. Before she OD's, she makes a series of tapes, each one about a different person she blames for her problems. She mails the tapes to the first person then kills herself. It's an original concept and I would appreciate it more if there had been even ONE logical explanation for why she offs herself. Sadly, there isn't. I'm no stranger to teen angst. I was bullied horribly in school and endured far worse than anything Hannah experienced. Yet, I didn't kill myself, which leads me to believe that Hannah--if she were real and not fictional--probably had a serious mental disorder. She was whiny, selfish, and narcissistic. She purposely put herself in awful situations then blamed everyone else when things when to hell. She could've handled every situation differently in a positive way. Sidebar I found the tapes to be their own form of bullying. Seriously, leaving behind tapes that blame certain individuals for your death? That's putting the weight of the world on shoulders that barely deserve it. I'm not sure if this book is supposed to appeal to the suicidal or the bullies. Either way, the only plus about this book was that it was well-written. I just wish it would've had more depth...or at least ONE valid reason for Hannah to kill herself.

For her senior year Maya moves back to the town where she grew up until the deaths of her brother and father. It's the first time in years she'll actually get to spend time at a school and in a stable environment. She feels guilty for moving away from her mother but living with her older sister Remy will at least allow her to finish school. On the first day back she meets Ben, an old classmate of hers. He advises her to stay away from him and tries to avoid speaking to her. Maya is drawn to Ben despite the fact that he's been an outcast since the death of his girlfriend 2 years ago. I really enjoyed this book, for a while it seemed like it was going to be about Ben and Maya learning to get on with their lives and how after both of them had experienced things that completely tore their lives apart they were trying to move on. There were some great characters in this book, Phoebe was definitely one of my favourites, personally I couldn't stand either Olivia or Hailey so she was a great relief from that. The end...wow, I wasn't expecting that at all. Things had been building up and I knew something bad was going to happen but it just didn't click until it was already happening. I'd have liked the epilogue to maybe be a little further on in the future, just to get a better sense of how everyone changed after what happened, but I liked it anyway. I'd recommend this book, there is violence in it, especially as the death of Bens girlfriend is discussed so readers should be aware of that before getting a copy. Edit I've just seen that a sequel is in the works. It's from Phoebe's point of view, she was a really cool character so I'm looking forward to it. I'm not sure it's totally necessary, I mean I felt like there was closure at the end of twisted so I hope it's not being written just for the sake of it. If it takes Phoebe but introduces new characters it should be ok though, just a crossover of a character as opposed to carrying on a story that finished really well.

I really liked this book, and it was sort of a surprise. I could tell from the summary that I would likely approve of the book with a big finally, representation in YA!!!! stamp, but I was not sure if I would like it on a personal level or as entertainment. It's a superhero novel, so you definitely have to suspend your disbelief a little bit. The plot was pretty good. I generally find YA a little predictable, but this wasn't too by the book, and the superhero stuff definitely helped mix things up. Jess is a fantastic protagonist, realistic in her teenage insecurities, but also self aware and confident and real. I liked her romance with Abby, which started with friendship and did not feel contrived or fabricated. Abby, though, I found less interesting and I thought it took too long for Jess to realize that Abby was in M's suit , which I could tell from the very start. I thought the ending was a little bit lackluster - there was a big build up and then they all just go home and Jess goes back to her life like nothing happened, like the villains of the story wouldn't come find her at school, etc. So, it wasn't perfect, but it was reeeeeeally good. And so overdue to have representation in YA!! So good to have a character already comfortable with their sexuality and to have a story other than struggling to come out, which we have all read a hundred times. 100 recommend and will continue the series!

After reading Jay Asher's Thirteen Reasons Why, I was so excited to read The Future of Us. Why? The concept was amazing!!! I mean, it sounded interesting and not cliched whatsoever. Sadly, my hype for The Future of Us was completely wasted. What was wrong with it? Well, nothing much. I found the plot pointless and boring. If The Future of Us actually had something worth mentioning happen in that book, I would have mentioned it somewhere. But no, it was a dry book full of worthless scenes and useless characters and dialogue. As much as I wanted to love The Future of Us, there was nothing I could love or enjoy. I do not know why I hated it... Maybe it was because I found Emma and Josh two annoying brats. So what if you find out your whole future on Facebook? You're all upset because it isn't a good future? Well there is nothing you can do about it except find a loophole out, right? No... Instead of trying to do something or preventing that outcome that is kind of impossible to do if you haven't met your evil spouse yet, Emma just mopes around and whines about it. I found it irritating and ridiculous. Instead of working to figure solving the whole problem, Emma just did well nothing throughout the whole novel. Pathetic. Josh was even worse compared to Emma. I mean, it's pretty obvious that this book is going to go somewhere in plot, right? Wrong... once again. The whole thing about Josh marrying the hottest girl in school turned him into a hopeless guy who doesn't what to do... Hm...... Should I be happy and marry the girl in the future, even though I have a crush on Emma, or should I just flirt with her because I feel like I have to? Dude, figure it out yourself. I mean, I understand the whole thing about men and hormones. But seriously? The whole dilemma Josh has is quite understandably a hard one, but Josh keeps on changing his plans. One second he will mope about his crush, the next is his future with pretty blonde girl. If you have to chose a future, Josh, choose one, ONLY one. The Future of Us just disappointed me so much. There was so much potential in where this plot could land. But sadly, Jay Asher and Carolyn Mackler turned the novel into a circle of torturous uncertain decisions that kept on being reconsidered repeatedly. Honestly, I am not sure whether I plan on reading Jay Asher's future books 13 Reasons Why blew me away, but honestly, The Future of Us is pitiful.

This review may contain spoilers. Also mentions of self-harming . This book was kind of hard to get into. Firstly, I struggled with seeing Hayley and Taylor as individual characters. They reminded me too much of Elizabeth and Jessica Wakefield from the Sweet Valley High University etc. series. They even looked like them. Unlike Jessica and Elizabeth, though, the apparent differences in their personalities weren't really shown. Also... a lot of the characters were really unlikable. And I couldn't believe that so many people knew that Katelyn cut herself, yet did nothing about it. These were teenagers and they didn't bother reporting this knowledge to... anyone? Even Hay-Tay gag , who were supposed to be these nice characters? There was one specific instance where a character is described as exaggerating everything. What does she exaggerate? Well, apparently there's this older guy who's quite creepy. This character Beth describes him as being forty. And the narration claims, 'He was actually nearer to fifty'. That's... not exaggerating. Beth saying he was sixty, seventy, ninety... that would be. Also, the constant changing between past and present was confusing. There was nothing to indicate a flashback occurring. I was struggling to keep all the different characters in my head. Most of them simply weren't given enough details to differentiate them from each other. Some thoughts were put into italics while others weren't. To be honest, I was getting something of a headache. Also, I figured out who was responsible for the e-mails pretty early on. All I was waiting for was for it to be revealed. I don't think I'll be choosing to buy the next book in the series. It's a pity, but it seems that Young Adult books - and especially Young Adult paranormal books - are really going downhill compared to what they were like when I was younger.

Brief Summary Sunday Woodcutter is the seventh daughter of a seventh daughter. She comes from a family where magical things happen all the time. One day in the woods she meets an enchanted frog he's really a man. When she kisses him, unbeknownst to her, he transforms and returns to his old life. He throws a series of balls to bring her to the castle, and re-win her affection. There is an evil lurking in the castle, though. One that will try to hurt her family. Can Sunday perfect her own magic? Can Prince Rumbold destroy the evil in his kingdom and in himself? Can everyone have a happily ever after? Review This book was set in a fairly-tale world. The author wove pieces of all the well known fairly-tales together to create this book. At different points in the book, Sunday and her family's life is like the story of the Frog Prince, Jack and the Beanstalk, Cinderella, and a whole bunch of other well known tales. I absolutely enjoyed discovering each character's fairy-tale role and his her unique brand of "magic." Sunday, herself, had the ability to tell or write any tale and it would become truth. The mystery in the book was centered around the king's apparent immortality, his deceased wives including Rumbold's mother and the evil fairy-godmother, Sorrow. She was the twin sister of Sunday's fairy-godmother, Joy. Once Rumbold became human again, he had very few memories from his former life. As a result, there were many confusing even cryptic scenes involving Rumbold trying to get to the bottom of the things. Although, the ending wrapped everything up nicely, this book never had the highs and lows of emotion that I really look for in a great book. It was just okay. Recommendation I am curious about Sunday's other sisters' stories, but I don't know if I would read the next book. I almost feel like in taking so many aspects of all the fairy-tales to create this story, the author weakened the power of the retelling.

So, the prologue was fantastic. And then the story actually began... I can sum up the plot of the entire book with one gif. That was pretty much it. The two main characters that the summary on the back makes you want to ship meet two other characters and fall in love with them for no apparent reason. I would like to start by saying that Disney's Little Mermaid is my favorite disney movie of all time. That being said... too many spoilers ahead to put it in brackets. read at your own risk I'll start with characters. Pearl is the main character... I think who really knows by the end? . I don't think it's spoiling much to say that she's a mermaid who doesn't know she's a mermaid because she grew up human after something happened to her when she was 4 yrs old. She is very honest and trusting, though gets bad feelings and bad dreams a lot. James is her best friend and the prince of the land. Kale and Faye are two merfolk who have been looking for mermaid Pearl since she disappeared years before. Kale is loyal and Faye is free-spirited and a careless , but that may be personal bias talking.... . That is all the characterization you get throughout the entire book. I want to cry. As for plot... This book clearly is not a modern fairytale. It is set in the undefined "past." I think the term that modern folk would give this book, based on the handling of love and marriage, would be "medieval." So as someone with a B.A. degree in History, I was quite insulted - because there is no time in history EVER when people took marriage as such a frivolous thing, and flung the word "love" around with as little respect for its meaning as in this book. Not even DISNEY as some people claim is this bad about that. To be fair to James, his line "I will marry the girl who saved me," comes almost directly from Disney's Prince Eric's mouth. But let us compare James and Eric, shall we? They are both princes who are under serious pressure to get married. They both have looked for a wife upon their parents' insistence and didn't like what they saw. However, James's best friend is a beautiful girl Pearl , albeit peasant, while Eric's best friend is a dog. Do we see the differences in their situations here? I would be very insulted if I were Pearl at James's assumption that he has no options. Eric, on the other hand, actually has no other options. So when each prince is miraculously saved by a beautiful girl, I don't think it is that much of a stretch for Eric to say "I will marry the girl who saved me," while James is saying those very words to his super hot female best friend whom he was about to propose to minutes before. All I wanted to do was slap James across the face. And that is only the beginning of the shallowness. Then we have Faye, the mermaid who is the one who MADE THEIR BOAT SINK in the first place, who is suddenly love struck after seeing this guy for literally five seconds. To be fair to Faye, Ariel fell for Eric while watching him on his ship after only a few moments. To be fair to Ariel, she picked Eric out of a crowd of men, watched him interact with people, and then fell for him. He wasn't just sitting in an intimate boat talking to ANOTHER WOMAN. Also Ariel did not cause Eric to nearly drown, while Faye did in fact puncture the hole in James's boat. Ariel also did not kiss Eric before actually speaking to him! I'm looking at you, Faye. She is a silly little love struck puppy for no apparent reason, and then kisses a guy she almost caused to drown while the waves lap at their feet tail. UGH. -_- The characters are just silly! Pearl is the only one who I wouldn't call silly, but the plot... lacked so much substance that her choices just seem ridiculous. The author wants us to want her to be with Kale... but there is nothing to their relationship! The same goes with Faye and James. Faye saves him... and that's the basis of the whole thing. At least Eric and Ariel spent time together! Good quality time in which she legitimately made him laugh for the first time in a long time, hurtled his carriage over a cliff safely, and had a wonderfully romantic boat ride in the lagoon together! This book shows NO interaction between Pearl Kale and James Faye except when they are info dumping about the "mystery" of the novel and shouting their love for each other. I can't get over this. The story had so much potential it kills me! The prologue was amazing, and the plot idea was really good too - unique and fresh for a retelling of this classic. But there was nothing to the story. They met, they fell in love at first sight, there may have been a few evil plots all over the place that were resolved in a page and then they lived happily ever after with the person they didn't know at all. The End

There you'll find me is centered around Finley love the name! , who moves for a semester to Ireland to follow her brother's footsteps so she can experience the love he felt for this place, and to get closer to god. You see, Finley's brother was murdered in a bombing in Afghanistan two years ago. Finley has basically lost all meaning in life, because she doesn't understand WHY it had to be her brother. I am pretty sure anyone who has ever lost a loved one had these kind of thoughts. So she heads off to Ireland to get answers? closure? a sense of direction? the presence of God? but ends up finding so much more. Then she meets Beckett. Beckett is basically the Justin Bieber, no, the Tayler Lautner much better of our time. He is charming, witty, and basically the Hollywood starlet everyone goes gaga over, except for Finley. Of course no one is perfect and has a perfect life. I love how 3 dimensional the characters are, each one has their own conflicts, struggles, and wounds that need healing. This isn't your normal light contemporary novel. The comfort, and sometimes snarky arguments, these two have when they're together is what made this book for me. It brought humor into the book and light into each other's lives. This book deals with deep and some what taboo themes without turning the story into a dark and depressing novel. I would recommend this book for anyone who loves contemporary books but wants more than fluff out of the reading experience.

I really wanted to love this book! The cover breathtaking. The premise so intriguing. But I couldn't quiet bring myself to love it. I liked it, but I didn't love it. Velveteen has a pretty sweet job in purgatory and she still finds time to haunt her killer. Actually, the parts with Velvet and Bonesaw were my favourites from the book. I love the idea of a murdered teenage girl trying to get even with her killer. There was a lot of world-building necessary for this one, since Marks constructed an entire society of purgatory. Overall, I thought the world-building was well done, but occasionally I got a bit confused when certain aspects were touched upon, but then never revisited such as the divining needles . Also, some of the secondary characters were very odd. Something makes me a bit uncomfortable about a 12-year-old addict Velveteen prides herself on being a badass, which I always appreciate in my heroines. However, in Velvet's case, she tried too hard and generally came off mean and bitchy. Now, I'm not claiming to be an expert in badass, but I always appreciate characters who 'are tough' more than characters who 'act tough.' Velveteen's commitment to repress any and all feelings drove me a bit nuts. Sure she had more than her fair share of trauma, but it made me frustrated at her as a character. On to the romance. Nick was confident and smooth, but at the same time comforting and vulnerable. Basically, he had the whole package of a YA love interest, not to mention that he's a saint for putting up with all Velvet's crap. My goodness that girl gives a lot of mixed signals! The pacing of this book was weird for me. It felt like sometimes the author would focus solely on one aspect of the book ie romance, Bonesaw, Velvet's job in purgatory and forget all about everything else for a few chapters. I would have really preferred it if the aspects were mixed together a bit more throughout. At one point I was so impatient for the romance to get out of the way so I could have more Bonesaw action! Morbid? Maybe. Overall, Velveteen is a good read, but it fell a bit short of being great for me. It's still worth a try if you like somewhat morbid ghost stories, but it didn't quite make my recommendation list.

What I liked in the series was the idea that thru magic, hunters have the ability to communicate with, even command, the elusive unicorns. I was taken by the time when Astrid was inside the enclosure and the einhorns another kind of unicorn encircled her and bowed. There was also the mystery of creating the Remedy, which, in my opinion, was still a little vague -- yeah well, maybe because it's the magic of the hunters' virginal essence that is used to create it, but still. Anyhow, I enjoyed reading the books albeit Astrid's lapses in judgment -- again, i'll write it off to her being a teenager. I finished Ascendant with a question, how will Astrid heal from her brain damage? Will Kaitlyn her step-sister give Astrid the remedy that Gordian has taken from her? What happened to Brandt, Giovanni, Reno and Isobeau Jager? Will Astrid choose to take that path Clothilde chose and leave the Order of the Lioness? or will she choose fulfill her legacy, with the aid of Bucephalus, as a descendant of Alexander the Great? Which in all leaves me to my last question, when will the last installment, Triumphant come out? Will it even come out?

Naif continues to be an impressive and strong young woman, trying to lead and fight, but also with a curious determination not to kill. She even tries to spare her enemies. It was also refreshing to see how those who remained in Ixion at the end of book one reacted to the events that unfolded at that book's end. The reader also gets to enjoy a deeper look into the workings of the world and I think most people will be excited and fascinated I was at least . An amazing conclusion and well worth a read. Recommended to anyone who enjoys YA and is looking for an astoundingly different world.

First, I would like to thank the author for providing me with an e-copy in exchange for an honest review. I always feel like I won the lottery or something when I have a review request in my email. - Jessica has a problem. More like an addiction. To Magic. In this world magic is like alcohol some people can use it responsibly, and others have to stay away from it entirely otherwise it becomes an addiction and can ruin their lives. Jessica has seen first hand the devastating effects. Her mom had a magic problem. They have gone from a happy family, to just the two of them living in little more than a shack. Despite all of that, Jessica is barely able to keep her own magic use down to a minimal level. Of course when her Amber, her best friend, has a vision of Jessica's mom dying in a car crash, she knows only magic will save her. She goes all out to prevent Amber's vision from coming true. Of course, there are a few distractions in Jessica's life, namely Carmen and Trent. It isn't as much a live triangle as many YA books there is a clear 'winner' and then a 'what if' guy. I preferred Carmen. But is he the winner or what if? I'm not telling. He did however have the best exchanges with Jess "Yeah, do I have stupid stamped on my forehead somewhere?" I glanced at his forehead. "No, looks more like loser, but I forgot my glasses." Jessica is pretty witty. Or maybe I am just old, and the kids these days are funny. Who knows. - I laughed, and that is what matters. I thought the whole magic as an addiction thing was a neat spin on the supernatural. It was an angle I had not considered before and it made me think twice about having powers. Overall, it was a god, solid YA book. There were a few minor editing issues those always jump out at me , such as using the wrong name once or twice, but I was pretty easily able to figure out who was actually being spoken about. I felt for the characters, their joys and sorrows were shared with me. The writing was good editing issues aside and I would recommend it for anyone who likes a unique YA.

I was completely enamored with the first book in this series, Hunger. Because I enjoyed it so much, I was really looking forward to Rage. Unfortunately, I was disappointed. With Hunger, I felt that the main character's issue, an eating disorder, tied really well to her becoming Famine. What Kessler was trying to achieve in the novel, provoking thought while entertaining, worked very well. I enjoyed the characters and couldn't put Hunger down. My experience with Rage was different for several reasons. First, I did not like Missy at all. I found her to be a very unsympathetic character. She was over-the-top angsty. I expected a certain amount of angst considering she is 1. a teenager and 2. a cutter, but she was so overblown and unlikeable that I couldn't make myself like her or care about her situation. Second, while a girl who is so clearly full of anger and is cutting herself when overwhelmed by her emotions might seem like a perfect fit to become War, it just didn't work for me. In Hunger, the central character's eating disorder coalesced with her becoming Famine perfectly. The story clicked together in all the right ways and places. Rage was the complete opposite. I felt like the author was forcing the story together. It didn't naturally flow from Point A to Point B. Missy becoming War and where that takes her completely did not mesh. It had the effect of jamming the wrong puzzle pieces together. Overall, I was disappointed with this book. I will still check out the next installment in this series, which is entitled Loss. I hope that Rage was just an unfortunate installment in this series and the rest of the series will be as amazing as Hunger was.

Spending time hunting with her father is her favourite thing but then her father goes missing and Yeva ventures out into the woods alone to find him. Becoming the Beasts captive, she isn't as strong as Belle is usually portrayed as, giving into the beasts demands and promising herself away far too easily. The most noteworthy secondary character for me was the beast, cursed to be a beast by day and human by night, he is constantly on the verge of losing his humanity and becoming all beast. The storyline is not the best fairytale retelling I've read as it sticks very closely to the source material. The pacing is OK but I do feel the ending was rushed. 2 stars, not the best book for me

3.5 Stars 'Enchantment Lake' is a young adult mystery novel that's targeted for readers around the ages of 10-14. The story follows our heroine - Francie - as she travels to northern Minnesota to stay with her two great aunts, after receiving a disturbing phone call from them about their neighbors' mysterious deaths. Concerned for their safety and determined to figure out what exactly is going on, Francie heads to Enchantment Lake and finds herself mixed up in the strangest mysteries she's seen from poisoned food and creepy unexplainable noises coming from the bog, to the legend of a treasure that's said to be in an enchantment - and mixed up in the middle of it all is a business making a lot of money in selling cabins and a road that nobody in the area seems to want built. Will Francie be able to figure out the mystery that ties all of these odd events together - before anyone else dies? It's easy to tell right from the beginning that this book is geared toward younger readers - more middle grade and young YA. As soon as I started reading, I felt that the story had more of a Nancy Drew vibe to it rather than a more serious and mature mystery novel. The main character - Francie - is a seventeen-year-old who, in my opinion, doesn't act her age. Her dialogue - both inner and with other characters - isn't very mature, which only deepened my feelings of her not quite synching up with her age in the story. She's a good main character - smart, a very loving and devoted niece, down to earth, and determined to see things through. There's not much character growth for her - or any other characters - throughout the book. Francie's great-aunts are an interesting pair of sisters and serve as some comic relief during the book. The plot was pretty predictable - especially if you read the description and paid even a little attention to the details in the story. I basically knew what was going to happen before I cracked the book open - but, then again, this book is geared more for younger teens and their reading level. The mysteries that Francie has to solve throughout the story are minor and I didn't even have to think it out to know what was going on. For the target audience though, I think the mysteries would be a great asset to the story and would help them be more immersed in the book. The author uses great details and vivid imagery throughout the book that made it easy to imagine Francie's world. I didn't exactly slip inside of the author's world, but I could definitely see how a younger reader would be able to. The story is told from a third person point-of-view, which made it feel more distant and unrealistic, in my opinion. If it was told in a first person POV with Francie as the narrator, I think it would have engaged me more and may have pulled me into the story a little more. Overall, this was a good book with solid writing and a rounded plot. It was very obvious from the beginning for me that the novel is targeted to younger teens and middle grade readers. Being an adult and not used to reading books on this level, I wasn't able to get the maximum experience that a reader who is in the target age range would have. Looking at it from that standpoint, it's a good mystery novel with fun characters and interesting occurrences, and is a well rounded story that mixes together action, adventure, mystery, and a bit of suspense and will leave the reader wanting to solve more mysteries with Francie. Disclosure I received a copy of the book in exchange for an honest review.

En fin, cuando termine de leer El lado explosivo de Jude lo primero que pense fue "menuda chorrada" y es que no me gusto nada, no me intrigo, no me entretuvo, eso si, lo que me dio fue mucha frustracion ya que al tiempo que avanzaba nunca pasaba nada interesante en la trama y ese intento de dramatismo de las ultimas 20 paginas del libro fue claramente absurdo. La historia es bastante cliche, el chico malo y la chica buena y blahblahblah, pero ni siquiera se le intenta poner algo original, obviamente la escuela a la que asistian tenia que ser una tipica escuela de pelicula gringa donde chicas 'hermosas' y deportistas tontos gobernaban la escuela, que me hace dudar seriamente si de verdad la gente piensa que la escuela solo reduce a la eterna batalla por popularidad que siempre se ve en las peliculas. Los personajes fueron insufribles, ninguno me parecio ni original ni nada, los personajes secundarios fueron casi inexistente, el pobre intento de triangulo amoroso me saco de quicio, y sinceramente Jude fue el tipico cliche de chico malo con un corazon bonito, que todo acerca de su historia no me sorprendio, ademas de que sinceramente si me encontrara con un chico como el, me preocuparia que todo el tiempo esta golpeando a alguien, ya sea personas, paredes o mismisimo aire, y cuando digo todo el tiempo, hablo en serio, me pregunto si la autora lo escribio por pura inercia o porque penso que un problema de ira era atractivo lo cual no lo es . Lucy es una protagonista que a ratos me caia bien, pero la mayoria del tiempo era mortalmente aburrido leyendola, les juro, a cada dialogo con Jude, existian tres parrafos completos de ella pensando en su relacion con Jude, en todo el libro, y lo peor es que decia absolutamente lo mismo en cada uno 'que Jude es malo para mi, pero no me importa porque confio en el' etc. El ritmo, a mi parecer, fue de lo peor, aunque si fue facil de leer que por cierto la traduccion a maldiciones mexicanas en el libro fueron de lo mas extrano parecia que la historia nunca avanzaba, todo el libro fue de Te quiero, te odio, me voy con el otro, te vuelvo a querer y odio al otro. Y asi sucesivamente, en todo el libro. En fin, ni siquiera me voy a atrever a leerme los dos libros que ni la curiosidad me ha picado, y es que en resumidas cuentas, El lado explosivo de Jude me decepciono aun sin tener altas expectativas y ni siquiera me entretuvo. Kanske ar det for att jag efter alla ar har en last pyramid av ungdomsbocker bakom mig, och sa har dessa bocker lart mig vad jag tal och inte tal med romaner oavsett aldersklass och genre. Men jag ar faktiskt inte sa imponerad av Katarina Wennstams nybakade ungdomsroman "Flickan pa hotellet" som jag trodde att jag skulle vara, eftersom hennes tidigare bocker varit vardefulla tillgangar i skolarbeten. En sak jag har svart for med romaner ar nar min egen inre lasrost och upplevelse blir abrupt stord av Forfattarens, for att forfattarens person med varderingar och allt gor sig sa oerhort pamind hela tiden i precis varenda karaktar. Till slut blir det som att se en enmansshow dar Forfattaren bara dyker upp i olika taffliga forkladnader och latsas inte tillrackligt bra for att vara nagon annan. Jag ser att det ar du, marsch av scen och skriv om tills jag tror att det finns ett persongalleri bakom scenen. En annan sak jag har svart for ar nar Forfattaren, som i den har boken, uppenbart har gjort mycket research pa Saker Hen Ar Forbannad Pa Med Ratta, skrivit av sig i ilska och forsokt gora sitt yttersta for att packa in alla dessa arga budskap i en och samma bok. En relativt tunn ungdomsbok dessutom. Det funkar inte riktigt, det blir spretigt trots att de inte saknar relevans. En film fylld med arga reklamavbrott, eller produktplaceringar av Saker Att Bli Arg Pa. Det ar borjan pa en trilogi, nog borde det ga att fokusera pa sorterade Saker Att Bli Arg Pa i varje bok. Sa det dar med att forsoka for mycket. Sveriges forsta kvinnliga domare som mormor? Att polisen inte fattar nagot jamfort med en introvert 17-aring som uppfyller precis varenda datanord-trope jag sett i hundratals andra fall, med undantag for att hon ar tjej? Det trottsamma pitchandet av missforstadda smarta ungdomar med nagra undantag och platta vuxna karaktarer som fattar noll och vars enda uppgift verkar vara att spy ut mys eller rattsvidriga klyschor? Gasp. Jag har forstatt att hon skrev boken pga flera bortglomda ouppmarksammade brott mot kvinnor i Sverige. Men verkligheten tranger igenom fiktionen har.

Now I ADORED "The Rain" the first book in this series, so I was really keen to read the follow up - I adored this one as well and the same thing is true of The Storm as was so with The Rain. Its all about Ruby. She is such a terrifically drawn character that you can't help loving her - although of course it could go the other way. If you love Ruby you'll love the book. If you don't you may STILL love the book but for entirely different reasons... Anyway, in "The Storm" Ruby is having some issues, all alone she goes through something of a mental breakdown and it takes a chance encounter with another person to make her realise this. As she returns more to her own sassy self, she sets off to try and track down her family yet ends up back in the place she once ran away from. Here she discovers dark deeds afoot and in her own indomitable Ruby style she embarks on a rather rambling attempt to sort everything out. There is a huge amount of character development for Ruby in this follow up novel - in the first one she was kind of shallow, although having to deal with killer rain did make her up her game a bit. By the end of "The Rain" she is growing up - and in The Storm she grows up some more. I have loved watching her from her humble beginnings, where even when everyone was dying around her she still found time to worry about how she looked, to the end of the first book and on into the second as she grows in stature but without losing her totally cool comtemplative edge. The other side of the story - the apocalypse side - takes on an even more sinister edge and is extremely well imagined. Human nature being what it is, nothing is straightforward, this part of the plot is cleverly constructed, seen as it is through Ruby's eyes to give the reader a hint of what lies beneath the surface before Ruby can actually get at the truth. The concept is beautifully frightening and the more "thrilling" aspects of The Storm are really very addictive. If you liked The Rain you will LOVE this. If you loved Ruby you will be so happy to have her back. Ruby Rocks. Overall a really really terrific read - I stormed through it yes that was on purpose and adored every sassy super moment of it.

If you love Sherlock as much as I do, but you crave the one thing that is missing from his life, then I think you'll love this book as much as I do. Sherlock with romance! He's not the actual Sherlock, but he's a similar YA version. He's realistically more immature and more emotional than the famous detective. He's also the author's own creation with his own backstory, which I think is very important. I like to read adaptations of classic stories, but I don't want an exact copy. Watts is also not a copy of Watson. She is Mycroft's closest friend, but she also focuses on other friends and her family. In fact, Mycroft and Watts are not isolated in their investigation. It is much more of a team effort with their friends, Mai and Gus, helping out. Still, there is an extremely strong connection between Watts and Mycroft that we know will escalate into more than friendship. We're waiting for it throughout most of the book, but boy does the author deliver! Those are some of the best kisses ever! I really enjoyed everything about this book. The characters, the romance, the mystery they solve and the one from Mycroft's past that is still unsolved. Also, the style of writing. I took a chance and purchased all three books as soon as I saw the tagline What if Sherlock Holmes was the boy next door? Judging by the terrific first book, I think it was a wise choice. I can't wait to read the next one, but I'm already hoping that someone writes an adult adaptation with a similar balance of romance and sleuthing.

I read a few Sweet Valley High books when I was younger, but when I found the first book, I thought I would give it a go as an adult. I have no problem reading children's books, I am a huge fan of the Babysitter's Club books, even now, and I last year I read a few Judy Blume books. I think it's important to remember that the books are written for teenagers. One of the reasons that I enjoy the Sweet Valley High books, and the aforementioned Babysitter's Club and Judy Blume novels, is that I like the fact that they are all about American adolescents at a particular time. This was before the internet, mobile phones and social media. My favourite characters would have their fun by talking for hours on the phone, meeting at the mall and going on bike rides. Maybe kids still enjoy doing this, but life is so much more complicated by all the new technology I know this makes me sound like an old lady rest assured that I partake in all this new technology myself, but also yearn for those simpler times! . The first book in the Sweet Valley High series introduces us to Jessica and Elizabeth Wakefield. The girls are identical twins identical that is, in looks, but miles apart in terms of personality. Elizabeth is the quiet, serious, sensitive twin, while her younger by four minutes sister, Jessica, is the wild one. Most of what Jessica does throughout the book is pretty low she sets out to steal her sister's crush, Todd, despite knowing that both Todd and Elizabeth are interested in each other. She accuses Todd of trying to force her into going further than a goodnight kiss after a dance. And she takes full advantage of having an identical twin by pretending to be Elizabeth when she gets into trouble with the police. The problem is that Elizabeth is the complete opposite to Jessica, and not in a good way. She's that annoying person that sees the good in everyone, and refuses to say a bad word about anyone. She resolves to be happy for her sister and Todd when she thinks that they are interested in each other, which would be fair enough, but surely if you've grown up with a sister like Jessica, you would be a bit more suspicious? She also forgives Jessica far too easily for the 'mistaken' identity with the police. A character who falls somewhere in between Jessica and Elizabeth would be much more likeable than either of these two prove to be in the first Sweet Valley High outing, but having read some of the later books when I was younger, I know that things stop being quite so black and white and get a bit more interesting!

Inspired by various mediums from films to classic horror novels to music, these fourteen short stories are filled with thrills, twists, and trepidation. And just when you think you have a story figured out, the surprises are fierce yet strangely satisfying. "After a while, Richard started getting the distinct impression that someone was watching him sleep. There was a strange weight in his room, as if the furniture or the walls weren't aligned quite right, and sometimes he would feel that weight press against his chest like a stone." Slasher Girls Monster Boys is a great collection of horror stories perfect for October. I'm familiar with most of the authors in this anthology, having read books by a large majority of them. Authors like Nova Ren Suma and Jonathan Maberry are sure to bring their personal brand of the strange and thrilling, but I was most impressed by authors like Marie Lu. Best known for her Legend series, Lu weaves together one of my favorite short stories in this book. The Girl Without a Face takes something as simple as a closet that won't open and turns it into a tale that had me glancing at my own several times, hoping it was empty. April Genevieve Tucholke's The Flicker, the Fingers, the Beat, the Sigh takes you for a ride where you end up rooting against key characters. This is my first reading experience with this author and it won't be my last. There were several stories in this anthology which were so good at introducing intriguing characters and exciting storylines that I found myself wanting the authors to turn them into full-length novels. Jonathan Maberry's Fat Girl with a Knife would make a perfect introduction to a novel about an unlikely heroine battling for survival. Jay Kristoff's Sleepless starts off like a cheesy horror-movie where you're screaming at one of the characters to be smarter, but ends up pulling the rug out from under you and begging for more in the end. Slasher Girls Monster Boys is fantastic for those looking for a quick scare during this Halloween season. While ghosts and killers may be the obvious choice for a horror story, many of these authors select more unconventional characters and what results is a really diverse blend of frightful tales that will surely delight horror fans.

How does he do what he's doing? Why? I have so many questions!
