more like 4.5 stars First off Yes, I didn't cry and yes I felt not as connected to the characters while reading as I did while watching the movie. However I have to say that this is a good, even great book, I really enjoyed reading. I especially liked Hazel's voice and her honesty. While reading I definitely felt like John Green was able to create a true picture of a teenage girl, not a girl, who is only defined by her condition. Hazel felt real. I also had the feeling that John has found himself as a writer in this book. Although I also enjoyed his previous works, I had the feeling that his thoughts and intentions were just more clearly portrayed in this book. I am definitely excited to see how his writing develops in the future. Coming back to the story It was raw and honest, without being too gritty and still keeping a sort of hopefulness, which was surly due to Hazel's personality. And although I thought that at some parts not as believable as at others, all in all I really enjoyed this read. Yes it was sad at times, and yes at some parts I needed to stop reading due to my feels, but I didn't cry? So am I heartless? Well I don't think so. Although this is a sad book, one of the saddest I have read up to this day, it never lost this sense of hopefulness, at least not for me. That is why I felt hopeful and full of believe in true love as a turned the last page of the book, and these are the feelings I associate this work with the most.

Another book that seemed to be split among my friends, Hallowed ended up falling on the "enjoyed reading" side of the fence for me. I usually HATE love triangles, but Hand stills handles the triangle here in a way that was believable and moving. I didn't like Christian at all in book one, but I liked him a lot more here. He wasn't pushy, or perfect or the OBVIOUS choice for Clara, and neither was Tucker. They are both viable love interests and not just because the author said so. One thing I could have had more of was clues as to everyone's "purpose". This book is also much sadder than its predecessor and I find that I have picked up a lot of books recently that have this sad and melancholic tone grief and loss seems to be a theme of many of my recent YA reads. It's a good thing I like sad, depressing, make-me-cry books.

Zombie novels are like crack to me. I just can't read enough of them. I can usually read them in one sitting because I get so emotionally involved, no matter what the length of the book is. When I found out that one of my favorite YA fantasy authors, Kellie Sheridan, wrote a zombie novel, I knew that I had to read it. Sadly, I was a little disappointed. The book takes place through four different character points of view, which kind of reminded me of T.W. Brown's Dead series. I liked seeing how all the characters coped with the zombie apocalypse in different ways. End Dayz starts after the zombie apocalypse has already begun, which I find interesting. Most zombie books start before the apocalypse. I thought it was a nice change of pace. I have mixed feelings on the characters. I thought Pierce was boring, and didn't really care whether he lived or not. The only time he impressed me was when he didn't stop to check on the voices he heard in another apartment. That was smart thinking. Speaking of smart thinking, I liked that Alex decided to leave notes for his dad at all the places they stopped. It's debatable if his dad would find them with all the different situations that could arise, but it's still a cool idea. Alex's story saddened me, but it was definitely my favorite in the book. I hated Belle and her father. They annoyed me so much. Actually, I disliked most of her chapter. Most of it was confusing. For being a leader, her father didn't have proper survival skills. There was no character intro for Grace. At first I couldn't tell if she was Belle's dad's girlfriend, or Belle's sister. Later in the chapter, it becomes clear though. Sometimes Belle seemed like a teenager, and other times she seemed like a child. I did enjoy Kellie Sheridan's take on zombies, and how they were starting to evolve differently based on region. I thought it was original. I also like how she made two characters stories intersect at the end. I'm hoping that all the characters will end up together eventually. Even though some parts of the book fell flat for me, I am looking forward to reading Morality, the first full length book in the series. I want to know whether the characters survive the zombie apocalypse or not. There are some that I hope do, and some that I hope get bitten.
Love this series. Maya Banks is awesome in whatever she writes.

Actual Rating 6 5 stars!! MAY CONTAIN SPOILERS Actually it does so BE CAREFUL Before I get to the good stuff, I'd just like to say that it took me about 5 days to push myself to write this. 2 of those days were spent reading Queen of Shadows which will have a review not long after this one if you'd like to check it out! and the other 3 were spent, honest to God, genuinely upset over the fact that I have nothing left to read until whenever the next book comes out. IT DOESN'T EVEN HAVE A PUBLICATION DATE!! I'm so sad. I've had a book hangover from this series for so long and it just won't go away. Okay, on with it then. Heir of Fire is Celaena's comeback book. This young warrior has been through hell and back and has received a small amount of care in between. Not only that, but she got her ass out of each and every deadly problem she had to face and survived, and is still surviving. After being sent to find the people who share what's in her blood, she must now deal with a new form of darkness that she had been repressing for her whole life. Only it's not darkness. It is the biggest chance of light she has had in a very long time. Leaving Dorian and Chaol and promising to return back to help the young prince, she sets off to strengthen a new part of her. Where she meets one of the strongest, unbeatable warriors of her time. Rowan Whitethorn is a whole lot of brooding and muscle in one man, and he has been assigned to help Celaena find the version of herself that she has long left behind up until now. It is up to her to master all the pieces of herself and bring them together to be the best version of herself that she can be, but can she do this with Rowan's lack of support? He is nothing like the Captain and Celaena can't decide whether or not it's a good thing. But she lacks the time and energy to dwell on it because the people that she cares about are in danger, she's in danger, and she has a whole lot of revenge heading into the king's direction. Okay. Okay okay okay okay. HOLY. I say this every time but Sarah J. Maas continues to surprise me with every damn book I read in this series. Heir of Fire was A M A Z I N G. I couldn't put it down. I have to be honest with you though, it did take me a lot longer to read than Throne of Glass did. I think Manon's storyline had slowed me down a fair amount because I was just dreading it at first. Don't get me wrong - it was interesting and I kind of knew where it was going with the whole Witch army thing, especially after Baba Yellowlegs' story was abruptly cut short and was not discussed ever again in Crown of Midnight. HOWEVER, I JUST WANTED TO READ MORE OF ROWAN'S CHARACTER. Honestly? I loved Rowan almost immediately. Chaol was getting on my nerves towards the end of the last book but I let it slide and let myself forgive and forget because he and Celaena were having a rough time figuring themselves out. But then he ships her off and kind of frowns upon what he discovers about who she truly is. YOU CAN'T DO THAT? This poor girl poured her heart and soul into showing you that she isn't bad. She was forced into a lifestyle that was impossible to escape at her age, and had nowhere else to go! What was she supposed to do?! Also her family just died!!! WHAT IS SHE SUPPOSED TO DO? RECOVER AND RETURN HOME TO AEDION?! I wanted to punch Chaol. That is all. Poor Celaena. For someone so strong and noble, she has so many scars to bear and they're still coming. She has lost more in this series than any character I've ever read about. I'd like to think it was over but we all know that isn't going to be the case. Not in the slightest. She not only has these scars, but she wears them as though she deserves to have them there. Rowan is honestly no help at this point because he looks at her like she's the scum of the earth, which is kind of how Chaol had seen her in the beginning during the Champion contest. The Champion contest.... You can't help but laugh about that now. We're in the third installment of the series and it's almost a joke to see that as hard after what she's had to face from then until now. I love how between Throne of Glass, Crown of Midnight, and Heir of Fire, Celaena's journey on how she became the woman she is today had been touched on throughout each novel. We learned new things we didn't know from the chapter before, and each pull on our heartstrings more and more for the girl who grew up too soon. We see her life change forever in this book. We got a piece of it in Crown of Midnight, but Heir of Fire is almost like an awakening. Actually... it is the reawakening of who she was in her past and who she is now living in harmony with one another to create the ultimate warrior that will rescue all those who need rescuing. A Queen. Because the real secret that she's held in for ten years is that she is Aelin Galathynius, Queen of Terrasen. What I love about this series, and I said it in my Crown of Midnight review, is the development in the plot and the characters. I don't know what water Sarah is drinking, but it has given her the gift of writing and I hope she never stops blessing us with her work. Celaena goes through Rowan's relentless attempts to bring out her Fae until finally, she does, and slowly but surly she is able to train that side of her that has been locked away since Arobynn found her. That asshole. Rowan knows of her past, and although it made him see her as a less despicable person, he still won't rest until his job is done. Maeve, Aelin's aunt, has ordered him to train her at his best and he obeys. What he doesn't expect is the amount of respect they end up having for one another, and the bond they form. Aelin's power grows day by day, and she turns into this remarkable character that you've been rooting for from the get-go and it's glorious to watch. I've never wanted a character to thrive more than I did her. Even with this growth, she still has the fierce nature she carried from day one with her, along with all the qualities you fell in love with. More importantly, she doesn't forget the lives lost to get to where she is. She's ready to see an eye for an eye on many accounts, but she does it with grace and stealth, and with an independence you've seen for three books now. She has a lot of catching up to do now that she knows she can wrap her head around what she left behind ten years ago. Aelin had abandoned everything once her parents were murdered, and now it's time for revenge, rebuilding, and reclaiming what is rightfully hers. Rowan stands as her reminder that she must be wary of who she trusts and becomes attached to. "The people you love are just weapons to use against you." Which has been proven true time after time in her past. So she puts her guards up, but not enough to keep Rowan out. Her only friend in her hell on earth, and someone who, like her, has something he's trying to overcome and scars that need healing. I hope this series gets turned into a movie or TV show. I know there might be room for error but I NEED TO SEE SOMEONE MAKE ROWAN REAL. He, like Chaol, was ordered to aid her in her training, but UNLIKE Chaol, shares the Fae blood with her. Not only that, but he understands why she's had to do what she's done to get to where they are today. He doesn't particularly let it slide, using it against her to taunt and push her into the right directions, but he understands. When I see the scenes with these two come up, not only am I filled with excitement, but I'm so mesmerized by the two of them. When Maas lays out the foundation of whatever it is they're doing that chapter, they almost dance around one another with their training. It's as if they were made to be in each other's presence. Am I the only one that felt that way? UGH. She describes these lighter moments with Rowan and if that doesn't thaw whatever ice heart has kept you from loving this man, I don't know what will. In the midst of my love for Rowan, I forgot about Dorian. Which upsets me because I really do love his character as well. After seeing his friend ship another off to the people of her kind, he seeks another companion who understands him better than he'd expected. Scorscha. He spends his free time talking with her and falling into this spell she's put on him with her genuine care for him. Dorian has risen above what he was in Throne of Glass, and has become this mature prince ready for the crown that awaits him one day. But, he knows the darkness that lurks in the castle walls and little does he know that he holds the power to counter that, with some guidance of course. But the shock and fear of what he is wins him over until one day he bursts and can't contain the power he holds. Scorscha witnesses his reveal and accepts him and hopes to find a way in which she can help him. Her healing abilities can only do so much. I already talked about my lack of interest in Chaol. I don't know what crawled up his ass and made him the stupid captain he turned into this book, but I was so mad. HE SHIPS OFF CELAENA AELIN? And then peaces out and ditches Dorian for the better part of the book. I mean he's still in the castle but he might as well have put an entire piece of land between him and his supposed best friend. Not only that, but this judgment he's place on the girl he's supposed to love was so annoying. What changed? Her history? This girl has done what she needed to survive and he's in a pissy mood because of what? Magic? No thank you. Chaol Westfall basically just disappointed me this time around. He was working with Aeidon which was great because I got to see his character fight for his family. The captain couldn't decide which side of Aelin he wanted to think about. He hated her one chapter, and understood and wanted her home in the next. Sorry bud, no can do. He, for some reason, refused to accept Dorian's power as well as Celaena's, which formed another wedge between them all. I'm glad Celaena Aelin and Chaol had this time apart though. I would've been even more sad for her had she been here to witness her former lover show what was basically disgust towards her. Manon and Aeidon are the newest additions to the character list. Aeidon is Aelin's long lost cousin, and is working his ass off to find her. Now he's working with Chaol to figure out what it is that is possessing those around them, and how it could be put to an end. Manon Blackbeak is her own heir, belonging to a long line of Ironteeth witches as well as the Wing Leader of the Thirteen. She is strong willed and shows signs of compassion towards the outcasts. She's also able to see the potential in those around her which makes her a great leader. I don't think anyone lost their hatred for the king of Ardalan. If anything it might have just intensified in this book. I don't even want to talk about him. Can someone kill this guy already?! I hate repeating myself, but I said it in book two's review - I love that romance is clearly a thought in this novel, but each character knows the responsibility that lies with them and don't think too much about loving someone. Dorian tries but that poor guy has lost his best friend and his newest friend, and doesn't really have much because his father is a prick. I said it last time and I'll say it again. Read this now. It has easily become one of my favourite books and I am obsessed with it. I know it's rough to transition to fantasy, but have an open mind and just know you WILL love this.

Kind of a fun story, but... It wasn't put together well. In fact, it was downright hard to read. Playing around with point-of-view ought to be done very carefully, y'all. Another thing that brought my suspension of disbelief crashing down was the insertion of modern beliefs about "equality". Give me a break. It's a fairy tale, for crying out loud. Let's have a little chivalry and some good old heirarchy! It fits the genre so much better. Modern mores just clash and jangle. The story has potential... Too bad it didn't quite live up to that potential.

I saw the trailer, did a little research, and immediately added the book to my library holds list. I WAS NOT DISAPPOINTED. The setting is contemporary America right after aliens have come to our world. They aren't your friendly E.T. characters either. The name of the book denotes the 'waves' of terror that the aliens inflict on the planet. The point of view flips between 4 characters as they navigate their new reality. The 'main' character is Cassie why are all of these young adult series books about a girl who never knew she had the strength within to rise up and be the hero? who is a fairly typical teenage girl and I don't think the book would work if she weren't able to believably carry the narrative. I don't want to tell you about the other 3 narrators because I think that would be too big of a spoiler. - Suffice to say that the book is sure to keep you on your toes and if you're a fan of sci-fi fantasy novels that center around aliens this is one that you should definitely check out. I've already made a note to pick up the second in the series, The Infinite Sea.

This book started out interesting, but then the main character really began to get on my nerves. Who wants to read about a self-obsessed, hot-headed, bully anyway? Even if he's going to go through some sort of profound change by the end, I'm not interested enough to stick with him. I probably would've kept listening despite the jerk protag, but the plot sagged near the middle and I found myself dreading the remaining CDs. That's when you know it's time to move on.

This book bothered me on several levels. I found it impossible to like Willow. Despite the fact she felt responsible for her parents' deaths, I couldn't muster much sympathy for her. That isn't a good quality in a main character, in case you were wondering. And the narrative style just felt so flat to me. But my biggest issue with the book involves the inclusion of a very personal note Kudos to making a very real problem such an important part of the plot, but the resolution was incredibly unrealistic. I was a cutter, have known cutters, and it is absolutely a mental health issue and an addiction. It's not something you stop because you meet a guy. And it isn't something that draws people to you. If anything, it pushes people away. If someone sees all your "tools" or that you have scars all over your arms, they're more likely to run the other way than they are to try and "heal" you. Additionally, other people cannot save you. As with any addiction, the only person who can get you to stop harming yourself is you. It's been a while since I read the book and I don't plan on revisiting it for the sake of accuracy, but I don't recall Willow seeking much professional help. As I remember it, she basically stopped because she had a crush on a guy and he pretty much kept saying, "Oh don't hurt yourself, Willow," and she thought maybe there was something to that. I also remember many graphic descriptions of cutting, so I wouldn't recommend this book to anyone who is squeamish or would find the content to be a trigger for their own self-injury.

The problem with that bull throughout the book is that it just detracts from the novel the entire time because I'm so ANNOYED. Plus, this novel as the one before was rather predictable. I'm all for satire, and I think Libba Bray is hilarious, but Beauty Queens was way too heavy-handed for my taste. Bray puts forth a valiant effort at making use of every single stereotype about teen girls that has ever existed, but it gets so confusing at times that it's not half as effective as it could've been if only a few of those stereotypes were tackled. Also, there's no real depth to it. Not that I expect huge depths from every satire, but I at least wanted to feel something for the characters, no matter how ridiculous they could be at times, and I didn't. I think this would've been a lot funnier more effective as a short story, or a novella, but at 400 pages it's just too much.

Great read. Loved this story. Twists and turns, LOL moments, this story has it all. Characters are well written and Kellogg Or am sucks you into her world, with her story telling. Read this book and see if Jamie the ice queen, heartless loaner can be thawed out. Can she possibly have a relationship without accidentally killing Ryan with her superpowers, or will Ryan or others discover she has powers like no other human.

4 Stars I really liked Paranormalcy and was SO looking forward to reading the second installment. Evie is such a likable character. She's funny, smart, adventurous, and has the kind of charm that can't be ignored. She really is fun to get to know and a very likable character. The story picks up a few months after all hell breaks loose at the International Paranormal Containment Agency, and Evie and Lend are all kissy kissy. That's okay, Evie deserves one minute of normalcy.... happiness. Things start out okay until other worldly things start attacking and trying to kill Evie. She's isn't too sure if all of these near misses are linked - she's kinda busy smoochin' and steering clear of Lend. need more Lend, please I was a little frustrated with Evie's choices in this story. Lying and keeping things from your ever understanding boyfriend is never a good thing, and although Evie is a teenage girl, I was hoping she wouldn't go in that direction. Ah, no matter. There is a new bloke, Jack, who can walk the faerie paths. He. Was. Wacko. My emotions for Jack were all over the place! He was funny, dumb, obnoxious, manipulative, and obnoxious. Oh, I said that already.... Jack and his "antics" add a playful feel to the story even though...his actions raise red flags. You know something is up with this dude, but you just can't put your finger on it. Well, ya do. In the end. Without a doubt the best part of Supernaturally is the personal growth of Evie. She really comes into her own in this story. Evie learns about her beginnings and starts to take charge of her own life SO heartbreaking , and decides how she wants to live the rest of her life. I was honestly proud of that girl by the last page. dabseyes Overall, fun and quick read full of more twists and turns than those creepy faerie paths. Keep me out of those!

The book was a good read but is already fading from my conscious. DNF at page 105 This book was a mess, oh my gosh. Let me start this out by saying that I absolutely hate DNF'ing a book. I rarely ever do it. However, I'm trying to take a new outlook on reading-- life is short and I don't have loads of reading time, so why waste time on something I'm not enjoying? If a book is boring, I may DNF it, but not rate it as the problem might be my own doing rather than the book's . But if it's bad, I have no problem rating it without completion. They All Fall Down was, more or less, pretty terrible. The premise is essentially that Kenzie Sumerall is at the beginning of her junior year of high school. Always the quiet, nerdy type, she is shocked when she makes it onto her school's top ten "Hottie List." Instantly, her life spins into a whirlwind of popularity, parties, and boys. It sounds all fun and great, until the girls at the top of the list start turning up dead in weird accidents. Kenzie herself keeps narrowly avoiding accidents and is receiving strange warnings in Latin. Clearly, something is going on. So, it sounds pretty interesting, right? That's what I thought. I was so excited to get my hands on a copy of this book. As fun as the plot sounds, it is poorly executed. One of my biggest issues with the novel is the entire idea of the Hottie List. I assumed that there would be people opposing the list. After all, it's super sexist and demeaning of women. But no, the only one in the entire town that seems to have a problem with it is Kenzie, and she's viewed as a super special MC because of it. Even older women covet the spots that they once held on the List and brag about it, as if it's their biggest achievement in life to be placed onto it. Once Kenzie was rated fifth, people immediately took notice. Even though she knew it was wrong, she still got caught up in the excitement of it. I understand that-- every girl wants to feel as if people like her. However, I didn't like that when guys started to objectify her, even calling her Fifth as a nickname, Kenzie never corrected or stopped them. It was gross. I wish there had been some more acknowledgement especially by adults of the fact that this was bad. Kenzie herself was not a great MC. Her tone was okay, but I got really tired of being reminded every five pages how smart she was. She wants to get into an Ivy League school and acts holier than thou to her peers, because how dare they want to party when college apps are approaching next year? She also doesn't act very intelligent. The second weird things start happening, she responds in dumb ways. She doesn't tell anyone about the threatening events occurring around her, even though she has plenty of evidence in her favor. She's also just hypocritical and weird in parts. Her personality seems all over the place and hard to grasp. The other characters weren't much better. Her best friend, Molly, was obnoxious and only cared about popularity. Josh was boring, and Levi was the "bad boy with a soft heart" stereotype 100 percent. Another huge turn off to this book for me was the love triangle. Kenzie mentions early on that she's had a crush on Josh since 7th grade. Once she gets on the List, Josh asks her out after previously never acknowledging her existence . Is Kenzie excited when her four-year crush asks her out? Nope. Immediately she loses interest in him and lusts after a bad boy she's never met before. It all happened so fast. By 40 pages in, both guys are already introduced romantically. And it's not subtle at all. Look at these cringeworthy examples "I can't help but compare Josh to the other boy who stole a lot of my thoughts today. Could they be any more different? At least on the surface, Josh seems so bright and harmless and golden. And Levi is dark and scary and sexy" 46 . Images of Levi Sterling and Josh Collier collide in my head, all dark and light like the embodiments of evil and good" 49 . Why don't YA authors understand? Love triangles are so overdone and unnecessary. If they're written well, I can deal with them. But that is a very rare occurrence. I could go on about my issues with this book forever. After skimming reviews, it seems like a lot of people did like it. I can see why, because it flows well and is oddly readable. I only stopped because I realized that I didn't care what happened anymore and the List stuff was wracking my nerves . In my opinion, the pacing was almost a little too fast. Weird, creepy events were happening nearly every 10 pages. It was sort of like Pretty Little Liars all sped up without the blackmail . The plot almost followed a certain pattern, as if the author said to herself, "Okay, first something scary needs to happen. Now Kenzie's mom needs to react, causing Kenzie to feel guilty about her dead brother. Now let's throw in some boy drama. Now another creepy accident..." and so on. It was strange. This brings me to my final point. Kenzie had a lot of family drama that I didn't care about. Her overly protective mother just seemed scarred by the death of her son. Kenzie overreacted to that. And a lot of time like 1 or 2 of every 10 pages was spent on Kenzie mourning feeling guilty over her brother's death. That's fine, but it felt kind of disingenuous because we never actually got to meet the brother. We're told about how he was popular and friendly and all that, but he died before the story began, so the reader doesn't get attached to him or feel sympathy for Kenzie. I've read books where it works when someone close to the MC dies before the story starts Saving June and Hold Still are good examples of YA ones , but this wasn't written well enough to pull it off. Instead, I just didn't care. As you can tell, I didn't like this one. I imagine some people will, because like I said, it's easy to read. It just wasn't for me. There were a lot of plot holes and the ending, which I read about in reviews, seems completely implausible and ridiculous. Why would assassins send threatening messages to a high schooler? If you're going to kill someone, just do it. Warning them and messing around is something someone only does for revenge and the drama felt like middle school behavior, not high school. I wouldn't recommend it. There are so many better things to read out there. 1 5 stars.

We are The Unofficial Addiction Book Fan Club, to know more about this book, go to the post in our website Until Friday Night The Field Party 1 by Abbi Glines If you are interested, you can visit our website The Unofficial Addiction Book Fan Club The Unofficial Addiction Book Fan Club's Review Rate 4 stars Review Until Friday Night is a story about loss, pain, romance and friendship. I'm beyond thrilled to have read a story written by Abbi Glines, but even more to know that she's back to writing YA stories. Because yes, there might be some intense moments, but all PG rated, so to me that's a YA story. In Until Friday Night we have two main characters. We have Maggie Carleton's life fell apart when her father murdered her mother and her way of coping with all the pain is to not speak. And then we have West Ashby's world seems to be almost perfect. However, he's scared and pained because his father's dying. We get two read from Maggie and West's point of view and I am always glad to have the two sides of the story. It was easier to see every single interaction between these two from a different perspective, the intentions of their actions and how the outside world affected them differently. Their story is unique, tender and dramatic. Pain brought them together, but love will make them last. I loved every single moment of this story and how this couple changed, grew and became more than just another young adult fictional couple. As an individual character, I have to mention that Maggie was more mature than West both on the inside and outside. West, on the other hand, if you read from Maggie's point of view you could get the sense that he was a bit more immature. However, reading his point of view blew your mind and totally made you reconsider this character over and over again. Maggie's definitely a strong character, as West says in the story. She's lived a traumatic family drama and she has found a way to cope with it, to keep moving even though it's even painful to breathe. But what's beyond admirable is that she had absorbed all those painful and traumatic experiences and transformed them into wise thoughts she decides to share with others in need like West. She's selfless the whole time in the story and I think that's one of the perks that makes this book so touching, emotional and enjoyable. Abbi Glines always tests their characters beyond a breaking point, and in Until Friday Night she did the same but with an original, honest and emotional story that will captivate you until the very last page. Don't let yourself fool you about the title, because it might have another beautiful meaning. You just need to get to know Maggie and West and their traumatic love story.

Warning not any big spoilers in here, but I do talk about specific characters and what they did or didn't do. I REALLY wanted to give this more stars, but I couldn't. The best part of this book were the last few pages with scenes between Devan and her mother. The positives first The setting and the author's knowledge of the LA area was believable. She has a great way of describing scenery to the point where I had a picture in my head of the area, the house, Devan's school...but everyone else was a blank face in my mind. Also, I liked the list that she kept on her mom as it seemed like a natural thing for a teen girl to do. The negatives First, I felt like I was reading a season of "Glee". I have teenagers and have been around their friends and I haven't heard any of them use so many "like" and "seriously" and "totallys" as the characters in this book do. I didn't like anyone in this book except Brad, Reece Malcolm's boyfriend. Everyone else was cliche from the gay boy, gay girl, to the love interests like "Glee" . Secondly, Devan fell very flat for me. She never really questioned why her mom gave her up and you are wondering all along what kid would just let that go by and never ask it? Spoiler you find out at the end why Devan went to live with her dad. Also,she never really talked about her friends back in St. Louis. After having uprooted my kids from their hometown and moving 500 miles away, I know it's hard on them and they talked a lot to their friends back home. They still do 18 months later. I found it very odd that Devan just kind of shrugged and never really cared what her best friend was doing back in her hometown. Her stepmother was never mentioned again it would have been nice to see what she ended up doing even though she had been awful to Devan. This woman was with Devan for 16 years and Devan hated her and the feeling was reciprocated, so why not give the reader specifics as to ways the step-mom showed this hate? There was only one scene we saw, a flashback, and that was it. Thirdly, the writing was choppy. I had a hard time following conversations and scenes because 1 there would be so much description in between a conversation, that when a character finally made a comment I would wonder what that comment was in reference to, so I'd have to flip back and re-read and 2 there were no scene breaks. One minute, Reece and Devan would be talking about themselves and the next line, literally, is what they ordered at the Mexican restaurant. In a nutshell, the book sounded so interesting and had the potential to be a unique book about a girl finding out who she is and who her mom is, but the depth to do that was just not there. After Devan found out Sai a new boy to the school she goes to was from St. Louis, I kept willing them--with all my heart--to compare notes about the area. When you move away from your home, and find someone who used to live in the same state or even the same county as you, you naturally discuss it. You talk about food, places, restaurants, sports teams, politicians but all you got here was "Yeah, I lived there too and we moved because ___." None of that happened and it seemed so unnatural to me. So, I'm sorry to say I didn't like this book as nothing resonated with me. Even when I dug back into my life as a teenager. I couldn't related to anything she did, which is maybe why I could only give this book 1 star.

The thing is I never know if steam punk exists in the modern realm with an inspiration to the past or if its something completely different. I loved the intricate descriptions of some of the inner workings of the gizmos and gadgets that appeared in the story. Adrienne thoroughly did her research and she did it well. Her scenes open up just like a movie creates the feeling of a time period, but what is great in the setting, lacks in other areas. The key driver for most books is plot. There wasn't a story that kept me from turning the pages. I had to stop and pick it up again and that is always a big sign that I won't end up liking the book in the end. I tend to get hooked into books very easily but if by the first 50-150 pages I'm bored, then I can automatically assume there's nothing worthwhile. It's good I'm stubborn though, because even if I'm bored, I'll keep going because I just have to finish the book. I'm glad I kept going because the story does pick up in the end, and it turned out to be one heck of an adventure. Characters Incredibly detailed and rich. Each main character has a back story, a personality, and a purpose Pacing Slow..Very slow to pick up in the beginning, but the end makes up for a great climatic ending. Cover Design Gorgeous. A Young Adult book with high-intensity action, drugs, and catching villains in the metropolitan city in the US of A. That sounds like a pretty good premise, don't you think? Reminds me of all those superhero books we all adore, except this one has young teenagers taking drugs to give them superstrength speed and whatever super-what-have-you. Reading this book a few weeks ago, it actually was pretty enjoyable... ...until it didn't. Here's the thing this book had potential. The first seventy percent was such an amazing ride. Here we are, introduced to a main character who is supposedly the best runner in her department. Her job as a teenage tool of the government? To use the Tetra which is the drug, if the cliche drug name itself wasn't self-explanatory enough to catch people using knock-offs of the drug to rob banks and risk public security. I loved the main character, Alana West, because she was so relatable - she wasn't the dreaded goody-two-shoes heroine, nor was she an annoying, reckless girl who thought the world revolved around her. She was level-headed, and at the same time, she was oozing with personality and had enough insecurities and self-loathing to balance her character and no, I am not being sarcastic, she was pretty well-rounded , and trust me I JUST LOVED READING ALL OF IT. I GOBBLED IT ALL UP. I loved the intensity of the first seventy percent in the book, and I loved how in the middle part there was this internal struggle between using the drug to do good and using the drug because you're addicted to the drug and the 9 minutes of euphoria it gives you. I'm not sure how exactly accurate it was, but I felt like it was somehow a sneak peek into the mind of an addict and how much they justified using illegal drugs. It felt so real and so intimate and so disturbing all at the same time how the hero became a zero all because of a drug and of course, some political shit, but hey, that's for you to find out by reading the book, right? and I just LOVED IT. And then the last thirty percent came, and it all went to shit. I don't know what happened with the book, but for some reason, the last thirty percent flushed down all the complexity, all the rawness of the narrative, all the GOOD THINGS, down the toilet and it become inconssitent, predictable, and just downright insufferable. Http shattering-words.blogspot.com Jocurile Foamei 2 Sfidarea By Suzanne Collins Parerea mea Theo Pentru mine cartea a fost mai mult decat un fel de transa din care a trebuit sa ma trezesc o data cu terminarea ultimei replici. A devenit un fel de drog a carui componenta principala nu o cunosteam nici eu. Un fel de ,,te vreau", dar nu stiu ceea ce esti! Dupa cum bine ne amintim din prima carte recenzia poate fi citita aici , Katniss si Peeta reusesc sa infranga povara Capitoliului, sa castige impreuna ca unul Jocurile Foamei, sa fie incoronati si sa aiba posibilitatea de a se intoarce in satul natal. Nu tu complicatii, nu tu rastalmacii, nu tu oameni cu priviri iscoditoare, nimic neinteresant. Un alt tribut - n cazul acesta doua alte tributuri - au reusit sa supravietuiasca, sa demonstreze lumii intregi ca ei sunt cei mai buni, sa nu devina sacrificiile aduse zeilor. Numai ca o data cu acest castig apar si pierderile de tip emotional si fizic. Katniss trebuie de acum sa sa traiasca impreuna cu familia ei intr-o casa luxoasa si cu o groaza de bani. Orice si-ar fi dorit orice om din orice District, numai ca lui Katniss nu ii face o deosebita placere aceasta schimbare de peisaj, asa ca ea continua sa vaneze si sa duca vanatul familiei lui Gale. Totul se desfasoara intr-un fel de durere continua, mai ales dupa declaratia pe care Gale i-o face. Ma simt si eu la fel de prinsa ca si Katniss, la fel de ingradita, la fel de nelamurita legat de sentimentele mele fata de cei doi baieti. Sunt intr-un fel la fel de sfasiata de dorinta unuia precum sunt de dorinta celuilalt, si desi niciuna din noi nu o recunoastem, stim cel mai bine care pereche de brate ne alunga cosmarurile si care ne lasa sa ne rasucim de pe o parte pe alta. Desi imi place ideea ca micuta Katniss sa se maturizeze si sa o vad mereu inconjurata de stilistii ei favoriti, mi se pare ca amandoua gandim din ce in ce mai mult una ca cealalta, iar asta ma face sa surad in incercarea mea nebuneasca de a tine pasul cu emotiile schimbatoare. Cand primeste vizita Presedintelui, ii simt deja inima si capul invartindu-se la mii si mii de miscari pe secunda. Nici ea, nici eu nu stim cum sa reactionam, asa ca acceptam cuvintele acestuia fara prea multe sanse de ripostare si nu incetam sa nu ne gandim la binele celui pe care il avem de protejat Peeta. Initial totul se invarte in jurul tuturor, problema este ca ne dam seama repede pe cine vrem sa protejam cu adevarat. Katniss sufera cateva schimbari pe parcurs pe care le ador, care ma fac sa imi simt pielea zbarlindu-se, iar corpul gata de atac. Este atat de imprevizibila si totusi atat de previzibila incat si tu poti avea cateva dureri de cap usoare daca nu esti atent. M-a maturizat psihic, cu cateva grade, comportamentul ei, pentru ca mereu imi dadea ceva de gandit pana la urmatoarea scena, pana la urmatoarea rasturnare de situatie. Momentul cand se anunta ce se va intampla la aniversarea de saptezeci si cinci de ani a Jocurilor Foamei, eu una inghet, Katniss are un fel de soc psihic si fizic. Un fel de modalitate de a recunoaste ca este prea mult, ca totul se intampla prea repede, mult prea repede! Asta este un fel de bonus imens adus cartii m-a facut mereu sa nu imi dau seama ce urmeaza. Cea de-a saptezeci si cincea aniversare a Jocurilor Foamei va fi formata din toti invingatorii in viata din fiecare District o fata si un baiat! Poftim? Exact! De acum sunt pe cont propriu! Katniss si Peeta trebuie sa se intoarca in Arena, trebuie sa infrunte din nou durerea, sangele, omorurile, totul! Haymitch nici nu intra in discutie, fiind dat la o pare cu usurinta de Peeta care se ofera voluntar. Katniss stie ce are de facut de acum, stie ce urmeaza si stie cum se va descurca! Va fi un singur invingator, un singur suflet care va ramane in viata pentru a povesti ce va urma, o singura suflare care sa asigure ca nicio alta Revolta nu va ramane nestabilita, neprogramata sau neiesita invingatoare. Katniss va sacrifica totul pentru Peeta! Capitoliul va fi inmormantat sub spaima. Districtele vor fi dezgropate din veneratie. Familiile vor avea parte de reuniri. Iubiri vor fi spulberate, altele vor fi cladite. Este acum ori niciodata! Esti cu noi, gaita zeflemitoare? Ofer cartii 5 5 stele!

Congratulations to Ruta Sepetys for tackling a lost moment in history. However, as a young adult novel, it fails to fully educate the reader about Stalin's attempt to wipe out entire nations and nationalities. Like the main character, Lina, the reader is left in the dark about the politics involved with the relocation and imprisonment of innocent people. It was as if the author was trying to protect us from trying to understand the politics of the time and protect us, like Lina's mother, from the true horrors of what was happening. While there are not many novels if any out there that deal with Russia's ethnic cleansing movement, I think the reader might learn more about ethnic cleansing reading Night, The Book Thief, Zlata's Diary A Child's Life in Wartime Sarajevo or Anne Frank's The Diary of a Young Girl. I do hope this novel inspires other authors, or even Ruta Sepetys herself, to bring to light the horrors and atrocities of the Stalin's government.

This book.....UGH this book... I probably read this book 5 years ago I found this book well written and enjoyed the dual perspective. I liked that this book was about suicide. It is a touchy subject and one close to home. I wanted to love this book. I wanted to This book had so much potential to be great. But it just wasn't there for me. This poor girl. Bullying is never okay but who's never been bullied? Everyone goes through it at some point or another. You stick your head up and keep moving on with life. Because things do get better. Eventually. Even if you can't see the light at the end of the tunnel. At 16,17,18 you haven't even lived a half of your life. Look around at all the people who have it so much worse! She was surrounded by people, she went to parties, she was so clearly loved by her parents, she had a nice, stable home, she was fed, clothed, warm. She made a choice to take her life before talking to anyone about what was REALLY going through her head. This book which, I think, was supposed to be there to help kids through suicide, just glorified it and made it appealing to those who think about it. It makes it appear glamorous, like once your gone, everyone will be talking about you. That shouldn't be the case. It failed to show the real effects suicide can have, the pain it causes, the emptiness it creates. The shear nothingness that awaits for you. And I feel like teens who are so susceptible to everything need to know and understand the finality of this. Had this book ended differently, had Hannah spoken up and got the help she needed, or failed to commit suicide and realized it wasn't the way out, my opinions and feelings towards the book would greatly differ. C'est la vie

I was excited to read SERPENTINE because of the setting, which is based in large part on China. I wasn't disappointed in this respect, but the setting was the only part of the book I was really able to get into. From the beginning, we're immersed in the setting. I loved how well the details came to life all throughout the story, and it was nice to read a fantasy novel that wasn't based on Europe. It also made me want to learn more about Chinese history, which isn't something I'm as familiar with. I wasn't into the characters at all. I realize that, as a handmaiden, Skybright is expected to fade into the background so as not to overshadow her mistress. But we spend the whole book in her head, so I was hoping there'd be more going on with her. For me, there wasn't. She spends the whole book centered on the people around her - first her mistress, Zhen Ni, and then the boy she falls in love with, Kai - and we don't really get to know who Skybright really is. While that isn't necessarily unrealistic, it didn't make for the most interesting narration. Also, the romance between Skybright and Kai fell flat for me, in large part because of my aforementioned issues with Skybright. The romance felt really underdeveloped for this reason. We also don't get to know Kai very well all I got was that he trains with the monks and that he's fascinated by Skybright, so I couldn't get into his character, either. The subplot with Zhen Ni was interesting, though. I don't want to spoil it, so I won't give specifics, but I'll say that it was explored very well through Skybright's eyes. I think people who prefer quieter heroines will probably have more luck with this one than I did.

Mila 2.0 In Short I really need to stop judging books by their first few pages. The Breakdown It's not even so much that I judged the quality of the writing. I completely misjudged the genre. I ignored most of the blurb before starting the book, because I REALLY wasn't bothered to read through 'as she unravels the mystery surrounding her identity' AGAIN. Which meant that I missed this either the basic premise of the story or the biggest spoiler you have ever seen, I don't know - it is in the blurb Mila is an android. Mobile Intel Lifelike Android. MILA. So for me, not knowing the android bit, even though it's stated plainly in the blurb, the foreshadowing and hinting at her nature was really good, and not too in-your-face either. We get clues about heightened hearing, missing memories and heightened strength, as well as the wariness of her mother, until one day she's with two friends and something happens which removes all doubt for the reader and means Mila is forced to learn about what she's really like - from information coldly dispensed, pre-recorded, from an iPod - in the form of a brochure, about her. And she reacts satisfyingly for once! She also experiences that peculiar sensation wherein once you discover something, everything reminds you of it and so many things are made clearer. And throughout the book, although she stubbornly refused it for a while, she begins to accept her design and eventually uses it as the advantage it is. And I loved it. There is such a huge contrast between the first few chapters of the book and the rest, which serve nicely to illustrate how much Mila's life has been shaken up. The first part has cliched, but enjoyable romantic fluffy beginnings between she and Harper, but the rest has thrilling action scenes and drama. I'm ashamed to say that I immediately assumed it was going to be some kind of high-school romance READ THE DAMN BLURB ROSE! , but even so, it was a good one! Even Mila's introspective bits, which were necessary because, did I mention, she's just found out that she's a freaking android, were concise and managed to fit in well with the plot of the book. Her natural, unbeknownst to her, fighting skills were VERY entertaining to read about, because who doesn't love a well-written fight with a teenage heroine? Also, we find out that her memory loss, which she had presumed was because of trauma following the 'death' of her nonexistent biological father dum de dum android , are because she really only has been alive for a few months, and she was 'born' sixteen. The meeting with Mila 3.0 was one of my favourite parts. Mila 3.0 is just an updated version of Mila 2.0, the protagonist, but without - many - feelings. Mila 1.0 was destroyed because she had too many, and too many pain receptors, which caused her to fail the torture test they're government-created spies , thus providing a potential risk for US security. I loved this because it was a real psychological blow to Mila 2.0 , teaching her that she really was just a manufactured machine. However, through the book she does change slightly, which her mother tells her is a point of hope, because if she can change and grow emotionally she is a person. The last challenge provided to Mila by Holland oh how I'd like to punch him was brilliant reading. Never mind how psychologically cruel and difficult it was to Mila. She was pitted against the updated, more skilled version of herself and forced to try to win for the person who matters most in the world to her. What more could a reader ask for? I also loved this part because it reminded me of the arena in the Hunger Games, in that it was really well described and I could visualise it clearly. There were a few parts that lowered my rating a star. The first was that her 'mother', who went everywhere with her and really provided little help, was SUCH a liability! I was probably supposed to like her as a person but I was just frustrated at her because she's just going to be an impediment to Mila's awesome android skills sooner or later. Seriously, she is nearly destroyed made torture bad things just because she insists on running back to some who she isn't even related to. I shouldn't be so cold-hearted maybe, but in this book I was. Having said that, there was a decently sad Prim Dobby moment, if you know what I'm talking about, at the end. Can I just say, Prim's death - WHY? The whole reason the story exists is because Katniss tried to save her sister! She can't just - GAH! Also, the way the set-up for the sequel was done wasn't exactly inspiring. And the ending - they just had to throw Hunter in at the end, when he'd had absolutely no involvement for half the story, didn't they? But again, it was quite cute and the set-up did serve its purpose. I would be very gratified if there's a Mila 2.1 also, although I doubt it. The description promises a breathtaking cliffhanger - read Catching Fire if you want to know what a cliffhanger ACTUALLY IS. The cover very nearly put me off the book altogether because it promised cliches and shoddy writing. Please ignore that and the publisher's description not the blurb altogether, they really don't live up to it. Overall, it was a very, very good book debut author! Wow! , and the 'faults' are mainly just my cold, picky heart talking. You can also blame the amazing book I read before this, which may have meant Mila should've gotten half a star higher. Anyway, I really enjoyed Mila 2.0 and highly recommend it. There is also Origins, book O.5, and two more to come.

"Catrina." He breathes my name like a secret. I caught you. "Stonefield." I run my hands over the hills and hollows of him, exploring the strange new land of his body. I let you. i think a big part of my affection for this book is tied to my love of its source material Wuthering Heights, and the fact that i have read a ton of retellings of Wuthering Heights, many badly done, but i always appreciate it when an author takes the basic WH framework and does something unexpected with it in this case, setting it in missouri during the american civil war, transforming heathcliff stonefield into a muscogee creek indian, and letting history have its way. as with any retelling, it's the author's prerogative to cherry-pick through the original material, borrowing some elements, rejecting others, adapting the leftover pieces as needed, and some of the choices are obviously going to work better than others. but i think as long as you, the reader, approach this book knowing it's a Wuthering Heights retelling, and you accept all that this entails, you'll be in good shape to enjoy the book on its own terms. because reading the many negative reviews of this book, there seem to be two major complaints 1 the romance feels like inauthentic instalove and 2 catrina catherine is childish, unsympathetic, selfish, and stubborn adjectives culled from several reviews most interesting to me is a review containing this line Catrina makes life harder for everyone but especially for herself with her reckless actions. now, i'm not here to single anyone out or poo-poo anyone's opinions, but that sentence right there is pretty much the beating-heart summary of Wuthering Heights, and the fact that the author made "her" catherine such a pill tells me she understands these characters and isn't prettying up the love story like so many others who have adapted WH. because i think people forget, whether they are influenced by the film-versions of WH or they're willing to forgive bad behavior that springs out of Great and Terrible Passions, that catherine and heathcliff were both insufferable assholes. or maybe they remember that heathcliff was one, because of all the vengeance etc, but catherine IS childish, unsympathetic, selfish, and stubborn. she's the worst! i mean, except for heathcliff, who is the worst! and Wuthering Heights is nothing more than a gothic predecessor of naughty girls need love, too, and a tale of what happens when two people who only care about each other ruin the lives of everyone they know. which, thankfully, is not many people. as for the instalove, while i definitely agree that catrina and stonefield are as insta-love as it gets, as long as you remember that this is based on a book whose most famously melodramatic line is "He's more myself than I am. Whatever our souls are made of, his and mine are the same" which is alluded to in this book with "Stonefield is my own self" , and you accept the idea - hokey as it is - that soulmates might recognize each other on first sight, it won't bother you overmuch. it didn't bother me, even though i usually eyeroll at instalove. but since i already had it in my head that these two were playing the roles of catherine and heathcliff, the expectation that they would be drawn to each other uncontrollably was already slotted in, and its suddenness is excusable. since this book doesn't have the benefit of catherine and heathcliff growing up together and having their intense childhood bond to springboard them into romantic love, the inclusion of catrina and stonefield's ability to read each other's minds was a pretty innovative way to identify them as destined to be together without having to provide a "falling for you" sequence. "we can read each other's minds and we think the other is attractive? must be love." and while it might seem odd to have this science fictiony superpower in the middle of a book about nature and war and history, it's no different from the ghost in Wuthering Heights - it's not necessarily supernatural it's more of a literary device used as a manifestation of their love and their unbreakable connection. in Wuthering Heights, the passion of the characters is mirrored in the wildness of the moors, and this one also celebrates the natural world - catrina has been creating her own version of installation art which i loved manipulating trees, rocks, water, and leaves into elaborate shapes and patterns, which stonefield observes and creates a "piece" of his own in order to get her attention. their love is conducted entirely out-of-doors, swimming, climbing, reading whitman and shakespeare together and celebrating their feelings and their bodies in their own little prelapsarian paradise, free and wild away from the prim and proper expectations of polite society. 'cuz catrina's definitely not well-suited to her time. she despises the corsets and dresses she's expected to wear - preferring trousers or full-blown nudity, frequently covered in mud, and she's reckless and impulsive and - yes - very, very selfish, but since stonefield is included in her definition of "self," she makes no distinction between his needs and her own. and their needs get pretty saucy. they are both very passionate and inspired by the fecundity of nature all around them. and once they start reading "song of songs" together, things are gonna get steamy pretty quickly. even before she meets stonefield, catrina wants a love that is intense to the point of destruction a passion heedless of its own safety I want someone who will climb right into me and explore every inch, knowing they might never find their way out. and this all-consuming love that burns everyone in its path? that's the very essence of Wuthering Heights, my friends... as a retelling, it's better than most. and kinder to its characters. henry hindley comes across way better than he does in w.h., effie nelly is fantastic in a complete character-makeover, and stonefield is far less diabolical than heathcliff. zero puppies are hanged. his role in the tragic turn of the events is less about him being a vengeful monster and more to do with him being bad at communicating. the only thing that really grated on my was this verbal tic of catrina's is it considered a verbal tic when it only appears in interior monologues? , where she prefaces way too many of her thoughts with the words "lord" or "lordy," but in a secular way -I think I'm falling asleep, and Lord, we're already at the parsonage the next time I open my eyes. -Lord, everything's topsy-turvy. -Lordy, his smile. -Lordy, just in time. etc etc etc all the time but for the most part, this book did not irritate me the way it irritated so many others, which might be down to my being a WH superfan and having a peculiar appreciation for authors who don't sugarcoat their douchiness. i've barely scratched the surface of what this book does well, using the whole review space to blather about inconsequential details no one but me cares about, so i guess you should choose to read or not read this based on your own WH feels, and not on this dummy's review.

This review will contain some spoilers for the first book in the series, Under the Never Sky, which I wrote about here. It picks up a few months after the end of Under the Never Sky. Perry is now the Blood Lord of the Tides, and Aria has been learning to use her Aud powers. They have a short reunion before spending most of the rest of the book apart Perry learning how to be a leader, and Aria searching for Olivia and the location of the Still Blue. This sequel fell flat for me, I have to be honest. The dual perspectives worked well in the first book -- when you have two characters together who are struggling to communicate, switching points of view shows the reader how their feelings and characters evolve and change, which can be a really effective device. In a book like this, however, I don't think it's successful. Because the characters spend so much time apart, the different perspectives are just recapping their journeys and it's more like switching chapters of two separate books. I thought Perry's storyline had potential to be more interesting leadership is a hard skill to learn, and being in charge of a whole tribe of people requires thinking fast. However, the whole process was sort of skimmed over. Aria's plot wasn't much better she and Roar go on a journey to find Liv. I would have liked Aria to do something for herself, like search for more information about her parents. The relationship between Roar and Liv was sort of interesting, but I didn't really understand how it related to the rest of the story. Apparently there was a novella about Roar and Liv released in between the books that would give a clearer picture. Extra material shouldn't be necessary to understanding the main story, though if I'm actually missing something by only reading the main books, that's a bad sign. Because Aria and Perry are separated for most of the book I didn't feel like their relationship developed in any way. There are some very feeble attempts at creating a love triangle, which just felt shoehorned in and halfhearted. At the end of the day, I just didn't feel like anything happened. There were a couple of plot developments at the end, but it seemed to me like this was just a placeholder until the third book. I'll still read the last one when it comes out, but I was less than impressed with this installment. Also, I hate the cover! I am on record as hating book covers with photographs of models on them, particularly when they don't look anything like the description given. If that guy is supposed to be Perry, then the cover designer surely didn't read the book.

Disclosure I received a request to read and review this book, but I purchased the book myself. Jenny, a farm girl from Utah, has few problems, but being being torn between two "first loves," is a biggie for a 16-year-old. This is a very gentle book, inoffensive, light on conflict, with a lesson appropriate for Young Women's. However, it has a few problems. The first and biggest problem is the voice. This is not the voice of a 16-year-old girl, nor the voices of 18-year-old boys. This is the voice of a grown woman, and all the characters' voices are the same. Some teenagers may talk and act like these characters do, and I would not be surprised to learn that the kids in the author's life actually do talk like this. But I found it unbelievable. Further, there were no smartphones, no texting, no email anywhere in the story, and one of the teenage boys said he looked up the girl's address in the phone book. In the age of Google, 4Square, Twitter, Facebook, and Tumblr, I found that completely unrealistic. I didn't find it particularly unrealistic that one of the boys would write a letter in pen and ink to the girl, but the letter itself was very adult, as in, middle-aged adult. Third was a the completely unnecessary introduction of a boy at the beginning of the story who was far too important to the protagonist, only to drop out of sight and b the sudden dropping-in of a boy who was never referred to until he was dropped in, compete with info-dump. Fourth, though the story arc was complete with room for a sequel , it was a bit boring. There was never anything on the line, no real conflict, and was written in an almost travelogue tone. The writing was serviceable, but the storytelling was lacking. I do think the author shows some promise as a storyteller, though, and I would encourage her to a find someone who can help her find her storytelling spark b not write about teenagers or c spend some time with teenagers and see how they talk, speak, act, and think and d catch up with how technology is used by digital natives.

Considering the subject and the plot of Wither, comparisons with Margaret Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale is, in my opinion, inevitable. Parallels will be drawn between the two books by readers who have read both books and perhaps the reaction to Wither will be coloured a bit by their exposure to the much acclaimed Handmaid's Tale. Let's talk about the good stuff first. The relationships between the three girls is one of the main joys of the book. Their interactions are compelling and the fact that it develops gradually rather than appearing as a matter of fact is one of the strongest points of the novel. Also, the flow of the prose is natural, there are no technical mishmashes that interferes with the reading experience. The narrative is compelling and the Rhine and the characters interesting enough that they provoke you into caring for them. That said, what prevented me from enjoying the book thoroughly is the inconsistencies in the plot. As I said at the beginning, I have read The Handmaid's Tale and the beginning to Wither is strongly reminiscent of it. However, there are such gaping holes in logic and reason that even when I was reading the book, I was asking these questions and not finding any answers to them. Let me elaborate. In the world in which Rhine lives, girls have a life expectancy of 20 years while guys live for 25. As such, the girls are require to reproduce earlier one of the brides is 13... and that's just disturbing . There are the "first generations" who do not suffer from short life expectancy and on whose shoulders the charge to find a cure for this "virus" rests. With me, so far? Okay. This obviously means that the human race is in trouble of extinction or we have become something like the "r-type" organisms as they are known in Biology. You know, like the weeds, that spring forth, die and then repeat in short life cycles? Except this does not compute because the r-type organisms reach reproductive age way faster than humans beings do. In the book, there is much talk about "orphans" because obviously their parents die but I have to wonder, why would people who are only going to live 20 and 25 years bother to have babies? I mean, the common people, not the wealthy ones. If they are going to succumb to the virus, why would they leave behind progeny to suffer when they are gone? I don't understand that. Unless evolution took place and women started reproducing at ten - even then, why would they trade their brief youth and life for motherhood? There's no logic to it. And the novel, unfortunately, does not answer these questions. It does not in a clear way, spend any time building up the dystopian world it has created for the purpose of the story. How can there be so many people as Rhine mentions once and again when most of them are dying? And then let's talk about the brides. Where in The Handmaid's Tale, there's a certain detachment the protagonist cultivates from herself, from her body because she cannot remain inside her body when it's being violated by the man who owns her, Rhine in Wither has it much easier. Much, much easier. She has a "husband," wealth, privilege, all the accoutrements and trappings of an ideal life. Except for "freedom." The husband "loves" her and she might even love him back if she would give herself a chance to do so. But then there's Gabriel, who unfortunately, is not developed enough as a character to warrant much comment. Linden is a better character at this point than Gabriel. I kept on questioning why, when Rhine was out with Linden in public, could she not simply leave? What was stopping her from leaving then and there? There's no mention of women not having the same rights as men so I presumed that they had the same rights and if they do, in that world, why could she not simply go? Leave? If the Gatherers the girl kidnappers do as they do in the dark or resort to trickery, it means that what they are doing is illegal - otherwise they wouldn't need the veil of trickery. So, why doesn't Rhine simply go to the police and demand that she's let go? Or get attention of the authorities in some way? Why? Is it because of Housemaster Vaughn? Who is not developed much either. He has a room in the basement where he experiments on the dead bodies of the wives before Rhine and her coterie. He is evil - his motivations are unknown - and he is The Enemy. It just...seems a bit like relying too much on stereotypes to create characters instead of doing so yourself. And honestly, they escape way too easily. I think that's the sticking point. It's way too easy for them. So easy that it's hard to believe and that compromises the integrity of the entire story. The series has a lot of potential. There is still Rowan to find. Still to see whether Rhine has any "cure" in her from her heterochromatic eyes. And considering that this is a debut novel, I am going to say that the potential is felt and I will read the preceding books in the series. As a reader, I would like it, however, if the author were to expand more time and words in developing to a greater degree the characters she created and the world they are living in. If she could answer some of the questions, work out the inconsistencies, consider logicality and reasoning, I'm sure her novels will much stronger for that.

'Cruel Crown' by Victoria Aveyard features two fairly short stories, spin-offs from 'Red Queen,' her first in the Red Queen series. What can I say? To be completely honest I was disappointed. 'Red Queen' was a five star read for me, and I had high expectations of 'Cruel Crown' as a result. The first story features Coriane of House Jacos, a poor noble family of little standing in the royal court. She catches the eye of Tiberias, heir to the Silver throne, and consequently marries and produces an heir but she is plagued with bad dreams of such magnitude that she fears for her state of mind! This first story did catch my interest, but it felt too hurried. The courtship rushed quickly to marriage and pregnancy, and Coriane's character struggled to develop amidst the speeed of the story telling. For me, the story ended too quickly and too suddenly, yet my sympathies had been stirred for the issues Coriane faced. I didn't even finish the second story, although I made a valiant attempt at it! The paragraphs regarding the 'missions' really put me off as they didn't seem to mean much. I ended up skipping them before giving up half way through. I don't like writing such a mediocre review when I so thoroughly enjoyed one of the author's previous books - but it just wasn't up to the same standard! Sorry!

This is one I checked out from my library system, as I have the ARC for the follow-up to it waiting to be read. This book frustrated me, and maybe it was supposed to. I generally enjoy books with unreliable narrators, but in this case, I just struggled with it. It's an ugly story it is about rape. Keir, the main character, is fed to the reader as this good guy and someone who would never hurt Gigi, his good friend and the girl he rapes. I think the way in which the book is written, from Keir's POV, leaves things too murky and makes the book come across as a rape apology or something. The way he explains everything away and how it's told from the POV of the rapist who acts as if he is just misunderstood is just too much. Eventually, the reader does more clearly come to see that Keir does not see himself clearly at all and is not at all who he portrays himself as through his narration, but it happens too late IMO. Too much of the book is spent making it seem as if there really was a misunderstanding and maybe he didn't rape Gigi. Rape is too serious of a topic to play with the whole unreliable narrator thing, and I was left feeling kind of offended at the end of the book and angry with the author. I also worry about what message it might send to teens who may think what Keir is doing throughout it is okay. We already have enough issues with "good" guys getting off easy when they rape girls and excuses being made for them because they are so "good". I'm still going to read the follow-up because I am desperately hoping that Keir does grow as a character and get what he has done and that someone beats the snot out of him too, as I was hoping for that through much of the book.

I gave this book five stars and shelved it among my favorites. Do I think this is Armstrong's best work? No. Do I think this is one of the best available in the Young Adult genre today? No. So... why the five stars? I gave this book the ratings that I did because I thoroughly enjoyed this story. I just got this book from the library today and have read it within five hours. That is usually a good indication, for me, that I am enjoying a read. The main reason why I enjoyed the story so much is mostly because this book has returned me to Armstrong's world of supernaturals. I loved nearly all of Armstrong's adult fiction series, Women of the Otherworld, and this story brought me back to the time when I first started that series. I had this huge nostalgia feeling while reading the whole book. It brought back good memories of old characters. If The Summoning was the first book I have ever read of Armstrong's, I doubt I would have liked it a whole lot and may have even decided to not read any of Armstrong's other work. I am very happy this is not the case, though, and I urge any reader that may have been put off by this book to please pick up some of Armstrong's adult fiction - you may be pleasantly surprised. So, enough of my excuses for a maybe-not-deserved five-star rating... Now on to what was good and bad about this book. I'll start by stating the good. Cue large letters -- OMG A YOUNG ADULT BOOK THAT INVOLVES A FEMALE AND ISN'T ABOUT BOYSZZZ??!?!! I am never disappointed with Armstrong and her ability to point out that girls women do not have to have their lives revolve around boys men. With the shit that the Young Adult genre is putting out today, it is nice to see a book that puts out healthy, positive messages to young women at least in this form . Boys is the last thing on young Chloe's mind, and thank goodness for that. The story itself was interesting but not overly surprising. Of course, the book was well written as is all of Armstrong's other work. Again, I'll reiterate from what I said above it was marvelous to read about Armstrong' "Otherworld" again. Like I said above, the story wasn't overly surprising and creative. As well, Chloe doesn't feel like a well fleshed-out character. I have a hard time understanding who she really is but of course, this could be as a result of the girl only being fifteen years old... and let's face it, I'm twenty-five and still don't know who I am . I hope that I can get a better feel for her in the next book which I am starting as soon as tomorrow if not tonight . The ending I have read a few reviews from friends that state the ending was lacking. I will agree here. I like full endings, not something that reads as if the book was just cut off from the next. This isn't too aggravating to me, however, because I can just pick up the next book and start it immediately. Overall, I have to say I loved it. I can't wait to get stuck into the next one!
