Seven-year-old Charlie is wandering alone at the pier one morning when he takes a tumble that would've been deadly were he not rescued by an older boy named Ant. Unfortunate circumstances led each boy to be at that unusual place at that unusual time, but fate smiled upon them that day. Charlie is instantly enamored by the older boy, and they proceed to spend the day together, palling around and having a bit of an adventure until it's time to part ways. Their interaction is all very sweet and innocent. Although the reader might identify Charlie's feelings as first love, Charlie is much too young to put words to his experience. He leaves Ant unsure if he'll ever see him again, but knowing somehow that Ant has made a lasting impression on him. I love Geoffrey Knight's voice in this story. The characters and their surroundings spring to life in vivid detail, especially the sights and sounds Charlie experiences throughout his day. There's also quite a lot of humor throughout the story, which made it all the more enjoyable. The Boy from Brighton is nestling into a cozy little spot on my favorites shelf, where I will revisit it often!

Hilary Duff adds yet another title to her multifaceted resume as she delves into YA writing with her debut novel, Elixir. As a fan of Duff since her Lizzie McQuire days, I had to take a read I LOVED when I was in third grade, playing her songs every day. I admit to being a bit hesitant, not sure what to expect as I never thought of her as a writer but a celebrity who spent more time with her career than writing tedious essays. I knew about the book when it was first reached bestseller lists, but I dismissed it as just her name selling the novel rather than her literary merit. Regardless, I am glad I delved into Elixir. The plot sounds like something out of a Disney movie, but with darker undertones. Clea, the protagonist, is a teen freelance photographer blessed with financial and social status. Her father goes missing, and her mother submerges herself in work. Her happy family is broken, leaving Clea with many questions regarding her father's disappearance. Clea doesn't care too much about romance but her best friend, Rayna lives for it until she gets weird, romantic dreams with a mysterious man the same man who appearances in her photographs. Then a photo assignment, sends her off to Rio, the place of her father's disappearance. Clea, desperate for answers, hops on a plane immediately. She bumps into this mysterious man, Sage, find out he is her soulmate along with some dark secrets, and goes from suspecting him to hopelessly in love with him. They have sex in a car. He keeps his distance from her, she breaks down. Along the way she uncovers dark mysteries of her past and her father's disappearance which are all tied to the coveted Elixir of Life. And her other best friend who is head of heels in love her, Ben, goes along for the ride too but he ends up to be a harbinger of horrible events It is clear we are supposed to dislike this poor guy throughout the novel. Immediately, I started to dissect the novel trying to separate Duff with her collaborator, Elise Allen.The words flow effortlessly through the page. I could tell Duff paid extra attention to her descriptions, unfortunately it was aimed more towards people than setting. Knowing her status as a celebrity and that she travels often, I was expecting vivid descriptions of Clea's home in Connecticut, the beaches of Rio, and the city lights of Shibuya. However, to my disappointment, there was more description in the Swaronski crystal Hello Kitty mirror she buys in the mall than in whatever country she's in. I have to applaud the writing in the scene where Clea takes pictures of her room to check if the mystery man will appear. She goes through the pictures on her computer, to find him in the picture of her closet. Read just like a scene of a horror film I swear a shudder went down my spine. You start to think Clea is an idiot when she trusts this creepy guy. The adventure is there, Clea runs through a forest escaping from creepy guys. At times, it feels like I am thrown into cliche CSI scenes enlarging pictures that magically turn high-res with zoom, decoding secret codes in a computer, and a password engraved on a watch. These scenes almost made me wince as they just sounded, for lack of a better word, lame. You start to wonder why is it all so easy and why it took less than a handful of pages to "solve" the "elaborate" puzzle her father created involving Shakespeare, a cribbage board, and his watch. The story was captivating a mystery, with a dash of paranormal, and a gallon of romance love triangle alert! thrown in for good measure. The sexual inferences didn't do it for me, I had to check the age level to make sure this book was not inappropriate. I've read teen novels with much more graphic sex scenes, but for a novel aimed at 14 year olds I am starting to wonder if I was just too sheltered. Compared to Ellen Hopkin's Identical, Elixir's sexual references are mellow but what bothered me is they just seemed to be sprinkled in there for the sake of it. The reader is already constantly being told that they are soulmates, we don't need sex in the car to consummate it. There are many points in the plot that just seems too convenient. Need to travel? No worries, Sage has a black American Express credit card, perfect for booking first class plane tickets. Clea's mother clearly does not check her daughter's credit card statements or wonder how her daughter flew home without buying a plane ticket. Need a password to the world's most precious elixir? No problem, her father is forgetful and scribbles his passwords everywhere, leaving them in the most conspicuous places. Got an ugly 500-year old talking corpse in front of you? No problem, she commits suicide on her own. However, even unlimited credit cards can't contain all my unanswered questions which I hope will be answered in the sequel. Where did that orchid necklace come from? If Clea is such a wonderful, "professional" photographer, why does she never carry extra lens, light modifiers, filters, model permission slips, or at least a tripod? and Why is Sage in all her pictures just because he is her soulmate? Do soulmates normally appear in pictures of your closet? If Sage has been playing for cribbage for centuries is dead even with Ben and Clea, does it mean the game is too easy, Sage isn't very smart, or Ben and Clea have past memories of playing the game? Why are those vials empty, do someone drink them and felt compelled to rebury them? What in the world is a small door along with a hidden chamber doing in the Shibuya 109 building, who built it? Why is there a store called The Little Door anyway? The Dark Lady is surprisingly nice, has has weird supernatural powers? Can we just kill Ben? I just picked up its sequel, Devoted today despite being awkward at parts, it was an addicting read with s good pace, and intriguing plot. I expect a better sequel from Devoted and I just want closure. While the plot seems to be full of holes, Duff has definite storytelling potential Hilary Duff, I think you just made a fan out of me...again. On a slightly related note, there's a line which reads "the odds are not in his favor." RANDOM THE HUNGER GAMES SPAZZ MOMENT

I'm not sure how to review this one, because I don't at all think the writing or the storyline are bad --- I just know that they were not for me. Initially reading DEARLY, DEPARTED, I came across a review calling it "one of the best steampunk novels". Steampunk? I'm not familiar with that. A quick trip to Google taught me that steampunk is a subgenre of either sci-fi or fantasy that takes a futuristic Victorian perspective of sorts. I'm still not 100 sure I understand the definition, but I think it should have been enough to tell me that this novel was probably not for me. This is basically the story of Nora Darling, a teenager in a strange futuristic setting that models the dress and etiquette of the Victorian age, except with a high tech twist to things. So, the ladies still wear long dresses, attend tea parties, and wait around to be courted, but they have cool gadgets too. Anyways, Nora isn't into the whole dainty female thing, instead focusing on the political unrest and military history of her homeland. Both Nora's mother and father have passed away, so Nora is sent to live with her prissy aunt, a Victorian-era gold-digger who wants to marry Nora off for money. So, Nora has a run in with zombies, then learns that her father was involved with a virus that reanimated dead people. He scientifically discovered a method to help some zombies maintain some semblance of brain power and manners, but of course they are still undead. Nora meets Bram, an undead soldier who becomes, of course, a future love interest. And, Nora learns that her dad is still alive well, as a zombie and struggles to learn the real story -- all while harboring feelings for a zombie who will eventually succumb to his zombie disease. I'm not sure exactly what did it for me. It just felt like there was too much going on. And, I'm definitely a fan of alternating perspectives, but we were seeing the story from way too many viewpoints here. It just got confusing and made the story too choppy. I'm sure there's a huge fanbase for this type of novel, but I'm just not part of it.

I dithered a bit about the rating on this one--I've been giving out high ratings lately like crazy mainly because I've been reading things that were highly rated and or recommended by friends , and there were minor, nudgy things about the writing in this one that may have gotten me to give it only four. BUT, the deciding factor was Goodread's definition of five stars "It was amazing." It was. Maybe more for me than for people who are way more tech-savvy than I am. But to realize that the things of which Doctorow writes are all 100 REAL was just mind-boggling. All he's done is to progress current events to their next logical step. I can't really even classify it is "sci-fi," though others have, because there's nothing in this dystopia as presented by Doctorow that isn't really already happening, at least in its infancy. There's some hope, now that Bush and his cronies are out of office, that it won't happen so fast, but it's still coming. Heck, the government already wants arphid chips in each and every one of my CHICKENS, for crying out loud. If you don't believe me, Google 'NAIS'. It's already happening on a "voluntary" basis. I've been wondering for years how long it will be until we're microchipping humans, for "convenience" and "safety." The book is targeted toward young adults teens, so the fact that the 17-year-old protagonist seemed, to me, unbelievably sophisticated and courageous is perhaps not surprising. I'm sure that if I'd read this at 17, it would have felt just right. Little Brother is also something of a love-letter to San Francisco, the city more or less becoming a character in the story. Parental advisory There is some discussion, in passing, of drug use mostly that of other, minor characters , but no descriptions of such. Language is refreshingly mild--I think you could count the four-letter words used in the entire book on one hand, and the most egregious one uses ___ in the middle instead of being spelled out. There is one account of sex happening, and some heavy petting, but nothing pornographic or really descriptive, even. More along the lines of, "we got naked, we had sex, and it was great." I was reading much more graphic stuff than this by the time I was 13 or 14, and I wasn't warped. Just thought I'd add this for parents who might be wondering. I just wanted to add a note to this review because I saw the book in a box the other day, picked it up, opened it, and the next thing I knew, I'd read it all the way through again. In one night. It's really good, y'all.

Let's Get Lost has so much potential but it falls flat. I did not enjoy this book at all. The first reason why this book falls flat it was hard to focus on a main character because it contains five stories. It was extremely rushed, each story was short and there wasn't enough time for a reader to get attached to a character. The only element that ties each story together is Leila because she helps each character. Leila is the second reason this book is a failure. Leila is such a frustrating character. She shows up out of nowhere and either fixes or fucks up the main character's life. I felt like she was playing fairy god mother by fixing lost grieving teenagers. Albeit Hudson doesn't fit those categories, he himself is a problem. Throughout reading this book I found it weird and unrealistic that every main character opened up to Leila. They only just met and their time with her does not exceed 48 hours. The formula of each story usually goes like this main character has problem Leila arrives they spill their story Leila fixes it. Leila didn't come across to me as a real person, she a plot device. Many reviewers categorize her as the Manic Pixie Dream Girl, and I completely agree. Hudson is the third reason why this book is bad. He just met the girl and he's infatuated by her. He instantly falls in love with Leila in one day. They JUST MET. Ugh, it's so painfully unrealistic. To be honest, Hudson is a creep and to prove this I have compiled a list of quotes proving my point. Click Here to see why Hudson is a creep. Hudson fixes her car and then takes her on a tour of all the sentimental places of his town. He then takes her home for dinner. This is so completely sketchy. Leila just met this guy he could a killer! At the end of the section, he was an asshole to Leila. I don't approve of this relationship. The last reason why this book falls flat where's the road trip? Leila's goal is to go see the Northern Lights. Alsaid doesn't write about her adventure going there, rather its Leila interacting with teenagers who need her help. Overall, Let's Get Lost is full of cliches, unrealistic romance, and inattention to consent.

I feel really guilty saying that this book is just okay, but it just didn't work for me. The author juxtaposes really complicated explanations of the context of a refugee crisis with extremely simple and uninspiring first-hand accounts of refugee children. For example, I'd read this explanation of what was going on in Kosovo or the Congo, and even though it was only 1.5 - 2 pages of context, I'd have to reread it several times to understand it, and still sometimes I didn't quite understand before I gave up. And I'm an well educated adult. Won't this be especially hard for middle school kids to comprehend? Massive numbers of casualties like 3 million would be the result of these complicated problems, but it's hard to have feelings about a number like 3 million. And going through the book, you see 3 million added to 60,000, added to 2 million, added to 550, 000....it's too much to be able to really process. Immediately after these confounding statistics and contextual descriptions, you'd read a pretty dull interview like "I really like America. I like Cheetos. My sister doesn't want to eat her vegetables. I think I'd like to visit my home country some day." This is not a real quote . Again, I feel tremendous guilt having anything negative to say about refugee children or this noble attempt to raise awareness. It's just....it is likely that I will well up with emotions and tears on any given day--I cry in commercials, I cry when I hear a single measure of beautiful music, you can pretty much say the word "suffer" or "abuse" and I can barely keep it together, so how is it even POSSIBLE that I felt nothing reading this book? I read half, and I don't really feel like I read any of it, but I gave it more than usual effort, even, and I just can't go on with it. I'm sorry! Sorry, sorry, sorry. I hope others will be intensely inspired and effectively educated. I hope it's just me.

This review will have spoilers but they will be towards the end, hidden away. There are some minor plot spoilers but they're very vague and shouldn't impact your reading much. I love V. E. Schwab's storyworlds, each one is unique and terrifying and enticingly beautiful. Of course I loved this book, however there were elements to the story that disrupted my immersion and I'm a little disappointed because the story absolutely didn't need them. That being said, I still really enjoy spending time in this universe with these characters. I would read a hundred books about this world because it's incredibly complex and interesting and two books didn't even come close to revealing the intricacies of the setting and plot. I could write so much about this story universe. The monsters are dark but understandable and the humans are very much the same. Schwab has intertwined good and bad and the complexities of moral grey areas so well without taking away from the fantasy aura of the duology. We only really get insight to Verity and a slight glimpse of Prosperity and it leaves so much of the rest up to our imaginations. I'd love to read about the various other cities and their own monstrous creations. The world feels way too big for such a short series. I love the characters and the changes we see them experience as their lives encounter obstacle after obstacle. They felt real in the best ways - not perfect and not trying too hard to be villainous. This is something Schwab does well in all of her books, but the one that comes to mind is Vicious. Somehow she takes these stereotypical characters hero, villain and twists them into something grotesquely human in nature. That is echoed in this duology, with Kate and August mirroring each other, but not quite as one would expect. Time to move onto the aspects of the story I didn't enjoy quite as much - namely, the romance. The book was progressing in a way that worked really well without the need for a romantic entanglement between any of the characters, so when it happened I was taken aback. I didn't expect it at all and, honestly, in my opinion it took away from the story more than it added to it. There wasn't that much build up to the relationship and even once it happened there wasn't much said about it. I just would have preferred a plotline more focused on the other aspects of the plot than the love lives of any of the characters. That being said, I understand that some may love this development and I support their opinions despite my disagreement. The other problem I had with this book was the climax - or the anticlimax. This is where the spoilers start to slip through, I'm afraid. All I'll say here is that the end comes along suddenly and, in my opinion, isn't planned out enough to give the reader the satisfaction they crave after such a build-up of tension. The entirety of the novel is focused on the Chaos Eater's rise to corporal form, but the moment that occurs, the Chaos Eater is defeated. Which leaves me wondering what the point of the story was if it wasn't to highlight how difficult it was to defeat the monster. Now, I'll admit that it wasn't exactly easy since Isla had to die to destroy it, but even that felt sudden to me. Isla was coming into her own, character wise, and I was attached to her but her death felt rushed and under-looked for the most part. Had it been drawn out into something more dramatic than Isla just... jumping onto the Chaos Eater, I think it would have had a greater impact. Or even if the Chaos Eater had been allowed to remain substantial for a while longer, since the tension is building up to what will happen once it gains enough strength and then we don't actually get to see what that impact would have been. Kate's death, and Alice's death in turn, also felt very sudden. If it was that easy to kill Alice, why was she still around? Another pressing question that was left open was that of Leo was he truly speaking to August or was August imagining it or something? I would have liked to see a bit more resolution. The end of the novel felt rushed and poorly written in my opinion. I would have preferred to have an extra hundred pages or so for the story to come to a more natural conclusion - especially with this being the concluding novel of the duology. However, that being said, I did still really love the book and in the overall picture I can overlook these issues because of the beauty of the world building and the majority of the plot. I seriously recommend picking up one of V. E. Schwab's novels if you haven't already. Side note Did anyone else have copies with a significant amount of editing errors? I mean things like a lack of spacing after a lot of the commas, plus a random change in font for one paragraph in one of the later chapters. Someone needs to hire a new editor.

I've read books I've enjoyed and books I've hated. I've read books that made me happy and books that made me sad. Very occasionally, I've read a book that leaves me enraged. "Amelia Anne is Dead and Gone" is such a book. Two hundred plus pages of an eighteen year old girl whining finally cummulating in the most ridiculous ending of all time. This is not a mystery, Rosenfield gives you very few clues to work with. This is not a coming of age story. The main character, Rebecca, is a recent high school graduate who's had sex and regularly drinks liquor. This is not a romance. People in this town wouldn't recognize romance if it gave them a hickey. Rebecca lives in a small town where no one ever stops smoking. EVERY character is constantly lighting up a cigarette to the point I assumed Phillip Morris did the underwriting . Rebecca just graduated with honors and has plans to go to the State University. She hates her town and can't wait to leave it -- except she's desperately grasping at any chance to stay. Her focus for this is James, her boyfriend. James is a high school dropout, with a drinking problem and a scary friend, Craig, who may be a psychopath. James knows he's the wrong guy of Rebecca. He's stuck in place while she plans to move on. So we get pages and pages of whining about this impasse mixed in with passages about a dead girl who's body shows up on the side of route 128 one morning. No one knows who she is. Details on how she died are sketchy. Rebecca thinks Craig might be involved. She's upset about her parent's imploding marriage but not enough to engage with them any time they try to talk to her. In the end there's a can-you-believe-this-got-by-an-editor fight scene in a parking lot where Craig gets hurt, Rebecca calls James and discovers what really happened to Amelia. You won't believe it because it's completely unbelievable. Then, despite the fact that Rebecca never hit anyone or lied to anyone, she decides she's completely at fault for everything that's happened. I'm embarrassed I spent money on this book.

This book wasn't my "cup of tea," but I can see how others might enjoy it. The basic story is that 14-yr old Jamie aka Punkzilla - after going AWOL from a military academy and living essentially on the streets in Portland, OR - discovers that his older brother is dying in Memphis, TN. Jamie embarks on a cross-country journey to try and get to his brother before he dies of cancer. Along the way, Punkzilla meets a broad range of characters that he tells his brother about in long, rambling, stream-of-consciousness letters. Stylistically, the book is a collection of letters - some penned by Jamie, some Jamie receives from family, friends, and authority figures. Some are sent received, some are written almost as a form of journal writing. The letters penned by Jamie most written but not sent were difficult for me to process due to the stream-of-consciousness quality. I found myself skimming in large chunks to get the gist of the story. What I did like was the convention of presenting a collection of letters - a lost art form that really gives people the courage to be "raw" and honest in a way that emails and other forms of communication just don't allow. On whole, I found it difficult to "dig deep" into this book due to the style, but there was gritty, in-your-face storytelling that could definitely have appeal for teens...particularly teens looking to read unconventional forms with a "street lit" vibe....

Can Tori and Christian overcome the law forbidding them from being together? I loved this book! My first thought when I began reading the book was "This is good!". As I got further into it and delved deeper, it changed to "This is fantastic!". I couldn't put it down! I must admit that when Tori and Christian first met, I rolled my eyes and thought, "Oh, no. I hope there is another book, as I would like to find out if Tori and Christian do overcome the law forbidding them from being together. I would definitely recommend this book if you like witches and vampyres

Words cannot describe how much I want to unwind this book and pretend it never happened. Unwind started with a horrific concept and some great characters. Connor was likeable from the series starting from about the third page on. Risa was likeable. Even Lev was likeable by the end of the first book. Unwind packed a powerful punch. It could make you laugh, and cry, and bite your lip nervously. Even though its premise was always unbelievable we would never be okay with doing this to unwanted kids , the characters lived and breathed and seemed real. Their actions seemed logical and consistent with their characterization. Even though unwinding itself was not believable, the characters' actions in given situations always were. This book, not so much. I felt just kind of like I read some medium content fanfiction written about the author died and never got to finish the series. The ending was just not believable, for a lot of reasons. The public at large had shown absolutely NO morals whatsoever up until what felt like the last 10 pages. Shusterman created a world where we sent difficult kids away to be unwound AKA killed , parts pirates lurk through alleyways to round up innocent teens to be unwound on the black market, and people get parts of Unwinds just because they're tired of their nose and want a new one, and no average citizen gave a crap. Unwinding was a part of normal life, kinda like pumping gas into your car once a week. And then all of a sudden it was like... Wow, guys... You know... this is like... wrong! I get that Shusterman really did try to pull out all of cards - Hayden's broadcasts, the 3D organ printer, Roberta being exposed, all those letters getting mailed out to the kids' scumbag parents, etc. - but I feel like Shusterman was kind of trying to justify his happy ending by reminding us all that "a few drops can cause a bucket to overflow" - or something like that he actually wrote . But it just felt unconvincing. Then SPOILERS BELOW SPOILERS BELOW SPOILERS BELOW HAVEN'T READ IT, DON'T READ IT Connor being unwound and then put back together again just infuriated me as it goes against everything the entire series has solidified for me. When someone is unwound, they die. Let me say that again. When someone is unwound, they die. They stop being conscious. When consciousness is broken, when that seal has been destroyed, that's it. The soul isn't there anymore. It's an act against nature that is irreversible. Consciousness is broken when someone is unwound, and then that's that. You can't just put them back together again and get the same person back. That's just dumb. It's kinda like saying if you take someone apart, they're just put on hiatus until you slap them back together, unplug them, plug them in again, and wait for the light to go from orange to green. You know, I kind of liked this series because I felt like the overall message was We are greater than the sum of our parts... but then Shusterman's like NAHHHH, just put Connor back together again, hit the reset button, and it's all good! Same old Connor. I guess I have to stick with Looking for Alaska.

Originally reviewed on my blog, Books from Bleh to Basically Amazing. Fixing Delilah is so much more than it appears. If this book is anything to judge by, Sarah Ockler is a writer to watch out for because she has an incredible ability to form realistic and wonderful characters, relationships and settings. I haven't believed so much in the actions of the characters I was reading about in a long time. I have been planning to read Twenty Boy Summer for a while now, but after reading this book, it's definitely higher up on my tbr now. Delilah used to be a good girl, who got good grades and never got into trouble, the same way she used to be close to her mom. But her mom's job is demanding, and over the years, they spend less and less time together until all they seem to do it fight. And, Delilah is facing down a whole bunch of crap at school that she can't seem to get a handle on, and no one seems like who they are suppose to be anymore. Delilah has legitimate problems at school and home and she reacts the only way she knows how. I was impressed by the way Ockler handled this. In order for Delilah to need 'fixing' she had to have some issues to begin with. I've read too many books in my life where the author gives us a 'troubled' teen complete with the stereotypical problems that are used to completely explain away and excuse bad behavior until some easy and magical fix comes along like a new boyfriend... . But Ockler never does that, not with any of the problems she sets up for her characters. She does give us reasons for the behaviors, but she never once treats them like an excuse. They are the catalyst, and perhaps the cause, but she always lets us know that her characters chose what their effect would be. I never felt like Ockler took the easy way out. I never once felt cheated as a reader. I thought that Ockler was able to create a very believable family dynamic and each of the relationships in this book were truly great. I can't say enough times how believable I found this story to be. Her relationship with Patrick was perfect- a childhood friend who maybe, just might start to become a little bit more. Emily was a great addition as well, a friend for Delilah when she desperately needed one. Even her memories showed relationships, her loving grandfather, distant grandmother and her imagined connection to the father she never knew. Both individually and in connection to others, Delilah was a very real character to me. I felt her pain and her happiness, despair and hope. This was a strong read, one I highly recommend. It answers each question it brings up satisfactorily without over-exposing. This book reminds me once again why I really do prefer contemporary fiction. If Twenty Boy Summer is anywhere near as good as this was, Sarah Ockler will land on my instant to-read list forever.

The story was ok, but when all was said and don't, I felt like it was a waste of time. I could have re-read something else and enjoyed myself more. The quote on the cover about what a great writer the author is... well, clearly that reviewer and I have a difference of opinion. I read this genre because the world building is so much fun to read and explore. Here, there really wasn't much of that. And the characters are very flat and there isn't much development of them either. The story is goes like this Sir Michael is a knight errant and Fisk is his squire. Michael rescued Fisk since Fisk is really a con man. They set out to rescue Lady Ceciel and it turns out that they help a criminal escape. So, their "adventure" becomes the quest to meet the conditions of Michael father's "probation" after he rescues Fisk and Michael from their troubles when it is discovered that they helped the lady escape. They now have to recapture the Lady and bring her to the lord so that justice can be carried out. The most exciting part of the plot was the escape from having been "cudgel-crewed". And the most interesting character is Lady Kara but we see so very little of her that we don't get a chance to know her. Fisk - we know he has a past, but we learn nothing at all and as a result it's hard to stay interested. We learn a little more about Michael because we see his father but it's still very one dimensional. The world that is built doesn't really get described very well. We learn that there is a furred god and that there are 2 moons, and this stuff called magica. And while its a safe and correct inference that magica is magic, for some reason it's bad for people to do. And animals and plants and stuff can be magica but to kill either one must make a sacrifice or something will come back to harm you. It's kinda like instant karma. But, we get no additional information. Zero. It's like the author was really only sort of interested in writing a book about magic. Until we get towards the end. And then Lady Ceciel seems to have some ideas about magica but we get, what felt like, the same chapter 3 times in a row. And we still really don't learn much that adds to the story. In fact, I was slightly disturbed by the "simple ones" and the way the author dealt with them as a class of people. And it made me hard to understand how experimenting on them should be something in a YA book. The alternating chapter narratives are a little difficult too. I don't mind alternating view points most times. But for some reason, it was often hard to track remember. I found that many times, I had to look back to the first page of the chapter to see who's name was on it to know who's point of view I was reading. I know this is the first in a series but I don't plan on bothering with the next. There just isn't enough of the characters to keep me interested. And the made up terms that aren't explained and the one-dimensional universe... too little to keep me interested at all.

Maureen McCarthy is one of the few authors whose protagonists are generally aged in their late teens or early twenties, embarking on university or finding their way in the first years after leaving school. I started university about the time Queen Kat, Carmel St. Jude Get A Life was published it has been republished this year by Allen Unwin and loved the book, quickly devouring the rest of her backlist soon after. It has been a while now since I have read anything by the author but I was thrilled to receive The Convent for review. Though The Convent is labeled as young adult fiction, I feel the novel will appeal to a much broader age range of women. A thoughtful, intriguing and heartfelt story, it explores the experiences of four generations of women whose fates are linked to the Abbotsford Convent. Nineteen year old Peach Perpetua has always admired the Abbotsford Convent's grandeur, now home to artists studio space, boutique stores and the cafe at which Peach works, but she was unaware of it's personal significance. Adopted at birth, it isn't until Peach receives a letter from her biological grandmother, Ellen, that she learns her grandmother was raised there and her birth mother, Cecilia, once served as a nun within the Enclosed order. While Peach struggles to come to terms with the unexpected information about her past, it is her present that she is most concerned with. Her sister is depressed, her best friend is pregnant and she is still reeling after a messy break up. As Peach navigates her way through her changing world, McCarthy traces Peach's lineage and their connection to the convent. Sadie was declared an unfit mother in 1915 after her husband abandoned her and her daughter Ellen taken from her to be raised in Abbotsford. Ellen spent her entire childhood as a ward of the nuns before marrying and her daughter, Cecilia pledged her life to God's service as a young woman. The author shares snippets of these women's lives and their hopes, dreams and regrets with alternating chapters. Through the the women's stories, McCarthy also traces the changing social and moral landscape for women over the century. Attitudes to women's rights, motherhood, marriage and sexuality have shifted seismically in the last one hundred years and the author acknowledges the evolution without any feminist rant. McCarthy admits that she has a very personal connection to this story. Most significantly McCarthy's own mother was raised in the Abbotsford Convent after being made a ward of the state at age 3 and while she rarely spoke about her time there, McCarthy was always fascinated by her mother's early life. McCarthy's interest in her characters and their experiences is evident in the care in which she has constructed the story. The Convent is a wonderful story, an easy read but with surprising depth for the thoughtful reader to ruminate on. This is a great choice for any Australian Women Writer Challenge participants given the relevance of its themes.

Tenley "Ten" Lockwood has spent the last thirteen months of the seventeen years of her life in an asylum. She was sent there by her parents for not making covenant with Myriad, the realm her parents want her to side with in the afterlife. See, it's an accepted fact that Firstlife is simply a rehearsal for what comes after death. In your real life, your Everlife, you sign with one of the two ruling powers Myriad or Troika. Myriad and Troika, deadly enemies, have been at war with one another for centuries and each attempts to recruit humans to tip the scales to their side. Both realms are willing to do anything to recruit Ten to get her on their side and each sends one of their top Laborers to win her over her eternal soul. Ten knows she can't trust anyone, but she realizes she may be falling for one of the boys sent to sign her soul to their realm - and he may not belong to the realm she's drawn to. All she has to do is survive long enough to make a decision. The concept behind Gena Showalter's Firstlife piqued my interest from the moment I heard of its release - the idea of multiple lives and that you know what the afterlife entails from the get-go - and look at the cover. It's fantastic. However, I did not like the execution of this novel at all - in fact, I couldn't bring myself to make it beyond page sixty-five, the second chapter. I have plenty of other books I'd prefer to spend my time reading, and hopefully enjoying, rather than continue here for another four hundred pages. Here are the main aspects that I didn't like the infodumping, the special snowflake syndrome, the assumed love triangle, and my disconnect from the main characters. For the most part, all of what I made it through is a giant infodump giving us the basics of the Everlife and who's who. It gets a little exhausting getting so much dropped at your feet all at once, especially when a good deal of it comes across as needlessly vague. I had a hard time telling the difference between Myraid and Troika. Although each has its own core values, those are constantly being undermined by the other side's propaganda. Both are willing to go to any lengths to claim victory to the point that the reader doesn't even know what to think. Not to mention that Archer Prince, the Troika Laborer sent to sign Tenley's soul to his realm, doesn't actually seem to embody any of the characteristics associated with his side. Now, for some reason, Tenley is a special snowflake. Supposedly, she will be able to turn the tide of the war for either side. Honestly, I have absolutely no idea why she's the most important soul currently living her Firstlife on Earth. I also have no idea why either side is willing to go to such great lengths to get her on their side, even after such a huge infodump. Also, I have absolutely no clue as to why she wouldn't have made any kind of decision in the first place. As far as I can tell, she could be doing it to spite her parents. If that's the case though, she can't be in her right mind to undergo torture and watch her friends die - just make up your mind already, or clue me in as to what you're trying to accomplish! If you couldn't tell, I just felt so disconnected from her and everyone else - like I was missing something vitally important about everyone. By the way, I fully expect there would have been a love triangle if I had continued on with this story between Tenley, Archer, and Killian the Myriad Laborer . I can just imagine how that could have gone - I mean, if she can't make up her mind to save her own life, how in the world is she going to decide between two boys. Overall, I definitely preferred the concept and the cover to the first two chapters. I gave Firstlife a shot, but unfortunately it just wasn't for me. However, I would like to try this author again - eventually I would like to pick up Alice in Zombieland and see if I have any luck there. Final verdict I was hoping for something more like this But by the time I was ready to quit, I felt like this Basically what I'm trying to say here

I knew by the time that I finished the first chapter that I wasn't going to like this book. Why? I mean, I get that she'd have to be tough to survive there, but come on. Everybody was scared of her? She beat anybody that touched her so badly that nobody could even look her in the eyes? Unbelievable. Then, she spends three chapters - maybe four, I can't remember - being the toughest person alive only to get rescued by someone else. She literally did nothing but observe as she was carried out to a helicopter at least, that's what I'm guessing a "roto" was supposed to be . And then she freaked out after watching her savior get killed. So much for Miss I-Killed-My-Parents-So-Don't-Think-I'll-Hesitate-To-Kill-You. The part that really killed me was when she woke up, she'd miraculously gotten a make-over from the best surgeon in the world and was basically a new person being sent off to live a new life with absolutely no information except her new name. Wow. So much for having it difficult. After reading to the 25 mark, Jenna had sort of done some cool things and I was interested enough in the story to want to know what happened next, so I skimmed to the end. Jenna's character only got worse, more soft, was saved twice more after failing to do anything that proved that she was as tough as she thought she was, and then saved the world because she actually just wanted to save her boyfriend. This book was such a bummer. I was really hoping to read about an awesome, strong heroine who works with the circumstances that she's given, but I ended up reading about a girl who was kind of tough, but really didn't do much at all except save her boyfriend. To be honest, I'm not sure that she even did that because I was only reading the first sentence of each paragraph by then.

spoiler alert Ughhhhhh... I didn't want to write THIS review, but after dragging this book out for days, I must. I expected more. More from Sarah, and definitely better. I expected a better story. Aelin holding Nehemia's death over him STILL and hating him for that is not only stupid, but also just ludicrous. Can we acknowledge the fact that Nehemia wasn't a great friend? She lied to Celaena, kept secrets from her, and had her own agenda. But she arranges her own death and I'm supposed to blame it on a guy doing his job?!?! Uhhhh... what? Chaol has always been honorable to a fault. If he were in the Song of Ice and Fire series, he'd be a Stark. Doomed. Oh, weird. Same in this one! That is not a flaw. But this pathetic attempt to make him unlikable and wrong for Celaena Aelin was overkill. To be brought up over and over and over again... I wanted to rip my hair out. Then she switches it to him abandoning Dorian. Sigh. Chaol's hatred and bitterness didn't make sense either. How do you go from loving someone to claiming they're a monster upon their return? There were so many hints throughout the book that the ship had sunk, so I didn't understand why it had to be dragged out. Aelin was a raging bitch to him whenever they were together. And I hated that Chaol's character just flatlined. He became boring and nothing like the one I fell for in Throne of Glass. Closure early on would've made reading more enjoyable. Maybe. But I admit I'm insulted by the destruction of my beloved to make way for a douchey Fae Prince. And Rowan. Wtf does everyone love so much? I couldn't really understand it in Heir of Fire, and I understand it even less after QoS. Yes, I get that he's a great fae warrior and Prince. It's been mentioned 74105062510046 times. Thanks for that redundancy. Holy gods, he is such a tool in this book. And no, I'm not sorry I said it. All I got from him while reading this was the mental image of an overgrown, horny teenage boy. I mean, some of the cheesy lines he was spilling were gagging me. If I wanted to read contemporary romance, I would. Not to mention the fact that their relationship is so damn boring. It's so easy. "We are both fae, so obviously we are the couple that makes sense." Why doesn't anyone else think it's too simple. After all of this, THAT is how it's gonna go down? Nothing happens except referenced sexual tension. I've never felt their romantic connection. When I have to be told that it's there, and it has to continually be alluded to, I know it's not real. This connection is completely contrived and not believable. He sniffs her, bites her, licks her I think, and I'm supposed to swoon? You're a hawk, not a dog, dude. Sorry. Blah. Just have all the sex and then become mates because, HELLO, we know that's where it's going! , save the effing world, have Rowan give up his immortality, and shut up. I also cannot stand their lame ass "silent conversations." And I saw someone else make a valid point. Rowan served Maeve loyally for hundreds of years and she's evil and conniving. She didn't come to aide when Terrasen fell. Yet, THIS doesn't manage to piss off Aelin at all. Somehow, with the almighty silver-haired Rowan, his honor is acceptable. It is only with the former Captain of the Guard that she cannot get past who he served. Regardless of how he broke his oaths while she was playing with magic in Wendlyn and kept Adarlan ALIVE. A partial solution, but stacking the guilt of her friends on top of that, and hey, the door to her heart is now open to Rowan. Was this how the ending was always meant to go? Was RowElin always endgame? I'd love to get that answer some day. The chapters featuring these two were the ones I sped through, and now there will be two more huge books filled with them. I'm not down with forced relationships. Yuck. Why couldn't she have had ONE relationship with a male that DIDN'T end up in romance?!?!?! It makes her look like a flighty woman. Speaking of unbelievable and unrealistic relationships being stuffed down my throat Chaol and NesBitch. Oops, Nesryn. I wasn't feeling that AT ALL. They had a fling prior to Celaena. That was HIS rebound, IMO. All of a sudden, now he wants more? I'm sorry, but that doesn't work for me. Never once did I feel any romantic connection between them. Absolutely none of the spark that was between him and Celaena. The tears at the end when she asked him to come back to her? GAG ME. More ridiculousness to attempt to sway us to Rowan's side. Aedion. YAWN. Another who cares player in the series. He's supposed to be this bad ass warrior and he's always whining about not getting his way. I'm so glad he was rescued. Let's get the Aelin Celaena one out of the way. I don't care what anyone says, THIS IS THE SAME PERSON. All that's changed is some emotional growth. But she also was unlikable for a lot of the book, and as the main character I'm supposed to be rooting for, well, it's disappointing. It seems like all the growing she did in HoF was lost on her trip home, and once she docked, she regressed into some teenaged girl who can't let go of a stupid grudge. Reading the story from her points of view was like reading someone with split personalities. Note the following are not true quotes, but paraphrasing. "Oh, Rowan. You are the greatest thing ever. I can't live without you and your hawk body." "I hate you Chaol. You killed Nehemia." "I'm wearing this slinky lingerie for you, my glorious fae Prince." "I wish I'd never met you, Chaol." Whatever. Most of this book she was a BITCH. I didn't even care about her, people. Surely I should've seen her growth. More on this later. I'm hoping that something in the next book will bring her back. Because this person? I couldn't give two shits about her. The best characters in this book series are Manon and Lysandra. I bet you didn't see half of that coming. And I'll be honest, neither did I. The witch chapters were the best parts of HoF for me, and it's again the case here. I don't know if I'd have been able to finish without them. Manon is a bad ass, but I almost hated her for awhile, too. Her subtle change at the end of HoF seemed to have disappeared, and I couldn't wrap my head around her NOT becoming good. If the world is changing, she's someone I hope makes it to the end. And hopefully with Dorian, which I've wanted since HoF. LOL! And I think it's gonna happen! Manorian is my SHIP! Lysandra is a BAMF. FOR REAL. All the secrets exposed --- almost made my brain explode. I gained an all-new respect for her, and was glad she got closure on things, too. The story. Whew, where to begin? I've covered some up there, but a lot of it dragged. It took forever to get to the "grand finale" and honestly, I wasn't super impressed. Obviously there's a hell of a lot to come, but with such build-up, this ending fell flat. While I'm talking about disappointment, I will say that I'm pissed how Arobynn went out. The King of Assassins VS. his protege should've been epic. Instead I got a crummy substitute and an easy death. No thanks. After everything, after SAM, I wanted him to die by Aelin's hand, while she raged at him for his treachery. He deserved to suffer, the way those he murdered did. I may never forgive Sarah for that part. I still weep over the loss of Sam. His death is still the most heart-wrenching loss of this series. Something unforgivable. He deserved a better revenge. I truly wish HE were by Aelin's side. AND WHAT IN THE EVER-LOVING FUCK DID WESLEY'S LETTER SAY??? Why don't we get to know??? Okay, I digress. Back to the story. Waaaayyyyyy too much campy "romance" here for me. The second Rowan showed up, I knew everything was going to change. Not for the better, either. What I didn't expect was all the contemporary shit that was to spew from Rowan's mouth. "I want to take my time with you... when I make you moan." The fuck? Did my fantasy book get lost somewhere? Do I have the correct copy of this book? Holy eye-rolling! I burst out laughing. That's supposed to be sexy? Overused, and LAME. I'd apologize, but I don't want to. There are several other "moments" they share, and I felt nothing. Well, nothing except a plea for them to get it on just so this bullshit would stop and I could get back to the important stuff. This centuries old warrior is talking like he's a human playboy. Barf. Then the bickering and Alpha shit between Rowan and Aedion. "She's my queen!" "No, she's mine!" "Mine!" "Mine!" Listen, dickwads. She's a bad ass and doesn't need either one of you oh wait, except for Rowan and his blood oath and their "connection" . Hundreds of pages of secret plotting, and the coolest parts of the book were wasted on smaller things - freeing Aedion booooooo . I get that Celaena Aelin is supposed to be a bad ass. It's been crammed down my throat for four books now. So the male posturing and expressions of awe can stop. Just saying. The witches give me the feels! Yes, those brutal, heartless creatures made me feel more than any other part of this book. Holy revelations! Can we get a book solely about the Thirteen? And Dorian, because, you know, MANORIAN!! So many things I never saw coming... and I love their story arc. I don't know what I'd have done without them these past two books. And now the ending. For all this build-up, for all this planning, I was a tad letdown by how things go down. Knowing it wasn't the true end, I figured it would be mild, but this felt watered down like a cheap whiskey. The coolest parts of the last 20 were led by Manon, Dorian, and Kaltain. I did have a second of pause when I thought my heart was to be shattered, but thankfully, Maas spared me that heartache. It's the least she could for what I've already gone through. However, the surprise character I haven't mentioned is a game changer. Not necessarily on her own, but with what she carries and where she's going. I think that and MANORIAN are what I look forward to most in book five. Someone tell me this book is just a bad dream. Or the vision the Valg Prince showed Aelin in HoF, because I don't like this version of events. Ultimately, it's a decent read, but it's not even close to the best in the series. Things are coming together, for which in thankful, but I really don't know what to expect next. I'm hoping the forced romance culminates so we can move past it. I'm hoping for my new ship to take off. I'm dying to know what Manon's plans are. And I'm hoping Terrasen will be more interesting than these last 600 pages in Rifthold were. For all my complaints and feelings of inadequacy, there are moments of brilliance woven in. Sadly, there just weren't enough for me to rate it higher.

This review was first posted here http dahlsdoll.blogspot.com 2012 07... I picked this book up a few months ago, but was wary to read it because of the mixed reviews I had been reading. Of course, my curiosity wouldn't allow me to let this one sit on my bookshelf, and I'm glad for it. Condie's writing style made for a very easy read. I seriously breezed through this book. The sentences were often short and direct. At first, this bothered me, but I think the writing was appropriate for the setting of the novel, in which everything is controlled and predictable. Speaking of controlled and predictable let me talk about the plot of this novel a second. Yes, the life of Cassia Reyes was quite predictable. Even the big shock that Cassia discovers, really didn't surprise me. And for that, I would not say this book had a driving plot. Actually, as far as plot goes, I wouldn't recommend this book to anyone. It's just too dull. Now, I could probably go on for a while on all the dullness of this book, but well, that would be just as dull. Let's just say that Cassia is completely unrelatable, and that her little love triangle is pointless and frustrating. Cassia, who is supposed to be our rebellious teenager, is too terrified to even cause trouble. Sure, she does little things like kissing a boy who is not her Match when she thinks no one is looking, but big deal. When it finally comes time for her to do something drastic, like leave her Borough and search for her true love, Condie places conveniences in her path, so Cassia can disappear without a fuss. I found this most disturbing since Cassia's favorite poem, her little artifact of the old world, states "Do not go gentle." Except, that's exactly what Cassia does. Someone please explain this to me because I really thought our heroine would put up more of a fight. However, despite all of my issues with the characters and plot of this novel, there is something that made me really glad I read this book. Condie's novel is driven by thought. There are many abstract ideas that I just loved thinking about in new ways. Condie toys with the ideas freedom, rebellion, and creation. The greatest thing that changed Cassia and myself in reading it was the idea of freedom, and the knowledge that man's greatest freedom is the freedom to create. Isn't that beautiful? I know these aren't exactly new ideas, but I'd say Ally Condie is one smart cookie. At least, Matched engaged my philosophy side, which, trust me, doesn't engage in too much. Seriously, philosophy can make my head spin. I think this is a challenge for all YA authors, to express ideas beyond the story. Condie would have nailed this too had her story been, well, better. Lastly, Condie wrote something that spoke right to me. On page 236 if you wanted to look it up Condie wrote, "Ky pauses for a moment before he answers, his eyes wide and deep like the oceans in other tales or like the sky in his own. "Even if he didn't live his story, enough of us have lived lives just like it. So it's true anyway" spoken by Ky after Cassia asks if the story of Sisyphus is true . Ky couldn't have said it better. This is the reason I read stories at all, and I suspect that is true for most of you too. No matter if a book is a work of fiction, I'll cry at the sad part and laugh at the funny parts because, to me, it's always real. I give Matched a three out of five foxes. The plot was slow and dull and the characters really didn't have any spark. It lacked action and the romance could have been spiced up. Condie's writing style was attractive and even very beautiful at times. Also, the ideas behind the writing were capturing and thought-provoking.

The author asked if I was interested and I said yes. The title certainly got my attention. It made me want to know more. There are some things about this book that might turn people away. I'm not sure if it has to do with last month being a not great reading month but this book is slow going and it isn't a long book. Does that make sense? I also think people might be turned off by the way a couple of characters speak. It was also really creepy how this one character showed too much interest in a thirteen year old kid. Oh excuse me thirteen and a half. The impression I get is that these two characters speak the way they do because the author wants to show that English isn't their first language. Some people might think they are typos or might be annoyed by it. I'm thinking it was done on purpose although I will admit that the two characters are pretty much the same when it comes to speaking so there could be confusion on who is who. I don't think it was really necessary. The concept of this book is really interesting. This world takes a step beyond what is already happening in the real world since Alexa is a program that you can interact with. It does make me think of Dollhouse a little bit because in this world peoples essences and brains are being uploaded to a computer. It also makes me think of The Matrix because you have these people who died but whose spirits live on in this virtual reality. I'm not sure if I was just in a weird head space but I did a bit of crying during the start of this book. It was sad because you have Rose a girl that's on the verge of dying which is sad because she's just a sixteen year old kid. I couldn't help but think of Alexa. This takes that a step further where you actually see the person and can interact with them because they retain the memories of who they were before they die. Shortly before Rose's death a man shows up promising to save her. Of course that doesn't happen but he shows up and the next thing you know Koren is able to talk to her sister again. Koren is used as the face of this new technology but I have to admit that it gets a bit creepy how they portray her to the world. It goes back and forth from the real world to the virtual world. It is easy to read and you do want to know what's going to happen next because you're wondering about what's going on in the virtual world. It is a good start to a series. http www.ficgal.com book-club aaru

Still a fast moving, mostly fun YA adventure romp. But the kids are showing evidence of two extremely annoying traits Whiney Potter - itis think Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince, the book that made me think Snape had a point, and the inability to learn from their mistakes. Seriously, in the last seven books, these kids have gone on quests where at least one of them has knowledge or "a secret," that if they shared insead of waiting until either the last minute, or after it would have been useful, would have made the quest less dangerous. I get that The Lost Hero quest group and the batch from The Son of Neptune may not fully trust each other, but they should tell each other everything within their mini-group. As should Annabel and Percy. I'd complain about Deus ex Machina plot effects, but Gaea is the "big bad," and the Greek Roman pantheons do make guest apperances, so that's to be expected.

This was my second foray into the "YA mermaid trend", and I'm glad to report that this book did not disappoint. Looking at you The Vicious Deep. It's well-executed. The author's take on the sea folk myth and the world she built was brilliant. Mermaids that are, well, half cannibals. Noo'kas. Razor fins. My favorite part is Hester, our main gal, going through this journey practically on her own. No damsel in distress needing help from a guy here. Well, there was Ezra but hey the guy was stranded on the beach. And they had just like two moments together. Monstrous Beauty is all tough and no fluff.

This book was very dissappointing compared to Lucy's other work Stolen A letter to my captor. I really thought i would like it because lucy wrote it, but i was wrong. The story dragged on and i got bored, i started skipping all thoughts and only reading dialogue. I just got sick of it and stopped reading alltogether. Im so sad that it wasnt what i expected from miss Christopher.

Every time I read a book from this series, it startles me that I can actually see the events taking place playing out. Miranda's voice actually jumped off the page at me. She's so vivid, and real and human, too - she complains, she worries, she sounds like a brat sometimes... I did feel that the story was a little rushed this time. Especially the romances. I mean, come on, you might be the last few people left on earth, but professing your love after two or three days when you barely know each other is a little too much. Miranda doesn't even know that Alex has a second sister! And Syl - who is Syl? How old is she, what kind of life did she lead Before, what was her family like... Syl was basically 'Matt's wife', and that's it. She wasn't Syl like Miranda was Miranda. Other than that, I liked it a lot.

It has been a while since I have stayed up until midnight and gotten up at five in the morning to keep reading! I love this series. The characters are fantastic, the plot is suspenseful, and the bad guys are despicable. Best books!

Hmm... I'm not going to go over the plot points, that is explained very well maybe too much information even in the description, however, I did not enjoy the first half of this book. I physically rolled my eyes so many times. So many Game of Thrones similarities which... I get, but still and also wayy too much of Andreus's damn secret. Ok, we get it. DNF - for several reasons... I just was not in to it. Paul's character had one interesting scene in the first book, and that's all we really have to go by on him. June is stuck -- in grief, in an abusive home life, and in a school where she is bullied on a daily basis. After losing her mother, June's father remarried, thinking he could provide June with not only a stepmother to fill the void but also a stepsister only a year older than her. What her dad doesn't know is that his new wife and daughter abuse June, forcing her to eat until she is sick, soaking her mattress with water and blaming it on June having wet the bed, constantly calling her ugly, and more terrible deeds when her father isn't around to witness it. The kids at school think these signs of abuse are just reasons to make fun of her and unfortunately, the teachers are too blind to see and June is too scared to admit to the abuse. But when June meets Blister, a local boy with a very large and poor, yet very loving family, she finally begins to see her worth and a brighter future within her grasp. But is it too late? June wants to prove that she is stronger than her abusive stepmother and stepsister, but she may have lost too much in the process. THOUGHTS As an educator, I was horrified by what June went through every day and how every adult in her life that could stop it, didn't. It was heartbreaking that June felt as though she had no one to turn to, and felt so little about her own self-worth that she couldn't tell the whole truth to the one person she trusted, a young boy named Blister. The before-and-after storytelling cleverly resonates as the plot reaches its climax, taking readers to the point of tears and then down to the depths of June's despair in the aftermath. The relationship between June and Blister, as well as her relationship with his family, the Wick's, are the brightest spots in this dark plot, and make the story worth reading until the very end.

Twigs is a nickname for Madeline Henry. Everyone calls her "Twigs" because she's small and in her late teen years she appears childlike. But don't let her size fool you. She's tough and spunky, qualities that she needs during the worst moments. There's her boyfriend, who's away at college and may not be as faithful as she thinks. Her alcoholic father is absent. Her mother and sister are inconsistent. Then there's her brother, who's missing in warfare. That storyline was the most real and heartfelt, in my opinion. Twigs also suffers at work from a horrible boss, thugs who harass her, and a crazy lady named Helen who attacks her with hair dye--although Helen becomes her friend and an important person to lean onto. I liked this novel, but there were too many conflicts. I know life can be bad, but throw together all these situations in a book and it's hard to focus on the main threads. My favorites were the brother, father, and boyfriend. Helen was important to the plot, but I didn't care for her. She stole the spotlight too many times and was unstable when there were already other unstable characters in the picture. Still, this novel was enjoyable and it was a quick read. I read this via NetGalley, courtesy of the publisher.

spoiler alert It's not that I didn't enjoy it... at times I really did. In both Carry On and Fangirl, I loved her characters. She has a great way of making them dimensional. But that's really all I liked. First off.... this book is written like a fanfic or a sequel in a series. Yes, I know it's based off Fangirl's fan fiction... but that does not matter here. If you decide to publish the story, then DONT make it a fanfiction. Or if it's written as a sequel to a book, WRITE the first book. There's just so much MISSING. There's barely any explanation at all for what's going on, and you feel you started to watch a movie when it was already in the middle. The plot is mediocre. I mean, there's just soooo much left to the void. We have no connection towards Ebb, who I suppose to be our "sob character". I mean, she and her brother were literally unnecessary to the plot. We also didn't need to know about Lucy, as she plays no role in the book. The mage could have had flashbacks, no need to make us think Lucy would be important to the story at all. Useless! Agatha had no redeeming qualities, she was a coward and a stuck up jerk. Simon never finds out about his family, which is pretty awful considering what we know. And the War just... what?? What happened to the war?! We don't have much explanation about it in the first place, but jeeze a war isn't something that goes away just because the head organizer is gone!! But above all... I couldn't get over the fact that this was an obvious Harry Potter-ish fan fiction. I could take it when in Fangirl, because the story there isn't important, its what the main character DID with the story. But here? As its own published book? No. It just felt wrong and obvious in all the wrong ways.
Parts of this book I really liked, parts of it I wanted to skim. Overall, pretty enjoyable. Interesting concept even if the characters are a little flat.

Although this book was kind of 'The Hunger Games' but mental tests mostly rather than physical only, it was quite good. The story pulls you in with graduation day for Cia in her colony. The Earth had a seven stage war, essentially humans caused one through four stages and then mother Earth turned on the planet. There were various extreme weather, volcanic explosions, tornadoes and the like and the U.S. was split up into colonies as they try to rebuild the Earth. Every year 100 students are selected for The Testing, where they begin with educational tests in a classroom and they just get harder along the way. This book was very entertaining and kept me reading and I'm excited to read the next one in this series that is slotted to come out in January. I do hope the author has a better ending than The Hunger Games though...

spoiler alert Fafa's Book Corner Wordpress Fafa's Book Corner Blogger This book was recommended to me by Evelyn ! Click on her name to read her review. DNF After reading Evelyn's review and the synopsis I knew I had to read it! Even more so after reading the tag line. I love the X-Men and Heroes! I thought that this book was written for me. Unfortunately though I didn't enjoy it. The book starts off with Ethan at a coffee shop talking about the amount of trouble he would be in if someone looked in his army duffel bag. It backs track a bit and explains the readers what is in the bag and the events that led up to a wrong gone bank robbery. Readers discover that Ethan has this Voice which sometimes takes over his own voice. The Voice seems to know far too much about people that Ethan has never met and more often than not the Voice gets him into trouble. You are told that while on a date with a really pretty girl-that was way out of his league-the Voice had spent all of Ethan's money trying to impress the girl. He doesn't drive and calling a cab would not work as he has no money. Ethan then decides to convince some stranger to drive him home while using the 'Voice' as his guide. On purpose Ethan bumps into a big guy who is carrying an army duffel bag. He lets the Voice take over and manages to score a ride with this guy. During the drive Ethan realizes that this guy is trouble. He try's to summon the Voice to get him out of the situation but nothing comes. Which means there is no way out. I didn't get that far to see what exactly led up to the bank robbery. But I did do some skimming. From what I gathered Ethan was at the bank with that former date of his when the robbery occurred. Ethan uses his the Voice to get him out of the situation. But it only made it worse. Apparently the voice knew the robbers name Jerry and the name of his daughter Kelsie . And revealed some other personal information. Somehow this whole fiasco made it on to YouTube. I honestly do not know why somehow would bother taping that. Assuming it was someone in the bank, that would be pretty stupid considering they were about to be robbed. Eventually Kelsie does come and hunt Ethan down to make him fix the mess that he caused. But that happens really far into the book. That was when I started wondering whether the plot would drag. And honestly making Kelsie Ethan's love interest seemed silly. Especially considering the mess that Ethan caused. I had two problems with this book. A The bank robbery situation could've been avoided. While Ethan does not have control over what the Voice says he does have some control over it. It is implied that he can choose to use the Voice. If he had just not let the Voice led him into loosing all his money, none of the events of the book would've happened. He knew it was stupid and a waste of time to spend with that girl so really he could've avoided it. B I couldn't wrap my head around the powers. While the Voice was interesting it didn't make any sense. I didn't understand how this power worked. I tried putting a name to it and that didn't work either. This really bothered me and I just couldn't continue. The only nice thing I have to say is I give the authors props for being unique in their superhero story and making up their own powers. Maybe had I done more skimming I would've had more nice things to say. Overall I didn't enjoy this but I don't regret reading it either. I would recommend it to fans of the authors, people who would like to read a unique story, and those who have been looking forward to reading this. If you don't fit in those categories then I wouldn't recommend it.

I picked this up with clear intentions I needed a no-thinking, no high-stakes, "feel-good" story that would soothe the anxiety, stress, and bookish hangover I felt after reading The Broken Eye. And this succeeded in doing what I wanted it to do. Still, that doesn't mean it was particularly good. Insta-lovey, ultra-superficial, extra-saccharine, and just...meh. Nothing extraordinary here. Do not recommend.

spoiler alert So I LOVED book 1. When I finished with book 2 I felt a mix between saying, "Meh..." or "Argh!" I mean, it was enjoyable. But at the same time it didn't move forward fast enough. And I like the character Zane, but I never felt as attached to him as I felt to David in book 1. And yet, she chooses Zane. I was expecting the whole time that she'd go for David in the end, but I was sorely disapointed. I'm definitely going to finish the series, because after all is said and done I'm still interested and still entertained by the plot and characters. This is a brilliant modern reinterpretation of a classic fairy tale, yet it has enough twists and changes to keep readers entertained. The characters were all really strong - Cinder wasn't a stereotypical, helpless Disney princess and makes a lot of tough decisions. I loved seeing the Cinderella plot unfold, always wondering how Meyer was going to incorporate it, although I would have liked it if there was a fairy godmother figure in there too. There were some very funny moments as well as some sadder ones, mostly due to the presence of the virus. As a Brit, I also really like that the United Kingdom remained a separate entity to Europe in the future colonies of the book - it was a feature that made me smile. I really struggled to put this book down, it was just so good and I can't wait for the next book, Scarlet, to come out. Especially since the title and description seem to be hinting at a Little Red Riding hood link. I can't wait to see what Meyer does next.

I usually have difficulty with YA books that focus on mental health issues however, I couldn't put this one down. Wolitzer has provided a novel with so many layers that it is difficult to describe. It is a story about friendship and self-discovery, but so much more. Educators teaching Sylvia Plath could use this as a companion novel. Others trying to get students to use journals could have them read this book. But it is also an extraordinarily well written book with rich characters who I came to truly care about. Although I know they could never tell me, I suspect this book was given strong consideration by a number of the ALA youth media juries -- or they should have!

ahhhh why did it have to end like that!?!?!?!?!!?!?!?

Skye is hopeful that THIS will be the summer she finally meets the boy of her dreams at the beach--but when she does, he leaves before they have a chance to exchange contact information. It's the following summer before they reconnect, and once they do, they know they are meant to be. It's not an easy relationship, with Seth working his way through college and Skye finishing high school, but true love will find a way. Skye and Seth tell their story in alternating chapters, introducing friends and families who remain in the background instead of becoming full characters in their own rights. The story spans three years in which not much happens they eventually have off-camera sex and one fight over ex-related drama , making the timeline a little difficult to follow. This latest title will excite established Colasanti fans, but is unlikely to win over new readers. High school appropriate.

Beautiful yet a very touching story. About a little boy, Sam, who suffers acute strain of Leukemia. His teacher Mrs. Willis encouraged him and Felix, although Felix did nothing but complaint about everything, to write a book on their own. Sam fills his book with list of things, questions about death, and what happened around him during those short period. For example his dad's reaction of his illness is portrayed like what most men is expected to react in such circumstances .. being strong and try to live his routine life. I think it's his way to hide his emotion, even from his son. Written in a point of view of a ten years old boy, it is appropriate to mark it as a book of laugh and tears. Kisah yang indah dan menyentuh. Tentang Sam, seorang anak laki-laki yang menderita Leukemia akut. Gurunya, Mrs. Willis, mendorong Sam dan temannya Felix yang juga sakit untuk menulis sebuah buku. Dan inilah buku itu. Sam mengisi bukunya dengan daftar banyak hal, termasuk hal-hal yang ingin dia lakukan seperti misalnya menaiki elevator turun, merokok, punya pacar, naik balon Zeppelin dan sebagainya. Atau juga daftar pertanyaan tentang kematian. Dia juga menuliskan tentang reaksi orang-orang di sekitarnya, ayahnya yang seperti kebanyakan pria diharapkan untuk tetap tegar dan menyembunyikan emosinya. Atau ibunya yang terlampau khawatir, bahkan adiknya Ella yang tengah malam datang hanya untuk memeriksa apakah Sam masih ada di atas tempat tidur. Dituliskan dari sudut pandang seorang anak lelaki, menurutku pantas buku ini disebut sebagai buku penuh tawa dan tangis. Dia mempertanyakan kematian, tapi dia tidak takut akan kematian itu.

I received a review copy in exchange with an honest review. The writing style in this book will enchant you with its hypnotizing symphony. I am a huge fan of the Splintered book Yes, I know that Splintered is actually a book series, but bookstores over here only have Splintered. No,don't suggest pirating the book online! I was mesmerized by Howard's writing Style as well as, her cleverly spun twists on the classic Tale. With Roseblood, I can easily say that she absolutely delivered. This is a retelling of Leroux's gothic tale of The Phantom of the Opera. Rune Germain is 17 years old girl who is having has a mysterious dilemma linked to her operatic talent, and a horrifying mistake she's trying to hide and understand. Her mother sends her to a French arts for her senior year to give Rune's talent clear direction. This school is located in an opera house rumored to have ties to The Phantom of the Opera! "One paragraph is all I needed to fall in love with this story !!!" I am not even exaggerating! The descriptions that build this book are absolutely phenomenal. The words are intoxicatingly lyrical and luscious, with a spoonful of Goth beautifully spilled in. This makes it one of the best lyrical, twisted tales that I have ever read. The beginning of the story is bit slow, true. But you have these pretty words to hang on until all of the oohs and Ahhs kick in. Every single aspect of the main characters, as well as the plot, is well fleshed out, making every single back story worth the wait. I don't want to spoil anything, but let us just say that A.G. Howard will manipulate your mood's auras to every single color known to mankind. GO GRAB THIS BOOK ALREADY, K????? Can't wait to read more A.G. Howard haunting stories. I give it 4.5 5 stars.

I love Maggie Stiefvater's writing. Her portrayals are layered and intriguing, and her use of language is gorgeous in this book. The plot is complex, which may cause issues for ambivalent readers, but Stiefvater packs some serious plot twists in. More in-depth review at opinion-not-fact.weebly.com.

Je ne m'attendais pas a grand chose de ce livre, mais ca tombe bien, cette semaine je suis malade et ma seule envie etait de me plonger dans un roman facile et plein de bons sentiments pour affronter cette epreuve. If you don't mind some graphic violence, you might like this. If you don't mind under-developed and one-dimensional characters, you might like this.
