Before I get started and completely forget, thanks so much to the publisher for sending me this book for review! I'm always looking for short stories like this during the semester. That way, I don't get demoralised if I feel like I've been reading the same book for weeks and weeks, and can chip away at my Goodreads challenge. When I first read the description for this book, it intrigued me. I was interested to see how they approached the issue of immigration, particularly with Brexit and Trump showing the lack of acceptance in or current world. In reality, the book didn't quite deliver all that I hoped, and I don't think I'd recommend it to any young reader on principle, but I'll get to that in a minute. I don't normally start a review by looking at the writing, but in this case I think it's necessary. As a Romanian immigrant, Nicu's English is stilted, and so the decision was made to write all of Nicu's chapters in Pidgin English. Throughout the course of the book, this became an important part of his characterisation, showing his history and culture. However, I'm not sure I entirely agreed with the concept... let me explain. Yes, it is understandable that Nicu would speak poorly, due to his lack of fluency. However, his thoughts would be in his native tongue, and this would be fluent. I feel like this decision really hindered our ability to get to know Nicu, due to his simple vocabulary. In terms of characterisation, I found both our protagonists very angsty, especially Jess. Now, I'm not denying that she had a tough living situation, but due to her woe-is-me attitude, I had a hard time feeling sympathetic. And don't even get me started on their actual issues. In a short book like this, I was hoping for something simple. But in reality, the main characters in this book were riddled with drama. It wasn't enough that Jess is in an abusive household a serious problem, that should be addressed , she also has to be a kleptomaniac, with alcoholic friends, an absent father, doing community service - she just had a lot of problems, which meant none of them could really be dealt with properly. This isn't the first time I've noticed this in YA, and it definitely wasn't the worst, but it still felt unresolved. Going into this book, I was unaware that it is actually middle grade the main characters are in 3rd Year in the UK, meaning they're 13 14 years old. This is yet another prime example of a book where the ages are clearly identified, yet appear older in their actions. To a degree, I think this worked for their situation, as it alluded to the fact that they were both forced to grow up fast due to their circumstance. However, it screwed up the timeline a bit. If Nicu is 14, it's another 2 years until he can get married arranged or not , meaning it doesn't really make sense for him to be going back to Romania in 3 weeks to get married. Speaking of marriage, in a world where diverse reading is said to be very important, this book threw up some serious problems for me. The complete condemnation of Nicu's arranged marriage was very disrespectful. I don't feel like the authors made any real effort to understand the traditions of Nicu's parents, meaning the story came off a little too westernised. The point of reading diversely, and writing diversely, is to attempt to better understand the cultures and traditions of others. 2 Irish authors condemning arranged marriages in Romanian culture is a dangerous territory. It didn't have to be much, a simple conversation between Nicu and his mother about her own arranged marriage, or a letter from one of his sisters who's just gotten married. Anything to attempt to better represent the the argument. Now, for the bit that really upset me - the ending obviously, there will be spoilers for the next paragraph . I hated that the solution at the end of this story was for Jess to run away. Imagine you're a 13 year old girl who's in an abusive household and you read this book. It promotes the idea that no one will understand or be willing to help you and that the only solution is to run away. In my mind, this is a terrible message to spread to young people, not to mention the fact that it just didn't make sense in the story - all Jess had to do was lift one of the old phones, filled with evidence of Terry's abusive nature, and bring it to the police, problem solved. Before I wrap this up, you must be waiting for my famous thoughts on the family dynamic! Throughout the pages of this book I didn't find a single admirable family trait. Yes, Jess said her mum loved her, but there was no evidence of any sort of affection between the pair at any point - they barely even spoke. Nicu seemed to be doing alright, in that he had a nuclear family, but they couldn't just let it be and had to make his father abusive too! Even one character in this book who was willing to help the pair would have been enough, maybe Liam could've given them PS50 and a flask of soup, or Dawn the case worker might have offered some advice, or one of her friends could have been slightly less bitchy. This would have helped immensely with the message of the book, never mind the general enjoyment factor. Overall, for me this book plays too much on the teenage idea that everything is the end of the world, and didn't focus enough on the different people who can help. It's sends a bad message, and I think would lead young people in a similar situation to feel even more isolated and alone. With all of that in mind, I gave it a 2 5 stars, which sounds really low. It isn't as bad as some of my other 2 star ratings ahem What Light but I just can't get behind a book with such a poorly thought out message. Although I didn't hate this book, it doesn't sit well with me, and I would be reluctant to recommend it to any young reader. The book comes out of 9th February, if you're looking for a fast read to bump up your Goodreads stats, you could always take it with a pinch of salt! What did you guys think? How important do you think the message of a book is?

This adaptation of the Faust story centers on five children, two twins and three others, all "stolen" from their families at age 10. The world has forgotten them until suddenly, at age 15, they appear with their governess in New York. The five become students at the Marlowe School, one of those impossibly difficult-to-get-into only-for-the-incredibly-rich-and-powerful schools. There, four of the five set out to take over, each with their own special "gifts". The fifth, twin Bice, isn't like the others. Her talent is hiding, learning, studying which she does by freezing time . Belle, her twin, is beautiful but with an awful stench that can only be hidden by bathing in emotions Val is a poet and seducer who can go back in time, perfecting conversations and events Christian is an athlete, bathing in some weird serum and sleeping in a coffin and Victoria is trying to be the most powerful, successful of them all. Clearly, all these gifts come with a price other than that black, only-seen-when-wet beauty mark. Madame Villeroy, their governess, continually plays one against the other, making deals and promises with no real method to her other than madness. At times, when talking to Belle, she sounded like Miss Havisham, but at others she just sounded stereotypically schemey. The five children manage to make enemies of almost everyone at Marlowe, with Belle the exception thanks to her baths and her determination to get Thomas . That didn't feel at all real to me why make their evil so obvious to all? And the ending, with Bice, Belle and Christian escaping, was overblown and moralistic. In between there were moments that were interesting, but the entire book didn't really hold together as a read. I also wondered about the chapter introductions. At first, I thought they were supposed to represent others that had sold their souls to Faust but Jacob and Laura? No idea who they were. If you're going to hit people over the head, make it with an obvious hammer.

Amazingly tense and yummy characters. Constantly kept me guessing. Wonderful romance, and devoured me in to the story. Great wrap up of what going on in this book, and nice stage set for the follow up book. Patch is dark and mysterious, never fully giving himself away.

Now, I haven't read a ton of books I'd say this year has been the only year so far where I've really started reading regularly everyday and developing my tastes. And I feel like I'm not that hard to please I tend to give most books about 4 stars and I don't always have a lot to dislike about a book but this one must've set me off somehow, because I haven't been so critical of a book in a long time. There are so many problems that I have with this book. To give this review more focus, I picked my hugest problem with this book one which I haven't seen a lot of reviewers of this novel address yet , the one thing that I feel really ruined everything for me, and made me lose a ton of faith in the series of Red Queen and that is the pacing. And I don't know about any of you, but when I'm reading a book, I like the pacing to be set like a steady voyage slow enough that it carefully leads me through the story and, also in this case, the setting, but fast enough that it doesn't leave me straggling through too much detail or unnecessary subplot. And the pacing of this book was way too fast for me. This one part is my personal favorite example of this About a quarter of the way through the story, after a failed attempt at robbing the local rich civilians and instead losing her family's only source of income after a struggle with the police, Mare gets a job in the nearby castle by some guy who pities her named Cal and she gets to work as a servant for a whole, whopping 1 hour - 1 HOUR - before she finds out that Cal is actually the Crown Prince future ruler of Norta, then falls off a balcony during the - whoa, what a coincidence - new queen auditions or Queenstrial featuring the various teenage girls of wealthy families and who most definitely serve as a stereotypical trope of bitchy mean girls , falls onto an electric forcefield which brings out her super secret abilities, and reveals her to be a Red girl with Silver powers. All within 1 chapter. Do you know how ridiculous that is?! She's literally a servant for less than a day and in the overview of this story, it's made to sound so much more important? And it should be! It's a crucial stepping stone for Mare's journey, made for her to reach the first huge plot twist of the novel Mare's true identity , which would've never occurred unless she got this job. And the author spends zero time developing on that and Mare's new life, which, might I remind you, is drastically different compared to her lifestyle at the start of the story. Mare goes from a poor, sarcastic thief for six and a half chapters, to a privileged, quiet servant for one and a half, and suddenly a powerful, refined princess for the rest of the book. It derails all suspense by rushing through this significant part of the story and ruins any sort of slow build-up whatsoever. And it's made me lose a lot of focus on what kind of perspective this book is supposed to have. Is the reader supposed to be a follower of the protagonist, fully immersed in this new environment? Or is the reader meant to be a bystander, who just watches the protagonist from the sidelines and sees the events unfold? After reading this book, it just feels like an ambiguously awkward mix of the two and reading it becomes so much less fun. And even if this was meant to be more of a bystander-kind of perspective my least favorite of the two , at least pull it off correctly. I can't exactly explain how, but there are various great books to take tips from. random note, but The Book Thief and Daughter of Smoke Bone trilogy does an excellent job at that But this isn't the only part problem I have regarding the pacing there are several other components throughout this novel that just pissed me off as I was seeing them. So here's a short list of them, in no particular order - Mare's education. Initially, Mare is depicted as the kind of person with higher street smarts than school smarts she never goes to her classes, because she's always busy stealing to help support her family, since she has no other particular talents other than pickpocketing. But somehow, right when she becomes a "princess" and starts attending her new princess classes, all of a sudden she knows everything and everything about the High Houses of Norta, from their trademark superpowers to their various unimportant flag colors. And there was no leading into this at all. There's literally tiny time skips throughout her first few months as royalty that remove any chance for the reader to learn anything with her about these Houses, until Mare magically provides facts about them in the narrative. And I know no one really cares about any of this stuff, but it kinda removes any sensation of going on this journey with Mare. Going back to the whole perspective issue, I think one of the best things an author can do is make it feel like the reader is a part of the story too, because it forges a connection between the reader and the book, to help them see what the protagonist is going through and maybe make them feel the same ways they learn as the protagonist is learning, they grow as the protagonist is growing. And I feel like the author just skimmed all of that so as you can imagine, I hardly felt any bond with Mare when she fell on the train to princess-hood or something. - Mare's acting abilities. Going over this part kinda bothers me, because I feel like it could easily expose me as a terrible reader, which okay, that's totally subjective and maybe I am a terrible reader. But when I was trying to analyze Mare's character, I never, ever, got the sense that Mare was a good actress. And if I missed that foreshadowing somewhere, well damn, I must be a terrible reader, because she turns into the Angelina Jolie of Norta immediately once she's declared a princess. It literally takes Mare no time at all, from her unexpected coronation to her quick integration into nobility life, before she's a passable, arrogant, stuck-up Silver noblewoman which is supposed to somehow convince all the Silvers that she's been like this her entire life, despite having grown up among Reds. Which shouldn't make any sense, unless if the Silvers are meant to be really that stupid, because they're well aware that Reds hate them. And honestly, I don't think any of the other Silvers ever doubt her faked personality they only snicker and sneer about her past and her carefully-shared political opinions, which she inserts way too well into her stereotypically tense, passive aggressive conversations with the other Silvers. To tell the truth, the most well-spoken I had ever seen Mare before this was when retorting semi-witty insults as comebacks. And remember, this girl is supposed to be only somewhat educated she skips the majority of her old school in the Stilts so she can steal. So how the hell did she become so good at blending in with a society that she's never been exposed to in her entire life? - Mare and Cal's romance. This one's a bit tricky, because I'm not the most cultured of romance readers around. But I think even I can say that the so-called "love" between Mare and Cal is pretty lame. I mean, when you think about their characters without reading what happens in the book, they sound pretty good together Mare is cynical, bitter, and somewhat withdrawn, while Cal is nice, friendly, and also incredibly generic, which is usually a trademark of a lot of opposite love interests. But the book just doesn't sell their romance to me. I might be bad at picking up on romantic cues, but do they actually do anything cute together other than walk side by side, grab each others arms, or dance together because Mare is conveniently terrible at dancing and Cal is not ? And besides, they hardly spend any time together. Cal's always off doing his crown prince stuff and Mare's always off doing her illegal, illicit activities of treason against the king. Not to mention that the relationship between Cal and Mare is literally identical to that between Mare and Maven. They're the same relationships with a different guy in each, and the 2 guys are practically the same person. Then again, at least Mare and Maven's actually makes sense they end up working together a lot well, more than Cal and Mare anyway on the rebellion, which is dangerous, scary, and totally breaking the law, and that would most definitely form a closer bond between the two. And what's Cal and Mare's excuse? That Cal has known Mare longer by one or two days since he got her a free job out of pity? "He'll always choose you," they said, after they'd known each other for a few months. Yeah, as if. Weirdly enough, this is only scratching the surface when it comes to the things I didn't like about this book, but I think I've gone over enough in detail. Overall I'm gonna say that this book was like the poor-man's Cinder the main characters are princesses and non-human, there are 2 races humans and non-humans , the non-human races have special powers and are notoriously bitchy, the non-human queens are assholes, the world is technologically advanced compared to our own now, and they're all at war. This quote also describes the book really well "You want me to pin my entire operation, the entire revolution, on some teenaged love story?" pg 316 I realize I'm being incredibly harsh, especially since this is a debut novel, so I'll add in something nice. One thing I didn't dislike about this story was the writing style it was occasionally interesting and filled with a ton of confusing figurative language, kind of like Shatter Me. P.S. Some additional things Cal and Maven are too similar both friendly and nice, despite being Silvers , all the main characters are white, the names of the High Houses are hard for me to take seriously, as well as the names of the Silvers with certain powers i.e. telkie for telekinetic, greeny for green warden? . Plus, that cool "whisper" guy from the first few chapters totally cool and totally unimportant to the whole story, so I'm disappointed about that as well. It would've been neat if that guy had turned out to be Maven, whose ability wasn't his fathers, but his mothers, which would've made him rare apparently.

I'm disappointed in this book. Even in the end, I didn't really care about Miranda. The death and destruction felt unreal. It didn't move me, and I cry fairly easily when engaged in a fictional world. My reaction bothers me because I have to discuss this book with a group of middle school students. I'm trying to decide what aspects of the book I enjoyed. If there is anything I want to point out about the story, characters or structure. Mostly what seemed unbelievable to me was Miranda. She is 16 and acts 12. Often. The thing is she doesn't justify it in her journal entries which is the format of the book . This book doesn't ring true as a teenager sharing their private thoughts in a journal. A typical teen would berate the other person to make themselves look faultless. Because she doesn't ever write this way, her change to a less selfish person at the end of the story feels fake. I didn't buy it. There was a lot in this book to stretch the realm of reality. The moon being knocked closer to earth by an asteroid, for one. The lack of news shared of tsunamis, destruction of coastal realms, earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. Apparently, the whole government folds beneath the weight of these catastrophes. The mother is flippant about the president. Miranda's friend Megan becomes part of a "Christian" cult that encourages her to starve to death, while offering all her provisions to the leader of the sect, of course. In the end, the government waits for people to come to them. Really? People are possible starving to death on the outskirts of our town, but we'll sit at City Hall with food until they come to us. This book will appeal to people who like end of the world tales. If you're looking for characters to admire, you won't find them here.

So much is going on and yet even more things occur. I wonder how Schuyler is going to do in book three? Can she really be turned into a Silver Blood?

Next thing you know, they've crossed the boarder and are up to antics that made ME want to spend a day in Mexico. I've got my bags pack, I'm ready for my hostage vacation! The real beauty of the book was the depth of the characters everybody had a back story, and a reason. The downside to this was it got a little confusing, especially with the ever changing perspectives and the characters all wanting to go to certain colleges, but everybody was so interesting, I felt very close to them. It fit the bill of a "Coming of age story", and I think the lessons learned were surprising but inspiring. Kylie had every right to be a Mary Sue, there was so much opportunity for her to be "Too Perfect" but in my opinion, I don't think she ever was. And that made me love Max all the more as he accepted this. Oh my god. Will was the perfect companion too, so fiercely protective, yet at the same time, he had his secrets too. I don't know, I don't think I can say any more other than, read it! Then come back and tell me your fav character, cuz I can't choose!

Feeling nostalgic for the books of my youth, I revisited Katherine Applegate and her Islanders omnibus editions first released as the Making Out series way back in 1993. Yes, I am that old... . While I found them to be overly-dramatic and a little bit cheesy on second reading, I think they would be loved by teenagers today. Reviews also on our site Readers In Wonderland This will be fairly short but I just wanted to share some quick thoughts on Matched even though everyone and their brother has already read it. First off, the idea behind this was great. I remember being at a Target about a year ago and being torn between buying Matched or Divergent and I bought Matched because I'm a sucker for a love triangle. And this "So when Xander's face appears on-screen at her Matching ceremony, Cassia knows he is her ideal mate . . . until she sees Ky Markham's face flash for an instant before the screen fades to black." is love triangle gold. I couldn't resist. The pages flew by but around page 300 I stopped reading for a second and thought about something. What exactly is happening? Ky and Cassia's relationship is progressing and Cassia has doubts about Xander as her match. Then I asked myself what was going on around page 100. The same thing. So, although I did not even realize it, I'd been reading pretty much the same thing for the last three hundred pages with itty bitty conflicts strewn in. Where were the huge plot conflicts? An actual action-y plot didn't kick in until what seemed like the end. The very very end and things finally got interesting. Don't get me wrong, I loved this book, but when the action kicked in it made me think of the rest of the book and showed me how much it lacked. Anyway, definitely read it if you have not already but what I've said above makes this novel at solid four stars from me.

This book was tolerable. The writing was stilted, the plot was thin and almost non-existent, the characters were one dimensional and not interesting, the love story had no chemistry or passion and it was a complete waste of potential. There were makings for a great book here. The setting being gorgeous, sexy places in Europe, good looking European men, amazing food and locales. It just falls flat. The author concentrates on the most boring aspects of the book and completely neglect the more interesting ones. The lead character is irritating and has this need to enable and infantilize everyone in her life including her mother who randomly suffers from agoraphobia. She also suffers from panic attacks like her mother but none of it makes sense and none of it fits in the story. What was the point of having the lead character have anxiety and her mother being agoraphobic? It had no point and added nothing to the story. Her best friend and her ex boyfriend storyline was boring and unnecessary. There were better ways to add tension or a foil for the sake of plot. This wasn't it. This also added nothing and served no purpose. As did the boyfriend's best friend. He was boring and uninteresting and somehow the lead character and him fall in love despite living far away from each other, being 19 and him being a player? I have no idea why he liked her, there was nothing interesting about her. The lead character babied her best friend even though she lived in another country and went to university on her own and then got mad when the best friend depended on her for everything. Her mother randomly starts to get better and her sister makes her feel guilty for actually wanting to do something for herself. Her father is non-existent. Where are the adults? Why is she forced to forgo her dreams because her mom refuses to take care of herself and her dad just abandoned the family to deal with it? Also what the hell was the point of this random mental illness storyline? Honestly, the only interesting part of the book were the different locales. Another thing that annoyed was that these girls had been dreaming of going to Europe all their lives, like to do cultural things and all they do while in Europe is hook up with guys, sleep late and just complain. Listen, I can be down for the hooking up with guys while travelling Europe, in fact I would've appreciated a storyline like that more than what was written, but at least visit some museums or something in between. At one point they go to Switzerland and spend an entire day in their hotel because it's raining. Seriously? You couldn't find SOME museum or fun indoor activity to do? What a waste of money and a great trip. The writing was not compelling at all. It felt like someone from high school wrote it and I am still unsure how this woman managed to publish so many books. A very generous 2 stars out of 5.

I had no idea what I was in for when I downloaded this as an audiobook to listen to of all places during a road trip with my Hubs. It sounded like a kooky premise and I liked that it was going to relate to mad cow disease in some way. It's a trippy book and lengthier than I initially thought but I stuck with it. I wasn't sure I liked it at first since it jumps around along with the narrator's swiss cheese brain and it appears he's headed toward death but we want him to live. In the end, I love that this book took me on an unexpected journey through craziness and I still remember it five months later to write this review. A pot-smoking teen with many flaws, all our narrator Cameron wants to do is graduate high school - and maybe get laid by a popular girl, Stacy. When 16-year-old Cameron is diagnosed with Mad Cow Disease, his life takes a crazy turn and we go along for the ride. A punk rock angel named Dulcie shows up and tells Cameron there's a cure for Mad Cow Disease with a mysterious Dr. X - he just has to go and find him. With the help of a dwarf named Gonzo who has some mother issues and a yard gnome who just might be a Norse god. Cameron is off on the road trip of a lifetime reminiscent of Alice in Wonderland or The Odyssey. I don't think its disjointed narrative with romance and adventure will appeal to all readers, but those that it works for will find a gem of a book. I didn't find it as laugh-out-loud hilarious as some other reviewers have, but I did find it to have lots of humor and lots of heart, which sometimes is a hard mix to pull off, Ms. Bray does it seamlessly. Cameron's observations about life, love, family, and friendship are all things that teens and even adults will relate to, and I think many readers will be nodding along to Cameron's words. Cameron sounded just like many teens I meet - he felt real and his voice was spot on. Not for everyone but a good little out-of-the-box premise for the adventurous reader.
This is a satire but it just didn't strike the right chord with me. I did not enjoy the over-exaggerated accents or the violence or the main character.

Wow, this was an amazing read listen. Something to rekindle the love of reading. Renee Ahdieh has a beautiful way of spinning an intricate web of a story. It was honey to my ears and I'm swooning over the lush description of the world, intriguing characters and exciting plot. Truly something to cherish and read again and again. I first experience this story via Audible. It was on my to-read list since I first heard about the book and I decided to listen to the audio version while traveling. I finished it quickly and immediately went to the book store to pick up a hard copy version. I had to experience this story again but with an actual book. It was just as beautiful to read as it was to listen to. The Wrath and the Dawn captivated me from Chapter 1 and I could not stop until I had devoured the entire thing. Each character is unique. Shahrzad is a strong complicated female lead whom I adore. There is more to the murderous boy-king than meets the eye. War is brewing. Plots are being plotted. Secrets are kept and broken. Vengeance is more complicated than first thought. My heart aches at the thought of having to wait so long for the next segment of this story. Literally, it aches. I must know what happens next. I've listened to it via audio, narrated by Ariana Delawari who does an amazing job in case you're interested. I've read the actual hard copy and am tempted to read it again. It feels as though it has been a while since a book has kindled this reading flame. - THE STORY - All though it is loosely based on A Thousand and One Nights I feel as though this story can stand on it's own because of the characters and the story within a story. There are so many parts it borderlines overwhelming but some how pulls it off. The word use and descriptions are sometimes breath taking and I applaud the author. If I were to hire someone to write my life, I'd give Renee Ahdieh a call. I wish my life could be told so beautifully. Her words paint the images in your mind and I'm intoxicated by the colors, shapes and culture I'm introduced to. It's the world we live in only brighter... warmer some how. If you're looking for something deliciously different, then this is the novel for you. I see this story being classified as a "high fantasy" and I can assure you it is not. High fantasy requires far more active magic, dragons, magical creatures and so much more. If anything it is a historical light fantasy read and heavy on the romance angst. LOVE that angst. - CHARACTERS - I could go on about the lead character, Shahrzad, for hours. First part of the book all she sees is her hatred toward Caliph and the justice she seeks for the murder of her best friend. She is willful, intelligent, brave, independent, passionate and straight up complicated. When she feels angsty, the reader feels angsty. Caliph is no cardboard stand in that looks good. He has real depth which makes things... delightfully interesting. It seems every character has a proper back story to drive the plot. Truly don't feel as though I am doing the book justice. Hoping to film a BookTube review soon but just trust me and read this book. Still can't believe I have to wait for "THE ROSE AND THE DAGGER"... which won't be released until 2016. heart aches

Review of Tiger's Quest by Colleen Houck Well, I think I just found my worst read of 2012. Simply horrible. Let me tell you a story. Once upon a time, a young and innocent girl was walking through the airport, about to board a flight home when she spotted on the bookshelf of a tiny airport boutique one the most beautiful and intriguing cover she had ever laid eyes on. It was a white tiger, a gorgeous white tiger surrounded by swirling patterns of blue. Immediately she rushed to the book, devouring the words on the back cover proclaiming it to be 'a sweet romance and heart-pounding adventure'. Young and innocent as she was, she did not know that words written by 'the New York Times best-selling author of Hush, Hush' were not to be trusted. She opened the book, intrigued by a summary whispering promises of romance and adventure, curses and myths. She told herself she must have this book. But alas, it was not meant to be, and the young girl returned home without her precious novel. So yeah, that was me. And it was only a little over a year ago, so I wasn't that young or innocent, though I do admit I had no idea who Becca Fitzpatrick was. Eventually, I did get my hands on a copy of Tiger's Curse and was disappointed to find it was not as magical as it seemed in that little shop. I did enjoy it though, but ''it wasn't as good as Twilight'', I thought to myself. Yeah, I can't believe not even a year ago I still liked Twilight. Hangs head in shame By the time I bought the second book, I was doubting the all around awesomeness that I had proclaimed Twilight to be. So when Tiger's Quest was an improvement over the original, I decided it was 'even better than Twilight'. Well, I was right on that one. Many months passed before I was able to purchase the third book, Tiger's Voyage. I debated over whether I should or not, after how long it had taken me to read Curse and Quest. But in the end, the cliffhanger in the second book convinced me it should be interesting. So when November came, I bought it and dived in, expecting it to be at the very least 'not too bad'. It wasn't 'not too bad'. It was just plain bad. It was so tedious and dull I couldn't get past 200 pages before giving up. Over the many months I kept trying to force myself to finish it, but I simply couldn't. By then, I had joined Goodreads and Twilight had dropped from 5 stars to 4 to 3 to 2 then finally to 1. I removed Voyage from my currently reading shelf and pretended it didn't exist. But it did, and I wasn't about to spend ten freaking months on a book and not finish it. So this morning, I took it off my bookshelf stuffed near the bottom with all the other horrible books and sighed in relief because there were only 150 pages left. I could get through 150 pages, right? Well, I could if I skimmed. So yes, I have finished. After months and months I have finished. The only question now is whether this would count as the worst book of 2011, or of 2012. I think I'm going to go with both. My review I have read many terrible books throughout the years, but I can safely that say few were as terrible as this. At least Twilight was entertaining. At least Eyes like Stars which was my pick for worst book read in 2012 prior to this had some imagination. This book had nothing, and I repeat nothing going for it. Problem 1 The pacing. It was soooooo booooriiiiing. Nothing freaking happened for hundreds of pages. If it had been 200 pages shorter it would have been a million times better and might even have gotten 2 stars. Even the action scenes had me yawning. Problem 2 The endless descriptions. Kelsey goes around describing absolutely everything she sees for paragraphs, often pages of text in a dry, boring voice detailing every single thing. There are paragraphs of what she ate for breakfast, how gorgeous Ren is, how pretty her clothes are. Plus she thinks in paragraphs. There are page after page of Kelsey pitying herself and agonizing over her relationship with her tigers. Sometimes even when she's in danger of getting killed. Problem 3 Kelsey. She is pathetic. Here's a short quiz to see if you are like Kelsey True or False? 1. You are the most gorgeous woman in the world. So gorgeous that 'gorgeous' is considered an insult. So gorgeous that every man who sees you wants you and every girl either adores you or is jealous of you. 2. You have a special power that nobody else has which makes you all the more awesome and better than everyone else. 3. Gorgeous bad-boys jerks who treat you like an object to be won are the best thing since sliced bread. 4. You would feel sorry for yourself if you had to choose between super hot hunk 1 and super hot hunk 2 because it's just so hard to choose between super hot hunks. 5. If you didn't have a boyfriend you would die. 6. You would lead one man on while dating another to avoid dying if the first man left you. You would be okay because you still had your boyfriend, right? 7. You feel unable to take care of yourself and stand up for yourself and need a boyfriend to do it for you. 8. If you an eel swam passed you, you would immediately freak out, thus hitting your head on a rock, passing out and almost dying. 9. If a shark had bitten off your leg, your only fear would be that no man would ever marry you and have children with you because you wouldn't be able to run around and play with them. 10. You would chose one man over another because he has given you permission to cut your hair how you want and the other hasn't. 11. If you found a magical fruit that instantaneously produces food you would parade around on a yacht making you and your two lovers delicious meals without a thought for all the starving people currently living in the same country as you. If you answered 'True' to any of these questions, then congratulations, you may not hate this book as much as I did. Now stop reading this review and continue to wish you were Kelsey and that super hot hunk 1 and 2 were real. Problem 4 Super hot hunk 1 and 2. I hated Ren almost as much as I hated Kelsey. He was a jerk. He was horrible to Kelsey and yet she was still head over heels in lust... whoops I mean love with him because they had a special connection. Forgive me if any of the following information is wrong since I just can't be bothered to go look through the book to check Ren dumped her for a bitchy girl who might have actually been more annoying than Kelsey. Bitchy girl was only there to show that Kelsey was so much better than her so it wasn't exactly shocking when Ren realized Kelsey really was the 'most amazing girl ever'. Riiiight. Anyway, Ren was a jerk and Kelsey was a doormat. When Ren dumped her, Kelsey went and immediately began dating Kishan because she'd die if she didn't have a boyfriend. Then when Ren realized that like every other man in Colleen's scary version of our world he wanted Kelsey again, he wouldn't leave her alone even when she made herself clear that she dating Kishan. And that brings me to super hot hunk 2. I liked Kishan in Quest. Why did he have to get so annoying here? Why was he downgraded into nothing but the steady guy that would always be there for Kelsey because she couldn't have Ren? Ughhh. WHY DID KISHAN FALL IN LOVE WITH HER? The terribleness just. Won't. Stop. Oh and how Ren fell to his knees because Kelsey was just so beautiful lol, it doesn't really get worse than that. Problem 5 The minor 2d stick figures only there to make Kelsey look better characters. The minor characters had no personality. They were completely two-dimensional, no scratch that they were one-dimensional. They managed to ignore every law of science and become the lamest characters ever to appear on page. Mr. Kadam's only purpose was to provide information for the characters in paragraph form btw . Nilima was there to tell Kelsey how amazing she was and to show that us Kelsey wasn't the only nice female character. The country-western guy, Wes, was to show just how desirable Kelsey was. Randi, the bitchy girl was to show that Kelsey was better than her. It's always about you Kelsey, isn't it? It sucks because these characters had potential. They could have been awesome if their entire existence didn't revolve around making Kelsey look better. Problem 6 The plot. Aka Which Super Hot Hunk should Kelsey chose? Yeah, there was this little subplot about running around looking for some necklace and 'battling' dragons and other really easily defeatable enemies but that came after all the endless angst. Oh, and like it's any secret whether Kelsey will chose Ren or Kishan. It never was. At least Twilight's pointless love triangle ended after 3 books. It seems this one will go on and on until the very end of the series. Problem 7 Is it really necessary for Ren and Kishan to be billionaires? And for them to have a tool meant to feed India's people and only use it for their super rich and privileged selves and Kelsey the goddess of the universe too of course ? I mean, really? Problem 8 The villain is laughable, pathetic and completely 2d. How she compared him to Voldemort? Hilarious. Problem 9 The dialogue is stilted and doesn't feel real. Problem 10 Oh look, a cliffhanger. Yeah, didn't see that coming. I'm just going to skip the next 1000 or so problems since I'm getting a headache. And finally Problem 1127 Kelsey almost got killed so many freaking times and every time I was just hoping so desperately that she would just die already. But of course one of the tigers or some lame deus ex machine saved her before that could happen. So that was the negative. Where's the positive huh? I've got to have something good to say, right? Well, I don't. The tigers, which were the coolest part of the series, were not even in this one. Ren and Kishan were men for nearly the whole book. And all that interesting mythology woven into the other books? Yeah, the only myth included here was some stupid love triangle between this beautiful perfect girl and two guys that was meant to illustrate Kelsey, Ren and Kishan's 'horrible' predicament. Oh, and some dragons who weren't really scary at all. So as my younger self who have said This wasn't as good as Twilight. Yes younger self, you are quite right. This terrible, wretched mess of a novel was actually worse than Twilight. I will not be finishing this series. 1 pitiful star.

Libertar Peeta e vingar o sofrimento imposto as pessoas dos 13 Distritos sao os objectivos de Everdeen. Estara proximo o fim do dominio do Capitolio? Eu e o Finnick ficamos em silencio durante muito tempo, observando os nos a nascer e a morrer, ate eu conseguir perguntar - Como e que aguentas? O Finnick olha para mim com incredulidade. - Nao aguento, Katniss! E claro que nao. Arrasto-me para fora dos pesadelos todas as manhas e descubro que nao ha alivio no acordar ... . O melhor e nunca ceder. E dez vezes mais dificil voltarmos a erguer-nos do que irmos abaixo. Com o pouco entusiamo resultante da leitura do volume anterior, parti para esta com as expectativas muito baixas. Suzanne Collins teria de subir muito a parada para redimir-se. Pior que nao ter subido, baixou. Amen! Sendo o 3o e ultimo volume da saga, a autora ja nao tem de continuar a encher este chourico de Katniss, Peeta, Gale e os outros. De entre os pontos negativos, o mais decepcionante deste volume foram as repeticoes. Collins pegou nas mesmas accoes dos volumes anteriores e mudou-lhes o cenario, pecado que ela ja tinha cometido quando repetiu a arena no volume anterior. Ninguem me tira da cabeca que havia material para escrever UM bom livro e ponto final.

This semi-autobiographical novel has exactly the right balance between humour and tragedy. The 14-year-old, Arnold Junior Spirit, who tells the story is a boy growing up on an Indian reservation. He spent his first 7 years suffering fits due to his hydrocephalus 'water on the brain', operated on when he was 6-months old , and all of that and more being bullied mercilessly. His father was an alcoholic and his sister coped with the world by locking herself in the basement. Mother tried to hold things together, but they all lived in extreme poverty. But there's a best friend Rowdy and eventually there's a teacher who sees promise and encourages Arnold to leave the reservation school and go to one in the nearby white town. And eventually .... This is a great story of finding yourself and of hope.

I ended up really enjoying this book, despite being very sceptical at the beginning! I absolutely loved the setting. I haven't read a YA book set in Arabia the Middle East before, and Ahdieh's really descriptive writing style made it feel so real. I could really imagine the world and I wanted to jump through the pages to experience it for myself. I don't really enjoy when books repeatedly talk about things like characters eyes, so I found that a little off-putting until I got further into the book. The romance in this book I was very uncomfortable with for the majority of the book, so much so that I am giving the book 3 stars. The two characters sleep together while she hates him and he is planning to kill her when dawn comes, and that really didn't sit right with me. I understand why it happened, but I wish the author had taken the time to discuss that more. However , the last 100 pages somehow made me ship it. I don't know it happened, it just snuck up on me! I had expected the main character to be badass, however the instalove ruined that for me. I was disappointed to see that she forgot her quest for revenge in a matter of days. She was also quite rude to her servant Despina for no reason, which I found a little odd. However I loved two of the other characters, Jalal and Despina - so I am planning to read their novella straight away! By the end of the book I had really warmed to Shahrzad and Khalid, so Ahdieh's writing gets points for winning me over. So to conclude, I had very mixed thoughts about this book however I loved the setting. I am a little unsure what the next book will bring, but I's curious so will be starting it tomorrow!

Find this and other reviews at Ramblings of a Daydreamer. I had high hopes for The Name of the Star. It was one of those books I was ridiculously excited about from the moment I saw it, mostly because I have a bizarre fascination with Jack the Ripper. I couldn't wait to get my hands on it, but when I finally did, I was slightly disappointed. Not like 'Nooooooo, whyyyyyyyy?!' disappointed - the book was good, and I liked the unique concept, but it wasn't as good as I'd hoped. I went into The Madness Underneath with no expectations. I was curious what would happen to Rory and the squad next, but I didn't have high hopes like I did when reading the first book...and that's a good thing, because this book was very meh for me. It started out well. The initial scene was wonderfully creepy and intriguing, but after that it took forever for anything else to happen. The story had moments of excitement that basically went nowhere and were kind of pointless. Not much happened in the entire book, and when something did happen, it was kind of random, and again, didn't lead anywhere. It felt like a bunch of things thrown together and tied loosely, but not much actual plot. I wasn't able to get interested or invested until toward the end, but when I finally got emotionally invested it was because something drastic and awful happened which I'll get to in a minute . As with the first book, I liked Rory for the most part. She had a great voice. She's funny and kooky, and while some people might not appreciate the almost 'stream of consciousness' feel to her thoughts, I found it all believable, plus amusing. There was quite a lot of angst in this book, which was mostly understandable, considering a Rory went through hell in the first book, and b she's a teenager. She was impulsive, self-centred, and made some horrendous mistakes, but it was mostly believable. I keep saying 'mostly' and that's because there were some things she did that seemed really weird and out of character, and went beyond impulsive and into 'what the hell is wrong with you?' territory. There wasn't much development or growth on her part, and the book was basically The Rory Show - all about her and very little about the other characters. In the first book I loved the secondary characters, but with the exception of learning a bit more about Stephen, the secondary characters seemed to just sort of...be there. Then there was the ending. sigh An ending like that should make me absolutely itch to get my hands on the next book, but it doesn't. I was upset half sad, half pissed , but it was almost a 'too little, too late' situation for me. It took so long for anything interesting to happen, and then when it did it was like a simultaneous punch to the gut and slap to the face. I'll read the third book, but I'm not dying to get my hands on it like I feel I should be after an ending that dramatic. Overall, The Madness Underneath was just okay for me. I still like the setting goes all heart-eyes over London and the unique concept of the ghost police, and it had a few creeptastic moments, but that didn't make up for the lack of plot or character development, or how the secondary characters, who were wonderfully vivid in the first book, seemed to get shoved aside in this book.

Find this review at Scott Reads It Thank you to Greenwillow Books for providing me with an ARC in exchange for an honest review Breathe had a lot of promise in my opinion but it really disappointed me. Imagine a world where people live inside a dome and outside is pretty much ruins Under The Never Sky then imagine that inside the dome people need oxygen masks to survive Masque of the Red Death . Breathe takes in place in a dome ruled by a government called Breathe. This book is told from the POV of three different characters 1 male, and 2 females . The POV was a bit of a problem for me because Alina and Bea sounded pretty similar and I had to flip back to see who was talking. I like books where the characters have distinct voices but this wasn't the case with Breathe. All the characters in Breathe weren't too likeable in my opinion. Be warned there is a cliche and typical love triangle! Quinn is in love with Alina even though he doesn't really know her. Alina doesn't really love anybody and Bea is obsessed with Quinn. Why is Quinn too blind to see that Bea has liked him since they were little? I'll tell you why! It's a stereotypical generic love triangle that we have seen so often in media. The male best friend always falls in love with someone new and foreign to him. He never opens his eyes and sees that his best friend loves him more than a friend. I am not a big fan of Breathe but it was a decent read. It had action and adventure along with romance. It was in my opinion, a typical dystopia even though the plot sounded original. Breathe in my opinion was pretty cliche and was very predictable!! I don't recommend this book at all but I'm clearly the minority here. I definitely won't be reading the sequel to Breathe. If you're in the mood for a great dystopian read Under The Never Sky instead!!!

"The Absolutely True Diary of a Part-Time Indian" is a funny little book that also carries a powerful emotional punch. Sherman Alexie expertly tells us Junior's story as he lives life day to day in one of the bleakest places in America, the Spokane Indian Reservation. In this place, people can rarely dream or hope because no one listens to their dreams or expects them to have any. Junior is a bright kid and understands how broken his community is. He therefore decides to do the unthinkable and leaves his current school in the reservation which is terrible to attend school with white people in the nearest farm town. This book is a delightful, funny, crass, and heart-wrenching book that is best experienced in one sitting. I say it is hear-wrenching because Junior is just a kid who grew up in an environment that was forced upon his people. All around him he sees violence, loss, and an omnipresent bleakness that soils his world view. Despite his claims that he understands that all people are flawed, I left with the impression that Junior idealizes whites and sees Indians as damaged. This mentality makes sense for him, as his life experiences provide ample evidence that this is the case--almost all Indians, according to him, are drunks and many die because of this and many of the white people in the story are wonderful angels! What ultimately redeems this book is Junior's unforgettable character. He is a nerdy, fierce, sometimes fearless, sometimes fearful young man who simply wants to have a good life despite the grim obstacles placed before him.

The second non-SpecFic book I want to highlight is The Vincent Brothers, the sequel to The Vincent Boys, which I reviewed two weeks ago. This book focusses on Sawyer, and we get to see how hurt and miserable he is after the events of The Vincent Boys, and how Lana tries to help him get over Ashton. Whereas Boys was all about Ashton cheating on her perfect boyfriend Sawyer, Brothers is about Sawyer coming to terms with all the changes in his life. His family has been shattered by the revelations about his father, his school life isn't so great anymore and his friends want him to get over Ashton quicker than he can. Into the midst of all this comes Lana, Ashton's cousin who's always had a crush on Sawyer but feels that Ash is so perfect, there'll be no competing with her. I liked the dynamic between Lana and Sawyer a lot better than that of Beau and Ashton, although to be perfectly honest I think that's just because Lana and Sawyer aren't betraying someone in the process of getting closer. Lana is quite strong and stands up for herself when she feels wronged, which was great to see, and Sawyer begins as a quite a flawed character he wants to use Lana to make Ashton jealous , but he soon gets over that and acts like the sweet boy we met in the previous book. We get to see a bit of Ashton and Beau though, and how their relationship is going. Although they seem happy, now that I can see their relationship from the outside it makes me feel uncomfortable. Beau is more of a possessive attack dog in this book than a sweet boyfriend. He's always described as growling and acting like an animal, demanding why people are on Ashton's driveway, why they are staring at her, etc. Not only is it tiring, it takes away from all the romance in their relationship, and I'm left with the impression that surely Ashton can't be too happy with him. But of course, she is perfectly happy. Abbi Glines has served up another entertaining read in The Vincent Brothers, and although this book concludes the series, I am interested in reading more of her works in the future, especially the paranormal-romance, the Existence trilogy.

It wasn't until the very end of the book that any real action or story telling took place, and then before I knew it the book had finished. There were heaps of questions that are left unanswered - and not in a good way that makes you excited about a sequel, but just annoys you instead. The were some positives - the characters did feel well developed. I was able to picture all the characters really clearly, instead of everyone looking really similar - a common problem I have with YA novels. Overall I felt like this book was designed purely to set up characters and a very vague plot, maybe the sequel will have a stronger story - I meant the dark shadows plot does have potential. This is a book that I really wanted to fall in love with and unfortunately did not. I tried for months to work my way through this book and when I hit the halfway mark and was still not invested I had to put it down making this my first Did Not Finish review. The book certainly had an interesting premise. It's about a world where the written word has been taken away and where literacy is illegal. All information and learning is controlled by a computer system called Verity. Our main character, Elle, is a Reader. Maybe one of the last ones. I never got far enough in the book to figure out if there were any others like her. Elle has to go on a journey to save the written word and save everyone from the control of Fell and Verity. There have been other books like this before of course and the ones I've read have been really good. I really wanted to see how Mansour was going to be able to pull off a unique take on a popular topic. My interest in the book went up and down. At first I was really excited to read it and then I wasn't and then I was. That's what kept me going for so long with it. If I could get excited some of the time, then surely finishing the book would be worth it. I wanted to finish it and see that the good parts outweighed the bad parts. I was rooting for this book. Not being able to connect with Elle is certainly a reason why it was hard for me to keep going. We figure out that she's a reader pretty early on in the story, but it never seems to occur to her how important that is. Yes, it's something that scares her as it should, but she should also be able to realize the power that she holds because of it. I would have liked to see her character develop a little more in the first half of the book into someone who realizes the strength she holds within herself. Not understanding a character is not something I usually have to deal with, but in this book I could not wrap my mind around just what Ledger was. When I first realized what had happened and the body that he now inhabited I thought that it was really cool. I wanted to see where she was going to take this, I wanted to see how the relationship between Ledger and Elle would develop. Every time the conversation turned the just what exactly was Ledger, I was confused. My brain cannot wrap my mind around the fact that the written word literally came to life and planted itself into the body of a recently deceased human. The written word. Came to life. Not like a movie adaptation, but actually and literally came to life. It's not something that I could make sense of. Ledger's relationship with Elle was also very odd to me. He is inhabiting the body of someone she was very close to and yet she can fall in love with this new being inhabiting the body as if she was flipping a switch. Yes, at first there was an awkwardness, but then almost instantly it changed and the relationship developed very awkwardly and not organically at all. Another thing I did not feel was organic at all was the speech patterns used in the book. They didn't feel real. She also had Elle ask a lot of questions for clarification. It was as if Mansour knew that the audience would be confused and wanted to make sure we understood what was going on. Once or twice wouldn't have bothered me as much, but it felt like it was all the time. It felt like there was a lot of telling and not showing in this novel and that's probably why the writing didn't feel as real to me as it should have. While the novel didn't have a completely original concept, I was disappointed in the execution. There were so many aspects of this book that had so much potential and could have made it amazing. Some parts were so clever that I had no choice but to keep reading, but unfortunately the parts that I didn't connect with got in the way of all of the good things. I gave this one star because I don't know if you can leave 0 stars on a book. I don't feel like I can accurately give it a star rating though because I could not finish it.

'All the Stars Left Behind' is a new young adult science fiction novel that fans will enjoy. It's the author's debut - which I think showcases her potential and talent. The plot might not be wholly original - there's aspects that I've seen plenty of times before - but the author gives it an unique feel that sets it apart. The story is one of star-crossed lovers that fall for one another but can never or should never be together. In this instance, the guy is an alien and the girl is actually a weapon that can save his endangered world. There's an obvious instalove situation between Roar and Leda, the main characters. I'm not a huge fan of instant "love at first sight" - at least not at the extreme. It was really intense between them right from the beginning and doesn't ease up during the story. I have to admit that I didn't like the way their connection started - these situations always make it feel cheesy and unrealistic to me in any situation . But as I got to know them each better and watched their relationship grow over the course of the story, I got on board. I liked seeing them work together to overcome problems and obstacles, as well as the romance - obviously. I just think it would've worked better for me, at least if it hadn't been so immediate and over the top. Just my opinion though - it's nothing against the book. Another thing worth noting and is always a big deal for me as a reader, was the writing style. I'm a huge fan of the first person point of view for several reasons and I almost always believe that it's the best way to go. Unfortunately for me, the book was written in the third person POV - from alternating perspectives of Roar and Leda. Don't get me wrong - I love that the story is told from both Roar and Leda's POVs. We get to see everything that happens from each of their viewpoints, which is always a great style, in my opinion. I really wish that it had been written in the first person instead. I think I would have connected easier and deeper with each of the main characters if it was done in the first person. My experience would've been much different, most likely better. One thing I love is getting to really know a character on a deeply personal level - it allows me to slip into their world more easily and I can usually identify with the narrator better. Again - this is solely my own opinion and preference - and has nothing to do with the writing or the story. I do recommend this book to fans of YA, science fiction, fantasy, dystopian, and romance. The Marked Son is a story that instantly takes ahold of the reader because the main character, Dylan, is just so enigmatic and alluring. His 17 years have been rough - with a mom that's constantly chasing the next fling - and he's as jaded as they come, but there's just something about him that will pull readers in. Maybe it's his unconcealed anger towards his mom or his ease in giving up, but I wanted things to work out for him from the beginning. Shea Berkley captures teen angst perfectly, then flips it upside down, throws in some serious abandonment issues, and adds a healthy dose of fantasy to the mix. The tidbits about Dylan's past and minute details hint at what's really happening, as do the chapters from an alternate, female POV, but the big reveal is something else. The mix of contemporary with fantasy is done flawlessly and seemingly effortlessly. The story progresses from a simple, angsty teen story, to so much more. Dylan's dreams and the foreshadowing escalate the tension and suspense, until the readers get that BANG moment along with Dylan. And once it happens, things go from uncomplicated to insane. And I loved it. The Marked Son is a captivating contemporary that turns into a surprising and unique fantasy. Dylan will find his way into the hearts of readers, as will his grandparents, the mysterious girl Kera, and the new friends Dylan makes along the way. If you're a fan of contemporary and fantasy, and love a mix of the two, The Marked Son is the perfect book for you.

Synopsis Addisyn White thought she had her new life, her after life, all figured out. Granted death had not brought her to the pearly white gates, she hadn't even left Earth. But death had its perks she got to live forever with her best friend and her assigned Link of Angels, in a beautiful beach house. Even with the changes she was going through to turn her human body into an angelic one, everything seemed pretty easy. Until a gray winged angel comes into her life, then all the secrets and lies her Link had been keeping start crumbling away, exposing a whole new world of dangers she didn't even know about. Now Addisyn must fill in the blanks before things escalate too far. Will she save her Link? Or will she be buried in their secrets forever? Review I am a dedicated reader when it comes to angel themed stories. I discovered Lauren Kate and Becca Fitzpatrick last summer, and devoured their stories. I quickly fell in love with their characters and daydream that the novel I am writing will one day live up to the beauty of theirs. This past winter I stumbled upon Susan Ee's Angelfall and embraced her apocalyptic angel-themed story as well. Hence, when I was chosen to participate in a Goodreads R2R, I was super excited. And, the cover is absolutely breathtaking. Thank you, Ms. Aple for choosing me to read and review your book! Therefore, I immediately dove into Aple's story, Neophyte, expecting the unexpected and hoping to be swept off my feet. Instead, I found myself floating somewhere in the middle. I read to escape my daily life-stay-at-home mom. I am the daily referee of two little boys and deal with whining and tantrums all day long. So when Addisyn fell into the category of "whiny" and "annoying," I quickly lost interest. I enjoy a strong, female lead. Addi tried to be strong. I just saw her as immature and irritating. One of the characteristics of the novel that I struggled with was the repetition of Addi's whiny-ness. She complained, a lot. She was angry, a lot. She irritated me, a lot. I truly commend Aple for writing and completing a novel. You go girl! I aspire to do the same and know how difficult it is. I also know that the first attempt isn't always the best. But, I believe Aple put her best foot forward, created a wonderful storyline with many new and entertaining details among the angel story category. She developed some fantastic imagery and detail. And I do look forward to any sequels there may be. I want to see Addi grow, as well as the rest of the supporting characters. While this story wasn't exactly in my top 20 list of favorites, it isn't on my list of top 20 despises. There were things that just weren't for me the repetitive nature and character development and other aspects of the story that I did like the idea of the Link, predestined angels and being reincarnated as an angel . And so, my impression is a bit wishy washy. I'm on the fence. All in all, I would give this book two out of five stars.

I've read a few modern young adult books. This is one that I really disliked. I very rarely hate books, it's like hating a piece of art- there are too many factors and opinion based parts . To be honest, after seeing this example of modern young adult books, I think I'll stick to Stephen King. The author describes the physical appearances over an individual's personality so much more- Katniss's appearance seemed to be featured in so many pages. The author didn't correctly judge what motivates people- in a corrupt country, would you be motivated by a girl reaching for a few berries, and then getting saved by the corrupt government she is rebelling against? I probably wouldn't- read 1984 if you want a book about dystopias. I expected for this government to have already fallen- it doesn't even bother to hide the state it is in, even decades possibly a century after the rebellion. Katniss participates in the game as openly as anyone else- she kills and brutally injures other participants at one point- this greatly diminishes the moral standards previously set when she saved her sister. As an example- say the contest endorsed Cannibalism- eat each other to win, last win to not be eaten survives. Would the readers feel the same, if say, Katniss ate the boy in revenge for him eating Rue? Probably not. There are more irregularities I.E. Why is peeta so useless? Why does Katniss seem so much like a feminist character? How did this book get published? - but I would rather not name them. This book is a manual- How to make millions if you're a young adult write in the 21st century- which is, write about teens fighting against a corrupt organization with or against fellow teens, give them uncommon skills of persuasion or abilities, and give them a useless lover both for "romance" and so they can run the main character's errands. The other thing I disliked regarding this book- it is classified as a Dystopia, and I certainly understand why- but what exactly, as a dystopian novel, is this story rebelling against?!?! To my knowledge, massive state sponsored killing contests of children was not a significant problem, nor ever- in the past or otherwise. Possibly in the colloseum, but currently- no. It is probably the most bizarre surrender treaty ever written- you must send your children to participate in our killing contest. It would just further enflame the rebels and fail miserably at quenching rebellions. Other dystopian novels- Fahrenheit 451, 1984, Brave New World- they all protested against some form of government tyranny- which was evident throughout the novel, and those protests were actual threats to our freedom. As a dystopia, this novel offers romance, emotion, etc., but if the author chose to protest against something more than the insignificant problem of state sponsored killing contests- I honestly don't know what to say about this book. If it is revolting against violence, which, I am sorry to say, will never cease , it seems hypocritical in a way, especially in cinemas. -Killing is awful- that is why we are showing you excessive and especially gory scenes of children being violently tore apart or completely losing a sense of humanity.
This story could've been really good, but the characters were hollow and vapid, and the story line was not as deep as it could have been.

Well, well, well. I didn't know what to think of this book when I first heard about it, if you want to know the truth. These were the days before "Mockingbird," before I had any sort of faith that a book about an individual on the autism spectrum could really get into their head. I mean, sure, I'd seen plenty of movies and read plenty of books about 'em, but for the most part they were all told from the point of view of neurotypicals. It's a big difference, you know. Those of us with autism do see the world differently, and the closest to accurate thing I'd seen up to this point was "Emma-Jean Lazarus Fell Out of a Tree," which never said the eponymous character had a disorder. But I digress. When I saw the reviews and that cover GORGEOUS, seriously , I was determined to read it, because I wanted to know if I had another "Curious Incident" on my hands. What do you know? I loved every bit of it. The first thing that I found particularly noteworthy is that the protagonist is described as high-functioning autistic, not an aspie. There is a difference between being high-functioning autism and having Asperger Syndrome, and while it's ultimately pretty miniscule it is nonetheless noteworthy. The protagonist of this book is more autistic than aspie, which is pleasing. This is a big deal to me, because I feel as if the differences should be known by many. I have high-functioning autistic friends and aspie friends, and Jason reminds me far more of the former than the latter. Second, the tone is just perfect. The life of an individual on the autism spectrum, especially during the tween years, is a difficult one indeed, and an air of melancholy permeates the entire book. It's not cry-rivers-of-tears sad, though, so there is none of that "woe is the autistic child" that could be found in many, many other books. It's remarkably clear-headed and free of over-exaggeration, which I by no means expected and in the end loved about it. What I loved most, though, is the incredible attention to details about the inner machinations of the protagonist's mind. He worries about when something is going to go wrong, he knows when something is going to set him off, and he is very, very much enamored of a girl who he's never met and imagines a relationship with her. And, especially, he is aware that other people have problems with those who "aren't normal" and is aware that he does have feelings despite not expressing them in the "normal" way. Real kids with autism that I know do all of these things, so it's very much refreshing to see a fictional depiction of one that gets it right. Any faults? The writing's too good. Seriously. There are times when it is very much apparent that this was "written." Twelve-year-olds generally are not as perceptive as Jason. And there are times where the book doesn't feel nearly as urgent as it should something tells me that a story told by an autistic individual should be a bit more dramatic. If these are all I can fault the book for, though, I will accept these flaws. This is a book of importance and, along with "Mockingbird," should be shelved in classrooms from fourth-grade onwards. We have indeed come a long way since "The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Nighttime," and I only hope that authors continue to make such great strides in attempting to accurately depict the experiences of individuals with autism spectrum disorders.

Jackson Pearce has once again created a unique twist of another retelling story. This time it's The Little Mermaid. As with the two other books in this series, Fathomless features more of the Reynolds siblings. This time it's the three and only girls, triplets, who have the powers to see the future, present and past. One night, Celia, the youngest and the seer of the past helps Lo, an ocean girl living beneath the waters just off the coast of Georgia save Jude, a young musician, from drowning. Since then, their lives have become interconnected and it's up to Celia to find a way to keep Lo on dry land and remember her former self, Naida, the human girl she used to be. As always, I really enjoyed Jackson Pearce's writing. This retelling was kind of different from the Hans Christian Andersen story we all know. Lo and her under-the-sea sisters not really related used to be human but are now trapped in the ocean though they can't recall the events that led to this fate. They are beautiful and grow more so the longer they stay in the water. They're not really "mermaids", they're not half girl half fish they have legs and just chill on a sunken ship waiting for the day the angels come and take them to the sky. They've all tried to sing and seduce men to drown and win back their souls but all have failed. Lo has forgotten who she once was and when Celia and Lo touch, it reveals that her real name is Naida if you read Sweetly, you know exactly who she is . Celia meets with Lo Naida more and more, trying to get her to become Naida again fully and never return to the sea. The Lo Naida "dual deul personality" aspect drove me crazy. It's not the book's fault, I've never been a fan of the "another person is living inside me" thing. It's an over-the-top concept that just turns me off when I find it pop up in my books. I loved Jude, he was cute, funny and I think the author did a great job portraying his love triangle with Celia and Lo Naida. She showed how he could equally be attracted to them both in a non-douchebag way. Celia's sisters were okay but kind of annoying sometimes. I feel like all their powers should've been incorporated more into the ending. And of course the Fenris make an appearance, as they do in every book. Out of all three books, Fathomless has the least action. It's also the fastest one I've read. I was extremely anxious to read about the love triangle that featured two girls after one boy which I hardly see in books but there wasn't a lot of adventure action like in Sisters Red. It also lacked the entrancing prose that Sweetly had where you just wanted to eat the pages. I love this series but Fathomless was the weakest installment. But I still liked it a lot. It was a fun read and if there's a Fairytale Retellings part four, I will definitely be devouring that one too. Cover Story Though I love the cover, it's a bit misconstruing seeing how these "ocean girls" have no tails or fins.
